title: Great multi-valve design & Not just for camping.
text:
I've previously owned a Klymit V without the "Luxe," but a piece of the one valve it had broke off in short order. This Klymit V Luxe has valves which *appear* to me to have fewer fiddly parts, and there are two of them--more on why that's good in a moment!

First off, these pads have a smart design. Although there is no railing per say, the Vs help to keep you on them which is good news if you do not stay in one place on a bed. The material keeps the air inside from feeling cold (and presumably from drinking in too much of the earth's cold).

The primary use I gave my original V was as a buffer between me and an extremely ill-suited new mattress while I desperately shopped for solutions. And although I've been a backpacker in the past, sadly, my primary intended use for the Static V Luxe is to act as a buffering layer when I need to sleep on other people's mattresses. I have considerable back health issues, and this padding is incredibly helpful for when I cannot be on my own mattress. I purchased this size this time because the original V is so much smaller than a twin bed that it was downright silly trying to use it for my purpose. Also I use a body pillow and change positions a lot. This will clearly be nicer for managing nights out of my own bed.

Now I saw someone complaining about the two valves because they are confusing. This person has probably never experienced the downsides of only having one valve for letting air out of a mattress. Sure, you need to be certain that the valve you are not blowing into is closed so that the mattress can properly inflate, but oh, my word, it is soooooo much easier to get the air out of this mattress pad! I could almost never get my original V small enough to properly stick into its dry sack. But this larger V luxe easily packs up smaller than I could get the original V to go. Ok, so maybe "easy" is relative. You do need to open both valves, roll it down from bottom to top, open it up again, fold a few times, and roll once more to get it maximally small. But it actually works and stuffs in the drysack.

I hope if you're reading this that you have more adventurous uses afoot, but I do recommend this Static V Luxe and wish I'd had one back when I was a backpacker!

title: Great machine!  It's strongest asset is cleaning sterling.  And I have some tips on using it for sterling.
text:
I have an older version of this produced in 2003 that lacks the convenient mesh basket and wall adapter. And, yes, I eBayed it for a steal. But this machine is definitely worth it, especially if you have (a) a lot of jewelry with porous stones, (b) a lot of sterling silver jewelry, or (c) a lot of jewelry and a strong aversion to noxious smells (the sparkle gem concentrate is relatively tame even to my multiple chemical sensitivities nose). I know of no other machine other than a professional jeweler's that can handle these things.

While I wish I could afford a lot of white gold jewelry, I have a lot of silver. Moreover, I'm not the sort of person who throws out a pair of earrings after it tarnishes. I search for what I want and do my best to preserve it. My skin is very sensitive to tarnish, so keeping on top of tarnish is important to me. And getting my hands very black while keeping on top of tarnish is less than ideal. The only downside that I'm sure would be a downside with sonic machines as well is that it may release glued in gems from their bearings. Also my instructions cautioned to only let hematite sit in the solution rather than applying the electrical current to it.

Now you may have noticed that the speed brite company only recommends something like 5 seconds for silver. There is a reason for this. If there is braiding or filigree or other little mechanical parts to your silver, these may either serve as catch alls where tarnish that is being freed accumulates, OR the oxidized bits that had accumulated in them will, if the silver is cleaned in this machine repeatedly, start to wash onto the shiny silver areas and leave brown, black, or purple streaks. Also, if your water is getting dirty, bends in smoother silver may take on some tarnish. That said, I find it useful to do multiple long cleanings on my silver with some special techniques and big caveats:

First off, when continuing on this long-cleaning silver path you do so at your own risk. I learned by trial and error and thought at first that I had ruined two pieces of jewelry until I figured out how to "fix" them. On the other hand, you will get WAY more of the tarnish off with the machine if you do multiple long soaks. One key that I have found invaluable when daring to clean my filigree or braided pieces at length with this machine is moving the hanging bar smoothly but steadily throughout the cleaning. This makes it much less likely that tarnish will stick back on. Indeed, this is important for all heavily tarnished pieces as well. If gripping the actual item with the clip, then varying where you attach the clip is also helpful. Making sure the water with the sparkle gem is on the cleaner side of things when cleaning filigree or braided pieces is also invaluable, as they will be especially susceptible to picking up tarnish already present in the water.

Sometimes I find an item that I want to resurrect from the dead that is throughly black, often with areas that are braided or actually intended to be oxidized. What I do in these cases is swirl constantly, move the clip constantly, and in between cleanings, wipe the smoother parts of the silver design under running water with my thumbs to wash off some of the tarnish. Basically I use the machine just enough on such pieces as to get the smoother parts of silver partially clean and then use a cloth. Also, I only clean these pieces when I am about to dump the water out so as not to ruin the water for other jewelry.

Now the sparkle gem ionic cleaner will not remove ALL of your tarnish, and as far as I know, it does not deposit any anti-tarnish coating on your jewelry. For this I have lately been using the Connoisseur jewelry cloths. However, if you have any plain old lint-free cloths around, it is useful to run the chains and so forth along these first (there will likely be some loose tarnish) as to save your chemical jewelry cloths for the final stage of cleaning. Especially with the very powerful Connoisseur brand, you can go through those cloths like crazy as they find layer after layer of tarnish on stuff that already looked clean.

I hope that helps!

title: DVD dysfunctional, GREAT company to work with.  Tips on ball sizing:
text:
For sitting long periods of time on the ball, going a size up is a good idea, but I have found that you want to stick with your size for the stretches and workouts to get the most out of them. For instance, I am 5'4" or 5'5" and definitely need to go back and buy the smaller ball for the workouts. But I prefer either the 65" or the 75" for sitting for any period of time. Getting two sizes is a really worthwhile investment, imo. I always sit on a ball or on a balance cushion (when not in a recliner) b/c of hip and back issues, and it makes SUCH a difference. [[UPDATE: the 55" is way too small for me. It seems what I'd really need are two 65" w/ one of them far less inflated for doing the workout... sigh]]

I had problems w/ the DVD from the go--it was a mess even though it wasn't scratched. The part I could see I really liked, but with medical disabilities, it was a little too hard on my body anyhow (do not underestimate the after-effects of swinging a ball full of air over your head--lol--amazing workout!). When I contacted Gaiam about the DVD, they sent me a replacement. Happily, it was different one that was more suited to my health, a beginner's workout done by a blonde woman named Suzanne. It consists of 45 minutes of mostly stretches. I've done it every day for a week, and my chiropractor cannot believe the difference in my spinal health and other parts of my body as well--even my g.i. So score for Gaiam as a company and for their videos! It may seem like a long time to just stretch (w/ a modicum of strength and toning), but it is proving to be so worth it.

As for the videos that come with this ball, they consist of far less stretching and more aerobic strengthening from what I can tell. I really like the woman who leads them.

I had problems getting any of the three plugs that came with the ball into the ball. The hole really was not shaped properly. I solved this by substituting the somewhat smaller plug from my balance cushion until I had stretched the hole out sufficiently. I realize, however, that not all of you will have another plug lying around and so thought I should mention that. Probably if you jammed the plug as far as it would go and sat on the ball for a few days w/o exercising, it would stretch out and go into the hole.

title: I added a inexpensive Velo 7 speedometer to see that my speed is consistent (important for road biking) and that works great too
text:
I struggled between the high-end spin bikes and this one. "You get what you pay for" kept going through my head. I eventually settled on the lower cost option since it was my first; I figured if I could get 2-3 years out of it I could upgrade later. The box arrived in pristine condition, which was a pleasant surprise. It arrived less that 48 hours from the time I ordered it. It took about 30 minutes to put together by myself, nothing was too difficult. I've been using it every day. It is "whisper-quiet" as I've seen described. I prefer more resistance and with the 46lb flywheel its a real workout. I had an elliptical for my pre-workout cardio for about 5 years (it finally completely broke apart) and the spin bike beats it hands down. I added a inexpensive Velo 7 speedometer to see that my speed is consistent (important for road biking) and that works great too. Although this spin bike doesn't have micro-adjustments for the handlebar and seat I was lucky to find a setting on each that fits my body type.

My only negative comment, and this is a real stretch to find something negative to say...is regarding the resistance pad/brake. I keep a can of silicon spray next to my spin bike and every 4-5 days give the pad a quick shot because it starts getting a little noisy. If/when I eventually do upgrade I might look at a spin bike with magnetic resistance but to get the belt drive with magnetic resistance you can increase the cost 3x.

I haven't seen any follow up comments to reviews for purchases 2-3 years ago and I'm hopeful that, with care, this spin bike will last many years with the occasional replacement belt and/or brake pad and regular maintenance.

To sum up my thoughts on this spin bike...it's inexpensive but its not cheap...it's well made and works great!

In addition to regular ( standard and Olympic) dumbbells and barbells, I have used Gripz on ropes, kettlebells, and pulldown and rowing attachments. Anytime you would want to use a "fat bar" type grip width, you can use Fat Gripz.
In addition, my clients and I have both used Fat Gripz to reduce elbow, wrist, and shoulder joint pain while lifting.

Third, Fat Gripz are rugged. I have several pairs of Fat Gripz for my clients that have undergone heavy use over several years and I have seen no degradation in their appearance or performance. They do not compress and lose their width like some other products.

Fat Gripz are excellent to use for grip training and forearm strength, but I use them on all types of lifts to increase muscle activation and train grip in a variety of positions. For example, try them on deadlifts, behind-the-back BB shrugs, rowing exercises, and push

title: the toughest, most reliable airbeds, but the pump should be sold separately
text:
First, it should be understood that these airbeds are not made to last all that long, even if used only inside a house. The periphery seams may separate, the plastic membrane is easily punctured, the ribbing may come unglued, the valve may develop a leak, etc. I use them in lieu of a regular mattress on my bed, with a smooth bedspring below, so nothing sharp around, very little dynamic stress (I don't bounce on the bed ;-), yet none has lasted longer than 2 years. Of course, that's for being in use every single night, not just for an occasional camping trip; it still makes them way cheaper than any "real" mattress.
I have tried several brands available on Amazon and locally; almost all died within a month or two, but the Intex ones all lasted 9-20 months. No punctures, no leaks, but they finally failed by losing their ribbing -- a rib comes loose, creating a big bubble of air; you can lose one rib and still do fine if it was on the side, but by the time you've lost two ribs, it's getting hard to use ;-)
Since none has ever leaked, no valve has ever failed, and we've never had a puncture (over 10 years of use of the Intex model), I suspect that, if Intex could (or wanted to) strengthen the attachment of these internal ribs, this would become a lifetime mattress. Perhaps their business model cannot accommodate such long life...
Since we use two of these and have to replace them every couple of years, we have accumulated quite a supply of these silly battery-powered inflation pumps (originally 8 D-cells, now 6 C-cells). title: 31.6 Be careful when ordering. Robust. Smoothed my ride.
text:
UPDATE: I weight 210 lbs. and the stock soft spring works great on pavement. In fact it works better on pavement than the hard, red spring intended for riders over 180lbs. It works better on pavement even with the preload set at zero (loosest). The optional hard, red spring is intended only for riders over 180lbs WHO ARE RIDING OFF-ROAD. Trust me. I purchased both. The good new is it is easy to change out springs in well under 5 minutes.

ORIGINAL: Be careful when ordering because the product page defaults to the 27.2mm diameter. How this is less expensive from the UK with free shipping and free returns is a mystery. Strangely, the optional hard (red) spring for riders over 180lbs does not seem to be anywhere on Amazon. I had to order it directly from Suntour.

The optional hard red spring is different than the 31.6 stock spring. The stock spring has a cast inner portion the fills the 31.6 inner diameter giving the spring greater stability. The manual states that the hard, (red) PKE100-20 spring (the only hard red spring on Suntour's website) is intended only for the 27.2mm post, that a hard PKE100-21 or -23 is required for the 31.6mm. Yet Suntour's website states the PKE100-20 is 'Compatible with all sizes of SR Suntour seat post.' I guess they found that the PKE100-20 could do the job on the 31.6 and they could phase out the -21 and -23. It works so I'm not going to worry about it unless something goes wrong.

The preload adjustment is not adequately explained anywhere. I adjusted it by trial and error. When I remove the spring for maintenance I will measure the depth of the threaded cap so I can duplicate my preload adjustment during reassembly.

There's a no-name brand at about this same price with only 20mm of travel so this is a good value with 50mm. Some more expensive brands have 90mm of travel which seems unnecessary because I weigh 210lbs and this one has never yet bottomed out on asphalt. I haven't yet tested it off road. Plus the one with 90mm needs close to six inches of exposed seat post. I have tall frames so the 90mm couldn't work for me anyway.

Even the bumps on asphalt were taking their toll on my aging bones but this fixed it. A very good and robust product.

title: Design flaw but still a great product. Only 91 grams; this thing is loud!
text:
This is essentially one of those compressed air horns you hear at sports events or a boat 'mayday' alert only this is rechargeable. It has a standard Schrader valve that can be pumped up to 80 psi (5.5 bars). I have the AirXwills Electric Bike Pump, another great product here on Amazon, that can refill the bottle in 10 seconds. It took a while to find a placement on the handlebars where I could press the trigger quickly. I ended up modifying my grip and mounted it on the grip.

The design flaw is that, to be useful in an emergency, the trigger must be mounted very close to the handlebar grip. But the very loud horn is forever married to the trigger meaning that the horn is just 18 inches from your ear causing significant discomfort. In one way this might be good because it will discourage using it in any situation other than in a true emergency. I would have liked the horn instead to be married to the air bottle which could then allow placement of the horn further away from the ear, like low on the seat down tube or low on the fork. There's a volume control but even at the lowest volume it is still very loud.

With this horn people complain about two things: 1) the bottle diameter is too narrow to fit securely in a standard bottle cage and 2) it's a pain to have to thread and secure the air hose down a bike frame tube to a frame-mounted bottle cage. The iUKUS Adjustable Bike Water Bottle Holder, another good product here on Amazon, solves both problems. It mounts to the handlebars so no worries about threading the air hose; just put the excess hose in the bottom of the cage before inserting the bottle. And it is adjustable down to the 2 inches that will accommodate the Airzound horn bottle securely. I can even mount the bottle sideways so it isn't so conspicuous and it's still completely secure.

These are my only other minor complaints: 1) the air bottle makes the entire setup a little bulky and 2) the quick release system for the mount/trigger assembly is a little flimsy and difficult to operate.

I think they are being modest when they state that volume is 115 db. Even at the lowest volume the horn can be heard in a nearby car with windows closed, air conditioning and the radio on. This horn turns heads. Great product, great value.

title: Wheel Builder Painted the Axle Threads Making Them Near Impossible to Service.
text:
These might be good wheels for the money. I bought two; front and rear. But ... the builder painted the axels so the nuts are near impossible to loosen to service the cones. The cones were torqued-down way too tight -- making the axels too tight to operate efficiently.

That's okay. I am accustomed to this. I can service my own hub/axle. But the builder painted the axles making it near impossible to open the hub to grease and adjust the cones.

I tried a 16mm socket on one end of the axle for leverage and adjustable crescent on the other. Slow going. Then a high-quality needle-nosed vice-grip on the crescent side. Still no love.

Now I'm reduced to overnight soaking in PB-Blaster to try to dissolve the paint. Next? Paint remover?

This is just too much work for a component valued at very close to $100.

I'm beyond the return period so I must make them work somehow. Just way, way, too much work to return them if I still could and too adjust and grease the cones.

Never again.

title: You need these for side visabilty
text:
Most headlights have a lens that casts forward, to amplify the LED(s) so that you can brightly see what is in front of you. This lens arrangement offers little-to-no side exposure to alert side drivers of your presence.

These lights are visible from the front or back (depending on your placement) PLUS from the sides.

I bicycle with four lights, solid and strobing white lights in the front and solid and strobing red lights in the back. Each of the front and back light has side strobe exposure.

I also wear a neon yellow reflective vest and drivers still turn right into me. I know to brake hard at a moment's notice and that knowledge has probably saved me an injury at least a few times.

After I brake hard and raise my hands in the air to say "WTF," the driver says, "I DIDN'T SEE YOU." Me, with all this regalia of lights and reflective strips on my vest, "Seriously?"

title: Best and Easiest for Simple Local Errands (Pros & Cons in review)
text:
Download the manual from the Burley website.

This is our second Travoy trailer. The other is still in use after 10 years. The new Travoy has some substantial upgrades:

• The new “kickstand” design keeps the trailer upright when parked with a load. The old one would tip over.
• New seatpost hitch allows a single hitch to be shared among two or more bikes. With the old one you had to buy more hitches.
• The tow arm now extends to accommodate rear bike racks and larger MTB wheels.
• Tow arm is now padded with foam for hand comfort.

The entire time we owned our first Travoy we mistakenly believed we should have chosen a flatbed instead. We recently bought a flatbed and don’t use it; bought a second Travoy as a backup. If all you do is local errands the Travoy is by far the easiest and best. If you tour or travel dirt roads a flatbed might be a better choice but you should want both a flatbed plus the Travoy because the Travoy is easier for local errands which are far more common.

The bags that are dedicated for use with the Travoy are costly and do not hold enough. Instead, wheel your Travoy into Target or Walmart and choose the largest clothes hamper that fits the Travoy form factor (see photo). Attach that hamper with three ratcheting tie-downs or four high quality, ADJUSTABLE bungees. Do not skimp on quality or number.

PROS:
• Lightweight, 10lbs +/-
• No tools or setup required. Screw the hitch onto your seatpost with the T-bold and you’re done.
• Folds to easily fit in a backseat, a trunk or an airline overhead.
• Holds up to $125 in groceries with the large hamper attached. Mind the maximum weight restriction (60lbs) and pack the heaviest items at the bottom (66% of load) and lighter items at the top (33%).
• With the Travoy you don’t have to bend over quite as far to reach cargo.
• Comes with a storage/carrying bag (although it’s mostly useless for carrying cargo).

CONS:
• You must adjust your riding style slightly. The Travoy is stable on level pavement but may tip over at significant road imperfections or surface debris. Slow down and approach handicapped ramps and driveways exactly at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to avoid catching a wheel on their raised shoulders. Avoid potholes and debris entirely. You’ll grow accustomed to this over time and it will not bother you. If the Travoy DOES tip, it doesn’t take the bike with it.
• If you run with the stock tires and tubes be prepared for flats. The availability of high quality 12.5” inch tires and tubes is extremely limited. All the tires from Asia that we tried are no good, even dangerous. We found very high quality 12.5 inch tires from the German manufacturer “Schwalbe” (available here on Amazon). Schwalbe currently offers the “Road Cruiser” for street and the “Black Jack” for trails and off-road (12/2020).
• 12.5” thorn resistant tubes are available here on Amazon but the Travoy 12.5 inch wheels require a 45 degree valve; otherwise there is not enough room to attach a pump or even a pump hose. These thorn resistant tubes had straight valves. To accommodate this shortcoming we found a "Air Inflator Hose Adapter" here on Amazon. Although it just barely fits, we can use it with both our floor pump and our road pump.

TIPS:
• In addition to thorn resistant tubes, we use the “Mr. Tuffy”-brand tire inserts on all our bike and trailer wheels (here on Amazon). Flats are now a very rare occurrence and we ride among numerous desert thorns.
• When using the hamper it is easy to cut a neon yellow reflective vest into three sections (left front, right front and back) and attach the sections to the hamper (left side, right side and rear, see photo).
• Reflective flags and flagpoles with mounts that fit your hamper are available here on Amazon. The flagpole we bought is high enough so that the flag can be seen above the level of a parked car (see photo). For added safety we now use this flag and pole on our bikes even without the trailer.
• When the hamper is inappropriate we use a cargo net. The cargo net is also handy if your hamper is overflowing.

Leave a comment if you have questions.

title: Poor Paint Job, Difficult to Use
text:
Update: Trailer frame has rusted at the welds after just two exposures to rain. I live in the Sonora desert where humidity averages just 20% and it rarely rains. I will sell this trailer or donate it to a local coop.

Original Review [now edited]
I had to invest a few hours in prepping this trailer. If you are not mechanically adept you might need a bike shop to prep and attach this trailer but this could also be true with any trailer.

• The fragile plastic bushing where the trailer mates with the fork cracked and split on the very first use ($12+ shipping to replace it on the Maya website.) I made an addition purchase direct within weeks and asked Maya to replace the defective bushing. They merely ignored my request.
• 16” wheel axle arrived with bearings inadequately greased and cones not properly adjusted.
• Without the critical axle brackets and washers you’re out of business so you’ll want spares $19 + shipping)
• Light is visible through seams in the dry bag. Useless. I use a rigid storage tub instead.
• The dark red flag has no reflective quality making it completely useless for nighttime riding. I made an alternate from a neon yellow reflective vest
• Wing nuts are an invitation to tampering or theft. I used common 3/8 x 24 axle nuts with the built-in raised, scored washer
• Manual states: “an additional axle washer (not supplied) must be placed between the rear fork arm and the Maya axle adapters …” . Within 2 miles with the washers in place, the wheel would suddenly shift to jamb against the arm/stay so hard that the bike couldn’t be ridden. Luckily I had a slightly shorter axle
• The selection of high-quality, after-market 16” inch tires and tubes is extremely limited. Extremely. Stout, 1½ inch thorns are common in my area so I added a Mr Tuffy-brand tire insert to the Kenda Kontact urban tire for greatly improved flat protection.

title: Somewhat inefficient compared to other bike LED lamps, perhaps more useful for other purposes.
text:
I purchased both lamps, the front (white light) and rear (red light). The rear red would a very good rear lamp except the amount of light emitted to each side (of both front and rear lamps) is very close to zero so they are effectively seen only from the front and rear -- not the sides.

The front lamp has no conventional lens with which to focus and amplify the light so it spreads a very wide beam when mounted horizontally or a very tall beam when mounted vertically. Essentially, it casts light to places you don't need to see. The front beam casts only to about four or five feet. I have a very inexpensive single-LED lamp (two AA batteries) that has a focusing lens which casts a directed a beam that is a little brighter and casts a few feet longer.

The lithium-ion batteries charge with a conventional mini-USB cable. A cable is included but no AC adapter is included. They require 2 hours to charge. That it is rechargeable is not much advantage. At the highest intensity the batteries last less than two hours. Most modest LED lamps using convention AA or AAA batteries will last in excess of 40 hours or more. On an overnight trip or a bicycle tour a conventional AA powered lamp would be a far better choice.

The manual states that "the battery may become ineffective at about 80% of its value after 300 to 500 charge/discharge cycles ... 5 years life span under good care." 300 charges sounds closer to 1- to -2 years in my cycling universe. The manual further states that the battery "loses 1% of its charge per day when stored at room temperature and 5% per day at temps over 104F degrees. Stored battery life decreases 50% at freezing and further degrades as temperatures decrease."

The white front lamp is perhaps better used for other purposes, a dark closet or cupboard, for example. I returned the red lamp but will keep the front lamp for a cupboard. Now that I have it for that other use it will still see some limited use on my bicycle but next time I will make another choice for my cycling needs.

title: Two broke back-to-back, poor quality control, plus update
text:
First, I had used these for decades. If the bike falls on the left side, any mirror is likely to break but I would always replace a broken mirror with this model.

There is a thin brass threaded barrel inside the base. That threaded barrel is there to accept the screw. Twice now, on two different mirrors purchased a week apart, that threaded barrel has come out of the base. In theory it could be glued back into the base but the barrel is so thin that it breaks at the slightest pressure of a pliers needed to get the barrel off of the screw, so that it might be glued back into the base. It really should be glued at the factory but recently it seems it is not.

By the way, the manufacturer sells replacement parts but asks $4 to ship what could be shipped for the price of two postal stamps. In my case it would cost $10 yet you can buy the entire mirror for $12 so what's the point of offering parts?

Update: I grew tired of replacing plastic mirrors every time the bike falls on the side with the mirror so I opted to get a metal motorcycle mirror here: [[ASIN:B005DSPO82 UNIVERSAL BAR END HANDLEBAR MOUNT MIRROR BLACK 6212041]]. I believe mountain bike handlebars are the same inside dimension as a 7/8 inch motorcycle handlebar (1 inch outside diameter) so most any motorcycle mirror should fit, especially the ones that mount in the bar end as this mirror does.

title: Seemed okay but the distanct between the rails seems non-standard.
text:
If you have the type of seat post where the saddle rails are sandwiched/clamped between two contoured plates this saddle might not work on your seat post clamp. This saddle comes with one of those rotary, rotating, claw-type clamps and the saddle likely works fine with that included clamp. However better bike seat posts can't use the included claw clamp type -- they must use their own sandwich-type. Technically, this saddle still should still mount but the distance between the rails was too wide. If you are confused about the difference do a web search for 'bike seat rail clamp' and you'll see the two different families of clamps.

I would have thought that the measured distance between saddle rails would be standardized but the rails on this saddle were just a very few millimeters too wide for both my sandwich-type clamps (it failed to mount on the two different seat post clamps I tried it on). The distance could maybe be lessened by clamping the rails, in a vice, for example, or using some other tool but I decided to return it rather than mess with it..

Otherwise it seemed okay, maybe quite a bit on the stiff side for a gel saddle.

title: Sometimes Tips Over, replace the tires immediately
text:
2016 UPDATE: Every replacement tire for this trailer (12.5 inch tire) is total junk, except one: the [[ASIN:B00I3U8MSG Schwalbe HS158 Wheelchair Tire - Wire Bead (Grey - 12 1/2 x 2 1/4)]]. Trust me, I tried them all by now.
UPDATE:
After three years I decided to change the tires on this trailer. By luck I discovered that there exist 12.5 in scooter tires and pocket bike tires in widths of 2.5 and 2.75 inches. I opted for a pair of 2.75 knobby pocket bike tires in the hope that the added width would prevent some of tip overs I describe below. HUGE DIFFERENCE! I could still make this trailer tip with little difficulty but it is far more stable with the improved tires. So if you're considering this trailer be prepared to change the stock tires immediately (<$20x2 with free shipping if you shop carefully). You'll still want to run with low tire pressure but not nearly as low as with the stock tires. If you opt not to change the tires, read on so you know what to expect and read the comments, too.

ORIGINAL REVIEW
For what it is (the materials) this trailer seems over-priced. It sometimes tips over (often enough) traversing street and sidewalk surfaces via a handicap ramp and driveways (and vice versa). If and when it tips over the trailer doesn't take the bike (and you) with it, but if you are traversing from sidewalk to street, it tips in the middle of the intersection. Not good.

The trailer tires call for 35 PSI Max and if those tires are fully inflated with an empty load, this trailer will bounce all over creation at any larger imperfections in the riding surface and is at serious risk of tipping over.

The tilted, upward-leaning design approach (like a hand truck) is a good one because the footprint is small, it is easy to maneuver when un-hitched and one need not bend far over to access the trailer and its contents. The footprint is small enough so I sometimes take it on a transit bus without concern. But I believe the upward design, hitching to the seat post rather than the rear-wheel axle, as with most trailers, is the source of the stability problems.

The strapping system (2 are included) is just okay. You can do just as well or better with quality bungies. I bought some of the bags that Burley dedicates to this trailer but returned them. I now just cinch a plastic clothes hamper to the trailer with bungies and the hamper holds a ton.

A few things can be done to minimize the bouncing and tipping:

1. when unloaded, reduce the trailer tire pressure to 10 PSI or lower. The problem with this is if you go from empty to a moderate or full load in the same trip, you'll need to inflate the tires mid-trip, closer to max PSI to accommodate the additional load.

2. traverse driveways and handicap ramps completely perpendicular so that you don't catch a trailer tire on the ramp's raised shoulders.

3. slow down (a lot) in anticipation of any significant road imperfection for when 1 and 2 are difficult or impossible.

After close to two years I still use this trailer almost daily for shopping but I've learned to slow way down when traversing from sidewalk to street and keep my tire pressure to 10PSI or less when unloaded or with a light-to-moderate load to prevent tipping. Even with the PSI under 10, there are particular handicap ramps that I traverse frequently over which, if I don't slow down significantly, the trailer will tip over. Every time. No exaggeration.

I'm not completely sorry I own this trailer; it has a lot going for it: small footprint, carry-on size for air travel, etc, but I believe it needs some type of suspension to prevent tipping to make it a better value at $299.

text:

Everything is a bit blurry with the round lens ones, above and below water. So annoying!

Although I’ve only been pool swimming a few years, I’ve gone scuba diving around the world and worked in the visual arts professionally many years I’m highly sensitized and particular visually.

After reading many swim goggle reviews on amazon, fumbling my way through to find a great pair, thankfully I came across a guy who is an avid swimmer and asserted he never even considers lenses that aren’t flat. It got me thinking… What’s that about?

It’s those funky lenses you see pro swimmers were - for a reason! Everything becomes crystal clear when you put a flat lens goggles on. These are not sunglasses or eyeglasses. Swim goggles are made from very different material that annoy does not uphold clarity when bent. No matter who makes them. (Hence the pros will only wear them..now you’re getting it ;)

I simply couldn’t believe how magically everything became beautifully clear and visible when I put the flat lens goggles on. It’s like wiping grease from a window that becomes a big picture window! All of a sudden you see all the beauty of the sky above, your surroundings, and dancing sunlight under the waterline while you swim!!

(I’m my pic they’re the ones on top)

Whichever brand you buy - BUY FLAT LENS SWIM GOGGLES!!

title: Learned flat lenses are the way to go, not these
text:
I’ve been pool swimming a few years now and I do wear glasses now since I’m over middle-aged.

I bought both the rounded goggles and flat lens goggles from these guys after reading an avid swimmers review speaking about only wearing flat lens. They’re the funky ones pro swimmers wear. Now I know why.

What a difference! I will never ever ever wear non-flatlands goggles again. I guarantee if you try each on, you will wonder why they even make curved lens goggles!

Goggles are made of a substance that does not lend itself to being curved. Every single thing is blurred. Above or below water. You put a flat lens pair on and boom! Every single thing is clear above and below water.

It’s such a pleasure. It’s like wiping grease away from a window and seeing clearly again. I thought I’d have issues with being near sighted… But of course water magnifies and with flat lenses, nothing was an issue.

All thanks to reading one of many reviews when trying to get to the bottom of what swim goggles on Amazon are great.

(In my pics the flat lens are the lighter lens ones reflecting my window better)

It's not perfect but it's a lot better than the pedometers I've used in the past.

I live and work in Japan. I have a few watering holes I go to relax. New faces kept asking me where I'm from. When told, few of them knew the name or where Iowa was in the States. I had brought back an Iowa Hawkeyes T-shirt and gave to one of my bar owner friends, but I never seen him wear it. He always wears a work shirt. This did not allow other patrons to see it. So the flag idea came into mind. The Hawkeyes car flag was the perfect size and of course looked cool. Right now there are two Hawkeye flags flying in Japan and when asked where I'm from we can point to the flag. It serves the Bar owners because it gives them and others a sense they are valued. It serves me because when I pronounce Iowa they spell it out as Aiowaa.
The Flags are of higher quality than I was expecting. It is not a single fabric with print on both sides. It was two fabrics sewn together or folded over and sewn. The emblems are printed and were very crisp. (No bleed over)The top of the plastic rod can be removed. This is probably so different flags can be put on or for you to clean the flag if dirtied. Hope this helps folks.

Once the bolts are in place simply decide how far forward or back you'd like the armrests on your cart. For this step I called in an expert. After my wife told me exactly where to put the armrests, I secured the final two bolts to complete the installation. Definitely looks great on our black EZGO cart.

As for the quality, the support brackets are solid and fit the arm rests perfectly. They were snug on the hand rail but that's the way you want them. The arm rest itself is much nicer than I thought it would be. It almost feels like a faux leather and seems to be waterproof as advertised. Might have to pick up a set or two for a few of our campsite buddies.

title: The most important add-on you didn't know you needed
text:
I usually keep my iPhone in one of the cup holders in my Ezgo. Sure, I can't see the phone while driving but when I hear that familiar ding I simply pick it up, flip it over (because it seems to always twist itself around backwards), fumble around with unlocking it (while driving), read my message and then try to type a reply while avoiding pedestrians, parked cars, and other obstacles in my way. Why I never thought to add a cell phone holder still mystifies me. Now I can see my phone while driving; a quick glance at the phone unlocks it; and I've become proficient in using Siri's dictation. I'm happy, the people I no longer almost run into are happy, and my phone is happy it's no longer be jostled all over the place while I drive.

As far as the fit goes, the hold is a little loose in the cup holder. Once I gave the adjustment knob a few quick turns it fit snuggly. The ability to adjust the rotation of the phone itself is great too. You can get the phone into the exact position you want. I've driven on some pretty bumpy terrain and the phone barely moves. This is a really well built phone holder. I'll be buying a few of these to give to our friends with golf carts.

title: A tube is a tube is a tube.  Went to local bike shop and wow. Not close to what these cost.
text:
You can't beat the price of these going to your local stores. If they even have them in stock. I think these were priced way better. My options locally were single pack or double pack. The price for these was half of what I could get and I got FOUR Tubes!

I liked that these were advertised coming from Taiwan. Most of my bike replacements have been from Taiwan so I was okay with that. They have had some great quality in my experiences.

These tubes are the plain ones without the green goop in them and they are the thinner ones. You can find ones that advertise thicker, puncture proof and with green goop.

My experiences is to just get plain tubes and order a large bottle of that green goop and put some into the tubes myself. Cheaper and they are also lighter this way. Not that i use these for competition, but always good to have less rolling weight.

Yes, they fit perfect in my bikes wheels. My bike has a set of wheels for city streets and a set for mountain terrain riding. My current tubes were over 10 years old and were made in Taiwan. title: Fantastic for energy gels! Lights are very bright as well.
text: I bought this for a half-marathon to keep my Clif Shot Bloks inside. At first I thought I'd only be able to fit one package in there, based on the way the belt looks in the packaging. However, it really expands and stretches nicely. It's more of a synthetic spandex stretchy type material than I was expecting. I was able to easily fit three Clif Shot Blok packages inside easily. The belt itself fits comfortable along the waist and I didn't even notice I was wearing it, just make sure you adjust it so it's snug. I actually left it on after my run while walking around the house without realizing I still had it on for about 30 minutes. The LED lights are nice and bright, and they come with three flashing modes (solid, fast flash, slower flash). However, I usually run during the day and have not used it while running but I'm sure it would be bright enough to alert drivers. Overall, a great little item if you need to store something during runs or bike rides. You could also probably fit cash, credit cards, and your ID inside if you don't want to leave them in your car or somewhere else. Or perhaps an emergency contact card if something unexpected happens. I don't think I'd use it for today's bulky 5-inch smartphones, but they would probably fit if you really wanted to. I also thought it might be good to store a small sized pepper spray bottle in for people that run alone and want the added protection. However, unzipping it and removing the item might be a bit tricky in a hectic situation. Just a thought!

Needless to say, after just a week, the first one fell off of my wrist while I was getting out of bed after some raucous activities (^_^) and fell about 3 feet (1 meter) to a carpeted hotel room. Imagine my surprise when I lifted it up and the display was dead (!!). I found a person in Bogota to replace the battery, but again, it died within less than 24 hours.

Sadly, I opened up my backup watch's case, less than a week into my 2 year journey. And after JUST FOUR DAYS, while I was walking the streets of Bogota, it started beeping beep beeping... and the screen got progressively dimmer. Until about a day later, it's screen was dead. I had the watch guy replace it, too, but it died within a week.

When I traveled to the Bahamas, I found a Garmin VivoSmart watch which does pretty much everything this does, and more, with an albeit worse interface, but it is wonderful so far and has lasted several months!

title: Bushcraft day complete. Bag approved.
text:
Just finished our first bushcraft day with this pack and loved it. LOVE the included D ring thank you so much I use it for so many things. The rubber flag patch is tasteful. I don’t even want to switch it out for anything. We started a fire in light rain and wind in upstate NY in 42 degrees. It’s not easy!

We packed clothes, binoculars, food and water, knives and a hatchet. First aid kit, hats, safety glasses, phones, chargers and work gloves. And it had plenty room to spare. It didn’t rain hard but my stuff stayed dry.

I like the side buckles and steals to decrease the size and really compress the gear into a smaller package so it moves less while walking. The zippers slide VERY smooth. My lady likes how it opens up full butterfly to pack it like a suit case! I think that’s cool too.

The chest and waist buckles are a must and appreciated on rock scrambles and hills. This is my new bushcraft bag and possible long hike back. (I’ll just throw my 2L water bladder in there). Plus the padding that contacts my back allows some air flow which doesn’t prevent sweat, but reduces back heat which I like.

It may also become my shooting range bag but we will see. But if you need a single or multi day bushcraft bag with a tactical look and feel, it’s solid.

title: Save your money for a better option
text:
NGL, it's a slick looking knife, but it isn't well constructed.

The blade looks good and the scales feel good in the hand. The blade definitely is sharp. The issue is the pivot point of the knife and the scales around the pivot point.

You'll notice that there is a nice index finger groove up near the pivot point. This is a nice ergo component, however when gripping the knife here the scales flex and cause a severe amount of blade play at the pivot point. Inversely, grabbing the blade towards the base and wigging it will cause the scales at that finger well to flex.

As much as I would like to write this off as a 1-off construction issue, I had an unrelated individual talk about the very same issue they had with this knife. They had sourced the knife from their local B&M and had mentioned the issue. I told them I had one in the mail and would check it when the knife showed up. Sure enough 2 instances of this knife with the same issue.

So buyer beware. I have heard good things about this knife maker and this knife so I decided to test the waters with this blade. I will be sending this knife back and I doubt I will be buying another Eafengrow even if it's another G-10 D2 for sub $20.

The other thing is that I had a trifold 4" mattress on top of it and even then it started to get uncomfortable after a 7 weeks. Without the mattress, I'm not sure I'd want to sleep on it. That said, if it did work as advertised, it would be a solid unit. It doesn't feel cheap. The last comment is that the reason for the additional length of the width bar beyond the actual sleeping space it is lost on me - there's like 5 extra inches of width and it takes up more space, clothing gets caught in it and it makes it more unwieldy. Maybe it's like that for a reason, but you'd think they'd make it a selling point if it was.

Next time be honest in your commercial and focus on the user experience more than on being cute.

My hip hurts now, feet hurt, heels hurt, knees hurt, shins hurt, hand hurts.... my lower back hurts from having to bend over because they didn't have the good sense to make the handle just a couple inches longer. It's TERRIBLE and just plain stupid. So any time i saved by riding was completely eaten up by having to lug it back - all. because the app is entirely unreliable, inaccurate, and the machine poorly designed.

the plastic is poor quality - things breaking off. The knee bar has broken 3 times!

THE WORST PART!!! the updates slow the machine down from 12 to 10mph. it feels like a mobile device for an elderly person now. 2mph makes a huge difference. and one of the things destroying my range is that it pushes back, trying to throw you off the machine. Literally. It thinks you're going too fast (when historically, those were acceptable speeds) and now it just throws you backwards. You have to completely stop and pause for it to reset it. Otherwise it is tilting BACKWARD - uncomfortable and DANGEROUS. esp so since the kneepads are now behind your knees so you have practically zero control over the machine. and lets not forget: thats eating up your battery. so you're wasting battery, to get there slower, all while being incredibly less safe and comfortable. How dumb could these people possibly be???

For $70 you can buy 3rd party software that turns off most of the STUPID TILTING BACKWARDS NONSENSE and gives back a few mph ....just ridiculous i have to pay extra for that and that its not included in the app.

These guys ruined their own machine and made it unreliable and unsafe.

title: Good water-resistant travel blanket
text:
Both sides of this are made of a water-resistant material, as you would find on a sleeping bag or jacket. I would not describe these as being soft or cozy. These are targeted at being travel blankets that should stay cleaner and drier for longer. A negative to this material is that it blocks moisture from escaping, so you can end up sweaty, especially if you are sleeping in a car without any airflow. This stores nicely in a case that can be used as a pillow. I got both the down and down alternative blankets. The down alternative blanket is thinner due to less filler material used. Both are sufficiently warm. The down alternative version should be more resistant to accumulating allergens. The down version offers more padding if you are lying down on this. Neither version offers significant padding if you are lying down on these as the filler is not dense enough to support body weight. The 45 x 80 size is enough to cover one adult unless you are obese. I washed both in a washing machine, and they came out fine.

My sleeping bag is made out of the same material on one side, and has more comfortable cotton on the inner side, with significantly more filling. It can completely unzip to use as a blanket. Depending on the scenario, a sleeping bag can be more versatile, although it takes up more room and is not designed to be used alternatively as a pillow.

title: Unable to scoop ice cream
text:
When traveling I like to carry a spoon capable of scooping Ben & Jerry’s ice cream since hotels usually only have disposable plastic spoons. This spoon fails the ice cream scoop test, although it puts up a fight before it bends. Since if fails that test it does not meet my needs. I did not get this for camping, which is the main use for this product. When I go camping I use plastic dinnerware which has worked fine for me.

Why does this “cutlery” set lack a knife? That is a significant omission for a "cutlery" set. $30 is too much to pay for a thin fork and spoon. These are lighter weight than flatware you would use at home, but they are about the same weight as all the other utensils designed for travel or camping. Titanium costs more because it is a rare metal, not because it is superior. If you are traveling by plane and security decides to confiscate your fork, you will be out $15.

For a $30 set that advertises that it is strong, I would expect to get a spoon that is capable of scooping premium ice cream without bending. I just reviewed a stainless-steel spoon that was of higher quality, was much stronger, and cost $3. I mainly use these for typical vacation and work travel, not multi-day hiking and camping, so weight does not matter much. If you are camping then this set is fine, but so is plastic.

title: Works as intended
text:
This CyclingDeal Upright Bike Stand gets the job done of holding my Cannondale mountain bike in place. My garage space is limited and I do not use the bike much, so I prefer the vertical configuration. If you use your bike frequently, it is easier to use the vertical configuration as getting it into the vertical position involves grabbing a dirty tire. The way this keeps the top wheel straight is better than another bike stand that uses a Velcro strap. The bike seems stable, but if I try to push it over I will be able to. I would not consider this kid-friendly in the vertical position.

This distributes the wheel weight well against three round points. Another bike stand I reviewed had the wheel rest against a thin metal bar that looked damaging to the tire.

You have to figure out how to assemble this yourself as there are no assembly instructions, just a parts diagram. They should have included instructions for the wheel rollers. The bottom wheel contact points can be adjusted into six available locations based on the wheel size. Find the correct size before tightening the screws. I did have to adjust the default center location. Adjusting these involves using two Allen wrenches. An improvement would be if there was a place to store the Allen wrenches attached to the product rather than have them mixed in a drawer of assorted Allen wrenches. I will tape the wrenches to the bottom.

The product box was damaged causing a bolt to fall out somewhere along the way. Their customer support team promptly mailed me the missing bolt.

Some of the other reviews on this product page are for a different bike stand. It looks like they swapped products after gathering reviews for the other bike stand. The current price is $70

title: You can get better poles for less
text:
The current price for these is $70. I can compare these to three other hiking poles I own:
Cascade Mountain Tech ($30) – My rating: 3 stars
G2 Hiker / Go2Gether Trail Star ($25) – My rating: 2 stars
TheFitLife ($21) – My rating: 1 star

The TE-K2 hiking poles look very similar to the Cascade Mountain Tech ones. I rate the Cascade Mountain Tech poles higher than these, and they are less than half the price. The TE-K2 poles have better thumb tightening screws, but otherwise, I do not see anything that could justify costing so much more. The Cascade poles have a feature that the other three poles lack in that the sections have flared end caps so they do not come apart easily. The sections of the TE-K2 poles slide completely out when they are not locked. I lost one of The Fit Life pole sections when it slipped out without me noticing when it was being carried. The same thing can happen to these TE-K2 poles if you do not remember to lock them while in a compressed state. The paint finish on the TE-K2 poles will scratch easily. For $70, you can get better hiking poles.

title: Not enough resistance. Has uncomfortable pedals. Schwinn is better.
text:
It folds up easily and takes up less space than most other exercise bikes, but that is the only advantage. The uncomfortable pedals have traction spikes on them, so you need to wear shoes. With most other exercise bikes designed for your home, you can use them with bare feet or socks.

The maximum resistance this offers is too low for fit men that want high resistance. There is no onboard computer to track anything or adjust anything. You adjust the resistance by twisting a knob. The bike has a smaller seat and backrest than most bikes, so it is less stable and there is no place to put a book or tablet, or water bottle while in the bike configuration. The bike is quiet, but it is noisier than many other bikes with bigger flywheels. The build quality is good and assembly was easy.

Schwinn bikes are more expensive, harder to assemble, and take up more room, but they are so much better than this bike. A good recumbent exercise bike is comfortable to sit on if you want to take a break. This bike does not have that level of comfort because the seat is small.

The current price is $460. A good Schwinn recumbent bike is more expensive, but it is worth the price if you regularly use it and have the space. The main benefit of Wonder Core is the ability to fold it up.

title: Missing the most useful tip for hiking
text:
These do not come with the most useful tips for hiking in rocky areas, which are the basic round rubber tips. I cannot imagine what this company is thinking with this omission. The shoe tips this comes with do not work as well for hiking and are notably less stable and secure than basic rubber tips. They are slippery. The shoe tips are for roads and gravel paths. Tips on hiking poles are mostly compatible across brands and I have a bunch of extra tips from my other broken poles that I will use with these.

These are basic low-end hiking poles, and what I expect at this $21 price point. I have also had TheFitLife poles and Cascade Mountain Tech poles. TheFitLife and Cascade Mountain Tech poles lasted less than 20 hikes before falling apart, and I would expect the same short life span from these G2 Hiker Poles. Most of my hiking is in the Appalachian Mountains, which are rocky and wet.

My low rating is mainly because these are missing the most important tip type for mountain hiking. I also rated TheFitLife and Cascade Mountain Tech poles low because of their short life span. The Cascade Mountain Tech poles bent in a situation that would have bent most poles, so I have rated that one the highest of the three brands.

title: Bowflex dumbbells are significantly better
text:
These JOVNO dumbbells go from 11 to 55 pounds. The Bowflex SelectTech 552 dumbbells go from 5 – 52.5 pounds. The Bowflex has a huge advantage in that they have more intermediate weight steps, and the weight steps are at logical numbers. The JOVNO weights have selections for 11, 22, 33, 44, and 55, which are unusual weight choices unless you convert these numbers to kilograms. If you want a weight around 15 pounds, you are out of luck with this product, while the Bowflex has choices for 12.5, 15, and 17.5. Unless you are already really strong, you will need these additional weight choices at the lower end.

The Bowflex has comfortable and grippy rubber handles. The JOVNO dumbbells have uncomfortable plastic handles that have grip ridges that dig into your skin. The Bowflex weight plates are covered in plastic to protect your floors, and the options stand they come with is great. The JOVNO weight plates are metal. The width of both products is essentially the same.

The current cost of the JOVNO dumbbells is $120 for one. Bowflex costs $400 for two. I bought my Bowflex ones in 2006, which means they have lasted for 15 years so far. JOVNO is an unproven Chinese brand. I recommend paying the higher initial price for the Bowflex ones. I really like the Bowflex stand. One of the main benefits of the stand is that you are at less risk of hurting your back.

title: Saves a lot of space. 25 pounds maxium.
text:
I can compare these to the Bowflex SelectTech 552 dumbbells with the stand. The Bowflex dumbbells have lasted me over a decade and they have worked great. They cost many hundreds of dollars, since they did not have much competition when they came out.

These dumbbells are 25 pounds maximum, versus the 52 pounds of the Bowflex. Most men need more than 25 pounds for gaining muscle, and even 52 pounds is light when doing leg exercises. Many exercises are enhanced with a lighter weight.

The actual weight I measure is 25.5 pounds, and every lower weight selection is a little bit higher than the target weight. The weight discs are made of metal. Bowflex coated theirs in plastic to make them less damaging if dropped.

This product is easier and quicker to use than the Bowflex. The ratcheting mechanism it uses seems superior in terms of simplicity. I question how long it will last and would be worried about it failing while exercising. This product is three inches shorter than the Bowflex, which is good since the long length of the Bowflex is a negative. These are quieter when being used than the Bowflex.

The current price is $90 for one. The current Bowflex price is $200 for one. I really like the Bowflex stand. One of the main benefits of the stand is that you are at less risk of hurting your back. Since these weights are only 25.5 pounds, the risk to your back is inherently less.

Compared to individual weights, or ones where you have to screw off the end caps to add plates, this type of dumbbell is a good investment. If you can afford them, the Bowflex dumbbells are great.

title: A good cooler
text:
It holds a lot and is more collapsible and lighter than a solid plastic cooler. There are bag coolers that have thicker walls than this, but this should be fine when transporting groceries home in the summer. I would not fill the entire product with cans and ice, like the marketing photo shows, since this would likely stress the seams too much. Use a solid plastic cooler for heavy items like that.

I would prefer if coolers had a plastic shelf on the bottom to keep the items away from melted water or spilled liquids that collect on the bottom. Most coolers do not have this feature. I have been using plastic liners that I took from my Tupperware produce storage containers.

The current price is $39. I see less expensive coolers that are probably just as good.

Features that some other coolers have are wheels for transporting heavy items, and some can be plugged into a car outlet or wall outlet for refrigeration. Other coolers collapse more when put into storage. This one is not designed to be collapsed, although it can be smooshed into a smaller shape when not in use. Good coolers can last many years, so you might want to invest in a high-quality one.

title: Not really a yoga mat

title: The concept does not work well
text:
This product is a fine rope saw. The blade is double-sided, unlike some of the ones for sale. Rope saws in general are not that great. You are not going to get the saw blade exactly where you want. If you have to somehow get it through a tangle of branches, all those smaller branches will get in the way of both positioning and the sawing. If you are dealing with a bare branch, that will be easier.

The chain binds up, and when it does you are going to have trouble getting it unstuck. That is going to be the biggest problem with these. If you cut a branch half way, then have to unbind it and it jumps to another location, you are not going to get it back in the prior groove. When the branch is mostly cut it will drop down and dangle while still attached. Detaching a dangling, but still attached, branch is another challenge for rope saws. Another problem is that this is a lot of tiring work that is hard on the hands. I used this on an Oak tree.

Throwing this up to very tall branches will be difficult. For weight, I put a tin of BB gun pellets in the bag. Some people recommend using a slingshot to get this over the branch. I do not own a slingshot, but trying to fling this over a branch by hand is difficult.

The low rating is more a reflection of the concept than this implementation of the concept. A rope saw is certainly cheaper than hiring a professional. If you can get to the branch easily and safely using a chainsaw, that will be the best method. This is for branches that you cannot reach with a chain saw or standard pole saw.

I am going to try the really tall Doca Pole saw next. My regular pole saw does not get up to high branches.

title: Poorly designed, low quality, falls apart.
text:
Caution: push the end caps on with much more force than you think. On my first two hikes, the tips kept falling off and I lost one. title: Works ok, but water condensation pools
text:
This served me well for three weeks on the road. The items you put in this need to start out cold and you need to buy a separate wall adapter for hotel rooms. I bought a cheap one from Coolbuy that worked well. This cooler does seem to keep the temperature cool when left in the car overnight though. This is easy to clean because the motor is on the top.

One issue I had is that after a couple weeks I noticed standing water on the bottom which soaked some items I had. I am not sure if that was from condensation or if a bottle leaked a bit. It would be good if this came with a small removable platform to keep items off the very bottom in case condensation starts to puddle.

The lid is heavy and can pinch your hand if it slams shut.

The cord placement is not ideal because it blocks some of the handle movement when plugged in. This is an issue because the handle needs to be in a certain position for the top to open fully.

Update. I have used this on more trips and have concluded that the condensation is from the cooler. The cooling fins ice over and then melt when the temperature rises high enough. I routinely see pools of water on the right side that soak anything underneath. This cooler is a damp cool, not a dry cool like a regular freezer. This is problematic for anything made of paper or cardboard in the cooler. I am lowering my rating to three stars.

My fix was to use plastic risers that came with some stay-fresh plastic containers meant to hold vegetables. It adds about one centimeter of space between the cooler contents and the bottom where the water pools.

title: A good investment
text:
This has been a good investment. I use it almost every day. I bought it to increase overall health and keep my blood flowing, not as a way to lose weight.

The desk it comes with is not very good. It takes two people to adjust the height, nothing should be on the desk as the height is being adjusted, and the height only adjusts to specific notches in the bar. I will look into buying a better desk to go with it, one where it is easier to adjust the height and one that has a larger surface area. I got the desk for free because of a sales promotion. If I paid extra for this desk I would be rather disappointed in it. It does not wobble noticeably at a high position, which some other desks might do.

The app that is associated with this desk is bad.

The controls for this desk could use some improvements. You have to hold down the stop button for a few seconds before you can power off the device, which is stupid and unintuitive for such a frequent action.

They should come up with a better way to lubricate the tread since that is routine maintenance. I cannot lift up one side of the tread at all since it is not centered on mine and the lubrication tube on my bottle is not long enough to reach the other side. I have no effective way of lubricating half of the tread.

Another improvement would be a dust collector for all the debris that falls off and collects at the back of the treadmill portion.

Overall this could use many improvements. However, these products are still relatively new and the competition does not have these problems solved either. Looking at the treadmill desks available for sale, this is a good one, even with the flaws.

Update: I ended up removing the console to use on a better desk and it worked without having to cut wires. I was able to pry off the hole covers and angle the wire connector through the holes in the desk leg to remove the long wire from the desk. I left the shorter wires in place for now. Before pulling the wire down through the desk leg I attached twine to it so that the wire in the leg is replace with twine. This allows me to pull the wire back up through the desk leg if I want to restore the original Lifespan desk. I am trying out an Ikea standing desk that is easier to adjust the height of and it has a bigger surface area. The markings on the long wire are: E146924 AWM I/II A/B 24AWG VW-1 300V. I looked for a replacement wire that I could buy and could not find one pre-made.

Update: this Ikea desk has been working great. It is much better than the supplied LifeSpan desk because I can lower the height if I want to sit down with the Ikea desk. The Ikea desk does not wobble at the highest setting. I am 6' 1".

Deflating became a game as the grandkids all wanted to take turns laying on it as the air went out. Although we are traveling, we will keep these mattresses with us because they are so useful.

I stored both mattresses and sheets in a 37 qt Sterilite gasket box (24x18x7) (see photo).

Addendum: This is the easiest way to help teach a child to not wet the bed without using pullups. Some kids aren't bothered by wet diapers but most don't want to sleep in a wet bed. Using this mattress, the child can get up in the morning, change, and put the sheets in the laundry without the trauma of fussing parents.

title: Possible Placebo Effect - Watch Out for Skin Irritation
text:
The first ingredient that might actually do anything is menthol which sometimes relieves itching, will temporarily cool the skin, but has the potential to irritate it. Camphor is sometimes used in cold sore medicine to temporarily relieve pain, also cools, but doesn't really penetrate into muscles. According to the nih.gov site, none of the ingredients have been proven effective for muscle or nerve pain.

Nonetheless, occasional use is harmless to most people and may have a placebo effect for relieving pain.

title: You Can Buy a Larger One for 20% Less
text:
I do not recommend the Alex Little Jumper Trampoline unless space is an issue. For $23 less you can purchase the significantly larger and more stable [[ASIN:B008BIV87M Bazoongi 48" Trampoline Bouncer with Easy Hold Handle Bar - Sunshine Yellow. Special Exclusive Limited Edition]].

The instructions are worthless. For example, one part states to "attach the bungee cord to the cord lock by pulling the knotted end of the cord tight". Can I just start by saying "What?" Well there is no knotted end, so you have to create it, though it doesn't really tell you how to do that. Then you have the issue of only three helpful images for the entire manual. And I probably need to start by saying I like to consider myself rather capable when it comes to assembling items and frames of structures having helped my father build our homes and additions. The instructions also do not elaborate where the knotted end should go in reference to the trampoline itself. You can figure out where it needs to go in the medal cord lock, but not on the trampoline itself. The only picture shows half of the trampoline having the cord wrapped around it so you are left wondering what the starting point looks like.

I hazarded a guess and just went with it at that point. Once I wrapped everything around and made sure that I pulled the cord tight several times I then tied it off. The instructions are then once again really vague; therefore I knotted the last end of the cord by itself and pulled it through the medal fastener. I then proceeded to knot the last end of the cord that I had just wrapped around with the beginning part of the cord to ensure an additional sense of security. The instructions mention nothing of this but after looking at the final results, with pieces of cord jutting out in random places, I knew that my three youngest would see that as an invitation to mess with it. So I knotted both ends together, and I did that twice. My kids can be rather problematic.

The directions then tell you to place the cover on the trampoline, making sure that it fits. Once again, the instructions lack on details. They do not specify that the cover should be placed in a specific direction. I used the writing on the cover as an indication for direction, placing the writing outwards where the handle will go. Otherwise, the cover does not fit. I found this out through trial and error, of course. There are also plastic clips that apparently must be clipped to the trampoline in some fashion, that you obviously have to figure out on your own. The most obvious thing was to clip them to the bungee cords that were wrapped around the trampoline.

The next step is to secure the handle. And yet again, those wonderful directions prove that they are pointless. I finally just put the small yellow bar into the curved handle portion (not attaching to the trampoline base yet) to get a sense of where it should go in the actual trampoline frame. I was then able to figure out which direction it faced, knowing that screws would be added at the end. REALLY not clear, but I was able to figure out having put together dozens of pieces before.

All in all, given that it was purchased at a discounted price, it will work out fine in addition to our other in home trampoline. This might be alright for one child, but it would definitely not work for my three kids (4 yr old twins and a 2 yr old) if I did not have the second larger trampoline. They are the ultimate test in terms of durability for any toy and this one is unfortunately not built for heavy duty usage. This might be fine on its own for occasional use from a calmer child, which none of mine are.

title: Reviewed Five Life Jackets - This Was the Winner
text:
We purchased five different life jackets for the 20 month old twins. The traditionally styled ones rode up at the shoulders. The Swimways Power Swimr System was difficult to get on and did nothing to keep the babies' heads above water. Nor did the Speedo UV 50.

We put the Stearns Kids Puddle Jumper on the first baby and she jumped into the pool for the first time in her life and paddled happily around for hours (see photo). The second twin took a little longer learning how to stay upright and she didn't want to take it off.

On plump babies, it's so tight in the arms that it is hard to get on and off. It's easier if you get both the jacket and their arms slick first (e.g, with sunscreen). However, neither twin complained once they got it on and there were no marks on their arms afterwards.

--------------------
5/12 Update. The twins are now three and can still wear their jackets although they take them off for swimming lessons. Their younger brother is a bit stouter and we have to grease up his chunky arms to get his on him. Another grandbaby on the way so I guess I need to buy a fourth one. The three jackets we have are also used by visiting kids so I realize that they are very tight on really stout kids and really loose on thin kids but, nonetheless, work well on most.

11/12 Update. The end of our third season and the three jackets are good as new. No wearing of the material and little fading despite having been left in the hot Georgia sun much of the time.

3/13 Update. The kids can all swim now but they still ask to have their water wings put on at time because they can just effortlessly float around. And, yes, they have already been swimming this year despite the 65 degree temperature of the pool right now.

7/13 Update. The fourth grandchild refused to wear the wings (or any life jacket). Fine with us since we are always with him and he's learning to swim. Love the new designs for this jacket. I need somebody else's baby to train now.

4/14 Update. Currently selling for $15 at Costco (fewer options)

12/14 Update. We still have the four jackets we purchased. All have faded a little but, otherwise, show no signs of their age.

The model before this (the 130) is what I was going to purchase at WalMart, it was cheaper but I would have to pay for tax & shipping (free shipping and no tax on Amazon.com) so it was only going to save me about $30 at WalMart (for the older model) so I am definitely glad I decided to buy the 140 at Amazon.com.
The previous model (130) was highly rated/recommended on the Consumer Report websites and that made me realize that a newer model would/should be even better. I live in a small apartment and although I wanted the recumbent one, I had to go with the upright. Not to mention, I figured I could work on my posture while riding upright. (ha ha) This bike is just what I need to get in shape. I have a leg injury and I am overweight and out of shape. I needed a piece of equipment that I could commit to and not feel like I was doing a dreaded chore. I can hop on this bike and watch tv, listen to music, talk with people around me, or just look out of my window.

At first I felt like the price was expensive compared to the other models, but it's true, you get what you pay for. As I mentioned, I am overweight and I needed something that would last while I pursued my fitness goals. The other brands are not built as well as the Schwinn models. Simply look at the frame work and tubing and you can tell.
After I put it together (without any problems whatsosever) I realized that it was of good quality and worth the money I spent. The setup was easy. I am a female with manicured nails and I didn't even chip my polish putting this bike together. I also didn't require any help. It was really easy. I had my laptop on my sofa with the manual enlarged (I went to the Schwinn website and downloaded it) so that I could see the images clearly, but I mainly used the paper manual that the bike came with.

I read the instructions for the setup of the user profile and everything went just fine.
~I read some reviews about little issues with customizing, but if you just take your time and read the manual, you will really see its not difficult. When you set up a custom workout, you have to realize that it goes through 30 levels so it appears as though nothing is happening, but be patient as you customize it and you will see that it is working right.~
~Also the Heart Rate monitor, if you simply plug it in on the side, it should work just fine. You just have to look for the spot to plug it in to.~
I have only used the bike 4 times so I can't give you any long term use information, other than the programs are nice, the resistance is great, and it has a lot of features on the console once you set up your user profile, but I can say that this is a very good investment for anyone considering purchasing a quality exercise bike. It is a good piece of equipment. If you have to save up a little to get the bike, start saving! If you are considering a different brand, forget about it! If you think that its hard to put together, get over the thought! If you are worried about it not being right for you, try it and you will like it!

I have a lot of weight to lose and I don't like going to the gym. I walk around my neighborhood which is ok, but now I can get a good little cardio workout. I am so glad that I got this bike. I am helping myself in the long run. This is the best way to spend over $300 and have something well worth it!

No missing/broken pieces, no damaged stabilizers, no damaged or flimsy box. I ordered and received in exactly 7 days. ***I'm NOT discrediting anyone's reviews about problems they had with their purchase, I am just stating that my purchase was problem free***

~I will add another review/or update in the future about how the bike is performing~ I hope this helps motivate someone!

title: Good scooter
text:
