title: Just what I was looking for...
text:
I had to submit my review after reading the other ones that didn't rate it so high. I have not had the same issues with my pack. It's exactly what I've been looking for. I've been running for two years and had previously used a standard pack that has one water bottle that sat right in the small of my back. However, I had been looking for away to attach my iPhone to it safely since I couldn't stand using an arm band.

I was so excited when I saw this pack in the store. It was just what I had been wanting. However, although it has the perfect holder for an iPhone, I was a little reluctant to purchase this at first because I was 1.) worried that it would be awkward running with a pack in the front; 2.) worried that the velcro would not be enough to keep the phone velcroed down and from flopping around....also the normal wear and tear on the velcro from flipping up the phone to note my pace on my RunKeeper app.

Admittedly, the pack doesn't work so well in the direct front as a runner...would probably be okay for a walker. However, there is too much bounce to allow that to be comfortable. It did much better when I moved it around to the back...however, it defeated the purpose of being able to monitor my pace as I was running.

I finally figured out that if I put it on my right side with the bottle toward the back part, that I could accomplish everything I needed. iPhone and app are easily accessible..in fact, I rarely need to flip up the phone to see my pace. I can usually see it by barely tipping it up. The water bottle is still handy and I'm able to use my arms without smacking it.

So, while I'm not strictly using it as designed, it suits my purpose just like I needed. I'm really happy with it. Some other things:

1.) The belt isn't that big. If your waist size is 40 inches plus, you might have a tough time getting it to snap.
2.) The water bottle holder is great. My old holder was all material. I like the reinforced strips that make it stiff enough to jam the bottle back in...yet is lightweight and holds the bottle tightly.
3. Water bottle is pretty standard...just right.
4.) The zippered pouch is bigger than I orginally thought. Holds spare key, chapstick, Gu and $ just fine.

1) I used the included ubolt and bracket to eliminate any up and down movement at the receiver. This is a bit of a pain to take on and off if you want to remove the whole rack when you get to your destination but it works well.
2) It had a bit of front to back movement at the pivot/hinge bolt that is used to tilt the rack. Since I don't need it to tilt at all, I tightened this bolt so that it no longer has any movement at this point.
3) Since it uses pins to assemble the pole and wheel supports there was still some side to side movement to the whole rack. I looped a tie down strap back to my tow hooks on each side so that it couldn't move back and forth.

It would be nice if it was a tight fit everywhere but it was REALLY nice to now pay several hundred dollars. For the cost of this rack I am very happy with the value I received.

I also looked at the Halex but the pictures didn't make it appear to be as sturdy or as easy to mount permanently at a later date. The Innova DISCatcher and DGA M-14 both appear to be made out of heavier material (from the pictures) and they may be better for a more public course, but at almost twice the price it wasn't worth for me to find out.

I purchased 3 goals and so far I am very happy with them. Assembly was quick and easy, they are very stable and the quality is good. Many reviews have mentioned adding a second set of chains (which would be very easy) but I haven't noticed a big problem with them. I will probably be purchasing the same goal when I expand my course.

title: So far so good
text:
I just received the Fitbit One yesterday, so I can't really give as detailed a report as some of the others I've read. I spent a very long time deciding which item to purchase - did I want a Flex? Did I want my heart rate monitored? I think the first thing to figure out is what you exactly want to accomplish.

For my needs, tracking my steps, calories burned and sleep is really what I wanted and the Fitbit One had outstanding ratings. As well, I did not want to have to wear anything on my wrist during the day. The clip vs. band was a huge plus for me. Plus the burgundy color is really nice (though where I clip it, no one sees it anyway).

I downloaded the free Fitbit app and created an account online as soon as I got it (you have to activate and set up online anyway). It asks for your goals as far as weight loss, in what time frame, steps per day goals, etc. You can make changes if you need to. Based on the goals you set for your weight loss amount and how hard you are willing to work for it (from easy at 0.5 lbs/week to very hard at 2 lbs/week), it will calculate how many calories a day you should be eating and then tell you how long it should take to reach your goal. This is the website or app, not the Fitbit One itself.

The Fitbit is small and I barely notice I'm wearing it. The clip is a rubbery material that is very soft, so it is easy to get the One into and out of the clip when you want to put it into the band for sleeping. I clip it to clothes on my upper body as per the instruction recommendations, and I don't remember it is there. You can set a message for when you first start it up, and then you can cycle through various stats, like # steps walked, stairs climbed, miles walked, calories burned, and then it will show the time all on the display.

On the website/app, you will get more details about all the areas that are tracked. When you meet a milestone, it has a little "hooray" for you - for example today I met my steps goal.

If you want it to track your sleep, you need to put it in the sleep band. I did that last night and it is super easy to get the One out of the clip and slip it into the band. I had to keep the band fairly loose so it wouldn't be uncomfortable - it isn't the softest material - but when I fell asleep I didn't even notice I had it on. In the morning, it gave me details about my sleep pattern and how long I was actually sleeping vs. how long I was in bed, which I think is super helpful.

This is a great tool, but like any tool the responsibility is still on the individual. You have to manually enter your food in the online tracker (or in the app), and it will tell you how many calories you've eaten, how many you have left, etc. It will also tell you how many you may have left because of the amount of calories you've burned. But that is all dependent on a person taking the time to put the information in and doing so accurately. For me, that's the hardest part (I've tried food tracker apps in the past). I think once I get into the habit and make it my routine, it shouldn't be so difficult.

Synching data from the One to the computer/app is done wirelessly. I noticed it makes it to my app (via bluetooth) much more quickly than it makes it to my computer. Sometimes I have to refresh the computer several times to get it to show the right number of steps, etc. However, there is so much more information in the online dashboard than in the app, and you can get into great detail about your sleep and other things that I really do want it to synch accurately (and quickly) with my computer.

My one complaint is that I didn't realize it already came with a clip and a sleep band so I bought them separately. That might be MY mistake, though, so I didn't take any stars off for it. But if you want to buy this, unless you want to have an extra clip and band just in case, you do NOT need to buy them separately.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this choice. It was a tough decision but so far so good.

I'll update if status after I've used it for awhile.

I have now tried FOUR of these, and wound up keeping two but I rather regret it. My original review stands. These cameras are wonderful in some regards, very temperamental in others. Workmanship is hit and miss. They use batteries faster than any other trail camera I have tried. The first one had a bad gasket so it was not weatherproof, and I returned it. The second one stopped recording images working entirely for no apparent reason, about 1.5 months in (Amazon graciously took it back after their tech team could not troubleshoot it, I had no interaction with the seller). I use them occasionally but they use too many batteries to leave out continuously as I had hoped to do.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I love so much about this camera - adequate (though not amazing) picture quality day and night, good review screen, and mainly I LOVE the ability to set the time of day it records at to minimize unwanted images. But. I had to return the first one because the gasket around the battery box didn't seal at all. The second camera worked great - for about a month. Then it simply stopped, for no discernible reason. After nearly an hour on the phone with tech support I was issued a refund (minus a restocking fee). title: Nice set! Will fit most rod tips under 3/16th of an inch in diameter.
text:
The picture on the left is the barrels of the largest and smallest rod tip in the set. The picture on the right is the eyes of the same rod tips. As you can see, the eye diameter is exactly the same on both. I'm not sure that matters. The set appears to be a quality replacement for smaller rods up to probably 100 lb class rods. The largest barrel is 4.5 mm or .177" or roughly, just under 3/16". If your rod tip is larger than 3/16" then this set is too small. These eyes are black in color. I had a hard time when looking at the pictures on Amazon, deciding what the true color was. Even the stainless rod tips looked black. These are definitely black with the inserts appearing to be dark grey.

I replaced allot rod tips when I worked in a tackle shop. It's pretty easy. This is how I was told to do it. First, when fitting these, always go by feel. Remove the old eye (if it's still attached) by warming the old eye with a heat source. We used a propane torch but a lighter or heat gun would work just as well. Don't overheat it. Just a couple of quick passes (never leave the flame in one place) should do it. Put on a glove or use a rag and pull the old eye off. If it doesn't pull off easily, apply more heat. Once it's off, make sure all the old glue is gone. Use a little fine sandpaper if needed. Fit the new eye to the rod by feel. Try different tips until the barrel tip fits snugly onto the rod otherwise the glue won't hold it for long. Soften the glue stick with a torch or lighter and smear the warm glue on the rod tip. Immediately place the rod tip onto the warm glue and turn the tip to be in line with the other rod eyes. There will be a bludge of glue just in front of the rod tip eye. Leave it. It will easily break off, nice and clean, when it cools. Leave the rod tip to cool for a few minutes. Usually, the excess glue breaks off after it has hardened by just pinching it with your fingers. Hope this helps. Tight lines!

PS, the third image to the right is a rod tip that I just replaced (10-25-19). You can see the glob of glue behind the tip barrel. When you pull that off (make sure you wait for it to cool sufficiently until it's cool and hard to the touch) pull it BACK toward the reel and not away from the reel, or you'll pull the rod tip off and have to do it again. The white spot on the rod is where I burned off the black epoxy that the original tip was made with. You can touch that up with some black paint if it bothers you. I won't bother as my rods take quite a beating anyway. Good luck!

I like that it has a bearing for the line roller at the base of the bail, and will be interested to see how well that performs and hold up.
There are actually several good spinning reel options at this price, so you do have some options. I don't know how well this one will live up to being 100% waterproof and better for saltwater, but that could give it an edge. This reel is pretty lightweight for it's size and capability, but, at the same time, has a bulkier look and feel to it than I expected from the pictures.
To be clear, I have not fished with this reel yet. This review is based on initial testing. I will update this review once I take it fishing, and continue to update should I experience any problems. I mainly fish in freshwater.
Overall, I like what I see so far. I expect to be happy using this reel, and anticipate it holding up well.
Update: After fishing with the reel, I can confirm that it performs well. The difficulty in tripping the bail is noticeable when using it, otherwise it is smooth and easy to use. It is slightly bulky feeling, but a good reel overall.

I have been fishing for my whole life, but this is my first baitcaster. There are a lot of instructions with it, but they are more general than specific for this reel. I watched a couple of videos, and was able to use this without issue. It is easy to adjust the drag, spool tension and magnetic brake. It casts well and retrieve relatively smoothly.
This reel pairs well with the One Bass casting rod (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0BFQPG9V3). They look and work great together.

title: Sturdy enough, and it works. Wish I had bought a different one.
text:

I have been doing the inversion at 45 degrees for a minute or two at a time, two or three times a day. I tried 60 degrees, but 45 is best for me. The table is sturdy overall, thought the leg and foot mechanism is a little shaky (I would not trust it if I were close to the 300 pound limit). It was easy to assemble - you just need to take your time and follow each step of the instructions carefully. There is one step that requires two people.
I am 6 feet tall and about 180 pounds. If I set the adjustable height at 6'2", I get perfect balance.
What I dislike is the head rest. It doesn't matter which setting is used to adjust it, the problem is just that it has a headrest that is thicker then the body. If the goal is to invert and allow pressure to come off the the neck and back, why do I want something forcing my neck to jut forward instead of being freely aligned with my back. If you are thinking of buying this to help with your neck, I would recommend a table that is flat - the neck and back supported at the same level (when horizontal, of course). I have enjoyed the inversion table, and have no problems with it's overall quality. I wish I had purchased a different one, though, due to the headrest.

title: Recommended
text:
I recommend this as a safe, effective and easy solution to use with a trolling motor. Once the battery is inside and connected, it can be used and charged without being removed. The circuit breaker has proven effective a couple of times when my motor got bogged down in heavy weeds.
The strap could be sturdier since batteries are so heavy. I have added some nylon rope as to help support it, and have had no problems.
There is a built-in tester to give a general idea of how much power remains. The auxiliary power port has been useful on a boat and at home to charge cell phones during an extended power outage.

title: Exceeded expectations
text:
It is not often that a product outperforms my expectations, but that has been the case with this trolling motor. I bought it to use with rental boats at a local lake. The boats I use the motor with are Jon boats, about 12 foot, and extra wide. The motor has more than enough power. Speeds 1-3 cover the range I like for trolling. On setting 5, it moves the boat along faster than I thought it would - so I can cover distance if I need to. Likewise, the reverse speeds cover the necessary power range. I have used the motor it with 1-3 people in the boat, and performance has been great in all cases.
I use a group 27 Everstart marine battery, and the Minn Kota Trolling Motor Power Center. (I highly recommend buying the power center and the upgraded weedless prop.) After about 5 hours on the lake, trolling and cruising nearly the whole time, I typically have 78 - 85% charge remaining. One could easily use this setup for an entire long day of fishing. With the added weedless prop, I have been able to move through heavy weeds. I only had a problem once in starting from a stop in some heavy growth.
I have been using the motor for two years with no problems. It has been dropped, banged on rocks, etc., and is very durable.
I can confidently recommend this motor.

title: Exceptionally poor sound quality.
text:
I bought this primarily to listen to Podcasts and some music while swimming laps. When it arrived, I was pleased with the hardware quality and ease of use. I loaded up some music and Podcasts and headed for the pool. It was relatively easy to clip the units to my goggles. The controls could be better, but are not terrible. I put it on, started playing a Podcast, put in my earplugs and started swimming. I had been concerned that my goggles might leak or come off during turns with these units clipped on, but it was not a problem at all.
The problem, though, was the sound. If sitting perfectly still underwater, it sounds decent. Pretty much on par with my 30-year-old one-speaker clock radio. However, even with earplugs, the noise of swimming and rushing water overpowers it. If I play familiar songs I can tell what I am listening to and somewhat enjoy them. However, forget about the spoken word. I had to turn the volume up really loud to be able to make out most of what was said on the Podcast due to distortion and background noise. And then it was just too loud to be enjoyable. In fact, I am sure that others in the pool could hear some sound from it. I tried to adjust it in every possible way, and followed the instructions precisely.
This seems like a good idea, but I am disappointed, especially for the cost.

Pros: Solid design, no earphones or earbuds, can still wear earplugs, easy to wear, stays on goggles and doesn't pull them off, easy to load songs.
Cons: Price, 1 GB of storage is a total insult, limited features and controls for an MP3 player, poor sound quality overshadows all else.

text:

Pouring fuel into the Trangia burner is far easier, it won't come open when inside or strapped to the outside of my pack. This bottle is STURDY, I don't worry about puncturing it like I did with the soda bottles. The seals are meant for alcohol use, so no concerns about a seal on a soda bottle going wonky and spilling fuel(aka my coffee and non-crunchy pasta) when miles from civilization either.

Possible downside is weight. I'm not lugging the kitchen sink into the back country, but I also don't do long hikes and I'm not cutting the handle off my toothbrush to save 0.3 grams. If that's you, the soda bottle is probably a better bet.

These bottles will also work with gasoline and kerosene. US law changed and so this kind of bottle can't be advertised for gasoline use anymore, but it's exactly the same bottle from before the law change, and is still used with kero and gasoline in the rest of the world. YMMV, this is not medical or legal advice, insert standard disclaimer here, etc etc.

One last thought, the .3l bottle has been great for single day or overnight hikes and is of course the lightest. Longer than that and I'd want a bigger fuel bottle. We like our coffee and tea and boil a lot of water. If you're just heating up coffee water or something on a day hike, then as long as the O-ring seal in your burner cap is good you probably don't need to carry any extra fuel at all.

Five stars, wish I had bought it sooner.

title: Great rations for emergency use, also made halfway decent s'mores
text:

Pretty neutral tasting, no strong reactions, good or bad, among ~10 people I've had try them. These are supposed to be coconut flavor, but I didn't taste any of that at all, they taste almost exactly like a graham cracker.

Texture is very crumbly, which is actually a good thing as it makes these rations easy to eat even for those with poor or no teeth.

Perfect, neutral and easy to eat is exactly how emergency rations should be. If you need to bust into these, there's no reason the rations should be terrible and make an already unpleasant situation worse by having to eat terrible food, too. At the same time, they're not good enough that anyone's going to be getting into them without a need. Not conducive to frivolous snacking. When's the last time you heard someone say "man, I'm craving some emergency rations!" Nope, me neither. Not being seriously yummy helps to make sure they're there when you need them.

The outer package is easy to open, the inner plastic shrink wrap on the individual bars was surprisingly difficult to get open. Completely doable, but a knife or sharp pokey object will make it easier.

They made OK s'mores. Not as good as normal graham crackers, but we had to find something to do with the leftovers from the tester packages.

Taste is almost exactly like graham crackers and unlikely to be rejected by anyone, especially after going without food for a day or two. That said, the texture is dry and crumbly, and will discourage most from eating these frivolously. The 200 cal bars are NICE compared to the other solid-lump-o-calories that we tried, and sub-wrapped(although not nearly as solidly as the outer wrapping) for usage over time. Very convenient, and possible for those with poor dentition to eat.

Thus far this is the winner. Will be ordering more.

title: Good concept, neutral taste, tough as a rock, not recommended for people with compromised dentition
text:
Bought locally to try before placing a large order.

Taste is pretty neutral, kind of like a fig newton without the fig. Not bad at all, and not good enough that anyone is going to crave them or get into them short of a real need. This is not a gourmet meal or an enticing snack, it is not meant to provide complete nutrition, it is meant to get a person through a rough situation, and allowances have been made for that.

With the above in mind, this product earned two stars because these are so hard and so compressed that anyone without solid teeth is going to have a really difficult time eating them. They do NOT soften in liquid due to the oil content(most compact way to add calories), and the individual bars themselves are too large to be eaten without being broken apart, which may also be difficult depending on what tools and abilities a person has.

Really recommend the Datrex brand survival rations instead. All the pluses, plus easy to eat. When the chips are down and you're busting into your survival rations, there's really no reason to make it any more difficult than it already is.

It's not a flamethrower, but for 99% of my needs, 80 lumens for 5+ hours is way more useful than 1500 lumens for 10 minutes. This light just keeps on trucking.

2/20/18 Still going strong, my everyday carry light.

1/16/17 Bumped up to 5 stars, the replacement light has been perfect. I lubed the tailcap threads and O-ring with petroleum jelly as soon as I received it, this might help.

11/15/16 Colorful Days replaced the light even though it was beyond the warranty period, quite nice of them. Will see how long this one lasts. Back up to three stars for now.

11/7/16 Downgraded to one star. Light flickers and is quite dim. Reacts to tailcap being unscrewed or tightened, and sometimes only works after loosening the tailcap slightly. Poor connection between tailcap and body of the light - useless.

So far so good. Solid little light and significantly less expensive than the Fenix and 4Sevens and Zebralight flashlights I keep losing. Headband is comfortable. The little case is nice enough but no one is ever going to keep the light in it - 5x more bulky than the light and headband alone.

With the cost reduction vs the brands mentioned above, some compromises are made. While it runs on rechargeable batteries, it's not really happy doing so. Much dimmer. I don't think the regulation circuitry likes the lower voltage much vs primaries much. The claim of 150 lumens is a joke, WAG compared to other lights I have, I would put this at ~80 lumens.

Can't comment on durability or waterproofness yet.

So far, while I'm happy with the light for the money, there's a reason I bought higher end lights. If my better lights don't turn up soon I'll just buy another one and this light will eventually get relegated to backup duty.

title: Great little stove, can't beat the value.
text:
Great little stove, love the piezo lighter. Fits inside a hiking pot with a fuel canister, very easy to keep with you and very fast to set up. Perfect for a hot cup of coffee or some soup while out in the woods or while taking a break from work. For the cost of a couple foofy coffee drinks from Starbucks, you can have fresh coffee wherever. This much utility for this cost can't be beat.

For those unfamiliar with micro canister stoves, there are some limitations. This is definitely is a backpacking stove, and nothing like a Coleman suitcase or even one of the older green single burner Colemans. This stove is optimized for light weight and compromises have been made in support of that goal. The pot supports are small and somewhat wobbly and the base is your canister, so smaller canisters are less stable. Definitely not meant for large pots, even a full 1liter pot is pretty wobbly. I've had trouble making enough coffee for 3 people with each of us wanting to fill our 20+ oz insulated travel mugs, even though the stove cranks out plenty enough BTUs. Wound up stacking up bricks around the stove to support the pot independent of the stove, so all the stove had to do was pump out BTU's. This is not a detraction, just something to be aware of, as heating 2+ liters of water for a group is NOT what this stove is designed for.

I use this for a quick cup of coffee or some hot soup while camping/shooting/wrenching/whatever. Morale booster, mostly. I've had no issues with reliability, but if I was in any kind of situation where the stove failing would be more than an inconvenience, I'd cough up for the peace of mind of an MSR. Sure it's 4-5 times the cost, but that's only $30.

Note: There are adapters all over the web to use these with the very inexpensive tall skinny butane cans, or even to refill the isobutane canisters with just butane. For the average hiker using a stove a few times per year, not enough fuel will be used for fuel cost to matter. If you're using it more frequently, one of those adapters could pay for itself quickly. Straight butane won't work as well as isobutane in cooler weather, but if you're getting into temps that low you should probably look at a liquid fueled stove anyway.

Wow that got long.

title: I know it's ridiculously easy to overfill tubed hurricane lanterns and get them to ...
text:
Short version: Pass on this. Buy a Dietz or Feuerhand or Kirkmann or other quality lantern.

Long version: I'm an experienced kero lamp and lantern user. I've owned lots of lamps and lanterns from multiple manufacturers for years. I know it's ridiculously easy to overfill tubed hurricane lanterns and get them to leak; even a quality lantern will leak if overfilled. That's not what happened here.

The base seam of the font isn't fuel tight. After leaving the lantern sitting with fuel in it for a couple weeks, liquid fuel has leaked out of the seam, wetting the seam and the workbench under it. There is no trail of fuel residue from the filler cap or the side tubes leading down to the seam, the seam itself is leaking. There are other areas of lacking quality that can be compromised on, but a fuel leak is not one of them.

I threw mine away.

title: Fantastic lantern. If you're used to standard big-box-retailer fare
text:
Fantastic lantern. If you're used to standard big-box-retailer fare, this lantern is a HUGE step up in quality and size and you'll be very pleasantly surprised. I've burned it ~12 hours and have yet to notice a drop in the fuel level. No smell when burning(except for a few hours after the very first use), even on plain ole kerosene. While it's attractively built and painted, this lantern is clearly built to be used, not just displayed. Packaging was GREAT, I was really surprised at how well this lantern was packaged.

Tips for use: The wick will probably need to be trimmed when you receive it, mine was uneven and had many loose threads. I used angle nippers, a sharp pair of scissors will do better. I just removed the whole burner assembly for easier access and trimmed the wick level with the wick tube. Burn it for several hours the first time OUTSIDE. The paint will be doing it's final outgassing upon being heated and greases and oils from stamping will be burning off during this period, you don't want that going on in your house. When you first light this lantern, turn it up a little bit and let the whole lantern heat up for 10-15 minutes before turning the lantern up to full brightness. Likewise when putting out the lantern, turn it down to a very low flame and let the lantern cool for a few minutes before actually blowing it out. The flame doesn't actually burn liquid fuel, it burns fuel that's vaporized off the wick. If you just blow out the lantern, full throttle to blown out, a bunch of that fuel is still vaporizing off the wick and that smells bad. This can be mitigated considerably by turning down the lantern and letting it cool, which will reduce the amount of fuel that continues to be vaporized after the flame is finally blown out. Odor may be less of an issue with lamp oil, but even with lamp oil, you'll still be inhaling the vaporized lamp oil, even if you're not smelling it. Not healthy.

Now, the one reason I gave 4 stars instead of 5 was that there was a chip down to bare metal on the font when the lantern arrived. As stated above, the packaging was amazing and undamaged, this lantern clearly sustained this chip before being shipped. I used a dab of nailpolish that was fairly close to the color to prevent rust in the future. This did not effect the use of the lantern at all, and I will be buying more.

5/21/16 update: I have several gallons of kerosene through this lantern now. Lantern has performed flawlessly, but I have found that it is actually my least used lantern. It's about the same size, weight, and cost as an Air Pilot, but puts out ~1/2 the light. Yes it burns less fuel, but if you turn down an Air Pilot to the same light level, you'll get about the same fuel consumption while still having the option to turn it up and get more light if you need/want.

title: Not for large or older people
text:
I purchased this unit, and it unfortunately arrived at my condo while I was out of town and my return window expired, or I would have returned it. I’m 63 years old, over 6 feet tall, and a large man. I go about 350 and ordered this unit because it will handle my weight, and it is built quite strong. I’m not sure where they got the child in the picture, but the unit just isn’t as big as it looks in the picture. The unit is built fairly strong, but is too low to the ground and too narrow at the base to be safe for large people. And there is no way to really adjust the pull force requirement, which is a lot if you are heavy.
If you are a large person and want to really use this machine, get a piece of plywood that’s at least 8 inches wider and longer than the base, mount 2 4x4s (stacked) to the front, and one 4x4 on the rear. Then mount the unit to the 4x4s and prepare for a real upper body workout. (Raising the front will allow you to get on the thing without the seat sliding downhill while you get on it). Overall, if you are a 20 year old 100 pounder, this is probably a good unit for you. If you are large, or over 30, you should look elsewhere.

title: Mongoose Trace - Adult user update
text:
I'm a 5'8" tall adult weighing about 170 lbs. This scooter with the air filled 12" tires is to replace another scooter I use to ride along with my grandkids. A scooter with smaller hard rubber wheels is hazardous when the sidewalk is uneven. Tree roots often push up part of a sidewalk, and a 1" difference in elevation is not fun. The more you weigh, the more difficult it is for the wheels to "make the jump." My other scooter also had a rear disc brake which is very nice.
As an adult, I found it difficult to find a kick scooter with big wheels and hand brakes tall enough for an adult. After much research, I chose this Mongoose.
I've been maintaining my own bicycles since the 1970s. One would think a scooter is a piece of cake to assemble! And it should be...except it's not!
This scooter is sturdy, nicely painted, the wheels are nice, although I would have preferred a slightly taller handlebar. The difficulty is with the caliper brakes.
The instruction manual points out how the left brake handle is for the front, and the right one is for the rear. So far so good. However, the actual hardware appears to want to accommodate both breaks from either handle.
Being made in China, maybe the Chinese do it differently. But Mongoose literature says they hail from Madison Wisconsin.
So, I've about finished with the front brake. After I removed a "double cable" and stretched the proper cable to the handlebar brake lever. However, the rear brake cable also has a "double cable" and the single cable from the rear caliper is not long enough to reach the right brake lever.
I shall try and contact the manufacturer tomorrow. Lucky for me, I happen to have a collection of brake cables from my years of home bicycle maintenance to make it work. But I should not have to do that.
Hopefully, Mongoose will get together with their Chinese manufacturer and straighten this out for future buyers. Might I suggest they move their manufacturing to Wisconsin where they hail from. They might also consider revising their instruction manual for more clarity.
ADULT USER UPDATE:
I've come to find out that this is a "Trick Scooter" as in circus. The twin rear brake cables allow for the handlebars to spin in 360 degree circles while "riding." I don't expect to use the scooter in this fashion.
Customer service was friendly and attentive. They shipped me a missing lock nut (in the mail) and noted by observations about the brakes. Although the brakes are fully adjusted, they require an unusual amount of hand gripping force to lock the wheels. I believe this is because the length of the caliper arms from the pivot point to the rim pads is exceptionally long. In my opinion, it is a design issue. There is a wide gap between the top of the tire and the single mounting point of the brake calipers. Therefore, the mechanical advantage to stop the wheels from spinning is very weak. This problem is compounded with speed and the weight of an adult rider. I would not ride this scooter on a steep hill. I believe a rear wheel disc brake would be a fine solution. That, or modify the frame design to enable installation of high leverage rim brakes.

As my purpose is ride and supervise young grandchildren and riding on mostly level sidewalks at low speeds, I will probably keep this scooter despite its shortcomings. But I should not have to settle for this due to lack of choice. An adult kick scooter with 12" pneumatic wheels and hand brakes without an electric motor is difficult to find.

title: Valuable Information about This Product (Vendor/ Manufacturer should take note)
text:
Although uncertain at first, this extension bar turned out to be a good fix to my stem problem.

Useful information the vender did not provide:

1. Flared section of the tube begins at about at center (approximately 4 inches). 4 inches of tube sticks above the headset lock nut.
2. When fully seated, a length of approximately 3.8 inches (97 mm) exists from the top of inner cap screw (which tightens the Quill nut) to the top of the extension tube.
3. The cap screw requires a hex head 6 mm (Allen) tool approximately 5-1/4 inches long if using L-shaped tool. If using a torque wrench, Neiko Log Hex Bit Socket Set, Metric 3 – 10mm (also sold by Amazon) will do the trick. This specific tool measures approximately 4-1/4 inches long from tip of Allen head to back of socket (face of ratchet). There is just enough socket showing to attach a 3/8” drive ratchet. Due to the shallowness of the cap screw and the required tightening torque, I don’t think a ball-end Allen tool will work. 3/8" drive extension bits should also work for shorter length sockets.
4. A specific torque was not provided. My research suggested 20 to 30 Newton-meter (170-260 inch-pounds)(You’ll have to research what is appropriate for your situation). Because I did not have a strap wrench and did not want to mar the finish with channel locks, I was unable to torque all the way to 170 inch-pounds (14.166 foot-pounds). The technique used is to tighten the bolt in short, sudden, jerks rather than smooth, easy pulls. With the jerk method, the outer shaft will still spin, but the bolt will also tighten. This will not happen with easy pulls as bolt and unit only spin in unison as it begins to tighten. I was able to tighten the bolt to sufficient tightness so that the extension does not spin with the installed handle bars and attempting steering while keeping the wheel from twisting.
5. One should also be prepared to change to longer brake and shifter cables and cable housings to accomodate the new, longer stem.
6. Hopefully these notes will guide fellow cyclists sufficiently through the process.

title: Revised Review: Clear as a Bell, but secure a bit of cloth or leather to the actuator.
text:
This bell has a nice, piercing, loud, distinctive ring. It is perfect for two lane trails shared by bicyclists, pedestrians, runners, families with strollers, etc. This bell is very effective at warning people ahead that a cyclist is approaching, and they instantly move or stay in their lane so the cyclist can pass unseen on their left.

The clapper is spring loaded requiring the cyclist to allow the lever to snap at the bell. However, under constant ringing, this can potentilly cause irritation to the bellringer's thumb. Thus the reason for only 4 stars instead of 5.
The clapper must "snap" in order for the bell to ring.

I would suggest gloves covering the thumb in winter, and otherwise practicing a technique whereby the thumbnail does most of the interaction with the spring mechanism. One could probably also wear some sort of protective bandaide or other covering on the thumb. The user will have to decide what is best for their circumstances.

There are other bells easier to ring, but this one is very loud and distinctive, and for me, worth the inconvenience of learning the "thumbnail technique."

UPDATE TO MY INITIAL REVIEW
I love this bell, and I would definitely buy it again. PLEASE NOTE: I added a modification that I would like to share.
Using Wedgewood Contact Cement, I attached a strip of tough polyester fabric to the metalic ringer mechanism. This tough but soft fabric protects the thumb from chaffing when ringing the bell (Please see photo). I suggest that a small strip of soft leather would work just as well and perhaps be even more durable. With this easy improvement, I can now raise my rating from 4 to 5 stars.

text: This is a light weight and then camp mattress. Lightweight is the key feature here! Very good for putting in a suitcase, a backpack, etc. Comfort is just OK. I think there’s a trade off between weight and comfort, as this is not a particularly thick mattress. Additionally, the thickness of the mattress makes it somewhat easy to inflate. The only real option is to blow it up by mouth, and it took me about 15 or so breath’s to do it. The pad is certainly much more preferable than sleeping on the ground, though it’s not as comfortable as thicker mattress is that would be heavier and be more difficult to inflate. The material is rather thin, and while I can’t attest to its durability just yet, it seems as if it would not be as durable as thicker and heavier options. Probably good for occasional use, but I would venture to say using it a lot would wear it out quickly. The material is kind of odd. It’s a little bit on the stiff side and also very slippery. This makes it maddeningly difficult to roll up and get back in the bag. It’s not that it doesn’t fit, it’s just very difficult to fold it properly and then roll it up without it unraveling and coming unfolded. It’s best to do it with two people, or you’ll spend a lot of time refolding, creasing, and rolling it up again. A minor thing, but if you had to do this every day at might try your patience. Overall, a rather thin mattress that provides a bit of comfort, but if you have the ability to buy something thicker or heavier I’d recommend it. title: Folds up on itself like a shirking violet at a homecoming dance
text:
I needed an umbrella for an upcoming trip to somewhere and this seemed like a decent buy. More to the point, it would arrive before I was scheduled to depart unlike some of the other choices. It was more than a tad pricey but the reviews were overall favorable so I went for it. Turns out I didn’t need it for that trip because the weather forecasters failed in their job.

Fast forward a few months to an actual winter rainstorm. Rain is coming down at a more-than-irritating rate. Wind is blowing at about 15 MPH with occasional gusts to 25-40. Umbrella is inverting itself about every 40 feet even without the gusts, and I’m not nearly as dry as I was when using my previous cheap Sam Walton special that was great but for the weak fabric. I want to rage-throw this pos across the parking lot, but that would be littering. It didn’t get better on subsequent uses.

Pros:
Mechanism to deploy it is smooth and fast.
If it’s not breezy, it will keep you dry, and do a pretty good job as a parasol on a sunny day (failed me in Puerto Rico’s mild breezes though).
Light weight and compact.

Cons:
It has vents that are supposed to prevent the inversion problem, but they are way too far away from the center to work even a little bit.

Opinion:
Buy it if you have no other option, otherwise avoid at all costs.

title: Right for the price with some issues.
text:
Seems like a few fake reviews on these... how 'bout a real one?

I bought these for a week-long trip to Alaska for salmon fishing on the lower Kenai River. My expectation was that I would throw them out at the end of the trip - instead I brought them home. They mostly met my expectations but are not a 5-star product.

Cons:
- The boots fit fine, sure, but the waders were otherwise too small. I'm 6'1, 270 lbs with a 55" beer gut, and have a 33-1/2 inseam. The bottoms went up to my crotch with a little slack, but the top and suspender straps are way too short. I had the buckles on the straps adjusted to the longest length without them constantly coming out (they did occasionally) and the straps really dug in to my shoulders. The straps should be at least six inches longer, but even better the upper part of the waders should be six inches taller. It was a bit of work to get them over my belly but I got to where I could do it over a hoodie and they were snug but not tight. If your inseam is longer than 34" and you're not going to get at least size 13, these won't fit.
- I could stand in them, but crouching or sitting without keeping my legs straight was impossible. There's no stretch in the fabric.
- The top of the pocket on mine is at my navel. Plus, no Velcro or snaps to keep it closed. I got river water inside, and constantly had things falling out. I lost a rented knife I had to replace and my $300 prescription sunglasses to the river.
- The boots don't have a comfortable insole and are really hard. I bought the $15 Dr. Scholls which worked fine.
- When standing in more than a foot of water the boot uppers would collapse and cause considerable pain to the tops of my feet, often to my toes.
- No breathability. My legs and lower trunk got nice and sweaty.

Pros:
+ All the joints are sealed and taped. I didn't have a drop of water on me from the outside.
+ Boots fit well.
+ Construction and materials are good for the price in my subjective opinion.

Neutral:
~ They are unlined. I knew this before buying them. Even wearing jeans my legs got really cold. Plan appropriately.

I wish someone had written a similar review before I bought these and had them arrive. I could have made the needed modifications before I left. With that said, I would not hesitate to buy these again or recommend them to a (very warm-blooded) friend.

It took us 10 times longer than it should have to get this thing put together because the directions suck so bad. text:

It is not worth 90 dollars or the 30 I paid for anyone over 5 feet. It doesn't rattle and it has a great brake. That's it. A small child should enjoy a Razor that doesn't rattle and it seems nice quality. The different sites or places that say this is 8 to adult 220 lb weight limit don't tell ya the bar height will be a little above your knees a little if you are 5'10".

The A5 Lux (which rattles but is adult human size) pictured with it shows how tiny the Beast is and the bar height I actually need and use. Beast. More like a Mini....mouse. I admit my mistake in not researching this better and thinking I was getting a great deal but this thing is tiny. Tiny.

title: Too much fun...adult opinion
text:
What I dislike?? I paid 67 last week now it is LESS....lol. But I will say it is worth the money. I am a 52 year old 5'10" adult and the last time I rode a Razor Brand kick scooter Harry Potter was in the theaters and I was "old" for scooters then. And had a very bad wreck due to the brake not really supporting my weight.
Rest assured ...I am under the 220 pound limit and the brake on this DOES work but not on a dime. Plan ahead.
The huge wheels make cracks and bumps easy. On smooth pavement it is a smooth ride....on rough pavement.....yep, rough ride. Will jar you pretty good. I use it for an 8 block radius. I have seen reviews of people who use it for much larger spans. I just WISH this product had existed when I was a teen or in my 20s. Also, if you meet a heel too steep to kick scoot, it is very easy to just pick it up or push it till you can easily go again. I think it weighs about 7 lbs. Don't quote me but that is something anyone can handle.

Here is what to know....as long as you an adult rider do not take this to a skate park, these days, no one is gonna laugh or poke fun. Scooters are hot now whether electric or kick and this scooter is great for people young or old. It is low to the ground, easy to kick, easy to ride, light weight...total fun.
I own the Razor E300. I wanted this for different reasons. It is 100 percent suitable for an adult human to ride. It IS a scooter and you could fall so wear your helmet. You already look a tad goofy....so don't worry what others think. Put that helmet to protect your brain and enjoy a fun ride!

title: Fun, fun, fun...wear a helmet!
text:
I just put some rubber bands on the throttle so it felt grippier. This thing is the most fun! I am 5'10 and weigh 180. It does have a hard time on hills but on flat land and down hill it can feel pretty fast. If you want to ride around town just choose flattest routes.

Like with a skateboard....once you learn the correct foot positions to ride comfortably, it is easy. I learned I put my feet on very similar as to my skateboards.

Since the throttle is either on or off with no inbetween....it can feel kind of jerky the first few times you ride it until you get used to that. You will learn it fast though....how to let off or turn on. Turning is not very tight radius so practice that if you arent used to riding one.
Prices are wild on these. I got mine last month for 260...the white e300 with the blue front forks. I see they are over 400 now. I think under 275 is a solid price if you want to play or plan to ride it to your local store or other near by places. Scooter laws vary state to state and where I am this is considered a toy and can be ridden on the sidewalks. Which....no one ever uses here anyway. We dont have bike lanes where I live either so I dont know if it would be legal to ride a bike lane in my state.

It is beefy and heavy and feels like a true machine rather than a toy. Mine charges fine, tires hold pressure fine, no issues at all.
I keep it inside because it flat states on the directions of use that extreme temps can effect the battery or even ruin it.
I have used it on street pavement, sidewalks, and fine gravel. I have never run out of charge on a trip but you CAN still kick scoot this old style if you do run out of charge.

I think it is fun, gets me out in the fresh air, saves some gas money.
