title: This is a perfect light for a tent or pop up
text:
This is a perfect light for a tent or pop up!

It's well made overall simple to use. The magnetic back makes it sure easy to place it any metal surface and the included strap can be used to mount it inside a tent.

The flood mode provides great coverage and puts out more than enough light up a tent. Hold the button to turn it on, then press it once to change the lighting mode from flood to spot to strobe and then to red for emergencies. It's convenient to be able to quickly remove it from the strap and switch it to spot light mode if you need to go out of the tent at night. When you get back you can just snap it back in place on the strap.

It comes with a fairly sturdy protective bag that can be used when you're done with it. Great little light, I'll definitely be taking it with us on our Prescott camping trip next weekend.

title: Mask makes it a pain to use

title: I dont know.
text:
Thought this will beat the traditional hay hats, wrong!
Hat is way too large in diameter. You will catch yourself bumping into everything. Sort of like wearing two numbers larger shoes, try it! it's annoying and so is the round hat, I guarantee you.
Next non-sense with the round hat is the side slits behind the mesh let the sun in. Rating sun protection 1 star as it defies the purpose of why I ended up buying this in first place; and If I posted picturet after first couple hours of wearing it outside in decent yet not extreme heat, you'd be horrified to notice the staining from sweat after it dries, in repeated sessions. It looks disgusting. Fabric, or faux leather, whatever the outer coating is made of, does not give an indication of long lasting life of a product, instead I expect it to peel soon, matter of fact, mesh on one side is already ripping off a good section at the lower seam due to not so precise stitching that skipped the mesh thanks to its large openings. The central insulation material that seem to be the same glossy flex aluminum you see inside the small refrigeration lunch bags is incredibly thin and expected to rip after a year or two of use - IF nothing else rips before it of course. (mesh pun intended)
Finally the inner blue "cooling" fabric that is to be wetted... impressions after handling it is nothing like what one thinks of when ordering this set. Thought it'll be pretty thick to absorb enough liquid to provide lasting cooling effect. What you will get? Another thin layer, to me these words immediately jumped into my mind: "A blue toilet paper, or is it actual fabric?" Yep, those are the impressions and the rating solely for the round hat so far.
I have yet to try the baseball type hat, but I dont see it to be any better except I wont be bumping my head against the firm hat that loves to bump into everything around you. On the other hand, sun protection is limited with baseball type hat as it doesnt cover in entire circle but a small section. Like I said in the headline, I dont know.
To me it seems that its rather a gimmick, poorly executed at that.
Not that it couldnt be a good product, if it was manufactured with PRO skilled team that would research, test and fix issues that I'm finding out on my own stupidity for wasting money on it even!
Only 5 stars are for the light weight but guess if I still wear it? After about a week? 10 hours of use I'm back to good old school hay hat I got good few years back and cant be happier!
Hope this reading helps you decide, better stuff your old hay hat with wet toilet paper and you'll be better with it than with this nonsensical pile of garbage that should never been manufactured as all it may do is pollute Earth with more artificial toxic materials causing all sorts of skin issues on humans, animals and foliage.

I am a weekly rider and often ride 30 miles a day to work, but the tandem is a ride in the evening with my wife bike and having a saddle that made it uncomfortable ruined many rides.

The WTB ProGel is not only comfortable but well built. The rails have a significant amount of fore and aft adjustment, the leather is well stitched and the padding where the ishium of the pelvis sets is well designed.

title: A great product.  Many uses.

title: Pretty good software, but hardware might need some help
text:
The app that accompanies this and the way it works is simple and very neat. I have yet to have a chance to check it vs more expensive industry standards like GC2 or trackman BUT for the most part these devices are accurate unto themselves and it's user error that throws them off.

It does NOT do carry distance (which makes sense if you think about it, it doesn't see what the ball is doing). If you duff a shot fat and hit the deck before the ball, it will register that as your strike.

It has a very cool animation and 3D manipulated graphic and pretty much all the important info in terms of face angle/path/AoA/speed/shaft lean. All very good for the home golf nerd that doesn't have regular access to the big machines.

Where it falls short and loses a star from my perspective is this: The mounting system needs a good bit of work. I left it in my car on a hot day inside the little carrying case it comes in (it latches to a little plastic dowel) and when doing so I THINK it melted the rubber grippers that grab onto the club shaft. So now it doesn't have enough tension to hold onto smooth steel shafts (like on irons). title: Great bag for the Price-lightweight but warm
text:
We ordered these bags for overnight/weekend backpacking trips. We aren't ultralight backpackers, since we stick to 1-2 nights, but this bag was still lighter than most we considered, so I was grateful for that. We have other Teton products that we use with car camping, so we are familiar with the company and their customer service and products.

First, the bags are fairly light at just 2lb 9 oz. Great for weekend backpackers. They also compress nicely in the sack they came with, but would do so even more if you bought a compression bag. However, they easily fit in the bottom sleeping bag compartment of our backpacks as is. The sack also has a strap on one end so you can easily attach it to the outside of your pack.

The bag is warm, and it's important to remember that sleeping bag ratings are for SURVIVAL and assume you're properly dressed for the weather you're using the bag in--dry base layer or naked, hat, etc. This bag should keep you comfortable at 40F and above if you're properly dressed/dry. If you go to bed in the same clothes you've been wearing all day, you'll get cold in any sleeping bag--always put on clean, dry clothes or sleep naked with a hat. :) If you're worried about warmth, you can easily add a lightweight fleece mummy bag liner--it won't add much weight to your pack, and the extra warmth can be reassuring if you need it.

I'm recovering from thyroid cancer and have gained 80lbs, so even as a plus size women at 5'10, 250 lbs, I have plenty of room to zip up and around me so that the bag isn't cold. I'm a side sleeper and I move around a lot at night, but I don't try to roll IN the bag--I roll with the bag. The cinch hood is a nice feature for a bag at this price.

Overall, yes, there are lighter and warmer backpacking bags--but for this price point, you'd be hard pressed to find one as warm, light, and soft as this one. If you're a beginner or just do 1-2 night trips from spring, summer, early fall, this bag should exceed your expectations. Add a lightweight fleece liner and you'll be set for even cooler temps. Teton never disappoints.

title: Alvada Hiking Socks 80% Wool? A simple test says not. Don't get fleeced!
text:
Alvada says these hiking socks are 80% Merino wool. But the moment I put them on, my feet said "synthetic".

But I don't like to leave a negative review without reason. So, I did two tests:

First, I took a pair out for a hike on a drizzly day. Real wool regulates temperature in the "Goldilocks" zone: not too hot, not too cold. Real wool also wicks moisture. The Alvada socks were too warm when dry, too cold when wet, and they did nothing to wick the dampness away.

Second, I used a test that is familiar to anyone who works with fiber: the flame test. Take a piece of yarn and a lighter. When held to the flame, real wool will shrink away. It will burn in the flame, but it won't ignite or burn on its own. When it burns it smells like burnt hair, and it leaves a powdery ash. By contrast, synthetic fiber will not only burn, it will ignite and keep burning. Synthetic gives off a greasy smoke and leaves a ball of burnt plastic.

I posted a video of my flame test on yarn from these Alvada Hiking Socks compared to a strand of yarn from a pair of Darn Tough 68% Merino Wool Socks. Spoiler Alert! The Alvada yarn caught fire and burned vigorously. Totally consistent with synthetic material.

POTENTIAL SAFETY WARNING:

Metalworkers (welders, grinders, blacksmiths), glass artists, firefighters and others who may be exposed to flames, embers or sparks look for wool clothing BECAUSE of wool's relative safety. Synthetic fibers can ignite.

Dont get fleeced and don't get burned by synthetic socks posing as 80% Merino wool.

title: You've Spotted a Good Deal with this Gosky 20-60x80 Spotting Scope
text:
I have a house with a fantastic view, including a field about 1000 yards off that is visited by majestic Roosevelt elk, and an airport about 4 miles out. My trusty pair of Leupold 8x binos really don't provide enough up-closeness for those sorts of distances. I tried a pair of BARSKA Gladiator 20-140x80 Zoom Binoculars, but was disappointed by two things: First, I'm no optician, but I really don't think the BARSKA is capable of 140x zoom. At the highest magnification, the image was no more zoomed than on this Gosky (actually, pretty sure the Gosky is more powerful). Second, at higher magnifications the BARSKA's images were murky and cloudy. (Other people using the BARSKAs say that the two eyes don't align very well -- but there's supposed to be an adjustment for that.) I liked the binocular depth perception of the Gosky, which was (surprisingly) apparent even at several hundred yards. But with the Gosky I got a much brighter and crisper view. (Also, for really distant objects, like the moon, I'm pretty sure that binocularity is lost anyway because the angle created by the separation of your eyes becomes insignificant at some point.)
I definitely appreciate the advantages of getting a (not included) lightweight tripod with this 'scope. The weight of the Gosky is considerable, and the magnification amplifies any movements. Put it on a tripod, and those issues are solved.
I have been using the Gosky spotting scope for animal- and birdwatching, plane-spotting, landmark finding, and looking at the surface of the moon. I can even pick out the ball and the plays when the kids play baseball in the field about 2 miles off.
I'm sure there are many more expensive, better made, connoisseur-quality optics out there, but the Gosky suits my needs and abilities just fine at this point.

title: Primus OmniLite Ti Stove -- Made in EU Quality Shows!
text:
[[VIDEOID:3e35f8b3c9ff2db1bc3918716d231bf8]] I have owned three single-burner camp stoves.

My first stove was an MSR XGK, which was lightweight, but was NOISY (like a jet engine) and could be adjusted to either OFF or INCINERATE. As an earlier model XGK it shared the light weight of its successors, but was not compact or easily stowed because it had an unflexible fuel pipe instead of a fuel hose. Those factors eventually made me sell it.

My second stove was a Coleman Exponent Apex II camp stove. This stove is quiet, compact, pretty lightweight, and simmers. But it's been 10 years or so and it now needs some maintenance parts, but Coleman doesn't make or sell them anymore. (That, by the way, is a real pisser, because I am the descendant of several generations of outdoorspeople who expected to inherit a Coleman product, maintain and use it for 50 years, and pass it down to their children for infinity.)

These experiences influenced my choice of a new camp stove. Simmering may not be for the real rugged types, but I need more versatility than just boiling water to reconstitute freeze-dried meals. Noise is something I want to escape from when I am enjoying nature, and I'd like to expect (although I'm often disappointed) that my fellow campers do too. Fuel source is another consideration: I was thinking of an ultralight bottled gas (as in not liquid) fuel stove, but just don't like the idea of all of those disposable cans tossed in a landfill (they aren't recyclable in my area, and I think I've heard about far distant lands that are littered with the things). I have also read that bottled gas stoves don't perform in cold or at altitude (although K2 is not in my immediate plans).

Before getting the Primus OmniLite, I considered a new MSR XGK. [[ASIN:B00G3PALBY MSR XGK EX Multi-Fuel Stove]] Cascade Designs (maker of the MSR XGK EX) is based in the Pacific Northwest and the MSR XGK EX is __ Made In The USA __ a BIG PLUS for me. Unlike my old version, reviewers say that the EX can burn at a simmer. But, many reviewers are suspicious of the XGK's plastic pump, and they also comment on how noisy the XGK still is ("jet engine" remains the theme).

A word on noisy stoves: For those who share my ethos about noise pollution, there is a product called QuietStove[[ASIN:B008129SEI QUIETSTOVE® SILENT MUTER DAMPER CAP for PRIMUS OMNIFUEL BACKPACKING CAMPING STOVE]] that probably does help a lot.

So, I opted for the Primus OmniLite, and since I might as well go all-in, I got the Ti version. This stove is light, portable, multi-fuel capable, reasonably quiet, simmers, and has a metal (mostly) pump. I have not yet taken it on a trip, but will update this review when I do. I did get the QuietStove module, which I will demonstrate on a video.

title: Poor design
text:
This is good example of why you can't rely on high reviews on Amazon alone. I consider myself a pretty durable sleeper; not overly picky or sensitive to sleep conditions. That said, this sleeping pad is next to worthless, especially if you are planning to camp on uneven/rocky ground. Its primary faults are that it is far too thin (about 1.5 inches when inflated), it is too small, and it slips around way too easily in the tent. With regards to thickness, if you sleep on your side, or if there are any rocks/pebbles under you, you will feel them digging into your hips. Compounding this problem is the fact that the pad is too small and too slippery, which makes keeping it positioned under the sleeping bag difficult throughout the night. It is CONSTANTLY shifting around.

Needless to say, it was definitely not worth the money for me. Do your research and don't just purchase the first well reviewed camping pad you run across on Amazon. A lot of them on here are designed similarly to this one. The good air pads are usually 3+ inches thick and quite a bit more expensive. Or, if you are just planning to camp a short distance from the car, go for a tried and true foam pad. They will be much more stable and provide more reliable padding.

text:

It's hard to explain, but it was basically wedged between the outer casing and the internal components, not just in the spool itself.

On the second one, the casting button was completely unseated on one side. The button has two small pegs which pivot inside of holes in the steel case. I had to take the bottom of the case off, bend the steel tabs that hold the pegs in place, reseat the button and bend the tabs back.

Both work great now and all the components seem pretty good, but this company has some serious quality control issues with assembly. It is pretty ridiculous that 2 out of 2 that I ordered were DOA, still sealed in the undamaged factory box. Luckily, I knew how to fix them, but most people who aren't mechanically inclined or perhaps know very little about reels would have had to return both of them. That is really unacceptable.

Still, they are great little reels now and they would be 5 star if not for the time I had to spend on fixing them. If you have some tools and are confident about taking things apart, I wouldn't hesitate to buy one. If not, well, you might be rolling the dice.

text:
A little background: I'm a righty, but due to disc-elbow problems (tennis elbow for disc golfers) I'm training my left arm to throw. The control issues are coming around, however so far I'm only getting about half the distance. When I started with the right arm years ago I noticed growth in the muscle over time as my distance improved. Hence my interest in this training device for the left arm. I want to quickly get back to the same success with the left arm.

I hooked this up to a couple of wall studs in my partially finished basement. After using it several times I can tell it's giving the arm a workout. I tried all three band combinations and can definitely tell the difference.

One concern is that the tension on the disc requires a very firm grip. Fortunately the device comes with a safety strap to keep the disc attached to your arm should your grip slip. My concern is that it might teach me to grip more firmly than needed on the course. I think I can adjust for that, so it may be a non-concern.

If you don't have something firm to attach to like a tree or a wall stud, the kit includes a piece to put into a door frame. A word of caution is to only use this from the side of the door where you would be pulling the door shut. You definitely don't want the door to open while you have the disc pulled back in full tension and have that door piece come flying at you.

My only complaint is that I found no instructions. It is possible that I overlooked them in the box and tossed them out. I was able to find what I needed in the Amazon description.

I'm betting that the next few weeks will see an improvement in my lefty distance!

I got these to replace the large oversized nail style stakes that I've been using for years. The big nails work, but they are sometimes difficult to insert and remove and are overkill for my needs.

For general use, I think these aluminum stakes are the perfect balance between the thin pin-like stakes that come with tents and the large nail stakes. The pack of 20 gives me enough for my 6 person tent and several spares.

I like the hexagonal shape of the stakes. I expect the size and hex shape will help prevent the stake from spinning around (a problem with the thin pin-like stakes). The shape of the hook itself should also prevent spinning.

I look forward to putting these in the dirt!

Update: After a weekend camping I think these are great for soft earth like in a campground or yard. In rocky ground I expect these will bend. For sandy ground I think I would want longer stakes.

But for normal earth these are great. They are better than the thin wire stakes that come with the tent, and yet small enough to store in the tent bag. I'm glad to have these.

title: Perfect for my go-bag.
text:
Fire starter is great. Whistle is great. Compass not so great.

This works as described for starting fires. The instructions are easy to follow. Scrape some magnesium onto your kindling. It takes a fair amount to get a big enough fire going, so keep scraping! Then quickly slide the striker along the rod to send sparks into the scrapings. I first did this with a paper towel so that I could see how much material was being scraped off. Due to the amount of scrapings needed, it might be best to buy magnesium shavings separately, but that adds bulk to your go bag.

Striking technique: I found that a motion similar to striking a match works best. I put the striker/scraper against the rod but pointed away from the kindling, with my thumb putting pressure on the striker. A flip of wrist slides the striker firmly against the rod and ends up pointing toward the kindling, sending sparks into your scrapings. This can be done without removing the striker from the lanyard.

The case serves as a handle for the magnesium rod, making it easier to hold onto while scraping and striking. The case protects the magnesium rod while not starting fires.

The case also has a small storage compartment that has a hinged rubber stopper/seal. There is no mention of this in the instructions nor on the item description. Another reviewer indicated that the compartment could hold wooden matches. I think that's a great idea. I tested with full-sized kitchen matches and found I could fit four, but only if I cut the matches to be a little shorter. Perhaps a better use of the compartment would be to store some magnesium shavings. It would at least be enough for one or two fires.

The whistle is loud and very high pitched. No doubt it will carry far in an emergency. It takes a little more effort than I expected. At first I thought it did not work. But then I really blew into it and sent a piercing note into the neighborhood.

Compass does not work well. I consider such glue-on compasses as gimmicks from the start and therefore no stars off. In this case the compass will not level itself to allow free spinning. If you fuss with it enough it may eventually point approximately north. It is better to invest in a quality compass.

title: A nice affordable small bag, but lacking usable pockets.
text:
My first bag, and I still use it. It holds ten discs easily, although more putters makes it tight (I carry two putters). It is great for those of us who don't want to carry more than 10 discs. The Midnight Blue color looks very nice. The small size of the bag means that it is prone to tipping over on uneven ground, but the discs usually stay put. Because of the lack of other pockets, I typically use the putter pocket for a towel.

The mesh pocket inside the top is unusable when not playing. The height of the discs makes it difficult to close the top, so anything stored in the top will interfere with closing. During play you leave the top unzipped, so you could keep a towel or marker disc in it during the game.

The bottle pocket holds a standard plastic water bottle, but anything bigger is very tight or too big. There is no tie for the beverage holder, so your bottle may fall out if the bag tips over.

Despite these drawbacks, I do recommend this bag for it's small size.

Dynamic Discs: If you come out with a redesign, I'd buy another if it has these improvements. Those of us who prefer to carry fewer discs still need some of the features found on larger bags.
- Ability to hold a larger water bottle would be nice.
- A full-width/full-height pocket for a towel and/or golden disc retriever on the back would be very nice.
- A marker disc pocket on the front of the putter pocket would be nice.
- A small pocket on the opposite end of the bottle holder would be nice.

title: Nice set, but not exactly for beginners
text:
Unless you know you want to start with a heavier set, consider finding a lighter weight set in the 140g-160g range. Most beginners will be better served by a lighter weight set until they learn to throw. That was (is) certainly true for me.

Excited to get started in disc golf, this 170g-ish set is the first set I purchased based on what I had read so far (and the value). After further reading, I also bought a lighter weight three-disc set from Latitude 64, and I'm glad I did. After a couple of months I'm barely starting to throw this heavier set reliably, yet I've bought more discs in the 150g-165g range to round out my "throwable" set. For now I'm doing best in that 150g-165g range, and the heavier fairway and distance drivers from this set are not yet in my bag. They say once you learn to throw the lighter discs, you will naturally move up to heavier discs.

Also, as a beginner you'll want to stick with the putter and midrange, and perhaps a fairway driver, so this five disc set is a little more advanced and may prove frustrating. The faster drivers are not effective until you learn the throwing techniques. I am barely able to effectively throw the distance driver in this heavier set, but I do pretty well with the lighter fairway driver in the lighter weight Latitude 64 set.

That said, these discs are great once you have gained the experience to throw them. The Judge putter (mine is 173g) has already become my go-to disc inside the circle. The Maverick was the disc used off the tee for my first birdie...in very windy conditions...and is earning it's place in my bag.

The Prime (DX) plastic is the least durable plastic used in the sport, but it is common in starter sets (and desired for putters due to grippy-not-slick feel). They will get dinged up when you hit trees (you will hit trees...sorry trees!). I've already started replacing discs in my lighter Latitude 64 set with the more durable Classic and Champion/Lucid plastics.

As for the colors, they do vary as indicated. I ended up with several pink disks. Pink is not my favorite color, but I'll take a visible pink disk over green or black any day. I typically buy yellow now. It's uncanny how effectively discs can hide in even moderate brush or in the dimming evening light. Until I can throw with reliable accuracy I'll pick colors I can find!

Enjoy the game...it's a lot of fun.

text:

It has two interior pockets (on opposite sides) for keys and such. I noticed that some tents have only one pocket, so that was a factor in my choice to not buy a different tent.

title: Great value rack
text:
Easy to use, easy to mount. The rack mounts firmly in the receiver (no wobble). I'm using a 1-1/4" receiver, but the rack comes with an adapter for 2" receivers.

Cons:
- When not carrying a bicycle, with the carrying arms folded down, the arms tend to rattle when driving. I was able to solve the problem by using a bungee cord to keep the arms from rattling. I simply wrapped the bungee around the arm-ends and one side of the center post, which is enough to hold the arms in place.
- Security. There are two places where a simple ratchet wrench is all that is needed to take the bikes, rack and all. The weakest link with this rack (perhaps all hitch-mount racks?) is the hitch-mount itself. The included hitch-pin requires a wrench, which is better than a pin alone. Also, the elbow that allows the hitch to pivot (for opening a hatchback or pickup bed) could be removed with a wrench. As a further deterrent, I use a long cable to secure the bikes and rack to my hitch bar. Unfortunately a cable is not much of a deterrent, but I think it's better than nothing.

That option does not work for my bike since the only handlebar space available is taken up by my headlight and bike computer. In comparison, the tail-light (at half-the-price of the front light!) comes with several mounting options. In fact, part of my solution for the headlight is an unused bracket that came with the tail light. Needless to say, I'm a little disappointed with CatEye for the lack of options. Otherwise I like the light.

title: While not perfect, this machine rocks enough for 5 stars...
text:
I've been using the total trainer for about 9 months now and I'm finally comfortable leaving my thoughts on it. Overall, I think this is the best value in a Total Gym type of machine and I would not hesitate to recommend it to others. I love mine.

---------------------------------------
Pros:
Huge glide board

Large range of resistance settings

Ability to add free weights

Comes with a curl bar (though I found it less than useful for actual curls) and other attachments that you may find useful.

Great price to performance ratio

Cons:
Some limitations for strength once you get into better shape, but with true, proper form which makes the exercises much harder and humbles guys who think they can really bench 260lbs because they hold the weight and move their arms 10 inches up and down 5 times in a row, this machine will last most average or out of shape people for quite a while.

The video that comes with it is pretty lame in my opinion, you're better off searching youtube for demonstrations of exercises on a Total Gym and doing those.
---------------------------------------

The machine can support up to 385lbs, so if you're 180lbs and add 100lbs of weights, you're still way under the limit. The maximum resistance levels are 69% without the glide board pulley engaged and 38% with. So technically, at 180lbs, the maximum resistance you're going to get is 106lbs and 193lbs. That sounds like a lot, but keep in mind that most of the common exercises seem to work better with the pulley engaged (and some would be impossible without it since the cable/rope is a fixed length and way too long to use without the pulley to take up the slack). For example, the instructions show you a way to kneel on the board, attach the mini-pulleys to the glide board and do a bicep curl with the curl bar. This is pretty unstable at resistance level 11 (the board wants to slide out from underneath you and you're really pulling yourself high into the air (I hit my head on my basement ceiling trying the exercise this way). While trying to keep the board from moving around underneath you is a decent way to work your core, it detracts from the exercise. I've found that bicep curls work best with the pulley engaged and the user hanging upside down, curling the fly handles up towards the chest (search [Total Gym upside down bicep curls] on youtube for an example). Still, for most people who are not in great shape, curling 106lbs isn't easy with good form (arms straight down at the sides on every rep reset, curl all the way up to the chest keeping the wrists straight and the elbows at the sides near the hip as much as possible). You could also invest in a weight vest to wear and increase the overall weight. Bayou Fitness could solve this issue by providing another, shorter cable that would allow certain exercises like the upside down bicep curl, chest fly, upright row and so on to be done without the middle glide board pulley being used.

Also, I'm not sure I'd bother with the squats on this machine, they don't allow you to have proper form because the glide board restricts movement (search [proper squat form] on youtube or Google to see what I mean). For some people the movement on this machine might not be a bad thing, but in my case, it causes pain in the knees whereas normal, proper form squats do not.

For those than cannot do a pull-up to save their lives, this machine can help with the large muscles involved (shoulders, biceps, triceps, upper back), but only actual pull-ups will work the stabilizer muscles. Still, if you're upper body is pretty weak or out of shape, this will get you more than 4/5 of the way there with the extra 100lbs (again, provided you use proper form and pull your elbows down towards your hips and keep your shoulders up and back and your head up during the exercise). Eventually, you'll need to start doing actual pull-ups to work the stabilizers and your core to get real results.

The instructions show a method of doing a bench press using the side pulley attachment points and thereby NOT using the middle pulley, which gives you a max resistance level of 69% of your body weight + 100lbs of plates on the bar attachment (this should be able to allow anyone up to about 230lbs to at least bench their own weight). However, the method they describe actually promotes improper form (but a slight adjustment will allow good form provided you aren't too wide). on a bench press, you want the bar to come down towards your nipple area, not your neck or collar bone (doesn't work the chest well and can produce injuries). Your elbows should be bent down towards your hips or sides. If you're willing you slide your body up on the board so that the side pulleys line up with your nipple area (which leaves your head hang off the board a bit and makes the cables come up underneath your armpit area but allows the proper motion for a bench press) you can get a decent bench. Two things with this. 1, don't wear loose shirts when doing this, they will get caught up in the pulley and 2, always keep the footboard attached for this exercise in case you cannot finish a rep, simply put your foot straight down to catch your body and there's no way for the bar to trap you or crush your chest. In essence, this allows you to bench as much as the machine will take without a spotter and without the same risk of injury that comes with lifting free weights on a bar (if you have good form otherwise you'll get injured even if you don't fail the lift). I do wish that the bar was wider for those of us with longer arms (closer grip stresses the triceps instead of the chest). There may be some ways around that last limitation, but I haven't found one that ensures that the cables will not slide on the bar that is also completely safe. zin theory, you could get a regular free weight bar and two 2.5lb slotted plates to thread the cable heads through so they don't move, but then you're adding 5lbs of weight plus a 25-45lb bar, which makes the exercise a bit more dangerous.

The few suggestions I'd make to Bayou Fitness would be a shorter cable to allow certain exercises to be done without the pulley, a wider curl bar to help isolate the chest when using that for benching and the ability to add more than 100lbs to the glide board weight bar. I'm not sure if the last one is possible (I'm assuming that the limitation is based on the strength of the bar and not the glide board), but the other two should be no problem. But overall, for most people looking to get into better shape, this machine and adherence to proper will get you there provided you put the time into it.

title: Not a bad machine, but easy to grow out of...
text: There's nothing inherently wrong with the machine itself, and if you're looking for a way to do circuit training (lower weight, higher reps, little to no rest in between sets) then this machine may last you a while. But without a way to add actual weight, strength training on this machine has a short lifespan. The resistance bands don't work well because they tend to pull the slider board out from underneath you rather than add resistance to the exercise. I guess if you were 300lbs it would stay put, but at 200 and 185lbs, I found it to be problematic. Still, for the $150 price tag, this is much better than any Total Gym knockoff that doesn't have provisions to add free weights in my opinion. I used this for about 9 months and then upgraded to a Bayou Fitness Total Trainer 4000 XL (a much better deal than comparable Total Gyms that have the ability to add free weights).

title: Great Power Tower for the money
text: It's hard to find something to say that hasn't already been said, but this is a solid piece of equipment if you're under 250lbs (the max weight that the 1700 can support). If you're less than 250lbs, then this is an ideal dip and pullup/chinup station. I'm 6'2" and 185lbs and it handles me fine. There is some flex/movement when doing pullups without proper form (erratic, swaying movement) and dips tend to flex the unit even with proper form (slow and controlled movement), but the overal the 1700 is still stable enough. I would suggest using the amount of movement or sway as an indicator of using proper form. If it's moving a lot, you're probably simply swinging yourself through the pulls and chins or dropping yourself down through the dips like a rock with no resistance (ignoring half of the exercise) without keeping yourself stable.

title: Very Good, but could be better for the old and the fat
text:
We took delivery three weeks ago. Relatively easy to set up, but be aware that the seat likes to slide to the end of the stops. Now that we are used to it, my wife and I use it every day, sometimes multiple times a day. We don't put it away, just leave it in place next to the wall, facing the TV.
My main issue is that it, like all the other rowers I've seen, sits too low for someone who (like me) is 76 and 250lbs, with bad knees. At first, I'd either fall the last three inches, hopefully onto the seat, or need some sort of support to get on and off. I solved that problem by wrapping an old belt around the body (see pic), which I could use as a grab bar to lower myself on and lift myself off. If Sunny would put a grab handle on the front, that would be a big help, and save on belts.
A secondary issue is the LCD display. Others have complained that it's not bright enough. The real problem is that it's at the wrong angle. I repurposed a chunk of plastic foam packing to lift the bottom enough to make it clearly visible when seated. Sunny could duplicate that with a simple folding frame.
I should also note that the labeling on the display is wrong. Label says: Time, Count, Total Count, Calories. Actual is: Time, Count, Calories, Total Count.
Finally, I note that almost all of the self-help videos on rowing emphasize managing your strokes per minute. The display doesn't show that. I'd be willing to give up both Total Count and Calories to get that in the display. After all, Total Count is only useful if you are the only person using the machine, and Calories are pretty much a meaningless guess without information like body weight.

title: We bought two
text:
It's not perfect, but it does the job. We liked it enough that we bought two, His and Hers.

Here's some hints on assembly:
1. Open the box from the top, using the 'this side up' arrrow as your guide. They have a clever trick to use the styrofoam packing as a frame to hold the bike during assembly, so you need to start out with the right relationship. At this point, you should Read The ....Friendly...Manual before you go off doing stuff.
2. The styrofoam is fragile. Be careful when you lift it off and put the bike body on it.
3. I found that it's more comfortable to work on the bottom assembly if you stack a couple of boards or bricks under the base end.
4. The first step has you trying to attach the base by screwing in four bolts and washers through four access holes in the plastic bottom. It's hard to see and hard to manipulate and the washers keep falling off. I solved that by removing the two middle pan head screws so that I could pull out the plastic bottom (which appears to be there just to keep out armadillos) and reach in to stabilize the screws as I put them in. If you wanted to, you could remove all five pan heads and not worry about bending the plastic bottom. When you are done, replace the pan head screws, and finish attaching the bottom cover by screwing in the final two pan heads next to the wheels.

It pedals very smoothly, and you feel like you are riding a unicycle. We have not had the pedal problems other have, but we don't use it that intensively. Like many other exercise bikes, it tones your legs, not your arms or upper body. You could carry weights in your hands, or you could just give up on that and read a book while you bike.

title: Fine bargain

title: YES!
text:
I get so many compliments on this chair! And I love it!

It is constructed very well. It supports my weight well (230 pounds...working on getting that down) and glides easily. I spent some time not realizing that the ball was not completely inflated, probably in fear that it would explode if I pumped too much more. Definitely follow the instructions for blowing it up - you have to let it sit for the night without 100% capacity - so don't buy this with the intention of using it the same day (this is true of any chair like this!) Don't skip that part! Then, when you finally do blow it up all the way, know that in a month or so you may want to blow it up further. When I refilled it, the ball didn't touch the group (even despite my weight!) and it changed where the back bolster hit me. When the ball was less full, the back bolster would hit me mid-back, which was comfortable but also allowed a lot of slouching, which was the main reason I bought this; to combat workplace slouching. Now the bolster hits me much lower and I am more in tune with my posture and less able to slouch.

In terms of aesthetics, I find that this chair is the best choice to use in a professional setting. Sure, it probably still makes me the "quirky" boss who does weird things like sit on a bouncy ball at work...but it also looks the most refined of all the exercise ball chair choices. I got the black ball and silverish-black metal for the most inconspicuous look as possible.

For a while, sitting in this chair would make me really sweaty in the pant area. But after a while, I got used to it and that stopped happening. Some people sell covers for that reason, but I found that the more used to the chair I got, the less sweaty I became in reaction.

Finally, I combat ADHD, and this chair is a fun way to get some energy out in order to "sit still" for longer periods. I try to make sure no one is watching or bounce discreetly. But it's super fun and helpful.

text:
I got two of the smaller size in the coffee color. I use it to pour and drink water out of throughout the day or sometimes to store food items in. title: Seams down the center/ Not 10 x 12
text: I can't imagine that this cushion was designed by anyone who meditates for long periods.  I suppose the first clue was how the description states that with this unique design you can sit on it sideways for more lift... as if they didn't already realize that monks and meditating enthusiasts have been doing that with the traditional round cushion forever.  But I figured perhaps they meant it gave more stability than the round cushion when turning it sideways or something.  The biggest issue is the large and rough seams in the middle from where the different colored strip on top meets the sides.  Those edges might not bother anyone who does short sits, but after a long day of sitting they can take their toll on the sit bones and buns.  They put more emphasis on making this cushion look "cool" with that colored strip rather than on function.  The felt material is interesting and is probably good for making sure you don't slide off the seat like some fabrics are prone to causing.  I thought this might make a good travel cushion because it's listed as 10" x 12", but my ruler measures it as larger.  So it's going back.

title: Longevity is questionable
text:
The first 2 weeks of use I loved this mat... but then I started to need a second mat to put on top of it. Many of the excercises I'm doing require that I stand on my knees and this mat provided great support... but after only a few days the imprint of my knees would stay on there longer and longer to the point where 24 hours later my knee prints are still there. Of coarse I move my knees around to different spots, but now my mat is full of knee prints. The mat gets thinner at these points and now my knee starts to hurt while I'm on the mat. I have to put an EXTRA mat on top of this one just so that it doesn't hurt now. I'm going to have to look for something sturdier that keeps it's thickness. In the meantime I've actually cut off the last 14" of the mat and use it to add extra cushioning for my knees while I'm using the mat. I'm short so I don't need the full length anyway.

I do think that this mat is great for yoga too and have had no problems doing so. However it's not good for a serious yoga practice because it's too thick and stretchy. For a casual practice it does fine.

title: hmmm.. not really gloves unless you're a guy maybe.
text:
So I returned the reebok 2lb wrist weights with the thumb hole because they were too big for my wrists. I then thought that perhaps weighted gloves would be better. Problem is that all the weighted gloves out there have their weight distributed only in the back of the hand. I liked that in the picture these looked like the weight wrapped around evenly on both the back and front of the hand.

Well, on me they are definitely more like wrist weights. They do not cover the bottom of my hand like in the picture, but rather go much lower onto my wrist. I think a person with larger hands would make the gloves go up higher towards the hands, but they would definitely need to make the thumb hole a little bigger. The thumb hole is fine for me, but if my thumbs were any larger they'd be a bit tight. Still they are better than the reebok ones and more attractive too so over all I am happy with the purchase. I weighed them and they are true to weight.

title: These are 1 lb weights not 2
text: When I put these on they felt really lightweight compared to our other 2 lb weights so I went ahead and weighed them along with another pair of 2 lb weights we had.  Our fears were confirmed.  These are 1lb each not 2lbs like the description says.  I'm not sure how much it's going to cost me to return them.

title: Great weights; DVD is a bit annoying
text: When looking for 2 lb weights I opted for these rather than more traditional weights because a) they looked like it would be possible to extend all the fingers while holding the weights if you want more length in the arm.  and b) They seemed to have the weight distributed evenly on both the palm side and the back side of the hand.  Previously, I thought weighted gloves were the answer, but they all have their weight on the back of the hand only, which exercises different muscles than if you were to have the weight mostly in the palm.  After trying out these weights I must say that I'm very happy.  These not only have even weight distribution on both sides of each hand, but you also have the option of letting go your grip and extending your fingers out fully while doing many exercises without worrying about the weights dropping.  The DVD has 3 15 minute workouts which are great for either a warm-up into a more lengthy workout, or for something quick in the morning to wake me up and get me going.  The only issue I have is the videography of the dvd.  The camera person apparently felt there was a need to switch camera angles every 5 seconds.  Very distracting. It wouldn't have bothered me as much if I was able to see the whole body of the instructor more often, but I've done the standing workout is the one I've done the most and often the video shoots the top half of her body without showing what she's doing with her legs... and switches to show her feet and not showing what she's doing with her arms!  I'm sure after I do it several more times I'll be able to just do the upper & lower half movements without needing to see her do them, but when you're first learning a movement is when it's most important to continually see it so that you're sure you get it right.  Especially if you're like me and don't get choreography down very quickly.  It would've been better if they just stuck to one or two camera angles and stayed there rather than switching constantly.

title: I have both the 1 and 2 lb versions.  2 lb version is too big.

But I may need to return them and get something else.  The 2lb pair is way too big and no matter how tight I try to wrap it around the placement of the velcro doesn't allow for a good fit and they wobble and shift too much during movement. I see others have mentioned the 2lb pair being too large for most women's wrists and I wish I had read them before purchasing. The 1 lb purple weights don't have this problem. 5 stars for the 1lb weights and only 2 stars for the 2 lb ones averages my rating to 3.

title: Tough and very well made
text:
I haven't had this gym duffel for very long, but since there aren't any reviews yet I figured I should offer one. This is the most money I've ever spent on a gym bag, but I took the plunge for various reasons. One being that my last two gym bags fell apart after a few years and this bag comes with a lifetime guarantee. And boy- after receiving it and feeling the nice thickness of the canvas and just how well made this thing is I must say that I definitely see this bag being able to go through hell and back for a lifetime without ever needing replacement.

Another reason I got it was for the separate base compartment in the bottom. I had a gym bag of lesser quality that had this and honestly I don't understand why more bags don't have it. It's a fantastic extra- because it keeps things completely separated from the rest of the bag. Some might say- Well, LOTS of bags have a separate compartment to put your shoes or whatever in... but I say no. Almost all bags their seperate compartments are designed in such a way that they actually take up space in the regular compartment of the bag. When you have a gym bag that has a pocket on the sides (like most do) once you fill it, the main compartment of the bag now has less space because the bulge is moving into the main compartment area. But bags with a base compartment like this one don't have this problem. You can fill the bottom compartment up without it getting in the way of anything you might have to reach for in the main compartment and without compromising any of its inside space. Really convenient. When I go to martial Arts class I can put my uniform and pads in the base compartment without ever having to deal with them throughout the day when I'm rummaging through the main compartment looking for basic things like my wallet etc. The full measurement of the bag is about 12" high/14"wide/11"deep (I did not have the bag filled up while measuring so my estimate might be slightly off) It has leather detailing on the handles for extra comfort. Duluth Pack has an even larger bag similar to this one made large enough to fit tall boots in the base compartment. I think it's called the Duluth boot duffel. That one was too large for my needs, but it might be ideal for those who need to carry more equipment.

Made in the USA... finally something NOT made in China. Excellent quality. Thick strong Zippers that do not look like they could ever break, that also zip easily. Comes with a lifetime guarantee.

title: LOVE LOVE LOVE
text:
I am SO HAPPY that they finally made a glass Camelbak!! I have it in blue but will be getting it in every color because I'm so excited they finally gave me what I wanted. For a couple of years now I had been using a kerplunk glass bottle and just placing the camelbak top/straw on it. But it didn't fit quite right. This bottle is great. There's no plasticy or metal taste to the water. Glass is the only material that doesn't leach a seperate taste to the water after it's been in there for a while. The only thing is that the straw is still plastic. I actually have some straws made out of glass that I sometimes use with the camelbaks, and they work, but again- there is a fit issue so I often can't use them. I wish camelbak would make a stainless steel version of their straw.

UPDATE/ March 2013: for those who are interested, I found a company that makes custom sized glass straws. It's called "GLASS DHARMA" and they have a website. If you order their "smoothie" sized straws and ask that they be custom cut to 7 & 3/8 inches, they will fit great with these camelbaks. I've been using their glass straws for years and they are really durable- last forever if you don't drop them on a hard floor (they are glass after-all), but this is the first time I realized they did custom sizes so I measured and ordered a couple and they fit/work great! Their straws come with a life-time guarantee. I even dropped my camelbak on the floor once and luckily it didn't break, but I lifted the lid and checked the glass straw to make sure it was fine- not a scratch. If you decide to use these you should wet the glass straw and inside of the camelbak lid before twisting the straw in- The lubrication will make it slide in without you having to worry about being too rough. The straws hold up perfectly inside these camelbaks. (Oh- and since they are glass I wouldn't use them in bottles that you use for sports activities or anything like that.) They look cooler than the plastic straws too because you can see the cloudy white plastic straw through the bottle vs the crystal-clear glass straw that matches better with the bottle (and the water).

I still use the plastic straw when I leave the house so that I don't have to worry about breakage during transport etc... but when I drink indoors (which is 99% of the time for me) I use these glass straws instead. The plastic straw is ok- unlike when I use plastic bottles which give off a plasticy taste almost immediately- the straw only seems to leech a plasticy taste if it's been sitting in the water for a couple of days or more... but Still I like to avoid plastic whenever possible and if you are like me you might appreciate this alternative too.

title: Favorite size

title: Good purchase- needs better directions
text: I've never needed directions for a carry-on before, but I did here.  I couldn't figure out how to remove the harness in the bag until I found the directions in the bag.  But the directions don't show you how to fold up the harness again so that it's nice and flat in the back pocket.  Also I was hoping there was an option to remove the belt harness without removing the backpack straps in case you only want to use those and not have the unused belt harness flopping around, but I haven't figured out yet if that's even possible.  Maybe it's because I've never had one of these types of luggage before, but it hasn't been easy for me to figure out. It's also not the lightest bag.  According to my luggage scale, completely empty this weighs about 8 and 1/2 lbs.  That means it weighs more than my largest peice of checked baggage luggage that is 30" upright.  What I like the least about the bag aside from it's not being easy for me to figure out the harness is that there doesn't seem to be an option for putting away all the loose straps and buckles.  There are buckles and straps on various places on the outside and if I don't need to use them then I have no choice but to leave them open flopping around outside. wish they had more colors.  For example on the picture you can see there are 4 buckles on the outside which  gives more compression to an over filled bag.  If you're on a short trip and you don't want to use the small backpack and don't need compression, you still have to snap on all the buckles unless you want them flopping around when you walk.  This means that this isn't a bag that you can constantly open and close to get things out if you need to- unless you want to go through the hassle of zippering AND clipping 4 buckles every time you close and unzippering and unclipping 4 seperate buckles every time you open. text:

As you can see from the photo the lower half of the tent is just the regular tent fabric and the amount of light is very obvious, and this is in a dim basement. With that said, I can easily see having the upper portion dark could really help with people like me who love to camp but struggle with the amount of daylight that comes through in very early morning or at nap time, but it is NOT full dark room tech.

I am also very concerned about the "hub" connection at the top; maybe a great idea but seems very fragile to me. I think they would have been better off using decent, stronger poles, and keeping it a regular dome tent set up, which is a super easy style tent to set up. The poles seem weak. title: Nice size U Lock for my needs, but problems with the cylinder on the lock I received.
text:
This lock is exactly what I need, but the lock I received from Amazon today had a cylinder that operates very difficultly. Kryptonite says the lock is a new design, and I wonder if they have all the bugs out yet. At one point the key would only go in half-way and I could see that the back layers of the cylinder were out of line with the outer layers. I don't know how many layers there are, but since the key would only go in half-way there was no way to turn the back layers so they would line up with the outer layers. Finally, after turning the key back and forth very gently for about ten minutes the layers lined up and the key would go in all the way. Unfortunately, the key continued to meet resistance as it turned in the cylinder and I had to ask Amazon for a replacement.

I would not trust the lock I received to operate properly away from home. I have several other Kryptonite locks and the keys all turn very freely in the cylinders. I wonder if I got a bad lock or if Kryptonite is going to have problems with this new design.

Update:

Looking at the lock further, I realized the black housing that rotates to cover the keyhole was also operating very difficultly. As I tuned the housing I saw fibrous plastic shavings visible under the edge of the housing around the keyhole. I removed several shavings with tweezers, and as I turned the cover back and forth more shavings worked their way out around the keyhole. As I pulled them out the keyhole cover began to rotate more easily. All of the shavings in the attached photo came from under the keyhole cover of the lock! If any of the shavings found their way down into the cylinder while the lock was being assembled, or when it was bounced around during shipping, that could explain why the cylinder is difficult to turn and the layers of the cylinder sometimes get out of line with each other as the key is inserted or removed from the lock.

Further Update:

Today, while waiting for Amazon's replacement lock to arrive, I looked again at the lock. Looking at the keyhole with a strong flashlight it appears the design of the metal body of the lock includes a narrow split that extends from the keyhole toward the black plastic end of the lock. I can't see how far the split extends, but I can guess that if it has sharp edges, and if the rotating black keyhole cover is shaped too tightly around the lock body, or if the keyhole cover has an uneven underside, the action of rotating the cover back and forth to uncover and recover the keyhole could actually cause the sharp edges of the split in the lock body to make the shavings I found. If any of the shavings work their way into the cylinder that, in turn, could cause the difficult cylinder operation I encountered.

Final Update:

One comment asked if the replacement lock had the same problem - it did not! I am happy with the replacement lock and so far it has worked fine.

title: A great, lightweight tire
text:
I recently bought a new Specialized Sirrus hybrid bicycle. Toady I swapped out the OEM tires and tubes for Clement Cycling Strada LGG 120 TPI 700cx28 clincher tires and Continental MTB/Race 28 700x25-32 tubes with 60mm Presta valves. The LGG tires weigh 233g each (my actual measurements), compared to 478g for the stock Espoir Sport Reflect 700x30c tires. The width of the LGG's on the stock 26mm (outside width) rims is 29.8mm, compared to 32.4mm for the stock tires. The Conti tubes weigh 140g, compared to 154g for the stock tubes. The overall weight savings was a surprising 259g, or 9.14oz, for each wheel.

Riding at the same tire pressure, 70 lbs front and 75 lbs back, the LGG tires had much quicker handling and the ride felt more cushioned. The more cushioned ride may be due to the heavy, relatively stiff carcass on the stock tires compared to the very lightweight and flexible sidewalls on the LGGs.

title: Great lock, and great service from Kryptonite
text:
My experience with Kryptonite goes back to the period when one of their their original locks was found to be easily opened with a ballpoint pen. I had registered two of their motorcycle disc locks at that time and as soon as they changed the design they sent me two new replacement locks. Since then I have become older and moved from motorcycles to bicycles.

I previously submitted a review of the very excellent Saris Bike Porter 2-Bike Trunk Rack, which has design features that enable bikes to be securely locked to the rack and also allow the rack to be locked to the frame of my car, under the rear bumper. Kryptonite's 2.25' New York Noose is just the right length to lock the top tubes of two bikes to the beefy upper section of the Saris rack with their Evolution Series 4 Disc Lock, and their KryptoFlex 3/8" x 7' Double Loop Security Cable is perfect to go through the front wheels of both bikes and lock the bottom frame of the rack to the frame of my car with one of the replacement locks they sent me many years ago, which is similar to their current KryptoLok Series 2 Disc Lock. Both of these Kryptonite locks, and the chain and cable, work perfectly and I have never encountered any problems with them.

We don't need this level of security for most of our bicycle outings, but when we head out for a vacation with our bikes that includes stays at multiple motels we always use our Kryptonite locks and chains.

One final note - Although I am sure no one else at Amazon would make this foolish mistake, when we left our B&B to head home from our last vacation I locked up the bikes and then left my cord with the keys to both locks draped over one of the handle bars while I checked the pressure on our car tires for the trip home. Of course I forgot about the keys and did not notice they were missing until we got home and tried to take our bikes off the rack. Luckily I was able to go into our house and get the spare keys that came with the locks. When I ordered replacements from Kryptonite they sent me new keys for both locks at no charge. Kryptonite provides excellent locks and they also provide excellent customer service!

title: First Fitbit worked great for two charging cycles - about eight days!  Replacement unit works fine
text:
We bought this Fitbit Flex for my wife. It worked great through two charging cycles and then went dead, refusing to take another charge. This must happen a lot, since Fitbit has a Web page devoted to suggesting ways people might get their Fitbits to charge - they say it could be a bad charging cable, a defective charging base, or that the Fitbit itself will not accept a charge. Since it is estimated Fitbit sells over 2 million activity trackers per year you'd think they could figure out how to make a unit that works reliably. Fortunately, Amazon Prime has accepted our return and will be sending us a new unit.

Our two star rating is based on five stars for eight days and zero stars after that.

During my wife's brief time with the Fibit on her wrist she learned two good hints for hopeful overachievers - if you vacuum a lot, or if you teach and write on a chalk board, Fitbit will give you credit for walking many extra steps! I imagine orchestra conductors also get incredible scores.

Update - July 7, 2015

We returned the first Fitbit using Amazon Prime's excellent return policy. We ordered a replacement unit and so far the new unit has worked perfectly! I am increasing our rating to four stars. The current unit merits five stars, but I am sticking with four stars since we had a bad experience with the first unit, which indicates some percentage of purchasers may encounter problems with their initial Fitbits.

title: DO NOT BUY. CAUSES ARTHRITIS-LIKE WRIST PAIN.
text:
Original review from Nov or Dec 2015: Fitbit, my relationship with you was ruined by the zip's disapproval of my sloth-like lifestyle. The frowny faces on days I considered "high effort" were judgmental and discouraging. So, when my APNP recommended buying a Fitbit to track sleep duration/quality, I was skeptical but compliant. I was hopeful that it would provide evidence of my lack of ability to sleep. So, I purchased the Surge, which looks like a monstrous thing on my bony little wrist. For some reason, everyone thinks it is an Apple Watch. I suppose my talking to it as if it had Siri probably is part of that. Also, it lights up in the dark randomly sometimes. I think it means to do that when you lift it up to look at it but doesn't always light up when you'd think it would.

The very first day, I had to work a table at a show and got badges for effort. I felt very accomplished but moreso, I felt tired and in need of caffeine because exercise is not my thing. So imagine my surprise when the very first night, it registered screen time as sleep time. So the very meager hours I obtained appeared to be a full night's rest with one time of being awake for 20 minutes (when I went upstairs to get ready for bed). The second day was a little off as well but the Surge quickly learned. And despite accidentally whacking it against a rock at the show, not even a scratch showed up. I am impressed by its hardiness. It also has gotten wet while sweating or washing my hands and still works great, though I haven't worn it during anything like swimming or showering.

Anyway, back to data--I started using the Excel data exports on the Fitbit site and comparing it to the data I log by hand. It is now one month later and the Fitbit has become more accurate but is still not perfect. Although, to be fair, I mostly just dislike it for how it tracks the exact times I sleep and wake up, thus evidencing how often I am late for work. But that's why I bought it so I can't be too uptight about that.

So right now, I am running my own self-study on my sleeping habits to provide to my prescriber. I compare their data to the medication dosages taken, exercise, diet, etc and provide to my doctor the raw data and summaries. This affords her greater insight to change my meds accordingly. I do wish it would sync better with my chart (right now I insert the data manually from their version to the one I use) and that they would offer the options to present data in hours+minutes rather than just hours. I also wish it would offer an easy way to track heart rate patterns over long lengths of time. But I'm glad for having this data, since it helps me to improve my sleep habits and med adjustments.

I don't like is how bulky it is. It's uncomfortable to even sleep on my side such that that wrist would be under the pillow but since I use it specifically for sleep, I need to wear it all night. I also wish there was a way to charge it without taking it off. It's also strange that there doesn't seem to be a very effective way of knowing who of my Facebook Friends also has Fitbit. Right now I have maybe 10 Fitbit friends and I am the biggest sloth of all of us since I am a counselor and most of my job is sedentary. That's discouraging for the competitions and such. I need more friends who slack at exercise at my level so we can have equally matched competitions. Then I might actually start liking the exercise parts of this. Although I giggle that sometimes I can get casenoting to improve my step count since it is on my wrist.

The floors climbed thing. No. You have to increase by 10 ft of altitude or whatever to get it to count. At minimum, I have to climb one full floor of stairs per day to get to my bed. Does it count? Not reliably. Yet it seems to sometimes count when I'm driving in a hilly area, oddly enough. And as for the whole exercise activities thing, nothing to comment since I gave up the gym membership a year ago and my exercise is mostly just walking, chores, etc.

The alarms and notifications. Okay, I love that phone calls make it vibrate. I ignore my phone and always miss calls. Everything lives on silent due to work. This way I can "check my phone" during a client session without seeming obnoxious. I just wish it would display the messages of a text rather than simply that I received a text. Also, I don't like that you have to adjust the alarms via the app or Fitbit web site rather than the watch itself. And I wish you could change the intensity of the vibration. The X you have to hit on the screen to get it to stop is so tiny that if I had a stronger vibration, I would actually wake up rather than silencing all of my other 6 alarms in my sleep (I have problems, I know). That would also help my clients with hearing impairments. Also, the buttons should seem simple but are not always super intuitive. But watches aren't my thing either, so take that with a grain of salt.

Lastly, the battery life is not as long as advertised. It seems to last a couple of days. I've always had trouble with Fitbit batteries though. My Zip eats them like me with Reese's Pieces. At least the Surge is rechargeable, unlike the Zip.

The band is okay but very bulky and not super comfortable. I wish it was more customizable.

In conclusion, it's 4 stars because it is still pretty awesome, probably even moreso if you're not as lazy as me. You don't buy this because you want a smart watch. You buy it in the name of pretending you care about fitness. But it still takes up your wrist space and if it comes down to this or other smart watches, unless you really need the fitnessy stuff, you can do better. [Unless, for the non-fitness people, you are the curmudgeon type like me who says "why buy a watch for what my phone can do?" In that case, don't buy a watch. You already have a phone that can do amazing things. And if you don't, you probably know how to do things like entertain yourself without technological reliance.]

It loses one star because of its bulkiness, lack of ability to do things other watches at equal/lower prices can do (both smart and non-smart, such as the vibration levels), and non-intuitiveness. But still a solid device with as many bells and whistles as you'll get out of a Fitbit device.

*****UPDATE FEB 2016: I am downgrading this to 1 star. Not only is the thing bulky and inaccurate, it also is actually causing me arthritis-like pain on whichever wrist it was worn. I've tried loosening and tightening the strap, changing wrist placement, and several other changes and the watch is just horrible. After a couple of days without wearing it, my wrists feel healthy again. I'm not alone in this either; google it. Lots of other people are having the same issue with it causing significant pain. I wish I could return it for a full refund.
