title: Proprietary charging cable; useless if you wear glasses; annoying to others
text:
I've had this for a couple of months, but just used it for the first time this past weekend while camping with friends. I will never use it for that again.

A) The wide angle sounds like a good thing, but it was really annoying to my friends. I had to keep the headlamp at the lowest possible brightness, and even then the light shining so wide was still annoying to everyone around me.

B) The led strip is very thin, resulting in the light source being behind the plane of my glasses. So much light was reflecting off the lenses of my glasses back into my eyes that I truly couldn't see much of anything in front of me. There's no point lighting a path if I still can't actually see the path.

Also, this headlamp has a proprietary charger. So you have to keep that specific single-use cable with you in order to recharge the batteries. And the batteries drain even when not in use. I charged it fully when I first got it a couple of months ago. Fortunately I tested it before my camping trip and discovered it was completely drained. So you can't just charge it and expect it to be ready when you need it. I had to fully charge it just before I left.

It is really very bright, so if you need something really bright, and you don't have glasses, and there's no one else around you who might be blinded by your headlight, then it might be an ok choice for you. But with so very many options out there, I recommend you keep looking. There are definitely better choices than this.

title: Incredibly bright, fantastic customer service, reflective material may separate
text:
First off, these are by far the brightest reflective anything I've ever bought, and I've bought >20 wrist bands, arm bands, leg bands, vests, .... Photons apparently hate this material: every single photon that hits it immediately turns right around and heads back where it came from. You will be seen when you're wearing these. They're so bright you may be seen from space. :)

Second, customer service can't be beat. I ordered both the the wrist bands and the leg bands, but only received the wrist bands. I contacted the vendor, Mark, and he sent the leg bands out within 12 hours of receiving my email. Later I had a problem with the reflective material separating from the neoprene on one one of the wrist bands, and Mark didn't just replace the one that failed, he sent me a whole new pair, and very quickly. So this is a low-risk purchase: if you have any issues, Mark will make it right for you.

One thing I'm not fond of is that the hook portion of the hook and loop closure is too long. Unless the band fits perfectly around your leg, a good sized section of the hook portion will be exposed, and can snag on cyclists' lycra gear. I wish the hook portion was just an inch long. The 3" loop portion would still allow a couple of inches of flexibility re length.

Also, I'm not sure why these have both extra long hook and loop closures and are made of stretchy neoprene. Both seem intended to allow the band to fit different diameters of legs + clothing, so I'm not sure why you need both. And the stretchy neoprene makes it much more likely that the relatively delicate reflective material will separate from it, as happened with 1 of the 4 bands I originally purchased. I'd prefer the fabric to not stretch to minimize the risk of failure, and just use the velcro to adjust the length. But since Mark backs up the product if it fails, this is a small deal.

Overall, I'm happy with these. I believe they're the brightest reflective bands you can buy, so if you want to be seen, these will do the job.

title: Great board, but doesn't twist
text:
I've had this board a few weeks now, and I really enjoy it. I use my standing desk so much more now because the motion this board allows is actually fun. The board is very sturdy and mostly stays in place pretty well.

I have two complaints:

1. The surface is hard, so my feet get sore after standing on it for more than 30-45 minutes. I just ordered a small anti-fatigue standing mat that I'll have to cut to fit this board - maybe that will help. But I wish this board came with the option of a correctly-sized cushioned mat. If my feet weren't in pain, I'd probably stand on this more than half time, if not full time.

2. The description says "Stand Still | gently rock, tip, twist | aggressively balance, move & surf". I bought this model specifically because it said "twist". But it doesn't twist. The bottom of the ball is grippy rubber with knobs that make it even grippier, especially on the thin commercial carpet typically found in offices. The grippy rubber knobs are good for keeping it in place, but they completely prevent the board from twisting. You can force it to twist a little bit if you need to move it 1/2" forward or back, but you can not absent-mindedly twist while you're working. Also, while technically you can tip / rock forward and back, really the only motion that's at all natural is rocking side to side. It's really good for rocking side to side. Any other motion requires enough effort to make it a distraction from working.

I'll keep this, because I really do enjoy the motion, and this is a very high quality board for this price point. But I'll probably also order a Fluidstance board because I really want the twisting motion, and I need a higher weight limit, so I'll end up ordering their top-of-the-line, which is ~4.5 times the price of this board. Alas. If only this board actually twisted....

title: Very light weight, no added bulk, very strong, good pockets
text:
I love this backpack! I commute by bike, and I wear those ridiculous spandex biking togs to keep cool whilst riding and not get my work clothes sweaty. Rather than packing a change of clothes every day, I take a week's worth of clothes in on Mondays. I like having the clothes in a backpack to I can easily take them to the restroom in the mornings to change, and keep the rest of them out of sight during the day. I was using a regular backpack, but that added weight, which is not great for biking, and it added bulk, meaning it was hard to fit everything in my pannier - I had to really stuff it in there and struggle a bit to fasten down the pannier's straps.

I bought this backpack in the hopes it would contain my clothes without excess weight or bulk. It's perfect! I have the 33L (largest) size, and it easily holds: 1 pair of (large) jeans, 5 shirts, 5 pairs of underwear, a couple of bras, a few pairs of socks, a microfiber washcloth and a small pack towel, with a bit of room to spare. It weighs virtually nothing, and adds almost no bulk, so now a week's worth of clothes fits easily in my pannier and doesn't weigh my bike down any more than absolutely necessary.

Since I have it at work anyway, I've used it to transport my laptop and other items, and it's plenty strong enough, and has enough useful pockets, to be an everyday backpack. My only small complaint would be that it lacks any structure. But that is, of course, by design, as it's meant to be folded up into a small package when not in use. But I never fold it up because I use it almost every day.

This was a great purchase. Very good value, high quality product, perfect for my needs.

title: Useless - don't fit Shimano Ultegra or PD-R550 pedals
text:
I have the [[ASIN:B00CTSKW3G Shimano SPD-SL Road Bicycle Pedals - PD-R550 (Black)]] on my e-bike, and the [[ASIN:B00CTSJZFC Shimano 6800 Ultegra Clipless Pedals]] on my road bike, both SPD-SL pedals. These Thinvik SPD-SL adapters didn't come close to fitting the Ultegra pedals. They at least came close to fitting the PD-R550's, but I pushed as hard as I dared and could not get them to engage. It's possible that if I pushed really, really, really, really hard I might be able to force them into the pedals, but I was afraid to push any harder for fear I'd literally never get them out.

It's too late to return these, but I ended up buying the [[ASIN:B07DL52T7J Acacia Bike Pedal Clip Platform Adapter For Clipless Pedals Shimano SPD LOOK KEO (SPD, NOEMAL)]] adapters. The Acacia adapters fit perfectly in both pedals, and require just the right amount pull to come out of both pedals. The Acacia adapters are the winners. These Thinvik adapters are useless.

title: Very light and easy to use
text:
I commute by bike, and I have to carry my bike up and down a flight of stairs 5 days a week. My bike is an e-bike that weighs 50 lbs without any gear attached. After adding a rack, trunk bag, lights, etc., it's probably up to 60 lbs. The bike is fairly expensive, and I work on a university campus, so I need a lock I can rely on. I originally purchased the [[ASIN:B005VMO49U Abus Bordo GRANIT X Plus 6500/85cm (33.46 in) black - Folding lock, Bike lock, Security level 15]] because of it's high security rating. But it's SO HEAVY!!! It's almost 5 lbs., which means it adds 10% to the weight of my already very heavy bike. Hauling my bike PLUS that lock up and down the stairs was just too much.

Now I have this lock. I love this lock! It's so light! It barely adds any weight to bike. It's also easy to lock. I like that I can remove the barrel, position the lock, and then replace and lock the barrel without the key. The security rating on this isn't as high as the ABUS, but I see so few of these in the wild that I don't think your average bike thieves are prepared to break this lock. At least I hope not.

As an added bonus, my e-bike has a cage mount on it's battery, and that's where I've attached this lock. So when I remove the battery to charge it, this lock serves as a very welcome handle for the rather heavy battery. :)

As far as I know, no one's tried to break my lock yet, so I can't say for certain how secure it is. But it has a good rating, it feels secure, and it's light and easy to use. So I'm happy.

title: No attachment points, no pockets, does not fit most racks
text:
These are nice looking and well constructed panniers. However, they have a few issues that leave me not fully satisfied.

First, there is not a single hook, loop, strap, or D ring for you to attach anything to. No place to attach a reflector or a tail light, no place to attach bungees, nothing. Seriously? Has whoever designed these every ridden a bike? There's always something you want to attach somewhere. How hard is it to add a few strategically placed D rings and maybe a strap for a clip-on light?

Second, other than the very flat zippered pocket on the top flap, there is not a divider or a pocket anywhere, inside or out. Everything you put in this pannier is just bouncing around with everything else in there. I like to keep my tools, my spare inner tube, a rag, a few wipes and a few zip ties with me at all times. I'd like to keep all these supplies in a pocket separate from my groceries, laptop, .... But no. There's not a pocket anywhere for a road kit. I had to buy ditty bags and put my emergency kit in those, and toss those in the bottom of these bags, where they continue to bounce around with everything else. But at least they bounce around together.

Third, I find these bags unnecessarily difficult to close. There's a bit of elastic at the back of the cover, near the rack, that does not glide smoothly over the body of the bag. Every single time I close these bags, I have to grab the elastic on both sides and pull it into place for a snug fit. It does make the bag look nice and neat when closed, and maybe it helps keep rain out. But it's annoying that I can't just flip the flap over and close the bag. Also, the clips that hold the top flap down are surprisingly finicky. I'm not sure why, but I have to slide the tab into the clip exactly parallel or it won't go in.

Fourth, the bags do not collapse when empty.They ship flat, and I assumed that I could collapse them at least a little bit when they're empty. But no. They ship with rigid pieces of plastic that you slide into very snug slots to give them structure and shape. You do not want to remove these every time you empty the bag and reinsert them when you load the bag. And even if you did remove them, the bag would just flop around loosely - you can't cinch it so it's smaller. So these bags are always the same (generous) size no matter how much or how little you have in them.

Finally, the bag claims to fit most racks. IT DOES NOT. The clips on top probably do fit over a variety of sizes of rack tubes. And the tab that releases the top clips is a really nice touch, and works well. The problem is the bottom clip, the one that keeps the bag from flapping around when you turn. It is a fixed distance from the top clips, and the distance is very short! I saw that before I purchased these, but I thought I'd be able to rotate the clip so it could grab on to one of the tubes going down to the bottom of my rack. WRONG. That clip does not move up or down, and it does not rotate - you can only slide it left and right. So if the bottom tube of your rack isn't exactly 7" from the top tube, the bottom clip won't connect. I had to remove the bottom clip, flip it upside down, then use a 10" bungee to stretch between the bottom tube of my rack and the inverted clip on this bag. It's a reasonably snug fit and it works well enough. But, contrary to its claims, this bag did not fit my rack - I had to jerry-rig it.

I'm keeping the bags, because I do like the quick on-and-off feature. And they're good sized, and they look sharp. But with a few tweaks to the design they could've been perfect. They're not.

title: Good light
text:
I commute by bike and I'm obsessed with seeing and being seen at night. I have a 650 lumen TerraLUX TT-5 flashlight (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009WFA4KU/) strapped to my handlebars as my primary light. I added this helmet-mounted light set as redundancy / extra security. I've had it about a month now.

This is a pretty good light. It's fairly bright, and I like that it has amber LED's on both sides of both the front and rear light. This makes you visible from any angle (hence the "360" in the name). Having gotten used to the blinding, virtual daylight of the 650 lumen flashlight on my handlebars, the 250 lumens that this light puts out on max doesn't seem quite bright enough to me. But I could get home safely with this alone if my flashlight were to fail, so it's bright enough.

Things I like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) You can aim the light wherever you need it. It's handy for checking out turns before you've made the turn. And I can now see the display from my bike computer without having to wait for a streetlight! And when I'm off my bike, I can see my lock, into my trunk bag, etc.
2) They increase visibility and therefore safety.
3) You'll probably leave them mounted to your helmet most of the time, so you're less likely to forget them. And if you're locking your bike up somewhere you'll probably take your helmet with you, so you'll automatically take your lights too - less chance of theft.

Things I like about this light in particular:
1) It's one of the brighter ones available.
2) It actively aims LED's in every direction, making you highly visible.
3) It's rechargeable and charges via USB.

Things I don't like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) They add weight to your head / neck.
2) They can get knocked around. I take my bike on the train for a portion of my commute, and when we near my stop I have my helmet on and am ready to get my bike out of the rack to disembark; meanwhile other riders are trying to get to their bikes. I frequently bang one or the other of the lights on the overhand above the bikes while we're all jostling around. Also, when I take my helmet off I feel I have to be more careful about stowing it so the lights don't get knocked about.

Things I don't like about this light in particular:
1) It's surprisingly heavy, and it's unbalanced. The front light is virtually weightless. The rear light, which has the battery pack, is surprisingly heavy. I invested in a very nice, "barely there" helmet that weighs virtually nothing. This light makes it feel like a brick. Obviously it's not that heavy, but it is heavier than I expected. And I don't like that all the weight is to the rear. This is okay when I'm leaning forward in riding position, but when I'm stopped at a light or otherwise upright, the weight is pulling my head back.
2) I find the rubberized button to turn it on / change modes difficult to feel and manipulate while I'm riding. If I don't take the train home, my commute is an hour and 15 minutes. To save battery I have it on low when I'm riding on well-lit streets and switch to high otherwise. I've had this light almost a month and I'm not getting better at feeling / adjusting the light. It takes concentration away from riding while I fiddle with it.
3) The tail light mode is not adjustable. It does this odd, slow fade-in / fade-out and that's it. You can't make it be always on, and you can't make it actually flash.
4) You can't have just the taillight on. Once the headlight's on, you can turn the taillight off independently, but you can't ride with just the taillight.
5) The battery is not replaceable. My flashlight / headlight runs on a replaceable, rechargeable battery, which means I can keep a spare battery in my pouch and be sure I have enough battery to get home. I can also ride with one battery while the other's at home recharging. With this light, if the battery runs out you can't use the light until you get to a USB charger. And it takes a good few hours to recharge, so you can't go riding for the hours it takes to recharge. And the low battery indicator is tucked away at the bottom of the taillight, and is only visible after you've plugged it in to recharge, so that doesn't help. So you'd better keep it charged.
6) You can change the angle of the front light, but only in discrete clicks. Each click is a very small angle of change on the device, but changes where the light hits the road by about 20'. I frequently want the light right in between two of the clicks and I can't put it there.
7) The helmet mounts strike me as odd. The front light slides into it's mount and clicks in place, but it slides in from the bottom. That means the if the clicky thing ever fails the light will slide out. If it slid in from the top gravity would keep it in place. And the rear light presses on with four tabs clicking into four slots. You really have to pull on it to dismount it. Odd.

Hmmm. Looking at this review there are way more things in the "don't like about this light" section than elsewhere, which makes it seem like I don't like this light. That's not true. None of the "don't likes" are show-stoppers. I'm keeping the light and I do like it. They're mostly just areas where I feel like the light could be somewhat better. If you buy this light you'll definitely be seen, you'll see where you're going, and you'll probably be happy you have it. These are just my observations for whatever they may be worth to you.

title: Not good, sending back
text:
Not good. The actual wheel is held on the Axis by two tabs with hex screws - but no other guidance, and no securing of the screw. The wheel will become wiggly as the tabs will shift. To make matters worse there is no form of bearing on the wheel, it's just plastic and it will become even more wiggly as that wears out.

What is worse is that the hand/foot pedals are also secured with single hex screws, but those sit in plastic. I couldn't even tighten both of them without overtightening one. There is nothing that helps both pedals stay in the same position horizontally or rotation-wise except these otherwise unsecured hex screws.

The outside of the wheel is made to look like it is a rubber tire. But it is simple hard plastic. You will not be able to use this on hardwood floor without damaging the floor, and it will slide on all hard floors.

MATERIALS: The mesh top combined with moisture-wicking material of the hat's construction makes this a must-have gear for my Texas summer running season, where pouring water on one's head is necessary.

WICKING: It does soak up some head sweat, but won't 100% eliminate the need for a headband or vaseline for humid days if you sweat a lot. The hat also dries out very quickly. I hang it on a wall in my garage, fully-saturated in sweat + drinking water and it's always dry in 12-24 hours for my next run.

POCKET: it's small and I haven't used it yet but perfect size for a key fob or even a small gel.

CONS:
WHITE/VIBRANT ORANGE: if you sweat profusely like me, the orange piping will bleed a little on this hat. Not obnoxious enough to be an issue for me, but for those that are OCD about that kinda thing, it's worth noting.

STYLE: I have a large head (7 3/8), so unstructured hats look much better on me than taller sitting hats. That said, this hat is extremely unstructured, by nature, and is not going to win any fashion awards for most head shapes. It's got a distinct "this has a very specific function" style.

title: Not for two similar sized bikes
text:
I have no one to blame but myself for trusting this rack would be suitable.
As others have noted, the single post with two locking hook design makes it very very difficult to mount two same frame height bikes simultaneously. But what's worse is that there's no easy way to load the bikes on the rack! If the locking post is upright, then the hook gets in the way of the bike. If the post is lying flat, then once you've put your bikes on there is no way to raise the post without removing the hooks first. Also, you can't keep the bike standing upright while moving the post, because the tire obstructs the locking hook, so you need to be prepared to have the bike lean on your car trunk. What a design disaster.
Make sure to try the rack before you buy. None of the youtube videos will point out these issues. And those guys showing how they easily get their ebikes on the rack? Good luck with that. You'll need to be in pretty good shape to do that heavy lifting.

title: An added layer of safety, but only to a degree.
text:
I like these mirrors, I typically ride against traffic, as it's easier to keep a lookout for drivers. The thing is, when someone is coming, I have to look over and see what the other lane is doing. That isn't always comfy, and I sometimes don't feel safe having to look over my shoulder. That's why I don't ride with traffic, because it's too often I have to look over myself to see what's behind me.

These mirrors help for both types of riding, but the problem is that even with them, it's hard to really see them until they're really close on you. It's better to have them than not, but it requires focusing on the mirrors to see a car from a fair bit away. I like the look of them, and the mounting isn't too bad, it has rubber pieces you can put into it to clamp down with, and once you do that, they're pretty stable. You do have really good visibility, and even if I can't see the cars from far away, it's a really pretty sight being able to see the world passing by you behind you. I like these, but I took a star off just because I wished I could see the cars better. Maybe if they were magnified they'd work better. Do get them, but if needing quick visibility on the cars behind you is very important, skip these, look for magnified mirrors more similar to car mirrors.

text:

The cool part about this design is what they did with all the utensils. It feels like absolutely nothing was wasted design wise. As others have commented, the fork is detachable, which at first I thought I disliked. Immediately changed my mind, with how secure it reattaches to the main part. Makes so much sense to be able to have a separate fork and knife or fork and spoon. Also just to make certain the knife is secure, it even has a little piece to block the knife from opening without that being out of the way. One thing I can't wait to do when camping is fold out the spoon, and fold out the fork when attached, and use it like a cooking spoon, as it gives it alot of length. It saves on having to carry cook utensils too for some meals.

I can't recommend this enough with the exceptional build quality, really cool inventive design, and such a cheap price. Absolutely pick this up for your camping gear, you won't be sorry.

That may sound like a good thing, I actually don't find it is. It's easy to lose things in the bag due to how many places you have to look, but the main compartment is very generously big. That is nice, as I can throw alot in there. I know right now I have an excessive amount of gear, and I can carry most of it in this bag or externally off of it. However, I feel that it can't support more than maybe 2 or 3 days of backpacking by itself with a fair amount of gear. It lacks internal supports for whatever that's worth, but it is comfy. I like the straps on it, it feels supportive, and I really can't wait to take it out in the woods. Soon as it cools off and I stop being scared of them.

I like how easy it is to adjust, and it does feel stable in the ground. Very easy to set up. I don't have any hesitation cooking on it, would love to eat some bacon cooked on this over wood fire, but the question is it worth the price? I think it could be depending on what you want it for. For most people though, backpacking means you're carrying just add water type food, and a butane/propane pot stove is just better at the cooking task than this. For legitimate cooking though, this is not bad. I like it, will carry it at least just to set up a good feeling camp, even if I don't use it. Very well made, but it is a bit of extra weight.

title: A really nice camp stove, and relatively compact as well!
text: I really like this. It's a nice small device that cooks and boils water extremely well. The camp pot has a good capacity for boiling water for any of your needs, I used it to boil water for coffee, then took it off, and cooked fresh sausage and eggs on it, no issue. Everything compacts down, if you pack it right, you can put the burner, fuel can stabilizer, pan stabilizer, propane/butane mix can, all in the camp pot/cup. The lid doesn't fit on it when you do that with the can of butane propane I'm using, but given the mesh carrying bag, it sits perfectly on top though once pulled tight, so it honestly doesn't matter. I do think the lid is poorly designed, as it's hard to get it off without burning yourself if it's boiling inside of it. It will shoot very hot steam directly on your hand, but it does secure itself tight. This is a good value I think, especially seeing how something like a Jetboil would cost you minimum another 30$ for something about as good. Can't recommend this enough, this will be brought with me camping!

I was a little nippy this morning, but a blanket would have definitely been enough. I think I'd be confident to take this down to 50 and maybe 40 degrees, but I don't think it'll go a degree lower. Not without using sleeping bags, top quilt, etc.

That also really does make it more of a 3 season bag, summer you may not even need it where I'm at, and it might work during all of winter depending on the year. It can be a 4 season bag, but only in very mild tempered climates. That's kinda why I feel I gotta knock a star, it works really good, I highly recommend it, but it's not the warmest.

text:

I did a ton of research and this tent has almost all the features I wanted. Full coverage rain fly but still good cross ventilation with the rain fly on. title: Get the gift of water travel
text:
This thing is amazing!! I've taken it out 6 times over the last month, for 2–5 mile jaunts, at local city lakes and sheltered bays, and a couple lakes in a National Park. At this point it's already worth its price: if it failed next outing (I don't think it will) I'd still be happy with it. For less than 100 bucks I have the ability to visit little islands inside lakes, get unbelievable views from the water, and explore wetlands and sloughs that landlubbers can't get to. I can't get over the novelty of launching, docking at some isolated rock beach or island to eat a snack, then coming back over the water. And having the ability to do this where there are no concessionaires almost feels like cheating! The experience is just that amazing. Not to mention ease of transport and storage.

As far as seaworthiness: yes, it tracks poorly even with the skeg but that just means more rotational practice for you. Stable in lake waves and jetski wakes, I've never felt close to capsizing. It's slow. Will blow with the wind if you let it, but you can easily paddle against it. It works, and it'll get you there.

Setup and teardown is easy but it does take some time. The pump is fine and it will inflate faster than you think. For durability: all components feels very heavy and solid, it's like bounce house material. The valves feel strong and actually take some effort to release the air. I take care not to beach the kayak, or set up/tear down on any surface too rocky or spiky. I also take lengths to dry it afterwards: I point fans at it for a few hours, making sure to get the inside crevices dry. I feel optimistic it'll be fine for a while.

Standard hacks: Get a large IKEA blue bag to carry the actual deflated kayak, use the included (flimsy) bag for the other components, pump, your PFD. Don't inflate the seat-bottom for more vertical leg room.

When researching this, I talked to 2 paddling-adventure friends and inflatable kayaks are perfectly respectable and even the choice of some extreme adventurers: see Audrey Sutherland's amazing books and adventures, and look up Grabner inflatables. Enjoy!!!

Things to know: the app is TERRIBLE. Other reviewers have already listed all the bugs in depth, but the app is unreliable for recording workouts and is not user-friendly. The bike also will not work directly with other apps (like Peloton). For that you need the converter, which costs another $200 on top of this bike, unless you buy the bike directly from their website. Then it is only $50. Considering they were discounting it 75% with purchase of the bike, I consider $200 a rip-off for what your bike should have done in the first place (work with other apps). I wrote customer service about the bugs. They agreed there was a problem and the developer would be notified. I was told I would be updated when it was fixed. I never was. The problem in the app still persists as of my writing this review.

Customer service: I wrote customer service via email. As far as timeliness, they wrote back quickly. However, if I ever had more than one question in my message, one, and only one, of my questions would be answered. I had to write back multiple times for my additional questions to be answered, so one simple email took several days to be fully addressed. As stated above, some of the issues never were.

I will update the review if any issues with the bike itself come up. I love the bike, how smooth it runs, and the huge range of resistances available. It seems well-designed and like it will hold up. However, there are some big annoyances that will cost you extra $$$ to overcome.

title: Device is good, though imperfect will suit most people, but FitBit customer service is frustrating & could use some improvement
text:
My husband purchased this for me for Christmas. I like the tracker, it is a better-looking device than the old Charge HR and does a decent job tracking steps, HR, etc. but has some flaws. HR is relatively accurate, but at times, and only when I am walking versus doing high-intensity workouts, the device will say that my HR is over 180 when my max HR for high-intensity cardio is more like 168. It also tends to under-count my steps, which I think is preferable to over-counting them, but still annoying. Also, it is hard to get my Charge 2 to switch between screens by "tapping it". It normally takes having to tap it really hard to get it to switch screens. Other than that, it gives me a rough estimate for my steps for the day, encourages me to move frequently (with the 250 steps/hr function), and gives me an idea of my HR during various exercises (not super accurate, but I'm only looking for a ballpark estimate/compare my HR across activities).

That said, the biggest physical flaw I'm seeing is with the new band attachment method. When I got my tracker new, I noticed that on one side of the tracker, the band wasn't attaching as tightly as the other. I didn't think much of it at the time, but over the course of five months, it has gotten progressively worse to the point that one side of the band will easily be "bumped" off the tracker and the whole device will detach from my wrist. I notified customer service about the issue and they did send me a new band free of charge, however, it was like pulling teeth to get them to replace a $30 band. I first received an e-mail from CS stating that I needed to take a photo of the problem with my case number present in the photo as well as the FitBit logo on my device, which was no small feat to accomplish given the location of my band's issue. I did take the photo for them (though it took two sets of hands to get everything in the photo the way CS wanted it), but I felt that the process of getting a replacement band was very frustrating and put a lot of ridiculous demands on the consumer to "prove" the problem, only to simply replace a $30 band.

In any case, I recommend the FitBit - it's not a perfect device, and customer service from the company is overly frustrating to fix a problem that's well-known (check the FitBit boards) and cheap for the company to fix without making the customer jump through flaming hoops.

title: Never Returning to Clincher
text:
I purchased Campy Shamal 2-way rims a couple years back. I then purchased everything needed to mount and maintain tubeless tires including Fusion 3s. I ride a '12 Specialized S-Works Roubaix and mostly do fast training rides about 3 to 4 days a week with longer rides beyond 60 miles fairly regularly. I weigh out at roughly 185 pounds.

Tubeless and ceramic bearings are somewhat in the same category these days in terms of bikers wondering if this equipment truly makes a difference. Well, I've ridden ceramic bearings in my crank and in my wheels...and YES...it makes a difference...now...I've ridden on tubeless for two riding seasons...and YES...they make a difference. Tubeless is the future...as it is in nearly every vehicle that has wheels from a riding mower to a motorcycle to a car...and mountain bikes. Why it has taken so long with road biking is understandable...change is hard...and manufacturers will go where the money is.

First, let me make this clear...putting the Fusion 3 tires on was a chore...and I mean...a CHORE. It will test your patience. Do NOT succumb to using levers as it will ruin the bead. Google tubeless tire installation for help but even then it will baffle you as to how you're going to get that tire over the rim...but...you will...and the benefits will be worth it.

Second, it takes a few rides to get the tires truly seated. Use an air compressed pump if you've got it...but...I had a "Joe Blow" floor pump that worked fine. I didn't install the sealant until after the second short ride and pump up. You will most likely lose quite a bit of air at first but as the tire seals over time...the air pressure stabilized. I do pump up my tires before every ride but it isn't out of the norm of my former clincher tires.

Third, I've ridden my fusion 3s at 90psi on the front tire and 100psi on the back. The ride is fast & super smooth. A lot of riders think super high psi is better but that is, (arguably for some), not true because at a high psi your tire is actually bumping up and down off the road which drains energy transfer over time. The benefit of running tubeless at lower psi is that the tire remains in more constant contact with the road which...over time...equals better energy transfer...and hence...speed, comfort, and endurance. Also, there is some evidence that without a tube you eliminate friction...I'm honestly not sure about that claim...even so, I can say from experience that I'm not going back to tubed tires...tubeless tires run as advertised.

Fourth, durability...I run typical roads here in Maryland over countless miles...up and down hills...less maintained side roads...and these Fusion 3s can go yet another season. The wear is normal with no unusual issues. I've NOT had one flat tire. I've NOT added more sealant since the first install...which I should've done...but...it hasn't made a difference.

Fifth, the only reservation I have is getting a flat tire but I guess it's a good thing that I'm not as use to dealing with flats like I had for my tubed tires. I have to say it has been a pleasure to not have had one flat for two seasons.

I'd like to try the ATOM version of this tire...and I think I'll get it just for comparison purposes. Not looking forward to the install and my expectation is that they will not fit my riding style, endurance expectations, and my higher weight...even so, I'm a believer in trying anything once...so...we'll see.

All in all...educate yourself but don't be afraid to go tubeless. It is change that we all seem to avoid but I'll never go back now that I've tried it out...and as the biking money goes...tubeless quality and selection will as well. ENJOY!

I have the Big Mouth, the Thule roof supports that it sits on, and the Thule fairing.  I bought the supports, then the Big Mouth so I can haul my road and off road bike, and then I had to shell out for the fairing because of the howling wind noise.  The major issue is that when you combine all three you have to begin modifying.  Due to the straps from the fairing, the long levers that hold the Big Mouth and the long bike strap levers all get in the way of each other.  To solve this issue I had to cut off half of the bike strap lever AND (since that wasn't enough) I had to cut off the lever that secures the Big Mouth to the supports.  In the end, it's a good product made less than average because Thule obviously didn't try it with different combinations of their other products (which you'll be forced to buy - ugh) and that's frustrating...for a product to be great it comes down to the details and no need for the customer who paid $$ to put in extra work to make things work...Thule has yet to figure this one out.

text:
The two big questions that you're probably wondering about. One, is it really worth the high cost, and second, which size is best for you.

Extremely comfortable, even for extended periods, with quality materials and construction throughout, so yes, for me, this is worth high cost.

Now, what size? I'm 5'9" and 260 lb, and decided on the Comfort 22" model, and it's about as perfect as I can imagine. The way I decided was to get a bunch of books and start putting them on a folding chair, trying various heights. I had initially thought I would prefer a higher stool, but after sitting at all the various heights for awhile, it became obvious that 22" was going to be the right height for me, easy to sit down and get up and very comfortable for long periods.

I really was surprised at how comfortable it is, and I think a LOT of that has to do with getting the right height stool, so spend some time before you order, and get some books out to try various heights to see what feels right for YOU, and do remember, it does sink an inch or two when you sit down.

It's not too loud and it's not too soft, it's just the right volume, and you can easily control the length of the brriiiinnggg, making it short or long. I have mine mounted on the left side, which lets me easily push the lever forward with my thumb. Again, the lever action is not too stiff or too loose, it's just right, allowing quick multiple rings if you like, but also giving excellent control for just a quick short half ring if that's what you prefer.

Quality seems quite high for such an inexpensive item. The attachment clamp (plastic) is nice in that it will close around small handlebars or larger size bars with it's long bolt. One point, be sure and watch out for the little screw at the top of the clamp (where the bolt screws into), as it can easily fall out and go missing while doing the attachment. It's VERY small and took me awhile to find, as it bounced quite a distance. All it takes is keeping your fingers on each side during the attachment process, not a big deal as long you know to do it.

Highly recommended for those who enjoy not only the wonderful sound of a traditional bicycle bell, but also getting a good value as well.

title: Excellent Bicycle Cover
text:
After going through 2 of those cheap plastic covers over the past few years I decided it was time to invest in a "real" cover for my bicycle which spends it's entire time outside my little apartment or where I work.

After measuring the bicycle (70L x 48H x 24W) and looking around on-line for several days, I got it narrowed down to this one from The Cover Store, and the one from Empire covers.

I went with this one because it had a fastener on the bottom to hold the cover in place (optional on the Empire cover), and I liked the tan color better than the black Empire cover.

I'm very pleased with the quality of this cover. I have my handlebars and seat set quite high, and often leave a small handlebar bag in place, and this cover still fits perfectly, covering the wheels all the way to the ground.

I'm not sure what the other folks that complained of a generic style cover got, but the one I received was obviously tailored specifically for a bicycle, and with the elastic hem fits like a glove.

I can't speak for it's durability or water resistance as I just got it, but a brief splash of water just ran off, and it seems to be made of very durable material.

I will say though, that I was so impressed that I just ordered another one.

Edit-Sept 28, 2011: I've had both covers for nearly a month now, and I'm VERY happy so far. I use my bike to commute to work, so I have a cover at both ends. Because of the elastic around the bottom, it took me a few times to figure out how to quickly and easily get the cover on and off, but here is what I've found works well for me:

First, after getting the cover on and positioned the way I wanted it, I used a magic marker to draw a fairly large triangle over the seat with the tip pointing forward and an arrow inside the triangle, also pointing forward.

Then I put a big L with a circle around it over the left handgrip and a big R with a circle around it over the right hand grip.

These 3 markers help me quickly orient and position the cover when getting ready to put it on.

What's important to realize is that the elastic around the bottom has a natural tendency to catch on things, so you simply have to learn what those things are on your particular bike and work around them.

I start by finding the triangle marker and placing that over the seat, then I get the elastic over the handlebars and down over the front wheel. Then I get the rear of the cover down over the rear wheel and around both foot pedals and the dérailleur. It takes about 2 minutes.

To get the cover off I just reverse the procedure, getting the elastic over the foot pedals and the dérailleur and then off the back wheel, then off the seat and finally over the handle bars. It takes about a minute.

This cover has plenty of room, but it's tailored in such a way as to fit nicely, and with the elastic around the bottom it's very secure. I'll report back after we get a few rains, but so far these covers are winners.

Edit (August 25, 2012): Well, I've had my two covers for a year of daily commuting to and from work, and I'm happy to report that they've met all my expectations for durability and water resistance. They still look almost new and I've had no problems with the seams leaking or showing any wear. Definitely a good investment.

Edit (September 5, 2013): Ok, it's been another year. I still use both covers for my daily commute to and from work, and they both still look really good. Only minor blemishes from being used outside all the time, but seriously, they still look very nice. Seams still all good, no wear. Elastic still like new. I've used the buckle several times during very windy weather, but probably didn't need to, because the elastic does such a good job. Yes, it still takes some time get them on and off, but I don't mind, and it's worth it to me for the excellent fit they provide. See you next year : )

Edit (January 16, 2015): Another year and a half. I really do love these covers. It's funny, people are always commenting on my "new" bicycle, and they can't believe it when I tell them it's over 15 years old. Yes, I clean and lube everything twice a year, but this bike lives outside, and it's these covers that help keep it in such good shape. A very worth while investment, and yes, the covers, although with a few stains here and there, still look practically new and function perfectly.

Some reviews have stated that the pad needs to be wider. I don’t disagree that it would be nice if they were, and it might be necessary for a large framed person. My husband is 5'9" and broad in the shoulders. I am 5'4" and its perfect for me. For close grip curls there is no issue, but wide grip you are toward the edge. In my husband's case, it didn't affect his workout. Everything works as it should and feels sufficient and sturdy. It only took ten minutes to put together and I was good to go. For me this was a good value to suit my needs and I am pleased with my purchase. As long as you are realistic about what you can obtain for the price you will not be disappointed. I do recommend this bench and will keep my eye on this brand for future items.

title: Heavy Duty Duffel bag, high quality
text: I have a bunch of duffel bags (sometimes I think I collect them); my favorite is a standard Nike bag, but this one is better if you are looking for really high quality stuff; the main black fabric or material is very thick and heavy duty, I think it will last a very long time.  In addition the main zipper is the heaviest zipper I have seen in several years on ANYTHING.  It seems to hold a decent amount of stuff; one thing that lessens the ability to hold stuff is the design (that's probably why it is called half dome, duh); it's kind of rounded on the top (not the usual squarish or rectangular design of most duffel bags I have owned), so you lose a little room on the top side.  It also has a nice little pocket on the side for an ipod or iphone or whatever small electronic device you want to carry on the outside of your bag.  The main shoulder strap is adjustable and fairly comfortable--but it isn't padded and if you are carrying any fairly heavy things, it isn't comfortable to carry about using the shoulder strap.  It also has a nice fairly solid rectangular bottom piece that fits in the bottom of the bag that provides support for the bag.  One thing I thought almost all duffel bags had was more than one decent sized compartment, usually two zippers with their own sections.  This unit only has the one main compartment (and the  other  really small one for electronic stuff  which does have a small zipper (again, really heavy duty).  It's like a heavy duty jacket zipper.  In sum it is a well made piece of merchandise; it will last years even with some abuse.  One final thing, the main reason I bought this is for airplane trips where you take carry on; this will fit in any airline compartment, and it still holds a reasonable amount of stuff (well, for us men)(I know, chauvinist pig), so it works for me for this purpose.

title: A Dandy little gadget that works admirably well for a while
text: My title pretty much says it all.  This little contraption has plenty of power (at least for my purposes) as I keep my tires on my Prius around 40 pounds of air pressure, and this unit pumped them up from 32 to 40 in about a minute or less.  The connector makes a good contact, and you lose little air putting it on or taking it off.  I've read of other evaluators who said their units lost lots of air, especially when removing the connector from the valve tip.  My only slight problem is the unit has a nice decent length air line which fits into the plastic housing.  There is a little piece of plastic that goes on top to keep the air line in the unit when not in use.  However, if you wish to leave the air line out, it is really easy to lose this plastic cover.  It's no big deal, but I hate losing parts, even non essential ones. Posstscript:  Unit basically stopped functioning after 6 months; the motor was burning up (you could smell it), and I was afraid to run it for fear of fire or other probelms. I don't think it is built to last, but when it is working, it does fine; the problem is it simply does not last. I  never abused unit and used it sparingly.  I am afraid (at least this one) does not hold up well. I bought a unit from Home Depot called "Husky" that has a two year warranty on it; this unit has held up for over a year (still all right).

The net, however, was not very good out of the box; that is, it is somewhat thin and doesn't tighten very well against the posts.  We used it at our club for a month, and people started complaining (too many easy net shots), so we bought a different brand (DHS) instead. title: Great for backpacking
text: I highly recommend this sleeping pad.  I recently did a multi night backpack trip with it.  I bought this as a second sleeping pad for car camping with the wife.  I had been using a big agnes pad.  While car camping the wife and I switched sleeping pads mid way threw the trip.  I had been sleeping on the big agnes pad the night before.  First thing I noticed is how much more comfortable the sleepingo pad was.  I sleep much better on it.  Which I thought was interesting because it was lower to the ground.  Fast forward to this most recent back packing trip and it was still just as comfortable in the back country as it was car camping.  Its a bit lighter than the big agnes pad as well.  Besides that there was two other added benefits.  The sleepingo pad is super easy to inflate and deflate.  Last thing you want to do after a long day of back packing is blow up all your sleeping gear.  This took half the amount of air to inflate.  The valve on this pad also makes it so quick to deflate and get all the air out.  Packing it down to its small size.  The last HUGE benefit of this pad is it doesn't make that squeaking noise when you toss and turn all night!  Which is huge.  I always locked myself in one spot before on the old pad because I didn't want to wake up the campers next to me.  Now I don't have to worry about that!  I highly recommend this sleeping pad for any type of camping.  At the price point you cant go wrong.

title: Yakima HighRoller Bike Rack
text:
I love this bike rack. It is easy to use. Before buying this i did a lot of looking online. I saw reviews that said that their bike moved around a lot and it looked unsafe etc. I am happy to report i have no such issues. I have a road bike with 700x23 tires. It holds my road bike in place perfectly. The only movement i can see is with the truck and no the bike its self.

That being said i was kind of disappointed when i went to try and install this. I had to buy the Yakima might mounts. These where not recommend thus i did not even think about it. The picture also lead me to believe that the mounts that came with it where the might mounts. This is not the case and i had to buy the $40 add on mounts. Also something to think about. This rack does not come with the SKS lock cores. If you want to be able to lock the bike rack to your cross bars and lock the bike to the rack you have to buy these. I was very disappointed that i had to pay a good amount for this rack, the "high end one" and it does not include these things. I will buy another one of these. I guess i know for next time.

GPS is accurate the the device quickly connects to the satellite and doesn't appear to drop at any point. But don't get me wrong I recommend Coospo. title: Oakley still cares about lens technology and innovation!
text:
I started my goggle search in the fall and was fairly convinced that I would go with a dedicated goggle company like Smith (my outgoing goggles) or Zeal with their automatic lens technology. I even bought some Zeal goggles but ended up not liking the lens or fit at all (none of their frames fit me and my Bern Rollins helmet well). I didn't really consider Oakley at first because they seem to be doing so many things outside of lens technology and innovation and had become a huge brand rather than the focused eyewear company of the 80s and 90s. The more I investigated this, the more I realized I was mistaken...

Prizm technology is the real deal and not just marketing fluff. I've been an avid skier for 33 years and these goggles are the best I've used when it comes to all-conditions contrast and overall visibility. Even the totch lens is good in overcast, snow/blowing snow conditions. The size of the lens and field of vision is also great with no visible distortion (another thing that I noticed with the Zeal). The anti-fog is not the greatest (in terms of initial fog resistance) but so far it seems to dissipate quickly when it does fog up. The only other complaint I would have is that the word "Prizm" in the lower left eye field of vision on the outside of the lens is a bit distracting. I wish it was smaller or not there at all. Neither of these things will drop a star from my rating but maybe a 1/2 star if I could. The point is that the pros far outweigh the cons and I'm a true believer in Prizm! Well done, Oakley. [...] This video on youtube gives a great in-depth look at what's behind Prizm.

title: Almost perfect but not quite.
text:
I'm torn between four and five stars.

Pros: this pump is carefully engineered and obviously high quality. The gauge is accurate and easy to use. It mounts to the frame unobtrusively. It isn't very heavy considering its form and function. Where other mini pumps struggle to get road tires up to full pressure, this has no problem. It's almost a work of art and I actually look forward to my next flat tire!

Cons: The pump handle could be a bit wider; I found it hurt my hand a bit to keep pumping at higher pressures. The frame mount seems a bit flimsy (the one from my PDW pump was much more substantial) and I don't like the velcro strap--it's a bit fiddly to get the pump securely attached while the hose is secured over the handle. As I was approaching 90 psi I found I had to be careful to keep the pump stable as it required a fair bit of force to keep pushing air into the tire. I'm concerned that I may someday crossthread the hose into the base by being clumsy or in a hurry.

Overall, a well designed and executed mini pump that's different than the typical hand pump. I would buy it again, but if I could, there's a few things I would change about it.

text:

In other words this flapper is like getting hit with the middle of a doubled over light belt where the Dom is holding on to the two ends. Getting hit with the two ends would bite more. Also the rounded loop at the end doesn't mark the skin as much as the crops with the two layered flaps. My other crop can leave distinctive teardrop shaped marks for up to a week if used with force. I doubt this one would. So either kind can be fun.

Regardless of which kind you choose, beware of crops where the shaft extends into the flapper very close to the tip. Getting hit with the shaft part is like getting hit with a cane and will definitely leave a welt. The fun of a crop is being able to deliver (or experience) a sharp sting in fun places with the flapper alone. Enjoy!

title: The best stretching method ever
text:
I'm very impressed with suspension strap workouts. Doing strength training, instant adjustments to resistance are possible just by adjusting by an inch or two how close you are to the anchor. And almost every strength exercise, whether for arms or legs, also involves the core. Which is amazing.

But the best thing about the straps are for stretching and flexibility. I can get deeper, longer, more supported stretches with these then with any other method I've ever tried. And my friends have called me a stretch fanatic for years.

This DVD gives detailed descriptions of 10 or 12 stretches, with progressions for each one. Their "workout" is about 45 min. long. Or you can use the "exercise library" which gives detailed descriptions of each with their progressions. Watch the exercise library for a much shorter stretch workout or pause with your remote to work an individual stretch longer.

You can probably find most of these stretches on the internet, but I'm glad I got this DVD which I got in a 3 DVD package that included a strength and cardio DVD. The strength is a pretty good workout. Haven't tried the cardio yet.

Notice I haven't mentioned TRX once yet in this review. Although I do own a TRX and like it, you can get VERY similar suspension straps on Amazon for $24.99. I got RopeInaBag and use it for travel because it is much lighter and more compact while still being plenty strong.

Regardless of the brand of straps you use, I highly recommend the stretches in this DVD.

title: It's a pretty great, very lightweight and so far durable tent.
text:
Honestly this tent is great, especially at the sale price it periodically goes down to. It is literally lighter than my previous 1-person tent. The stakes it comes with are great which is rare, plenty of guy-lines already attached and coiled up at the tie-off points, no issues with ventilation or heat retention in the 3-seasons it is designed for. The rainfly, footprint, and base of the tent all clip together quite nicely and have adjustment sliders to keep them correctly tensioned. The single piece pole assembly is a little counter-intuitive, but it works great once you orient it.

HOWEVER: get the footprint for it.

I bring a scrap of tarp to throw under the footprints of all my tents anyways, because a sharp, half buried rock can always ruin things, but you don't need to. A significant amount of the versatility and convenience goes away without the footprint that is designed for it, like the ability to throw the footprint and rainfly together as an emergency shelter in a few moments, or use it in an ultralight configuration to save even more weight.
The only potential concern i have is that with how light this material is, I don't know what long term durability will be. It is VERY light material, and that usually trades out durability. Time will tell.

My friend is 175lbs, they had the exact same issue to a lesser extent, but they could at least get it moving.

I have used hard body and iSUPs before without issue, and have since bought a 6in thick board, and have had no issues whatsoever.

title: Not perfect, but they're $4
text:
I initially forgot how affordable these are, and my review was a bit more critical. Once I realized they cost less than 1/3 of what I figured they cost, I was delighted. They're useful for $4. I use these, some of the orange screw stakes, a pair of tarp poles, and a tarp to build a makeshift shelter or a tremendous rainfly. Sadly most tents nowadays lack hardcore waterproofing, so if it may rain, I put the tarp together, and all of teh elements play a role.

These help with tie downs, especially if the the existing grommets are poorly made, poorly located, or both. These hold much stronger than grommets, as they inherently require a hole in the tarp. These don't. It can take a bit of work, especially on thicker tarps (those don't tend to make great awnings anyway), but it's worth it.

Anyway, they're not brilliant, for for $1 each, they do what they do well.

title: Great for camping
text:

I have a large basement, but it still is sad to see a cubic foot always being occupied for use twice a year. These have all of the benefits of the hard plastic reusable ice while being able to take up as much space collectively as one block. You likely can fill these with contraband not allowed in parks too!

Highly recommended.

title: More portable than DIY alternative to Kan Jam
text:

Most folks have some level of Frisbee skills, and most folks have played a game with a goal/goalie. This piggy-backs off of that common knowledge.

While the game is fun, the parts in this kit are basic. This helps keep the cost down and keeps it highly portable. Both are sound choices, but it would feel better if the actual cost were a bit lower. I'm thinking $25-30 more than close to $40. Price aside, it doesn't take up that much space when storing, and it's looking plenty durable.

I'd definitely recommend checking out Kan Jam and related Frisbee games. They're fun! As far as the hardware, this is definitely something I can recommend, but I cannot see why this would be better than another competing product.

text:

I might have still someone gave this 5 stars (titanium is that cool!), but alas there's the serrated edge. It's not really useful, and when combined with the wide fork, it means you'll be tearing at you gums unless you have a huge mouth. That's kinda a dealbreaker. Still gave it 4 stars if you have a big (or at least wide) mouth.
