text:
I originally got this for our twice a year camping outings, but I've also found this useful for occasional camping outings, pot lucks, and even a big lunch bag. It's rather nicely made, and holds quite a bit. It won't keep stuff cold forever, and I'd use it for things other than raw meats and whatnot, but it's not exactly marketed for those uses anyway. It's great for keeping things relatively cool, especially if they entered the bag that way and are bunched together. It's great for cans, but it also works for hot or cold dishes. I found this great for some of the BBQ I make at home and bring to friends and family hot to go with whatever dishes they are making. Thye size is perfect for wrapped pork buts, brisket, ribs, etc.

I really like this and find it to be a steal for $15

title: Tremendous fit, but price is steep for lackluster lenses
text:
I own a variety of sunglasses from Serengeti, Ray Ban, Oakley, Tag Heuer, etc... All are get marked up a lot due to brand names and Luxoittca's grip on the market, but all have excellent lenses, especially the Serengeti and Oakley lenses. I tend to pay $100-150 for these (often shopping around and waiting for deals), so seeing these for $127 raised my expectations, despite being well aware of Magpul's heritage for reliable, often ugly, and occasionally overpriced bits of plastic.

These are reliable ugly overpriced frames. Well ugly is a bit harsh, but compared to designer eyewear brands, these look more like $30 frames than $130 designs. They are especially reliable in terms of grip., I've never had glasses more glued to my head than these. They don't move at all when upside down, shaking my head, etc... Great work there. Comfort is Ok. Not great, but considering how well they stay in place, it's not bad. The optics are OK. Nothing special in terms of clarity, color rendition, or contrast. Not at all in the same league as Serengeti, Oakley, or even Tag Heuer.

I'd be much more forgiving at $80, but these are $130. The overall image is comparable to $10-15 knock off lenses from eBay. I'm sure these are decent quality in regards to UV and whatnot, but in terms of clarity and contrast, they're just so-so.

If these had lenses on par with my Tag Heuer Sennas, I'd be in love. Sure they're not the best looking frames, but the sure grip and wide field of view would make up for that. These are functional glasses, not fashion ones. Sadly the functional quality of the lenses just falls short.

title: Not the most comfortable
text:
OK...I would get a different travel pillow
I am a buckeye through and through, so I was excited to see this Ohio State branded travel pillow.
The fabric feels extremely soft. The embroidery looks really nice.
The downside is that this pillow is so overstuffed that I could not get comfortable on the plane.
A lot of likes about this pillow, but I would not bring this with me if I had any intention of sleeping.

title: Wonderful bag for my laptop and papers
text:
I've used a variety of bags to bring my PC into the and out of the office, and this is my new favorite. It's slim, svelte, and ergonomic. Everything else I've used is just too much. Granted those were moreso travel oriented, and Marmot makes a larger weekend bag (also great) that fills that niche. This one is allowed to just do the basics. That doesn't mean that there's a lack of features, as there are ample pockets and organization bits. There's even a handy powcket on the outside for my compact umbrella!

The ergonomics are phenomenal. I'm 6'7" and 300lbs, so my body type is a bit beyond the norm. This bag accommodates my frame as well are more common ones. The chest strap makes carrying the heaviest loads quite bearable.

All my other bags have been retired. This is my new daily bag. Love it!

title: Very good fitness watch
text:
This is a great fitness watch, but it's not that good of a smart watch. I wouldn't suggest cross shopping this with a Samsung Gear or Apple Watch, as they can do quite a bit more than this. Likewise some of the newer Garmin watches are a bit more capable, but if you're looking for a fitness watch (with some smart watch features), this is a very good option.

It sets up quickly, although the charger is more akin to what I expected from 2015 than 2018. It clips on, and it charges reasonably quickly. It has a guided setup and decent instructions that will help walk you through using the watch. I'd rely on those, as it's not the most intuitive watch. Apple and Samsung have them beat there (I haven't used a Garmin). In regards to use, I find the GPS to be quite accurate (compared to phone) and the heart rate and steps to be accurate (compared to a Fitbit). Both do well compared to my own non-scientific tests (ie the heart rate looked right and the recorded journey matched my recollection).

I would say that a Samsung, Apple (if you use iPhones), and Garmin would be more broadly recommended. This is a bit of a fitness watch for fit people (the Garmin fits the bill there), and it's not a "lifestyle accessory" or gizmo. I found the focus on fitness to be refreshing and a bit of a reminder of what I'm trying to do, but I couldn't send tunes to my earbuds or other stuff I can do with some of my other watches. I find it to be a solid tradeoff, but it may not be for you.

4 stars for being a bit niche but not being absolutely amazing at that niche.

title: Great for holding down huge inflatables in the wind
text: Great for holding down huge inflatables in the windLast year we bought a 9 foot tall St Bernard lawn inflatable (it's a Christmas thing), and before long we were watching the poor guy barely stay on the ground (we tied one leg to a tree) with all of the stakes tore out.  We replaced the two big line stakes with the larger version of these and each of the legs with one of these smaller screws.  No issues whatsoever.  We actually had a couple lines snap with the stakes remaining placed in the ground.  Installation is a breeze with the included tube to help twist these in, and they come out easily as well.  Great stuff!

title: Great for holding down huge inflatables in the wind
text: Last year we bought a 9 foot tall St Bernard lawn inflatable (it's a Christmas thing), and before long we were watching the poor guy barely stay on the ground (we tied one leg to a tree) with all of the stakes tore out.  We replaced the two big line stakes with these and each of the legs with a four pack of the smaller screws.  No issues whatsoever.  We actually had a couple lines snap with the stakes remaining placed in the ground.  Installation is a breeze with the included tube to help twist these in, and they come out easily as well.  Great stuff!

title: Great, but they're a bit small and run warm
text:
I've used a few Ringside gloves, and all are great. I like these easy on velcro gloves for quick sessions or light bag work. I don't use these for heavy hitting, so I cannot say I've really tested the padding, but they've worked well thus far. The weight and balance are spot on, and they're almost perfect. Almost.

They run small compared to other Ringside gloves. These are as tight sans wraps as others are with them. It's not a huge deal, unless you barely fit normally, and that's me. This these almost don't work for me. They also run hot or rather sweaty. Again, relative to other Ringside gloves, these just fall short. It could be related to the size issue, or it can be a separate one. Either way, the pair just doesn't work great for me.

For the right person, these could be great.

title: Poor stitching makes it unsuitable for much
text:
My wife is a Buckeye, and she was excited to show her school spirit when traveling. She doesn't lug a PC or really anything heavy. Just a battery pack for her phone, a few cables, some knitting stuff, and whatnot. That along has caused the stitching inside to stretch and give up. The materials don't seem much better than the stitching. This is a $5 backpack with Ohio State branding.

I cannot recommend for most people. It's just poor quality

title: Solid build and a great price
text: These are better than the balls that came with my cheap table, but I cannot say if they are "tournament" grade or not.  They do have a nice feel to them, and they're the right size for my table.  More than anything, the vibrant color is the biggest positive.  So much easier to track.  Note that these are a specific size, and not all tables use the same size ball.

title: Sturdy and functional
text: These are hardly good looking, but for a kid, it's a great way to look like a big leaguer.  It does so while providing UV protection and filtering out the sun.  Nothing remarkable in either regard, but these have proven sturdy and resilient.  Drops, scrapes, and getting sat on only begin to chronicle what these have endured, but they look almost as good as new.

title: Solid soft bag for beginner/intermediate users
text:
This bag is well made, easy to hang up (you'll need a hook or another mount (it comes with chains). It starts a bit fluffy, but it settles in to being soft, yet firm. You can use with or without wraps (I wouldn't use it for hard boxing without wraps/gloves). The bag is nicely filled without any lumpy bits. The length is rather long, and it appears a bit longer than listed. It likely won't be an issue, but it could also drag on the ground. Speaking of the ground, it lacks a means of attaching it to the floor (it's not a traditional boxing heavy bag).

After a few months, the bag has held up rather well. It hasn't settled weird or gotten lumpy. The outer shell still is in great shape (no cuts, tears, etc...).

title: A cheap toy that could be so much more
text:
This is a poorly made cheap toy for younger less demanding kids that will see few tears when it gets given to Goodwill. It's value comes from the inherent novelty, and air hockey is loads of fun. This manages to suck the life out of air hockey with tiny paddles, pucks that don't glide, and an overall feel of a cracker jack prize.

A better made version could be a fun table top game to enjoy with a beer or two at a party. This fails in that, which was my hope. 2 stars may even be generous.

title: Great for novice players
text:
I'm by no means an avid dart thrower. I play enough to justify having a set of my own, but the weak link is me, not the darts. That being said, these really elevated my game. Perhaps better players wouldn't see much benefit or they already have something similar or better, but for me, these made a ton of difference.

The biggest benefit for me came from the balance and heft. I'm 6'7" and 300lbs. I have big meaty hands, and I think smaller lighter darts are too much of a challenge for my lack of dexterity. The heft likely helps the most, but the slight front weight bias seems to help these stay on target.

If you're a novice player lacking in dexterity, maybe these are for you. If you're beyond that point, perhaps other reviewers would be more relevant for you.

title: I love Ringside gloves, but these are oddly small and offer limited protection
text:
I've generally used large Ringside gloves (with wraps), and these don't fit well at all. The fit is compounded by being an odd fit (not just small). In use they offer limited padding even when used on a padded heavy bag.

I love Ringside wraps, bags, and gloves, but these are a bit of a let down.

title: A great addition to a camping bag, but it's pricey
text:
We go camping twice a year, and this lantern has earned its place in the camping bag. It can light up a pop up canopy, tent, or trip to the bathroom. The size is compact, the light is bright, and it's very light. The build is top notch, and the waterproof rating seems spot on (didn't get wet, but it seems very well sealed).

So much to like, but the price is a bit rough. It's a much better lantern than various 3 for $20 sets, but for many, it's hard to see how it's worth it.

title: Could be longer
text: These wraps are good value for the money, not great but good. I personally like thinner wraps, they are easier to get around my hands and in-between my fingers. They could stand to be a bit longer, the reason for 4 stars.

title: A simple, portable, and durable game
text:
This is a simple, portable, and durable game of ladder ball. The price is right, and as noted it's durable and portable. The game itself isn't new, but it can be new to many players, which makes it a nice addition to bocce, crochet, horseshoes, and the all to ubiquitous corn hole.

Anyway, it doesn't take up much room in a car, on a shelf, or wherever, and the price is right.

title: A simple portable game of horseshoes
text: A simple portable game of horseshoes.  There's not much to say beyond that, save for it does everything right.  It's lightweight yet has enough heft for the game.  It's durable.  The price is right, and the kit doesn't take any room in a car, on a shelf, or whatever.

title: An absolutely wonderful backpack from a company known for them
text:
Thule makes amazing bags. My wife and I have a couple Thule camera bags and three Thule duffel bags, and all continue to impress with wonderful attention to detail, tremendous durability, and unmatched ergonomics. The duffels are quite big, so I tend to get the honor of lugging them around, but this one is for my wife. She's average height for a lady, but as even then torsos differ, she appreciated all the options to adjust the way the load is carried on her shoulder and hips. The pack has the right amount of storage options to allow for storing small bits here and there while not forsaking a large compartment. As she doesn't wear backpacks much (and she sees me bump into things constantly with mine), she appreciates the relatively compact nature of this bag and its lack of things to snag.

The only con is the price. As all of our other Thule bags continue to look and work better than any new bags after years of use, I think the price will prove to be worth it. I'd strongly consider this, especially if you anticipate on using it often.

title: Look and feel great
text:
These darts look great, and they work just as well. The shaft is easy to grip, and they throw great.

In the end, these are pretty steel darts. There are better ones, but for the price, they look and feel great.

title: A flawed set of darts
text:
These have an unexpected balance and don't fly like the rest of my darts. They also struggle to stick in the board. Worse still, when they do stick, the tip sometimes comes off!

The case is OK, but given the issues above, it's just not a great set.

title: A fun set! Will hold darts if you adapt your style
text:
This is a fun set! The board is a decent quality plastic electronic dartboard, and it works well in that regard. Soft tip darts stick as well as most, which is to say it's not the same as a traditional board, but pretty good. Some darts will bounce out, and if you throw poorly (or heavily), it will likely see more bounding. This is all normal for electronic dart boards. The games are nothing remarkable, but it's also comprehensive--you won't be missing any games.

The darts? Well they're crap.

title: Another great bag from Thule
text: Thule makes great bags, and none have let me down.  This is no exception.  The bag is amply sized, has great zippers, and makes handling the gear a breeze.  The hand grips are ergonomic enough, and there's rollers, but I'd also like a should strap.  Snowboard gear isn't that heavy, but it would help.

title: Rather nice novelty ball
text: It's a nicely made novelty football, which also can be used for informal tosses around the office.  The fit and finish are good for the price, the printing is crisp and vibrant, and the laces are well done. Mine has held air nicely (not a Patriot's style ball!).

title: Compact, cozy, and great
text:
I'm a bigger lad, so I tend to use bigger heavier sleeping bags on our camping trips, but we like to have an extra for whatever comes up. This fits the bill perfectly with it's modest size, hypoallergenic nature, and vegan build.

It's a bit snug, and the interior feels better than the exterior. The zipper is less than ideal, but I'm convinced every sleeping bag I'll ever use will have that curse, so I'll refrain from docking a point.

title: Well made, but comfort lacking
text: While I camp, I unpack a large SUV and carry my gear less than 20 feet to its destination.  Thus, I'm not the target audience in terms of needing something that packs into a tiny space.  I do however have a big head that likes to be comfy, and this is not it.  It's well made, and it holds its air.  Neither seem to help in terms of comfort.  It does better when laying on my back and it's very poor when laying on the side.  It's definitely better than nothing, but it's not great.

title: I wish I tried these sooner
text:
I never thought I'd wear electric socks, and don't get me started on how far fetched the idea of remote controlled socks would have seemed. With that in mind I love these despite the quirks.

What's to love? Well they keep my feet nice and toasty, work well as socks, and generally are comfortable. I can get the temp right without having to fiddle with my socks (I know it sounds lazy, but boots and all...). The socks are even machine washable!

What's quirky? You can tell there's wires in there. Not so much because you feel them, but rather because they stretch a little odd. Nothing big, and I suppose other similar socks do the same. No biggie. Sure beats cold feet!

title: Took a bit to get used to, but worked well
text: There is absolutely nothing wrong with these lifting straps. They are well made and have held up to my abuse. I started using lifting straps years ago and became accustom the old style canvas wraps. I thought transitioning to these would be easy and more convenient. I find myself going back to my canvas style wraps purely out of comfort and familiarity. Like I said, nothing wrong with these as they are well made and I am sure they would serve anybody well.

title: Great for occasional sparring and bag work
text:
I tend to prefer the ease of gloves with velcro, which these are not, but these are great gloves, and they have me appreciating the benefits of lacing up (I don't box at all and a spar sparingly).

The gloves are solid and comfortable, well balanced, and feel great. The feel is better than velcroed gloves, though I cannot put these on by myself (not a con of this specific model, but one of all laced gloves). The gloves seem to fit a variety of hands with and without wraps (I always wrap and have a large hand).

In the end, if someone is handy to tie them on, I use these over my other gloves. I really like them.

title: Bungie failed immediately.  The rest is just ok.
text: The included bungies are rubbish.  The rest is ok, but it's a glorified duffel bag.  I used a bag of play sand and put that bag in here.  It worked well, but feel like I paid too much for such a simple doodad.

title: A very roomy starter pack, but it can quickly hold more than you can comfortably carry
text: This is a decent starter external frame pack.  It's lightweight and does the basics well.  It will struggle if you try to tie too much on it (even a bulky winter weight sleeping bag could be too much), and it's not the most ergonomic.  These faults aren't deal breakers for me (occasional 3 season use), but they're things to consider.  The interior is huge!  It's got a good number of pockets, so stuff can be somewhat organized.  The weight distribution is relatively well managed, but a lot will come down to fit.  The bag has a few options you can configure, but depending on your body type, the bulky interior could carry more weight than the shoulder straps can comfortably transfer to your back.

title: Lightweight, well padded, and ample targets.
text:
These are functional enough and does a good job. The padding is ample, yet not too bulky or cumbersome. The pads create a sizable but practical target. The only fly in the ointment is that these always seem to be slipping off. I do have largely hands, but I wouldn't say unreasonably big ones.

Folks with smaller hands don't seem to have the issue, so I guess most folks will be happy. I'm delighted otherwise.

title: The thick neoprene keeps everything safe and the zipper works every time
text: There's not much to say about a paddle cover, but it fits well, is nicely put together, and gets the job done in while also being stylish. The thick neoprene keeps everything safe and the zipper works every time.

title: Nice beginner set for occasional use.
text:
This is a handy set for occasional divers. It could even be worthwhile for a trip or two, as it sure beats renting. The mask is comfortable and neither too tight or loose. The snorkel does a good job managing water, and the fins have a nice wide and not to long shape that makes it a bit easier to move around.

The snorkel strap is flimsy, and the fins don't have the most robust straps either. Both likely would be an issue in the longer term, but for occasional use, they've worked well.

I'd judge this more harshly as a frequently used set, so if that's your use, I'd shop around a bit. For tourists and occasional users, this is great.

title: Cute, functional, and easy to stow in our camping bag
text:
This is a simple, cute, and useful lantern which we used to great effect in a recent camping trip. The light is just right for a tent, as is the clip. The glowing function is rather nice.

I love this, despite the 3 AA battery requirement (just use 4!)

title: Totally legit
text: This is incredibly well made, easy to mount, and does a phenomenal job mitigating noise and vibration from a giant heavy bag swaying.  All hardware needed is included (you'll need a drill and a socket set--some wax to lubricate the bolts help).

title: Pretty darn good for the price
text:
I'm a large dude, wrap my wrists in lengthy Mexican style wraps, and use a padded bag--oh, and I got the 16 oz / large size. With those things in mind, I really like the gloves, but they're not perfect. The fit is true to size and the gloves are kinda comfy. They don't fit as tight as I'd use for sparring, but the ease of putting them on and off (I can fumble around to put them on myself). The padding is good, but not great--rather great but not the best. It's fine, especially with a bag with some cushion.

For the price, the purpose, and the overall experience, these are a good set of gloves. If I was hitting a bag for hours a day, I'd get gel gloves, but these do just fine.

title: Great looking comfortable gloves that breathe
text:
These are attractive and comfortable gloves for sparring or bag work. I like how well they breathe and overall comfort, though they are a bit tight (narrow). There's the right amount of padding where needed and they simply "feel right".

So far they've worn well after a few month, and they look great. My coach loves the bright contrasty colors which makes it easier to see the point of impact and technique. All in all, I highly recommend these gloves.

title: Fun for a while, and it makes for a fun drinking game
text:
This is a well made though not too engaging table game. Booze makes it much more fun! We use it for a change of pace during Foosball, and save for the noise and lack of complication,

it's fun! It's hard to give this 5 stars in that context, but it's hard to give it only 3, as it really is fun.

title: Sometimes they do make them like the used to
text: I'm not, nor have I ever been, an expert in the world of wristbands.  These seem like what I used as a kid, and they're a bit of a throwback in terms of quality.  It's got cheap glued on logos, and softness is kinda there, but kinda not.  It's absorbent, but again, I'm used to much better in regards to towels, robes, etc... Basically, while everything else in my life has gotten richer, more luxurious, and more functional, these are like 1985.  The price isn't bad, and you know MLB got its cut, and these seem rather durable, which is a concern.

title: It could add a couple pounds and be better, but pretty good
text: This is a nice tea that's not without opportunities to improve.  It excels with its easy to adjust to many hitting locations ability, and I haven't had any issues with it holding up.  It struggles with a few other reviewers having bad luck (more than I expected to see) and a lack of heft.  A bit of added weight would greatly enhance the experience.

title: Classy, fun, and nothing bulky to store
text:
I learned bocce in my high school recreational sports class (one of my favorite classes), and I always appreciated the class and simplicity. No complicated setup, no permanent structure, no bulky gear in the basement. Plus come zombie apocalypse, you have weapons!

This set lived up for decades of nostalgia and visions of recreational bliss. The balls are well made, come in a smart bag, and appear ready for years of use. The latter is good, as I plan on using this regularly for years. No cornhole at this house!

title: A PITA and the back
text:
Ugly, uncomfortable, and hard to get in and out. I suppose I should say more, but that's all you need to know.

I guess it's well made, but even if it wasn't, it would last forever due to no one wanting to use it. It folds compact, but since it's all but useless, it's actually bulky compared to nothing.

title: A mighty fine home table for casual use
text:
This is a nice home table. I can see it even being used in an AirBNB style vacation rental. It lacks balanced players and likely cannot handle years of abuse, but it also has a modest price and gets shipped right to your door in a couple days!

With casual (though loads of fun) home use in mind, it's great! It took some time and effort to assemble, but once built, it's built to last. As noted, it's not a commercial grade unit, but even vigorous home use won't do this any harm. The players spin and move freely, and the ball isn't overly keen to fly who knows where.

In the end this is a MDF table, not a hardwood or metal one. It's heavy, and it won't last forever (I think multiple moves would be the death of it--that or moisture if used where that's an issue). I think 5-10 years of use in a home rec room is a reasonable expectation however. For the price, it's worth it.

title: Great mask for occasional use (great seal, excellent visibility, and dry breathing)
text:
I've had good luck with this set. The mask seals well (larger head), doesn't fog (after basic treatment), has a great view, and doesn't take in water (well a few drops here and there). Comfort is good rather than great (no harsh seal or dramatic mask ring), but for masks that's still rather good. The strap grabs my hair more than I'd like, but otherwise no cons.

If I were a frequent diver, I likely would seek a better solution, but for occasional use, this is great.

title: Lightweight, comfortably, and well made
text:
These gloves offer a great balance of light weight, long sessions of BP comfort, and a nice level of grippiness. The lightweight is accomplished while still using a fair amount of leather, and the leather is generally well cut and stitched. The gloves fit ... like a glove, and there are no unwieldy seams that lead to odd bulges or opportunities for blisters. Speaking of that, these hold up well to lengthy BP sessions and leave me free of blisters, while holding on to the bat with a nice grippy texture.

The styling is a matter of preference, and they can be a bit loud (though not more than most gloves), and fit can be a bit subjective (seemed true to size for me).

title: Solid lightweight paddle that may be the right one for you
text:
This is a great $50 paddle; a borderline great $60 one; and an OK $80 paddle. As it's currently $60, I'll give 4 stars. I

It's crazy light, has an ample (though not the biggest) sweet spot, and handles well. As you'd expect for carbon fiber, it's crazy still, but also rather quiet (the noise it makes does have a pingy sound).

Larger paddles are nice, and some would gladly trade a bit of weight for that extra size. Also, some may actually prefer a slightly heavier paddle.

title: Holds all cans and keeps everything ice cold
text:
This handy coozie not only holds normal 12oz cans, but also accommodate the skinnier ones from Coors. No matter the composition, the contents remain cool and delicious. It supposedly can handle bottles too, but we tend to use cans when camping, and well we're not that fancy!

The exterior dimensions makes this easy to hold, and it helps reduce accidental spills and party fouls. All the while, your hand won't get the chills. That's a win-win.

title: No incline, and starts to slip slightly at 7pmh, but otherwise a pretty darn good basic treadmill especially for walking/jogging
text:
So this is a rather nice basic treadmill (well by today's standards), that comes in a relatively compact (like fits in a minivan compact) box that's crazy heavy. Mine arrived in good shape, though the box had some battle scars and FedEx kinda locked us in by pupping the box so the door wouldn't open. The console and electronics would have been top notch 10-15 years ago, but it's not some web connected device with monthly subscriptions to live trainers ... then again, you don't pay for all that either. When not in use, it folds up, and gives you space for stretching or whatever.

The running platform is comfy, wide, and able to handle longer sessions. It could use better handrails (they're small, yet always in the way--I guess it helps you keep your form), and treadmills that cost twice the price are better made... then again, this isn't twice the price. The belt stays firm up to 6mph, where it starts to slip. That's enough for a walk, jog, and some running. At 7mph the belt starts to slip forward (only slightly) with each landing. Serious runners (and arm swingers--those handles can hurt!) may want to look elsewhere.

The only other nit to pick is a short cord (nothing a good extension cord couldn't remedy).

It all comes down to needs and cost. If you need or really want more, well this isn't for you. If you're looking to walk before you run (so to speak), this is for you. The price is right, it's built to last, and if you outgrow it, you could recoup much of the cost.

I'll update the review as needed, but I'm very happy.

title: Great bag for the price
text: This is a rather well made leatherette bag. It's nicely filled and free of lumps, has moderate protection for wrists (wraps or bag gloves are your friend), and while not one if the nicer leather bags, is pretty darn nice for the price.

title: Great bag is the height is right for you
text:
This is a well made and well designed bag for boxers looking to train at new angles (especially uppercuts) or folks looking for a mixed martial arts bag. The bag is well made (it has a nice durable shell), and should be easy enough for you to mount (you'll need to figure that out based on your needs). I definitely wouldn't skimp on the bottom bungee.

The biggest negative is that it's a bit hard to use at different heights.

title: If you have a hitch go that route, but this works well save for blocking plates.
text:
As others noted this can obscure license plates, which may or may not be a good thing ;-) I didn't have any issues with straps loosening, and it does hold three bikes securely. I don't feel that long term use would do any harm to my paint--may leave fine scratches in finish that can be polished out. For now, I've yet to see any issues.

4 stars due to blocking of license plate.

title: A wonderful setup delivered promptly
text:
I'm an aging man who still likes to shoot some hoops, so my rim hanging days and blocking shots off the backboard days are over. That being said, I haven't used a nicer hoot outside of a gym (and even then they often aren't this nice). It's all glass and steel, and while 54" is a bit smaller than an official 60" backboard, it's common for outdoors and doesn't offer any real limitations (and after lifting the 160lb box for this, I couldn't imagine how much a 60" box would have weighed!). It's also a 4" pole, which is less than some other models that have 5" or 6" poles. If Lebron were coming over to jam, I would definitely want the extra build, but 4" is fine for me (used to be all you saw).

Delivery was prompt (Amazon used a local delivery company with a box truck/dolly who called ahead to arrange for delivery and brought all the way inside my home. title: Spacious, easy to set up, and dry
text:
Prior to getting this tent we borrowed a tent for a camping trip, and while we thought it set up quick and seemed nice, we were greeted by a deluge pouring through the seams on the roof. My wife was about ready to swear off camping, but we pushed on. We weren't going to let that happen again, so when I saw this tent, I pounced.

It comes in a rather large box, and the bag within is big for a four person tent, but not too large. The real bonus was the expanding bottom of the bag, which makes it nice and neat for before the sale but expands to be a more realistic container after the first trip, where things don't tend to fit in their original bags.

That trip was eye opening. Not only is the sixty second assembly more or less legit (it kinda doubles when you include taking it out of the bag), it's an ample tent. I'm 6'7" and while I couldn't stand in in the tent, it's broad tall roof is such a blessing. Likewise the sides go up at a steep angle making all but the outer inches rather tall too. It's nice and airy and makes a very generous two person tent, though you could turn it into a flop house and squeeze 4 in. I'd say 4 is doable, and 2 is luxurious, which is more than I'd say for any 4 person tents. Well done!

No leaks, quick setup, quick break down, and stylish looks are a big pluses.

Minuses are few and minor--mostly size of tent for storage (as the description notes, this isn't for backpacking). It's not the most compact, but really it's a slight difference and the quick setup is a great trade off and makes you want to actually use the tent!

title: Holds a lot of weight without losing any air

The first night I mistakenly suggested filling it extra firm (we're both side sleepers fond of softer beds) thinking that it would inevitably lose air. It didn't :-( It was rock hard, like we inflated it. It didn't lose a single bit of air. The second night we took that into account and let a bit out, and it was much much more comfortable!

Inflating went easy with a Coleman AC air pump, and deflating went easy enough with some body weight and rolling. It was a bit tough to roll it nice and neat, but we got it rather compact again once we tried a bit harder at home.

My only complaint, and it's minor, the weird flocked side grabs dirt and cannot really be cleaned. We use sleeping bags and a sheet on it, so it's no biggie, but once a tiny bit of mud finds this, not even a clorox wipe will help.

That aside, this is an air mattress that can hold some serious weight and not lose any air. That's amazing given some nightmare experiences that I've had.

title: Not for everyone, but great for dedicated players looking to make practice more productive
text:
To be honest, I wouldn't have ordered this if it weren't a complementary Vine item, but I'm glad I did. I never even heard of such a ball, let along did I think it would work--it works!

A friend of mine is a basketball coach, so I dropped by with this ball. After getting curious looks of disbelief and questions as to if I missed the deadline on April fools, we started trying it out. The players really responded to it. It felt like a normal ball (a good one at that), but they could immediately track their stats. That's the real genius here. Most of us can seen when the ball goes in the net or not, but keeping track of shots made/missed in practice can be tedious. Plus you can hook some speakers (preferably bluetooth) up and have this make solo practice a game and keep tabs. It really works!

Wow, this sounds amazing! It sure does, but there are some limitations. For now iPhone (or iOS) only (works on iOS 9 btw). Android is coming. It also isn't for tracking layups or dunks, rather it's designed for 7+ foot shots. It's also not perfect. I was hoping for 95%+ accuracy, but 85-90% accuracy (requires a net to work at all btw). That's still amazing, but there's room for improvement. Also it's more useful in solo practice, as there are plenty of other ways to make group practice interesting. That's not to say it's not useful there, but $200 can probably be better used in that context.

As a solo practice tool, this is awesome. Like a fitbit or other modern doodad, this aids in accountability and adds a game like aspect to a mundane activity. Sure great players have always driven themselves to taking thousands of shots a day, but not everyone has that focus. This can definitely help, and while the accuracy is still a work in progress, over thousands of shots, it will show trends (and hopefully improvement). Plus it talks to social media, so if by chance you and a buddy have one, you can share stats and trash talk on Facebook. Isn't life grand! On a more serious note, it can show coach, dad (or mom), that you're using it and getting your reps in, to help justify that expensive summer basketball camp.

So is this a gadget for early adapters and hard core basketball players? Mostly. We all have different budgets, and for some $200 isn't much, but for many it is, and yeah, it's a niche. It'll do more to help your game than a pair of fancy shoes or expensive athletic wear, and for the gym rats who put in hours a day working on shooting, this is a great (and novel) addition to the arsenal. For everyone else, maybe wait a bit.

5 stars if you're in the niche

title: Failed after 16 months
text:
***Update after 16 months of gentle use***

Fell apart after 16 months of gentle use; largely in an office environment. Was a five star item, but honestly I expect at least 24 months of life in this scenario. Until then the band worked well, but the heart rate feature was hit and miss.

**Original Review**
I got this for the misses to help her keep track of her activities and keep things somewhat interesting (she likes the Fitbit app). She previously had the Fitbit Zip, and I wanted to find something that was harder to forget in a pair of pants (and thus get washed).

Getting this set up was a breeze, though like her Zip, this was easier to get working on her Android phone than Mac Pro. A nice (though not unexpected) plus was the ability to simply replace one device with another and keep her progress. Here are some general observations:
Pros:
The stair tracker is great! It only counts full flights going up and doesn't get tricked by elevators.
The pedometer is very good, though like most wrist ones it's far from perfect. I'd say it's the best we've used.
The ability to see steps, stairs, etc... on the screen is great. You don't really need to always use a phone to know your progress
Bluetooth phone integration is surprisingly useful (she doesn't always have her ringer on or have her phone on her person, so she no longer misses calls!

Cons:
Heart rate tracking is cool in theory, but it tends to read high (always 90bpm or higher). My wife has remarkably fair skin (almost clear), which I though would help, but perhaps too much!
The thing is bulky. There's no getting around that this is more a watch than a bracelet.
Proprietary (or at least very uncommon) charger--boo!

I'm still giving this 5 stars overall, but consider the version without the heart rate tracking as just about as good as this.

This is one of those cheap and easy (seriously, two allen keys and 10 minutes) upgrades that will have you wondering why you waited so long on your stock pads. If you're one of those people who feel the need to spend money on their bike to feel faster, or you can't imagine having an American component on your Italian thoroughbred, go ahead and get the SwissStop brake pads. title: These lights are plenty bright enough for easy visibility at night or in the fog
text:
These lights are plenty bright enough for easy visibility at night or in the fog, with a flashing mode to draw eyes for greater safety. They pop on and off with ease and store in a saddle bag or jersey pocket. I like to have as much light shining in as many directions as possible when riding in low visibility, so I use one of these on each wheel, a headlight, a taillight, and a flashing light forward and back. These are a good light source to alert drivers to either side of you in conjunction with your head/tail lights.

To be more quickly identified as a rider in the dark, I recommend having reflective or lighted elements on your body, as well--something on your helmet, as well as on your joints. Drivers will be able to more quickly identify the light show coming down the road as a bicyclist if they can make out a person moving along than just a number of little lights.

The light output is amazing. the light gives you a lot of down and side light, as well as distance lighting spot beam. it was well appreciated on the trail last night. It has a nice metal housing, and big button in back for high, low, and high-flash. which is really bright, and i don't see using that ever. The charger seems to be of low quality, but it works. my only ride so far has been an hour on high beam.

The only complaints i have are as follows:
1. the battery cable comes detached at the connector with vibration. I had to tie the connector together, and this problem was resolved. make sure you fasten these together, because there is nothing like going down a trail at night when your light goes out. luckily i was on a straight section of trail.
2. The mount takes a bit of getting used to, make sure it is really tight, otherwise it will move. it is hard to get real tight because of the weird mounting clip, vs screw. it worked though in the end. I would have preferred a twist tighten mount.

Overall, this is a great little light for the money. I am happy with my purchase, but cannot say anything about durability as of yet. i would recommend this and other SecurityING products.

I am rating two stars because it does NOT perform as promised in an important area AND because the company never responded to my request for support.

First, I'm an experienced swimmer; I'm 60+ but I can still swim a mile in under 30 mins and complete a 200 IM, so it's not like I don't know what I'm doing in the water. I've tried and tried -- and really tried -- to love this.

Pluses: SWIMMING with the Powerbreather is a breeze, and I actually enjoy the stress it places on my lungs, forcing me to breathe deeply. When I am swimming point to point I can work on my stroke, don't have to gasp to breathe, etc.

Negative: But doing flip turns is a nightmare! No matter what configuration I try, when I flip the tube fills w/ water and, because it is LITERALLY screwed onto the head, I have to race to release it before I am breathing water. Choking, gasping... this is not my idea of a good time. I've re-read all the literature, and everything points to my being able to do flip turns, which is specifically why I purchase the most expensive version, the Wave. I've reviewed all their pictures and videos, and notice that NOWHERE do they demonstrate anyone doing a flip turn using the device. Interesting. I've written to their customer service on their website asking for help and complaining I can't complete a flip turn w/o taking on water and is there any help they can offer and... crickets. Nothing.

I even had a swimming buddy try out the unit, thinking that "maybe it's me... maybe my flip turns are off." Nope, he took on water, as well.

title: Good water bottle tracks your consumption
text:
The WATERH bottle looks and feels solid. It's comfortable to grab for a person with large hands like me, but I wonder how a person with smaller hands would feel about it. I have certainly used other "non-smart" bottles that feel better in my hands. The cap is functional, though I would have preferred a type of cap that has a spout or similar mechanism. For example, I love the Zojirushi cap that (1) keeps any parts where you place your lips clean (WATERH does that), (2) can be operated with one hand (WATERH does NOT do that; you need a hand to hold the bottle and the second one to open the cap), and (3) is easy to clean (the WATERH cap has some tight spaces that are hard to clean).

The bottle has a water sensor inside, as well as some kind of scales at the bottom of the bottle that helps the app determine how much water you have consumed. The bottle needs to be charged by resting it on a USB-C base charger, included with the product. I've been using the water bottle for a couple of days, and the bottle battery is at 97%, so apparently it will last quite long.

The bottle has a led ring near the base that reminds you when to drink. The led light is also used to display when the bottle is charging, when it is fully charged, etc.

The application is pretty basic and bare bones. The Apple Store display pretty bad customer reviews. I haven't found it to be bad. The only missing feature that is important to me is an automatic connection with Apple's Health application. Adding that feature would make much more useful to me.

The manufacturer states that "WaterH is equipped with a built-in TDS (Total Dissolved Solids) sensor meter so you can know exactly what's in your bottle. Stop guessing the quality of your water through taste or smell." The sensor is likely there, but I have found not way to access those results. There are no instructions, and exploring the app yielded nothing.

Bottomline: the WATERH water bottle is a fun gimmick, but not really necessary. Regardless of how you do it, drink plenty of water.

title: Convenient, easy-to-use water bottle with filter
text:
I like the size and shape of the Water-to-Go bottle. The shape is a bit asymmetric and fits well within my hand. Good capacity (about 18 fluid ounces). I also like that you can use the dishwasher to clean the bottle--many other bottles advise to handwash them.

This is an expensive water bottle. The bottle by itself is worth only a fraction of the price. The one feature that makes it worth buying the Water-to-Go bottle is its filter that is advertised as removing not just superficial dirt, but microscopic viruses, bacteria, parasites, pesticides, etc. Unfortunately I don't have the skillset to personally test whether "99.9999% of water-borne contaminants" are actually removed by the filter. I've read several external reviews, but I haven't seen an independent scientific, technical test of the filtering system. If the filtering system is as good as advertised, then I am OK with paying the high price of the bottle + filter. In long hikes, it is highly valuable to carry less weight because most of your water needs can be met by refilling this bottle.

title: Not for large feet!
text:
The foot warmer seems to be made of good quality fabric and leather.

The foot warmer has three temperature settings: 38C (100F), 42C (108F), and 55C (131F). When I turned the foot warmer on at room temperature, it listed 22C. I adjusted the temperature to the hottest setting of 55C. I kept it going for 45 minutes, with both my feet in the warmer. After 20 minutes or so the warmer stabilized at a temperature of 43 to 44C. 25 minutes later, the temperature had not changed, never reaching anywhere close to 55C. 44C was warm enough, but not what was promised.

Besides the temperature limit, two drawbacks for me (may not apply to other people):
- The foot warmer has USB-C input, and it comes with a USB-A to USB-C cable. Note that the warmer only accepts 10W, and if you try to use a USB-C to USB-C cable that delivers higher wattage, the foot warmer will not work. Ideally the foot warmer's electronics would be designed to take as much wattage as they need, and no more, in the same way I can connect an iphone and an ipad pro to the same fast-charging brick, and each device would accept only as much wattage as appropriate, instead of burning out or shutting down.
- This foot warmer seems to be designed for those who shoe sizes 11 and under. I wear size 13 shoes, and my feet barely fit, with my toes partially curled. Pretty uncomfortable. The product description makes no reference to foot size, and unfortunately for me, I cannot use this foot warmer effectively. Otherwise, it does its job well.

title: Great for backpacking and emergencies
text:
Very light (less than a pound), great for backpacking, and certainly useful in emergencies when no clean water is available. Claims to remove 99.9999% impurities, though I have no way to test this myself.

The instruction manual has some information missing. In English, it does not state the maximum life of the filter. In Japanese, it seems to say it is 1000 liters. The Amazon page information states information that seems contradictory. On the one hand, it states that the water filter has a lifespan of 30,000 liters (that information is reinforced by two illustrations). On the other hand, it says that the filter element needs to be replaced after 1,000 liters. Perhaps the pre-filter element needs to be replaced after 1,000 liters, while the main filter in the device itself lasts for 30,000 liters? The translation from Japanese does not seem to be completely accurate. I checked the Amazon page for the filter + pre-filter replacement, and it states they last for 30,000 liters. title: Innovative twist for a hand warmer
text:
I own four other hand warmers, all of them one-piece batteries. At a first glance, this hand warmer looks very similar, but you soon realize it has double the number of ports and buttons of a typical hand warmer. And that’s because this one warmer is actually two halves attached magnetically. You can use it as a single unit, with both sides heating, or you can split it into two independent halves and put each half in a different hand or pocket, or use one half as a warmer and the other half to charge your phone. The caveat is that the external, rounded part of each half is the only one that heats. The internal, flat part that can attach to the other half magnetically does not produce heat. I don’t think that’s a downside. If you are holding one of the halves of the warmer in the palm of your hand, the heating side perfectly fits your palm, and the flat side is only covered by your fingertips, so any heat would be wasted anyway.

Each half warmer has a 5000mAh battery, so in theory you have a combined 10000mAh.

Bottomline: I like the concept of two independent batteries that are shaped so they can also function as a single unit. That concept distinguishes this warmer from the other four I own.

title: Perfect holiday gift!
text:
Beautiful packaging! Excellent for a gift, much better than the standard packaging of most hand warmers (I have four)

The hand warmer itself has an elegant design, with covered ports, a stylized drawing, and golden touches that contrast with the blue/grey color of the warmer.

As pretty as the hand warmer is, it is thicker and shorter than most other hand warmers (see photo for comparison) and even a hand as large as mine can only cover one of the sides of the warmer, with the fingertips holding the other side.

A window shows the percentage of charge left in the battery. That is unusual in a positive sense; most hand warmers have three leds to show the charge left, as well as the intensity of the heat setting (only listed in celsius/centigrades).

Three heat settings: 98 F (normal body temperature), 113 F, 125 F (the highest setting feels very warm, almost uncomfortably hot).

Even though the manufacturer promises 5 hours at the highest heat setting, my unit kept working for over 10 hours--very warm all the time!

Time to charge from 0 to 100% through micro USB (only input): about 5 hours

Because of functionality (easy to use power and heat buttons, heat display, power display) and aesthetics, this is the hand warmer I like the most out of the four I own.

This hand warmer would make a very nice holiday gift!

text:

The battery is easy to operate. The only button cycles through the four heating settings: auto; high (60 degrees centigrade = 140 F); medium (50 C = 122 F); low (40 C = 104 F). [See photo] On the high setting I could feel the warmth, but it did not feel like 140 F. I use hand warmers that get to that temperature, and they feel much hotter than the socks. When worn with shoes or slippers, the heated socks on high are just fine. Sitting in the living room with the socks on high, my feet started getting cold.

Charging via USB-C port.

Bottomline: the socks work well when worn with shoes or slippers (the purpose stated on the manufacturer's description), but they do not appear to be designed to be worn on their own when lounging at home (my hope, but not something promised by the manufacturer).

I'd give these heated socks 4.5 stars (since they do not get as hot as 140 F), but I'll round it up to 5.

title: Bladder failed at a critical moment
text: I purchased this hydration backpack with the 3L water bladder in mid April, in preparation for a long US roadtrip with several visits to national and state parks. With lots of hiking in hot weather, I needed a reliable hydration source. Unfortunately this product wasn’t it. I tested the bladder system at home, and it seemed OK. However, the bladder didn’t survive its first real world test. In Canyonlands, Utah, with 100+ degree weather, two things happened: (1) the suction end got punctured within minutes. It still worked and didn’t leak, so I kept on using it throughout the day. (2) At the end of the day, back at the hotel, when I tried to refill the bladder I couldn’t get the bladder seal off. The hard plastic handle/seal doesn’t budge at all, and it almost seems as if it has fused closed (I don’t think that’s possible, but the reality is I can’t slide it at all, and yes, I am doing it in the right direction.) Bottom line: I am at the beginning of a series of hikes, left without this key component of my hydration system (fortunately I have backups, though I’ll miss having a hydration backpack/water bladder, and it’s beyond the return window, so I’m out of money as well. I know that the vast majority of the reviews are positive (that’s why I bought this item!), but based on my experience I cannot recommend this product. One star from me.

I keep looking for a higher quality pump, and with a large SUP, I may pre-pump a couple minutes to reduce blower time & over-heating. The first stage draws about 8-9 amps, and the 2nd stage only 4-5 amps.

title: Very solid, assembled, basic, low drag trainer that got me going.  Finally got it totally quiet, and a good hard workout.
text:
This trainer is a very basic, low friction (Light workout) trainer that is very easy to set up.
It is solidly made, and very quick to assemble (really no assembly)
Very nice that it comes with wheel quick release rear wheel skewer to fit the trainer, and front wheel stand.

However, for low noise & a hard enough workout I ended up buying:
> The red trainer tire: Slick for no noise $40
> A shimano cassette that has a tiny 11 tooth high gear $20
> Small 26" tube and rim tape to support the tiny red tire $7

Note: don't make the mistakes of did. I bought a second wheel for $40 to have a quick change from quiet trainer to road-worthy. My bike has a 7 speed Shimano back cassette. The new wheel had a 7 speed Shimano FREEWHEEL WITH 13 teeth high gear. They both work on this bike, but do not share inte changeable cassettes. A "freewheel wheel" is cheaper & weaker- the way the bearings support the axle. (Per good Sheldon brown webpage). And I had to adjust all the derailleur stops to have it shift properly on the freewheel wheel. I needed a 11 teeth high gear to get a good workout, so had to move the red tire & tube to the old wheel with cassettes & get a 11tooth to 28 tooth cassette.

Finally loving my quiet workouts!!!

So, this is a very basic entry level trainer because it has:
> Light drag for the rear tire; just a little magnet drag; no air drag squirrel cage; no flywheel; no fluid drag system. Just a light magnet drag.
> No quick release to get bike on & off; must screw these bolts in & out and fine tune.\
> no quick release for roller pressure on rear tire. Bend down and screw it in trial & error for enough drag without much noise.

About noise:
For me it was a balancing act to get enough of a workout without overtightening the roller which creates a lot of tire squeaking/ deforming noise. I tried tire pressures from around 50 up to the max of 87psi. Still hard to get a lot of trainer drag without slick tire squeaking/ clicking noise.
1. It is not really that the TRAINER that makes any noise at all. It is quiet, but creates very little drag with it's little one-setting magnet.
2. A TIRE with ANY tread will generate noise. Even at a slow low gear for Physical Therapy for an ACL injury, my neighbors were looking over the fence for the strange noise.
3. With a SLICK tire, the noise ranges from near zero (with just enough roller pressure so the tire will not slip on the roller), to "Pretty squeaky/ clicky-noisy" if you press the stainless roller too much more into the tire to increase the workout intensity. The tire simply deforms so much around the roller it has to squeak and slide around, making a pretty loud clicking sound.
Edit: I realized the tire only squeaks loudly a couple mnutes, then gets totally quiet when it warms up. These tire "clicks" sound so mechanical I could have sworn they were coming from inside the roller /drag mechanism. But it's the tire / roller slip that goes away when it gets warmer & stickier.
4. So the actual noise occurs even with a slick tire if you want a hard workout because the stand has very little built in magnetic friction. No flywheel/ no air or fluid drag. So for a light workout it can be quiet. (I'm going to my highest gear on my 21 speed to get more drag)
5. A partial solution for me is to change shimano cassettes and go from a 13 tooth highest gear to a 11 teeth high gear. This makes the wheel spin faster> harder workout> still low enough roller pressure on red trainer tire to be very quiet (only chain & sprocket noise).

I read other reviews saying they wished the bought a better trainer. After a day using this, I understood why. (Low drag on this one, no quick release roller or bike holder, Also, the magnetic drag is sort of a clicky on & off drag ,as if your chain is contributing vibration into your ride; but it's really the magnet drag working properly. So air drag or fluid drive trainers can create a lot more drag without the little clicks, and a flywheel on a better model trainer makes for a more realistic ride feeling

I would also like to point out that the rubber lasts a LOT longer than the cheap garbage that they normally put on premade rackets. I've been using this paddle for about 35-40 hours of game play and there is almost no loss in grip.

Overall the racket has a nice crisp response and pretty good speed. It's a little bit faster than the average racket and has good control. The feedback (feel) from the blade is good and I haven't noticed any dead spots when striking the ball.

The interesting thing about this racket is that the rubbers are designed to peel off easily so that they can be replaced. (Almost all premade rackets have non-removable rubber) A lot of Amazon customers seem to be complaining about the rubbers coming loose. ITS SUPPOSED TO PEEL OFF EASILY! If it's a little loose on the edge just glue it. I plan to eventually peel off the forehand rubber and replace it with something more aggressive when I get better at looping.

The only complaint I have is that the wood finish on the handle is a little rough. Some people like that, but I prefer a smoother grip.

title: good alternative to older Spoke Lit model
text:
I got these to use in place of the larger/bulkier Nite Ize Spoke Lit wheel lights (the rubberized ones that snap on to a spoke), and have been satisfied so far. I'm using these on 2 bikes, and have attached them to traditional round-spoke wheels as well as wheels with flat/"bladed" spokes, and they fit both and stay on (haven't had one fly off yet). These use different (smaller, CR927) batteries than some other Nite Ize lights, and I haven't used them enough to rate battery life yet. I got these mainly because the Spoke Lit model had a habit of getting loose and banging against the fork.

-smaller than other spoke lights; haven't had problems with them rubbing the fork, brakes, etc. on mountain or road bike
-seem to stay in-place a bit better than the Spoke Lit model (at least one they're positioned correctly); these fasten with a clip instead of just a press-fit
-lighter than the older Spoke Lit model

Bad Stuff:
-not as bright; will be visible, but if you want a lot of wattage on the wheel, may need to double-up
-only light the wheel in one direction; thus, a pack of 2 would cover 1 wheel
-no blink mode; just solid-on or solid-off

title: good way to mount a light
text:
Got this to mount a MiNewt 150 on my helmet, and it's working well so far. It's kind of a tie-down thing with some pipe-insulation-like rubber under the plastic foot/pedestal to keep it from sliding around on the helmet. I've had it for about 2-3 weeks, so I can't comment on durability, but it has the same quick-release setup as the handlebar mount packaged with the 150. It tilts front and back, though not side-to-side. I'm using it with a Bell road helmet, and had no problems mounting it right in the center--as long as you have symmetrical vents in your helmet, you should be ok.

Good Stuff
With the right adjustments, you can get a good view of what's (well) ahead of you, and having it helmet-mounted allows you to pan and sweep the road ahead for pointy stuff and potholes. I also use it to alert drivers when approaching intersections--a quick look left and right gives a flash in their direction to get attention. The on-helmet setup seems to allow for longer "reach" from the light as well. One added bonus--drivers of high-profile vehicles (monster trucks, etc.) are more likely to see you since the light is well above the handlebars.

Notes and Concerns
If going for long rides in the dark, I'd recommend keeping a small blinky on the handlebars to complement the helmet mount (if you're not looking straight-ahead, your light isn't either). The mount is also made mainly of plastic--not sure what that does for long-term durability--may want to take it off if not doing night/dark rides, to minimize UV damage in the sun, etc. The mount does make the light sit rather high on the head, so it's not going to improve your aerodynamics or get you any style points (like a Roman centurion helmet profile), and it of course adds a bit of weight to the helmet.

Overall
I'd recommend this, especially for anyone who rides in the dark frequently or for long periods of time.

title: good side-vis option for the price
text:
Good Stuff: These fit fairly well on traditional spokes, and actually work on my flat/bladed spokes as well (Aksium road wheels). They produce a decent amount of light (I'm using 1 per wheel), and apparently get attention, and I've had the occasional stare or hoot from passing motorists, etc. These increased my side visibility a lot, and I use them on early-morning and night rides. I get a good amount of light from the blinking mode, so I suggest using that to conserve battery unless you're looking for a specific lighting effect, etc.

Bad stuff: The rubber/plastic body is kind of a press-fit on the spoke, so they'll wear down if you're moving them from wheel to wheel a lot--may not stay on the spokes quite as well after a few changes. Putting the light on the spoke also involves kind of a twist-and-slide motion, so you'll want to be kind of light-handed to avoid affecting the wheel's alignment/truing. As other reviewers noted, I got mine in with nearly-spent batteries (one had been on in transit, in the solid-on mode), though I bought the 25-pack-of-2016's, and it's been working OK so far. Also note: if you're riding a bike with narrow chainstays or a narrow front fork, you may want to check the positioning before riding with these--may not have a lot of room between light and frame because of the dome-shaped power button. I was able to make mine fit on a road frame (Orbea Onix), though I have be pretty scientific about where I position the light on the rear wheel.

Overall: for the price, I'd say these are a decent buy, and a relatively low-cost way to get some side visibility.

title: Perfect for hassle-free riding
text:
Used it, Loved it ... on the single wheel on my electric unicycle (EUC).
Where the rubber meets the road, it seems, doesn't get enough love here. So I thought I'd start a thread to share opinions about tire pressure, maintenance, etc. (starting with some of my opinions).

I find tire pressure to be one of the most important components of handling and ride, and I'm a bit obsessive about it on my EUC's (probably carrying over from motorcycles and bikes). There are three things that make tire pressure a challenge with EUC's:

EUC's only have one tire, low pressure has a direct impact on ride, and tire failures are unforgiving
EUC's have unique bent valve stems that make it hard to find inner-tubes, and a pain to fill (you just don't want to do it)
EUC tire pressure is a bother to check compared to any other vehicle, because the valve stems are hidden in the EUC cavity, and difficult to attach to a pump
... and there are probably other things. The net result is that you want to maintain the tire, fill to pressure and forget it.

To that end, I've Slimed (https://www.amazon.com/Slime-10056-Tube-Sealant-oz/dp/B003V9XYNW/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1487706156&sr=8-2&keywords=slime+bicycle) both my V8 and Zero. I used about 1/3rd of the bottle on each one. There is no effect whatsoever on the feel of the wheel, and I think it provides a certain security. In Chicago, I can take my bike into any number of convenient shops to buy and install a new inner-tube; but the same shops would just draw a blank with an EUC, and the inner-tubes are hard to find. Best to maintain what you have.

I like to keep my tire pressure up at 3 bar (~44 psi). The sidewalls of my V8 and Zero tires both recommend 40-65psi pressure, and the V8 comes from the factory at 2.8 bar (~40psi). So for me 3 bar seems the right pressure, and both wheels feel good at that pressure. It's a real bother to fit a pressure gauge on the valve stem because they are bent against the wheel. I almost never get a seal on my gauge without several tries.

So instead, I pumped the wheels up with my Lezyne pump (https://www.amazon.com/Lezyne-Steel-Floor-Drive-Black/dp/B005UND3CY/ref=sr_1_3?ie=UTF8&qid=1487706504&sr=8-3&keywords=lezyne+pump) -- I recommend Lesyzne as the absolute best bike pump on the market -- and then put a Gozens 44psi cap (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01HRIKIY0/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o04_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) on the wheel. That way, I can easily check the pressure at the start of each ride. You do need to buy the Gozens at a particular pressure (BTW, they have bluetooth systems, which I think are a bit of overkill) but you get 4 of the basic caps for $9, so NBD.

title: Believe the hype
text:
This is easily one of the best camping gear investments I've ever made. I initially cringed at spending so much on a sleeping pad, but it was worth it.

There are simply no other pads out there that are as warm and light. With an R-value of 5.7 it's rated for use down to about -4 F. Practically speaking, it can be safely used year-round. I've used it in the high 20s F and it's insanely warm. But in the summer it remains comfortable — I've had no issues using it in temperatures up to 65 F.

The reason that the pad cost so much is that it manages to be so warm and so light. The first time I used it on a 4 night trip backpacking trip and I was desperately trying to cut every ounce from my pack I could, I knew then that I had made the right choice spending the extra money on this pad rather than going with something heavier to try and save $50.

title: Good for shallow water
text:
While gravity filters have become the most popular backpacking water filters because no pumping is required, pump filters are still essential in situations where you only have access to shallow water sources. And that's why I went with the MSR SweetWater for a 5 night backpacking trip in the Grand Canyon backcountry — all of the water sources were shallow streams.

Pump filters aren't fast, but only having to filter 3 to 4 liters a day for myself really wasn't much of a chore. If this was the only filter for a group of people, then I'd say figure out a way to use a gravity filter.

I never got sick, so I suppose that's some kind of sign that the filter worked. It didn't, though, fully remove odors from the water. The water at one of the places I filled up had a slight swampy smell to it that was still there after I filtered.

The Nalgene attachment that it comes with is quite useful. The overall weight and size are also good for backpacking.

Note: You absolutely have to always use the prefilter. If you don't, tiny pebbles will get sucked in and obstruct the plunger. I don't get why MSR makes the prefilter an attachment rather than permanently part of the inhouse. Well, actually I guess they do that so you can replace the hose without also replacing the prefilter, but they're just inviting people to use the filter without the prefilter. Speaking from experience, if a pebble does get stuck in there it's not to hard to get it out. But always bring a backup filter.

title: I was happy with its performance
text:
I recently took the 3L Crux on a 5 day/4 night backpacking trip in the desert. Some days I had it filled up all of the way, other times just to the 1L mark. I was happy with its performance.

The Crux feels well constructed -- it should be able to withstanding getting banged around in my backpack for many trips to come.

I liked the feel of the bite valve and the divided compartments in the bladder is a smart way to reduce sloshing.

My major complaint is that it's a bit too easy to incorrectly screw the lid on. Looking straight on from the front it can appear to be sealed but it's not and water leaks out. Before you leave the water source where you're filling up you need to tilt the bladder downwards to check that the lid has been properly sealed (if you look at it from the side while twisting the lid you can see if it's going on wrong or right). I suppose this is the price of having the bladder opening on the side — as opposed to the top — which makes it easy to fill holding with one hand, especially in shallow sinks.

title: Solid bike rack if not a bit over engineered
text:
This is clearly a sturdy, well constructed bike rack. There's no reason to fear that it will come loose on long trips.

Unlike most other bike racks it uses tight ratcheting cables for mounting to your car instead of fabric straps. Does that make a difference? Probably not. I've had a Saris Bones rack for over two years with about 1,000 miles on it -- I've never had a problem with it.

Unlike the Saris Bones it does not have side straps (just top and bottom of the trunk). But, more of the rack's surface area is pressed against your car, so the side straps are probably less necessary.

Mounting to your car: Very simple. Once you get the hang of it, it will maybe take 2 or 3 minutes. And it's a one man job.

While it should be able to fit on practically any kind of car, before buying you should still consult Thule's website to confirm that it will fit on your car. They have a very long list of cars that it has been rated to fit onto.

Attaching your bikes: Also very simple. It takes just seconds.

As for the "patented No-Sway Cage prevents bike-to-bike contact," yes it works, but plenty of other bike racks are built to prevent mounted bucks from swaying into each other.

Storage: It folds up flat, so it doesn't take up too much space in your trunk.

Competition: Thule's major rival in the field of bike racks is Saris. I don't think you can go wrong with the Thule, but to some degree it feels over engineered. Saris' design is much simpler, and significantly cheaper (though the Saris is hardly a budget rack). The only advantage I'd give the Thule over the Saris is its ability to quickly fold flat. So I'm taking a star off because I feel that price is unnecessarily high -- you can get the same level of performance from the Saris at a lower price.

title: Great Laptop Backpack
text:
[[VIDEOID:mo363W3UY9IZ8Y3]]Let me start by saying that I've been using various Timbuk2's bags since the mid 1990s. While the prices may be a bit high, I've consistently found their bags to be well built, durable, with excellent water protection. In fact, I recently used one of their camera backpacks on a three week trip across Japan where the bag was subjected to a number of downpours; no water ever pierced the bag's envelope.

In terms of size, the volume of this bag is comparable to the laptop briefcases that came with laptops in the 1990s through the early aughts. As you'll see in my video, the laptop is housed in a compartment on the back of the bag in a heavily padded sleeve. In the video I have a 13" MacBook Pro in it.

There are two other compartments for storage and numerous small zipper pockets. On one side there is a water bottle holder, and on one of the shoulder straps a bottle opener (a standard feature of all Timbuk2 bags).

There's heavy padding on the back of the bag (where your back touches it) as well as on the shoulder straps.

As the the video shows, it's not a large bag, and that's the point. It's meant to hold your laptop and several documents -- whatever you may need to bring home from work for the night or the weekend. It's also small enough that if you're going out after work and you have it with you, it will easily fit under a table. And, it will fit under any airplane seat.

Finally, I also like that there's no indication that it's a laptop bag. In fact, if someone were going through it, they probably wouldn't even notice the laptop compartment in the back.

title: Great valve
text:
While this can seem like an instance of someone inventing a better mouse trap, the valve on this bottle really is frustration free compared to typical bike bottles.

The valve is essentially open all of the time, but water will only come out if you squeeze it -- not so easy that it will come out when handling it, such as removing it from the bottle holder, but still not requiring much force. So you never get into instances when you're using your teeth to open the valve, sucking on the bottle or putting a death grip on it just to get the water out.

As for its insulation abilities, reviewers are grossly overstating just how cool it will keep liquids. There simply isn't much insulation -- and not room for much -- so on a sunny summer day the ice will still melt pretty fast. Don't expect that it will keep your liquids ice cold for much more than an hour after filling it up.

title: Decent air mattress
text:
I personally wouldn't spend much on an air mattress because no matter how expensive they are, they always have an ephemeral life cycle. It's just the nature of them.

The construction quality feels a bit heavier duty than other mattress in this price range. So far it is holding air well -- I've kept it inflated for 3 and 4 days without having to refill.

It feels as comfortable as any other air mattress I've used -- certainly comfortable enough for guests staying a few days.

While it doesn't come with an air pump, the air pump I have for my car works with it (it has an attachment specifically for inflating air mattresses and rafts). And based on the price, it looks like you save some money by not having a pump come with it.

My one complaint is the design of the valve. It does not have a way to allow air to flow in but not out at the same time -- so if you stop inflating, you have to immediately close it. I've had other air mattresses where the valve could do that.

title: Excellent bike rack
text:
After doing a lot of research, I settled on the Saris — I didn't care about cost; I wanted something that would hold my bike secure and not scratch it or my car.

And keeping my bike secure was a huge concern. I have a 15 mile drive to where I bike out in the country — and half of that drive is on the interstate at 70+ mph.

After 6 months of use I only have praise. The Saris does in fact keep my bike secure, it doesn't scratch anything, and it's quite easy to mount to my car -- it takes me about two minutes. And it's very easy to place and secure my bike onto it.

You should be aware that it does mount to every car a bit differently. On my car the side straps mount lower than pictured on the directions because of grooves on my trunk, and I have to pop the trunk to put the lower straps in place.

My only complaint is that the front wheel will move unless you secure it with a bungee cord or velcro strap. Saris sells a separate wheel stabilizer strap; it really should just be included.

One last note: I see people who leave their Saris rack on their car all of the time. It's so easy to remove that there's really nothing to stop someone from stealing it off the back of your car when left unintended. So I always take mine off when I'm done cycling.
