title: Great mosquito net that doubles as a one person tent
text:
This net is great and can even be used as a one person tent in clear weather. This seals completely, unlike the big hanging nets that hang down around you but leave the floor or ground exposed.

Setup takes all of 10 seconds, including taking the tent out of the bag and throwing the tent in the air to let it pop up on its own. You don't have to worry about tying anything off, but it does come with stakes if you want to use it outdoors as tent. Storage is easy and it folds float in about a 30" ring.

I'm 5'9" tall and overweight, and I had plenty of leg room and room on either side and could sit up and move around inside the tent. I also have room for a few vital pieces of gear that I wanted to keep with me. If your over 6' tall your mileage may vary.

I set my tent up on a cot at our local Boy Scout summer camp inside a permanent canvass tent that didn't completely seal. It fit pretty well on the cot, with just a little overhang on either side of the cot.

My son and his tent mate each had one of these, and they had to reposition their cots so they ran from side to side instead of front to back to avoid downward pressure from the sloping tent roof. The sloping ends of this cot then fit the roofline of the tent very well.

I have slept in this for 3 nights so far and my son has slept in his 6 nights. It seems well made and like it will hold up well.

title: dead after a very short time
text:
UPDATE Feb. 2016
I've changed my rating to 1 star. I think I was able to use this a total of 4 or 5 times before it died. You can see some of my experiences below in the original review. That creaking got louder, so I added a bit of WD40 into the roller (not the belt), which seemed to have solved the problem. Then at the end of last week, I was walking on it, and the thing suddenly froze up completely. Rollers won't move, belt won't move, nothing. It is DEAD.

To be fair, Paradigm (the manufacturer) did offer to replace the thing for me. But they had never even heard of this happening; I had no confidence that they really knew the product that well. If they replaced it, I'd have to pay for assembly AGAIN, and have no guarantee that the new machine wouldn't have the same problems. So we decided not to replace it with an Exerpeutic machine but go with a different brand entirely, and purchased from a local store that will give us support.

My original review:

I vascillated between giving this 3 or 4 stars. I like it, but am unsure about how long it will last. Firstly, we paid for the professional assembly and I'm glad we did because it took him over an hour to put it together. The packaging was poor, as other reviewers have said, and a couple of pieces were broken. One seemed to be a plastic bit that wasn't serving any purpose, so we cut it off with some tools.

In terms of workout, I like it quite a bit. Yes, the incline is fairly steep, but that's why I appreciate it; it's helps me break a sweat easily. The advantage of a manual is that you can speed up or slow down on your own time; you don't have to fiddle with buttons.

In terms of noise, it's louder than other Exerpeutic exercise equipment. In addition to the constant swishing sound, the treadmill creaks a fair amount. I'm hoping our downstairs neighbors won't be bothered (so far they haven't complained...we'll see). The creaking certainly doesn't instill confidence in the longevity of the product. But for the time being it's working and I'm grateful because we have a small apartment and could never fit a full-sized treadmill in here.

title: Great sunglasses, but like the Maestrale better
text:
Having gotten several years excellent use from glass-lensed Serengeti drivers and 555nm polarized sunglasses, when the frames on those finally broke it was time for replacements. I decided on the plastic lensed, more wrap around styles. First, I got the Maestrale in Drivers Polarized. Really love that one! I wanted something neutral for bright, clear days, and also when doing photography, so thought I'd try the newer Erice in the CPG lens. I will compare the two...

The main attraction is that the Erice is more open on top, so ought to ventilate and not fog up as much as the Maestrale. Surprisingly, it is not any better in practical use! Still fogs up easily in certain situations. Also, my eyebrows generate a lot of oil, and I have to clean the Erice as much or more than the Maestrale. The eye-side of the lens on the Erice is coated to reduce reflection, but this also makes it more "sticky" to clean.

On the other hand, the Maestrale, with it's closed bar across the top, really hugs the eyebrows and keeps the sun from peeking of the top.

The frame is thicker and rounds outward a bit more than the Maestrale. Sometimes this interferes with winter hats, etc. Also, it weighs a bit more, so won't stay on top of my head as well as the Maestrale.

Ultimately, I like the Maestrale better and hope they keep it in the line for many years to come.

By the way, both units come with the same semi-hard case and cleaning cloth, and both are made in Japan. They cost me about the same, too.

title: High hopes, but some flaws make it less useful than I thought
text:
This is my fourth "serious" cold weather hat purchase in recent years. I bought this from another vendor because at the time Amazon did not have my needed size 7-3/4 in Black. I normally wear 7-5/8, but ordered a bit larger as recommended by others. I will compare it to three other hats:

1.) Mountain Hardwear Dome Perignon, XL - Windblock fleece that fits over my large noggin and protects my ears and much of my neck. In this comparison, this is my first, warmest and still most favorite hat if I don't need sun protection. Wish it didn't have the large logo on front! Quiet under a hoody. Can store easily in many pockets.
2.) Outdoor Research Rando, XL - Goretex shell & inner fleece hat with earflaps that fold under cap. Smallish, wire frame bill can be bent up, offers some eye protection, but not enough when sun is low in sky. Wish it didn't have the large "OR" logo on front. Noisy under a hoody. Most portable, take anywhere hat, but ultimately not as good as...
3.) REI Crestrails Winter Cap, XL (2015 model & doesn't seem to be available this year) - My favorite overall hat. Almost as warm as Mountain Hardwear Dome Perignon, but with long bill for sun protection, and REI's proprietary wind/rain shell over cozy fleece layer. Also, drawstring can adjust earflap snugness and keep hat from blowing off head in strong winds. Has very small logo, so doesn't stand out. Noisy under a hoody. Stores well in down or storm shell pockets.

And, now we come to the mighty Stormy Kromer Rancher, which I had high hopes for. I expected with all that wool and bulk that it would be warmer than the others. Making exact comparisons about relative warmth is challenging because the weather can vary and how physically active I am makes such judgement tricky. Still, I got the consistent experience that this hat isn't as warm as any of the other three, especially if there is any wind at all!

It is by far the bulkiest, largest hat of the bunch, and as many have commented, may not be all that flattering to one's head at least in urban environments -- not that I care if the hat is functional. There is a fairly stiff band around the inside perimeter that tended to press uncomfortably on the side frames of my wrap-around sunglasses (Serengeti Maestrale & Erice - love 'em both!). Didn't care for that, and none of the other hats had this problem.

The earflaps didn't hug my ears very well, and the wind blows right through them. Very disappointed in that, and adjusting the front bow-tie didn't make much difference, except when really tight, but then it was too tight for my head. I eventually discovered that if I left the flaps folded up, then pulled the band over my ears, it still covered almost all my ear, but with two layers. This arrangement is warmer and snugger, but still lets some wind through. Perhaps I can put a dark band of plastic between the layers for wind protection? Hmmm, I'll try that.

OK, so what do I like? The construction and materials are top notch, and it seems a good value for an American made product. I like the lack of a logo -- though the big size draws attention in other ways. The material is very quiet under a down hoody or storm shell hood. No swishing sounds here.

Overall, I have all I need in the REI Crestrails and Mountain Hardwear Dome Perignon. The OR is the most minimal of all hats, and one that I can keep as a spare in the car, backpack or camera bag. The Stormy Kromer, unfortunately, was a $50 purchase I wish I had not made based on my experience with other hats.

Of course, it may work for you, as witnessed by the many 5-star reviews here and elsewhere.

title: Good value, but a bit too long for this 5'11" Male
text: This is a well made strap and a good value.  However, it is a bit too long for me, a 5'11" male with a fairly long torso.  I use a bottom grip on the body, and attach the strap connector to the lug opposite the grip side.  With a sling style strap, I like the for the camera to hang on my right side with the lens dangling in front just above my hip joint.  This way, when I walk my leg isn't constantly hitting the lens barrel and making the camera bounce.  The way this strap is designed, as you shorten the sling loop, the plastic tensioning collar begins to come back around towards the front.  The two attachment points for the camera (I use only one) are forced toward one end of the pad attachment by the length tensioning collar.  So, as I shorten the sling loop, the pad rotates around so that most is on front.  When adjusted to my ideal length, only 3-4" of the shoulder pad is on my back, with the rest across my shoulder and in front.  Not ideal, but there is still enough padding for the strap to do it's job when I have the camera riding where I want it at my hip.  If you are shorter than me and want it to hang the same way, this strap may not work for you.  I am not aware of a shorter version.  OpTech, why not make one?

text: For some reason my initial review was flagged for violating community guidelines, so I want to be clear why I have a problem with this hammock. For backpacking, weight is everything. I have been considering investing in a backpacking hammock as a lighter-weight alternative to my backpacking tent, which weighs just under 3 lbs. But I've never camped in a hammock before and I want to know that I enjoy it before spending $200+ on a setup from REI. When I saw this hammock, the price was great and the advertised weight was 1.8 lbs, so it seemed like the perfect option for what I'm looking for. When the hammock arrived, it felt heavier than I was expecting right out of the package, so I put it on a scale. Sure enough, it weighed in at 2.6 lbs, nearly as heavy as my backpacking tent. This is disappointing to me, and the seller should update the weight on the page to reflect the actual weight. In backpacking, a pound is a big deal. This is not what I signed up for. That said, for the price point I will probably hold onto this and take it on a one night backpacking trip to try out hammock camping, but at 2.6 lbs, this won't be a long term solution for me.

title: Not quite as good as the original.
text:
I used the original (CycleAware ViewPoint) for many many years but it seems they are no longer available. So, looking for a substitute, I'm trying this brand.

The ball socket isn't as tight. This may mean loosening over time but so far it's not a problem. I have not yet had them flop out of place while riding. Since adjustment is really only necessary during initial setup I sometimes put a drop of super-glue on to prevent it from moving over time as I clean my glasses. But I spend at least a couple weeks using them before making the set-up permanent.

The original had foam based tape. Theoretically this gave it better surface area adhesion on typically curved glasses. The thin base of this product is a little flexible and seems to conform to the glass so I appear to get similar adhesion. Those who complained about bad adhesive probably touched the tape or tried to mount onto unclean glass/plastic. The tape I got was good quality. You should use a pin and tweezers to handle the tape. Also, make sure you don't touch/contaminate the mount face and insure your glasses are very clean.

The reflective surface, so far, seems at least the same as the original product. I must guess a bit because my ViewPoint's are 10 years old and a comparison may not be fair. This product could be worse but the original has degraded over time.

There are definitely several ways this COULD be inferior but so far they appear equal. Only time will tell more.

I found a package that I believe was purchased in 2002 with a price of $10.99 on it so, comparatively, the price isn't completely horrible although it is still high.

Note: For road bike use, mount it as high as comfortable on your glasses so you don't end up looking at your shoulder when on your bike. Also, be sure to have your helmet on to insure it's not in the way of your view.

This is a real workout that will tire you in ways regular running cannot. For the runner looking to strengthen his endurance and body overall, this is good tool. Your knees will appreciate the break.

The Nautilus E618 Elliptical Machine has several important numbers on the display. Speed, distance, calories burned, and pulse rate. Meanwhile, there are several workouts to choose from (once you get in shape -- these aren't easy).

You can have as many as four profiles so if you are a multi-athlete household (as we are), this is nice. I've set mine to reflect my body size so that calories are better figured and that I can track my progress without confusing it with anyone else using the machine.

Where it lacks is that the speakers are weak as is the fan. In my opinion, both are useless. I cannot offset both with a room fan and through Bluetooth speakers. Meanwhile, the distance counted seems off (much less than expected). I'm hoping there's a solve for that, but it is frustrating.

After a few miles, when I just a quick look, it can be a nuisance while running through a shady area. In fact, while lit, unless in a pitch black environment, the numbers are actually more difficult to see.
* The description says, "The Night Mode feature allows you to illuminate the Indiglo night-light for 3 seconds with any button press, regardless of the mode or function." I was unable to get this to work with any other button.

For the price, I would like to see better engineering. While I understand this is an entry level pulse monitor, set-up is an unnecessary challenge.

title: Good, But Overpriced Treadmill With Some Frustrations
text:
The most important feature to me on a treadmill is footplant comfort. This nails it. It as comfortable of a treadmill I have used. If I run enough miles on a cheap treadmill, my Achilles and knees ache. However, there is more to a solid machine.

The speed eases up smoothly and sensibly. It never jerks. Similarly, the incline is never abrupt. Very nice feature.

The heart rate monitor, the one on the handle bar, is sometimes inaccurate when compared to my [[ASIN:B000P8VWRC Timex T5J031 Unisex Digital Fitness Heart Rate Monitor Watch]]. While it is only a few beats off, I expect a machine at this level to be better.

The buttons are an issue, reacting in a finicky, frustrating way. My make-do solution is, instead of fumbling with typing in numbers while running, I punch one of the walk-jog-run buttons, which takes me to a given speed. From there, I use the faster-slower button.

Entering my weight and speed and incline and it shows my calories burned. For me, this is just a curiosity, but it shows consistent data.

99% of the time, all I use it for is long long distance, up to 10 miles or so. For this, I am completely happy. There are plenty of other features I never use (the HeartSync workouts, for example). The buttons are a hassle, but once set, I'm good to run.

title: Useful for Indoor Track Workouts
text:
Anyone working out on an indoor track will find a counter helpful. At 12 laps a mile, counting laps is difficult. Counting is easy; remembering how many laps I've done is hard.

The Sportline counter fixes what my math teacher could not, allowing me to turn my mental energies toward my workout, or toward a conversation with my running partner.

---Necessary on a Practical Level---
I tried a system of using my fingers on my right hand to measure laps 1-5, then using my left hand to measure how many laps in groups of five. That is, two fingers on my left and three fingers on my right would equal 13 laps. It sounds easier to employ than it actually is.

The Sportline counter has five worthwhile features:
* It counts one per click, up to 9,999. I won't run more than that, so, for me, it is plenty.
* The display is legible while running. The white digits are large, on a black background.
* The size of the device is small enough to carry.
* The finger loop fits nicely in my middle finger.
* The reset dial quickly zeroes out the counter.

The only two drawbacks are
* The reset dial would be more comfortably located on the left, not the right side of the counter, or otherwise better engineered for right-handed users.
* The weight is heavy. It is small, but can feel like baggage during a longer workout.

The Sportline counter is sturdy, does as advertised, and serves well as a tool for anyone walking or running a lot of laps.

Anthony Trendl

title: Perfect size for bushcraft or camping! Don't hesitate to get one, totally worth it.
text: I have experience with 4X ESEE knives, and there is a tool for every job - I love them all.  I bought this one to "downsize" from the ESEE Laser Strike which I found to be way too heavy to carry all day, and while a phenomenal knife, was not as well suited for smaller tasks.  This one I found to be the perfect size for just about everything you do in the outdoors.  Also, for folks with smaller hands, or a desire to work the blade more deftly, the smaller handle drops weight and is more easy to manipulate vs. it's larger cousins. After much experimentation, I've settled on carrying this knife as well as the tiny fisherman version which has a very small blade (2.5 inch) and is perfect for squirrel and fish work.  The two together cover most tasks well.  I also purchased an aftermarket fire steel with a kydex sheath which I added later. I then had to MOD the blade by ever-so-gently using an electric wire brush to remove just about an inch of the blade coating on the spine of the blade right near the handle so you can effectively spark the fire steel.  Now, that will require extra oil maintenance to prevent rust, but if you take care of your tools, they will take care of you.  I would love to see ESEE create a sheath which could house all three items (anybody listening?).  Now if you are bushcrafting, remember to always carry a folding saw (safer) or a small axe.  With those four tools, and a sharpening stone, you can rebuild civilization!  If you have never had an ESEE knife, you will love this, so don't hesitate as it is bomb proof and will last you forever.  If you could only have one blade and your life depended on it, this is the one.  I may make some videos on this knife and when I do, you can find them at "Thecameracommando" on youtube.  Cheers and happy camping!

A sleeping bag will just compress and your butt will freeze at night, even in summer.  the quilt is outside of your hammock so it maintains loft and warmth.  Do some research, figure out your proper hang height and distance, use a ridgeline, sleep at an angle, put a small pillow under your knee on your outstretched leg and or bend the other leg and you will sleep like a king. I once slept in an Eno double nest for two years straight and I miss it.  Hammock camping is the BEST, and I highly recommend it for grown ups who hate sleeping on the rocky ground. title: Apex
text:

The higher the ramp, the less the accuracy. It does increase your distance, significantly, which in my opinion makes the APEX worth it for that alone. The negative is the time it takes to take it off your barrel. With 4 little screws to remove, it's nothing you can do on the field of battle. I made the mistake of using cheap paint and paid the price. Once the paint made it into the APEX after a break, I had to remove myself from the game, get out my screw driver, take off the APEX tip, and douse it with water to clean it out.

At the end of the day, for $25, I'm pleased. Again, not a miracle worker, but allows you some creative shots that will make your opponents "think twice" before camping out behind a tree.

text:
I was a little bit skeptical of this thing when I first started looking at it. They advertise it more as a camer accessory than an actual night vision monocular. I decided to buy mine used as I am new to the night vision thing.

I love this thing! So here it is

Pros:
Solid
Functions as expected for generation 1
Comes with an illuminator
Great light gathering without the illuminator
Lens caps
Commonly used batteries cr123 for it and 9v for the unit
Carrying strap
Rubber eye piece
Huge objective lens around 80mm
Adjustable diopter
Adjustable objective
Long range 200yards on a crescent moon night without illuminator

Con's:
Heavy!!
Lots of focusing of the objective lens
Awkward to hold/the illuminator gets in the way a little
No actual on/off switch-just a button to push to charge the intensifier last about 2mins a push
Battery is awkward to put in

Overall this thing is awesome, especially for a beginner!

I paid less for it because it wasn't brand new, but it is well worth the money. I highly recommend this to new night vision users.

If you have been using other gens, this probably isn't for you.

title: Uncertain at first
text:
I purchased this knife as a semi-impulse buy. I had been looking for a new edc for a couple months, however I was skeptic to stray away from my kershaw of 5 years.

After my initial purchase I read many mixed reviews, and after a month of carrying here are my thoughts.

PROS:
1) The low profile pocket clip doesn't scratch the crap out of my car paint as my kershaw did.
2) The metal is not as good as my kershaw, but it is VERY VERY close.
3) A ceramic hone works best after sharpening.
4) You can get this thing RAZOR sharp, but it dulls after a moderate amount of use.
5) It is SUPER light, and very fast.
6) Initially the opening mechanism is weird getting used to. However once you do, it is actually very easy to use.
7) The short blade does NOT impede its performance as I originally thought. You can think the belly of the knife for this, it adds a nice additional cutting surface.
8) The anodized aluminum is fairly slip resistant.
9) The thumb studs protrude enough for you to get a good open on it.
10) It is very sleek looking and the POP is an attention getter.
11) It is pretty ergonomic and it fits in the hand pretty well.

CONS:
1) It is difficult getting adjusted to the opening mechanism.
2) The "safety" makes me feel like this thing will jump open in my pocket if I don't have it turned on.... even though it probably wont.
3) I don't care for lock back knives as it impedes one handed use. I now can use it one handed though which took some practice.
4) The metal is odd, things you think would dull it won't.... but the things you don't think would will.. I.E. it cuts through weed eater string like a beast but a couple pieces of thin cardboard has this blade spent.
5) Tape and other adhesives stick to this blade BAD... My kershaw had a Teflon coating. Something I wished this one had.
6) the top of the pocket clip sticks up about 3/16 of an inch from the knife.... it is just odd to me. It doesn't really affect the functionality however.

Even though I questioned my purchase at first, I am very happy with my purchase. For this price you get a PERFECT edc knife. Just make sure that you have at least an 800-1200 grit diamond stone and a ceramic hone for quick sharpening.

It is quiet and sturdy, it makes no noise at all and doesn't move at all when I ride.  I stand up on it a lot too! The seat is very comfortable and not tilted. The digital controls are simple but I didn't need or want to pay the price for a complicated computer system. title: Solid folding bike and great customer service.
text: This is an updated post.  I received this bike and it was easy to put together and everything worked great.  I felt like the resistance was not hard enough for me (I am an avid cyclist).  I contacted the company and they sent me a video showing me how to increase the resistance.  It still wasn't hard enough for me so they sent me a new bike that is a different style.  The customer service was really amazing!  They really worked with me to make sure I had the bike that I needed. I think this folding bike  would be great for most people who are looking for a smaller bike and don't need the bike to have a ton of resistance.  It had a really small footprint in my bedroom, and folded up nicely. It pedaled quietly and smoothly. All the folding bikes by necessity are somewhat recumbent, that's just how they have to be built to be folding, you should just know that going into it.  And because they are compact and folding they won't have the same level of resistance as some of the other larger bikes.  They are not designed for instance to be able to stand up and do a big hard hill climb.  I think that's just a trade-off of having a folding bike.  But I thought the bike was very comfortable and well-built.  The seat was comfortable, it was easy to put together, and everything worked well.  And again, the customer service was awesome!

Good:

Bad:
* It's quite large. We'll see how long it lasts on my MTB before it gets hit by something or breaks off under its own weight.

* The transmitter magnet can spin on the spoke and face the wrong way. I wound up using my old Bell 200's magnet since it screws onto two spokes for this very reason.

title: Use a longer belt and this bike is not so terrible
text:
This is a low resistance exercise bike. The design is surprisingly solid, with one major problem: the belts are the wrong size!

This is why most people have torn belts in these things. Belt replacement is a major repair, requiring box/socket wrenches and allens, belt routing and careful tension adjustment and alignment.

The good news is that I figured out what belts do work in this thing:
4PJ610 (the wide belt, this is the same as OEM)
3PJ610 (the narrow belt, this is longer than OEM which was 3PJ584).
You can buy belts from Ametric, that's the only place I found.

You could probably get a shorter wide belt instead, but the combination above works pretty well - if tightened sufficiently, there is quite a bit of resistance in this bike.

The reason you want a longer narrow belt is because the tension adjustment is done on both belts at the same time, and the narrow belt is then overtightened and soon rips. Hope this helps you.

I also discarded all the plastic body parts, it's a naked bike now. After taking this thing apart twice, you'll want to do the same...

I sit on this bike when I work at my height-adjustable desk, sometimes all day.

title: Loosens up, but that can be fixed with a bit of work
text:
As others have already pointed out, this rack has a tendency to loosen up and potentially lose bikes. The reason this happens is because the main vertical tube is loose (has some free-play in the lower holes and rocks forward and back). Every time the bikes rock forward/back, the restraints move slightly up, no matter how tightly you screwed them down. There are several solutions (which can be combined for added safety):

1) Throw a tie-down strap over the bikes, attaching the hooks to the bottom bracket. This will keep the bikes from falling, and even moving at all if the strap is tight enough.

2) Prevent the free play in the top tube. The way I did this was as follows:
- Overdrill the hitch pin hole to 5/16" or even 3/8". The small 1/4" hitch pin loosens the hole over time, resulting in wobble. Use a 5/16" (or bigger) hitch pin, available at big hardware stores or amazon.
- Reinforce the holes in the tube. I did this by epoxying in a 5/16" coupling nut cut to length, then drilling it out so that the bolt/pin fit tightly.
- Reinforce the holes in the frame. I did this by epoxying on tight-fitting washers (1/4" washers I drilled to 5/16").

3) Permanently epoxy or weld the vertical tube to the main unit, giving up the fold-down feature.

title: Harsh ride, but probably worth it if you can't afford a flat
text:
There is a major difference between this tube and its non thorn-resistant counterparts. The difference translates to a 3x larger package and a 3x stiffer inner tube. Whether this means that it will intercede on your behalf when penetrating objects attempt to derail your day, time will tell. But I can tell you that:

1) It takes some effort to stuff this piece of salami into your tire. It doesn't bend willingly.
2) It takes some getting used to on the road. Your tire will absorb less shock from road imperfections, resulting in a harsh ride. It's not like riding on solid rubber, but it's not as soft as a regular inner tube.

In my opinion, the harsh ride is worth it on a daily commuter, where reliability is paramount. I'm not sure if I'd use this on a recreational bike. A suspension bike may be fine.

Update: after a week or two, I stopped noticing the stiffer ride quality. Also, I have about 50lbs extra on that rear wheel, so my experience may not be typical (it's an e-bike).

title: A comfortable sitting ball
text:
I got this to replace my desk chair, as I wanted something that would force me to stay upgright and not slouch.

Sitting on the ball is fun, comfortable and almost forces you to bounce continuously, much to everyone's amusement.

My back does not feel tired after sitting on it all day. I even started to balance on it while typing, keeping my feet in the air. The 75cm height seems ideal for a standard desk height sitting position for a wide range of body types: both 5'10" and 5'2" work best on the 75.

The foot pump that the ball comes with is not adequate for regular inflation/deflation, but it will do if you're only doing it occasionally. It takes 10-20 minutes of obnoxious squaking to get the ball inflated with the little thing. If you have a "Double Quick" type pump or any high-volume inflater, the fittings appear standard and it should work fine.

The ball comes with two plugs (one spare) for the inflation hole, and I have not tried to remove the plug once inflated, but it may be difficult.

Overall, the ball does exactly what I need it to, so I have no complaints.

Also, my cats (2) seem to stay away from it, so my concerns about them puncturing the ball seem unfounded.

title: Life changing!  Increased theft prevention of bikes by 100x
text:

Mountain biking is life. I’ve been transporting 2 MTBs on a $500 kuat rack, on the back of my truck, for 8 years. Traveling to destinations all summer. I’ve had bikes stolen off this rack twice! Once in broad daylight at moab brewery. Once in idaho when I went in to get a coffee and breakfast burrito for 10 minutes. Professional thief's used cutting tools to grab 20k worth of bikes in 1 minute.

I bought this and installed it in my truck bed that has a cap. Now, our 2 bikes are hidden in the truck bed. They aren’t exposed to the weather on a long drive. I’m not paranoid about bikes being rear ended on roads. I’m not worried about going inside the gas station to buy something. I’m not worried about theft when eating with friends after a ride while they go outside every 5 minutes to check.

The attachments have fit all of my bikes thru axel/fork sizes as well as my friends bikes! One size has truly fit all!

These have been through the ringer and held up. Attached bikes to them at least 200 times this summer.

title: Great for my needs, not perfect for extended typing.
text:
Update: Fixed the wobble: I found a board in the shed about the width of the other leg, cut one end at the same angle as the desk, painted it cherry and bam! No more wobble at all.
I read all the negative reviews and though they do have a point, but for my use, this works, and I like it. If it doesn't hold up over time I'll update my review.
Pros:
*price is right
*easy assembly
*looks nice
*Allows me to adjust my chair high enough that my legs are at a 90 degree fold which is much more comfortable than having chair too low at my regular desk.
*Having my screen at eye level and tilted really helps my neck, especially since I can't type without looking at the keyboard.
Cons:
*Yes, a little wobbly
*not easy to adjust height if you will regularly want to do so.

To address some of the wobble concerns, the individual components are sturdy, where the desk part slips into the base is where the wobble comes from. I took a plastic "wobble wedge" (available on Amazon) and secured it in the gap, not a perfect fix, but improved the situation. Use real tools to tighten all the bolts and screws, not the tools included in package.
I also used a common plastic door jam to wedge under the uneven wheel.
I do data entry on a calendar, I type for 30 seconds at a time in between calls. When my hands are on the computer, I try to keep the heels of my hands steady, too much hand motion will create a slight wobble. If you are using this for a business where you type long emails or are a student writing papers, you might want to invest in something sturdier. title: This is a great concept. I never purchased the original fitbit because ...
text:
This is a great concept. I never purchased the original fitbit because I wanted a heart rate feature. The problem is the heart rate accuracy during CrossFit/HIIT/strenuous-type exercises. The accuracy is spot on during the day, and seems equally accurate during mundane exercises (running, cycling, rowing machine, etc). The inaccuracies show up during virtually any other style of workout. I have corresponded a substantial amount with fitbit, and they say they are working on improving the algorithms. Who knows if they can figure it out.

While I would like to see it being accurate during my workouts, one of my biggest complaints regarding it's accuracy is the "lag time". Meaning, how long after the activity is over does the fitbit take to begin showing an accurate heart rate. I would think a few seconds is reasonable. Well, it takes 30-45 minutes!! I don't understand why, and fitbit was unable/unwilling to tell me why. I have tried wearing it on both wrists, at varying tightnesses and locations on my wrists, and taking it off for a few minutes and then putting it back on. Nothing helps, it still takes 30+ minutes for it to be accurate again.

So how is it inaccurate? It reads REALLY low. It will typically read 50-60 bpm low during and immediately after an intense workout. My actual heart rate is 160-180 and the fitbit will say 95-110.

I gave it 3 stars because everything else about it is great and useful. So if your workouts are walking/running/cycling or other similar types of activites, it will work great for you. For those doing similar exercises as me, it will only be useful for monitoring heart rate throughout the day and while sleeping. I decided that was useful enough to keep it, though it was close. It becomes a personal decision as to the value of it.

I researched a couple of options - even considered just grabbing an old bike rack off Craigslist (the kind you lock bikes to on the sidewalk). Fortunately, I discovered the Dual Touch. I read a few of the negative comments about the stand falling. I can believe changing temperature causing the stand to fall, but I haven't experienced any issues living in the Pacific Northwest. title: Just hit the slopes with my Matrix FSX Skis...
text:
and they were awesome. This was my first experience with snow blades and I bought them on a whim. I am an experienced skier and usually opt for longer skis (180ish). The skis came pre-sharpened and waxed from the factory.

I took them out to Whiteface Mtn in New York. Took me about 2 hours to get used them and transition from normal skies. By the end of the day I was able to hit the double black diamonds and technical trails without any trouble. Snow blades are a bit different as they excel on packed powder, ice, and machine groomed snow (which, sadly, is what you usually get at most mountains on the east coast!). In light powder, the blades tend to sink due to the low amount of surface area, which slows you down. Additionally, I found that the blades were not as stable if you try to rocket straight down a hill- carving your way down is the best technique for snow blades.

Lastly, I found that the blades made it a bit harder to land jumps well. Since they aren't as long as normal skis, you don't have the same amount of forgiveness with your landings and need to make sure that you come down straight & balanced.

Overall, the skis are totally worth the price considering a regular pair of skis is easily 4x the cost.

The grip is super easy to install and have the little 'extras' to make it simple. For example:

1) The grips come with a clear saran-wrap coating on one side that you need to peel off before wrapping it around your racquet.

2) The wrap comes with one end cut at an angle so that you get a proper wrap angle.

3) The tip also has a piece of double-sided tape stuck to it to keep it in place while you start wrapping.

4) It comes with a pre-cut piece of tape to finish taping the final end to the racket.

The wrap is also not too thin nor too thick. I did remove the original, factory wrap on my racquet before I put this on.

It also seems to have a very nice wear level. I have played 4 weeks now (3 games a week) and have no wear holes.

title: Outstanding no frills workout machine
text:
I decided to pick one of these up from a local dealer about two months ago because I hate going to the gym. I reasoned that if I had a treadmill in my apartment, I would have NO more excuses when it came to working out. Luckily, this has paid off for me - I've used the treadmill nearly every day since it was delivered. I really love this treadmill so far.

The Precor was more expensive than similar models, but they seem to have a better reputation when it comes to quality, reliability, customer service, and repairs when things DO go wrong.

When I was testing out treadmills at the store, the Precor definitely did feel more sturdy and well built, even though it's one of their cheaper, Chinese made models. And even though the 9.23 is made in China, I was told that replacement parts are stocked in the US (if that means anything to anyone).

I use my treadmill for walking on an incline only. The manual says that it supports users up to 550 pounds for walking only, and 350 pounds for running (which is much higher than other, cheaper models). I started using the treadmill when I was about 330 pounds, and have never had any major problems with it (I'm down 8 pounds last time I checked). The motor doesn't jerk or hesitate at all, even for someone as heavy as me.

One thing to note regarding the maximum weight: the dealer told me to add 50 pounds to the maximum if you're going to run, so I would have exceeded the 350 pound max if I had done so. This didn't bother me though as I had only planned on walking at an incline anyway.

The only minor issue I've had so far is a slight bit of belt slippage under my right foot. There isn't anything in the manual about this, but after doing some research, I figured out how to tighten the belt a bit so this wouldn't happen. The belt would also go off center as well due to it being too loose. I haven't had a problem since tightening it.

The manual talks about centering the belt using the bolt on the right side of the belt only. To tighten the belt, you just have to do equal clockwise turns on each side of the belt while the treadmill is set to around 3 MPH - maybe a quarter or eighth turn at a time making sure the belt stays centered. I was very conservative about this, testing for slippage after each small turn, and I didn't have to tighten the belt much. This was pretty easy, but Precor will have the local repair people come out if you are at all uncomfortable doing this yourself.

I also called Precor customer service about the belt slippage just to be safe, and I also wanted to see how that whole process would go. When I called, I got connected to someone in the US nearly right away. The customer service agent directed me to the local repair guy, who confirmed what I had found about tightening the belt (he didn't need to come out). The agent seemed rather knowledgable about the product, and cleared up some wrong information I got from the dealer as well. So far, I'm pretty happy with Precor customer service.

The dealer told me I'd need to lubricate the belt, but the manual for the 9.23 says you never need to do this. Customer service confirmed that the 9.23's belt does NOT need to be lubricated.

The sound of the treadmill running and my footsteps are rather loud, but nothing too annoying when you wear headphones and listen to music. If others are in the room, it might be disturbing to them though.

The treadmill has a rather strong odor to it at first that DOES seem to diminish over time. The best way I can describe it is a plastic and/or electronics smell. It's not terrible, but it's not exactly lovely either.

The electronics are ultra basic - just what I wanted. You get a few programs and start, stop, incline and speed controls and that's it. I actually prefer this since I only ever use manual controls anyway, and I have other gadgets I use to do anything fancy.

The 9.23 doesn't have side rails, which is a bit uncomfortable at first, but I've gotten used to it. The next model up has rails and a few other things, but I didn't think it was worth the extra cost even though I really would prefer rails in order to steady myself. This is a minor issue that I've learned to live with.

There is a small ledge under the screen that's perfect for a Kindle or a tablet. I have a [[ASIN:B00HWMPSFQ Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 10.1 Tablet (Black)]], and it sits securely on the ledge even at 6% incline. I listen to music and use the Kindle app to read, or I listen to Audible audiobooks, and the time flies by. I have little trouble motivating myself to walk in the mornings.

The treadmill has a built-in heart rate monitor when you grip the handles. I have found this to be practically useless though, as the reading jumps up and down way too much, and it takes way too long to get a reading. I wanted to track heart rate, so I bought the Polar H7 heart rate sensor and paired it to my phone, and I use the Polar Beat app to track heart rate, time, and calories burned. So far I'm really loving this system.

The last thing I'll mention has more to do with modern circuit breakers than the treadmill itself. When I first got the treadmill, turning it on would trip adjacent breakers if there was a certain load above maybe around 100 watts on it, like a bathroom light and fan for example. I had never heard of a device tripping a DIFFERENT circuit breaker, but apparently this is very common with treadmills.

Apparently, treadmill motors emit some type of interference that trips newer types of circuit breakers (AFCI). Luckily there is an easy fix for this - all you have to do is plug the treadmill into a [[ASIN:B0000513O4 Tripp Lite ISOBAR4ULTRA Isobar Surge Protector Metal 4 Outlet 6 feet Cord 3330 Joules]] or something similar. I've also tried the [[ASIN:B0000510R4 Tripp Lite ISOBLOK2-0 2-Outlet Isobar Premium Surge Protector 1410 Joules]] but it didn't work. I know other similar surge protectors with EFI/RFI line noise filtering have been reported to work too, but I've only tried the Tripp Lite.

Overall, I'm really glad I spent the extra money on the Precor. It feels sturdy and meets my basic needs, and I have confidence that if I do have a problem, I'll be able to get it taken care of without a ton of hassle.

title: Quality, functional
text:
Functional, water-resistant, floats, accurate, relatively stable, protective housing, luminescent and fair price.

Use as a bearing compass and backup heading compass.

Allows reading a bearing while being gently pitched, rolled. Scale is in 1* increments. Under flat conditions easy to read down to the 1*. Dial settles down to a stable reading relatively quick. As a person needing 1.25 reader I found no issue with seeing the readings without the readers. Easy to read scale in the daylight while wearing polarized sunglasses. Luminescent "greenish" color allows for easy night sightings without killing your night vision. No batteries required:). Worst case situation would be a short exposure to a light source to recharge the luminous dial.

More or less floats on the surface of freshwater with no obvious moisture intrusion. Did not note any IPX rating on the packaging(long gone in the trash). Soft rubbery like housing allows for secure grip with bare wet hands or lightly gloved hands. Housing material should provide some protection from the eventual drop and the every day bumps. Neck lanyard and light weight should reduce drops and allow for all day wear. Housing should protect the unit from swing bumps.

Accuracy checked against an older Silvia Ranger type15 and Garmin GPSMaps 78sc. Prism (hand bearing sighting) view is in degrees only. 1* increments. Viewed from above you have the degrees in 30* numerical with 5* marks and the cardinal points.

Personal preference for "cheek" style vs. "arm" style of bearing compass. 5-year warranty from an established(+50 years), reputable company. Good real world history of reliablility and function.

title: Good product with the potential for becoming a better product.
text:
Bit biased Solio "fanboy". Second Solio product purchased. Bolt user for 3 seasons of heavy use in some relatively extreme conditions. Only issue with the Bolt has been the expected loss of battery capacity due to use. Solio has provided a replacement battery free of charge. Reliable product with over the top customer service.

Charged up the hub using a wall plug. Have been sitting here on the deck under a partly cloudy sky with the panel plugged into the Hub, the Hub plugged into the iPad Mini Retina. Over the past hour the iPad battery has gone from 68 to 69%. The Hub capacity has dropped from 100 to 60-80%. iPad Mini Retina battery capacity is +6000mAh. Hub capacity is 2000mAh. On paper the maximum topping off charge should be ~33%. Under current levels of sunlight the panel as expected cannot maintain full Hub charge.

Conclusion:
Option for Apple specific charging protocol and minimal risk if you charge via the Hub to your device are big positives. The big negative is not specific to this charger. The neg. are the limits of today's solar panels.
This is a small, relatively light in weight and compact solar panel. The rate it charges the Hub has to be balanced against the panel size. If you can deal with the charging rate and are in need of a compact, lighter weight unit you will probably like this
product. Limited capacity of the Hub battery are IMO a negative. The Classic2 has a 3700mAh battery. Would be happier if
Solio could increase the capacity of the Hub. Test of time and higher capacity battery for today's higher energy needs limits this solar charger to 4****s for now.

title: Least effort of any small pump to reach 90psi
text:
Over the decades of commuting, racing and just fun riding I've owned too many frame/mini pumps. Frame fit Silca Impero was still the standard against a handful of Zefals, Crank Brothers used. New top pump is the Lezyne Road Drive large size.

Strokes to reach and level of effort at 100psi:
Road Drive= 150 strokes at an easy-moderate effort
Pressure Drive (med) = 140 strokes at a moderate-hard effort
Silca Impero 520mm size = 120 strokes (90psi) at hard effort

The Road Drive is ~3mm narrower than the Pressure Drive. Maybe why it takes less effort at any psi above 70. Longer stroke more or less made up for the difference in air volume delivered.

The Lezyne pumps required a threaded valve stem. The pump is connected to the valve stem by a flexible length of hose that screws onto the pump when in use. Stored within the pump. Reduces the chance of snapping off a valve stem.

Found out the pump is relatively sturdy. The old Kirkland seat wedge pack has a pump sleeve. The large size Road Drive sticks out ~6cm. It ended up popping out hitting the pavement & bouncing a few times. Outside of couple cosmetic scuffs the pump works fine. A velcro strap now makes sure the pump stays put. At the Lezyne site rebuild kits are available. Nice not to have to chuck another pump into the landfill when time & wear ends a pumps usefulness.

title: Inexpensive, functional.
text:
First non-roof or truck box rail mounted rack purchased. Was in need for an inexpensive rack to put on the old Chevy Prism(Toyota Corolla) to carry a single bicycle. When unboxing I had some serious doubts. Chunk of light weight plastic. Nothing substantial like the Thules & Gorge Racks owned. Gave it a try. After a few uses I'm happy.

Set up is pretty much idiot proof. I leave the lower straps adjusted to fit the vehicle length. Loosening or tightening the top straps to remove or attach the rack. Take less than a minute. Rack when not used sits inside the trunk. Compact size takes little space in the Chevy's small trunk. No loose parts to lose.

My private driveway and mile of "gravel" township road traveled to reach pavement are by any standards poor. Pot holes, dips, bumps, washouts and rumble strip sections make for a harsh ride. Concern for the bike's paint job & my trunk door resulted in couple additions to the rack. 2 sections of foam pipe insulation to protect the top tube where the bike attaches to the rack and a velcro strap to keep the front wheel from flopping around. Saris incorporates a strap to keep the crankarms from rotating and pedal bumping your vehicle. Rack so far has functioned as advertised. Securely attached bike to the rack. Rack securely attached to your vehicle on smooth paved highways to bumpy gravel roads.

Only couple issue so far. 1st is more due to the road conditions & type of (trunk mount system). Dust & mud kicked up by the vehicle's backwash ends up on the bike more so than a roof system. 2nd is bike security. The rack to be removed at least on my car requires opening the trunk ~1" to release the lower mounting clips. Bending the clip with a small pry bar or just cutting the poly straps would allow for quick thief of the rack. Locking the bike to the rack requires some form of aftermarket cable & lock system. But then the thief could just take the rack with bike attached. Will need to think of some form of locking system to reduce the chance of this situation from happening.

title: Does the job, but the design could be refined further for a significantly improved user experience
text:
Generally speaking, this does what it sets out to do - namely, it has enough room to store two bicycles vertically. However, I think there are some dramatic improvements possible here.

For one, the unit is just barely sturdy enough for my 2 full carbon bikes with a combined weight of under 30 pounds. If I had to store a couple traditional aluminum frame bikes, I would be concerned at the stand collapsing due to its stability. As an enhancement, it would be nice to have adjustable height between the two bikes.

Second, the bike frame holders are not necessarily thick enough. It works fine for a road bike, but triathlon or mountain bikes would need a cross bar to comfortably fit. I think it would be nice to have slightly lengthier frame holder, especially since the footprint is already there.

title: Essential Ham Radio Field Day Tool
text:
Are you a ham radio operator tossing portable antennas up into trees? Don't like the idea of sling shots and potato launchers? Hate that tangled mess of mason line? Looking for reasonable elevation for the weekend? I recommend this.

I hate rope, string, wine, wire, cable, and anything squiggly that is over 25 feet long. It is certain to become a tangled mess and cost 30 minutes to an hour to straighten out just to have it wrap around your ankle and trip you up. Happens to me every single time.

Some smart ham out there suggested I try this throw line bag and weight. After it was delivered I brought it out to the backyard and started tossing it around. I made about five or six long low tosses without any tangles and three or four high tosses over the tree without a problem. I'm sold on it. My slingshot is going to see a lot less use and I still don't have the guts to try my potato launcher.

The bag is more than storage. After a toss you just stuff the line back in the bag without concern for winding it properly. Just push it down in the bag. When tossing the weight you just let the line play out of the bag. I have yet to experience a tangle. I'm sure there's some added resistance and I might be losing a foot or two of max height but for ease of storage and deployment you can have the foot.

When done, stuff the line in the bag along with the weight. Cinch it up and toss back in the truck until next time. Not a whole lot of fussing.

A warning... wear gloves. The rope they use burns! Me and one other person found out the hard way. Ya... I didn't tell him. But even after that he went out and bought his own kit so maybe the burn wasn't so bad. Still, wear gloves.

I think I got the 12 oz weight. Then next one down might have been a little better. After a few tosses of the 12 oz weight I was getting real tired and my height/distance was dropping rapidly. Good argument for doing it right the first time I guess. Still, 8 oz might be some benefit.

I know it's tempting but don't toss this thing at your buddies. The weight is substantial and if you hit them they won't share in your amusement. Not that I did anything like that but you know. It could happen.

That's it. Wish I found this a long time ago. Until now I had been using my slingshot with a 1 oz weight and a Zebco 33 and 20 lb test line. Then I would tie the mason line for the second pass. The tangles were unbelievable so a spool of mason line was a one-time-use item for me. The rope in this kit is strong enough to hold up any wire antenna for a weekend so you only need a single pass.

title: Beautiful Looks, Wonderful Performance
text:
I'm loving this reel. It replaced an Ambassadeur 5500C. The differences are pretty obvious. The Patriarch includes both a friction and magnetic breaking system. This might be a good thing if you have experience but it does take some time to get used to it. Nearest I can figure, the magnetic breaking is most effective at the beginning of the case where the speed is highest while the mechanical brake operates across the whole cast. When I change lures I usually turn up the magnetic to 8-10 and then adjust the mechanical until I clean casts. Then I back off the magnetic for the same result. The end result is nice long casts with fewer rats nests. Then - to add to the complication - you can pop off the side and adjust how many magnets are active in the magnetic breaking. I keep two on and four off (must be done in pairs). I get a few more yards (5 to 10 maybe) from the Patriarch compared with the 5500c.

Reeling back in is smooth. The moving eye lays the line smoothly on the spool but I notice that during casting the eye stays in one place. I can't remember for sure but I thought the 5500c eye moved during casts. Careful when you release the spool. The tension on the line may be enough to get the spools spinning and you can end up with a rats nest without even casting.

The Patriarch fits nicely in the palm while on the rod. It allows me to keep a finger on the spool and keep in touch with the line out the front. I have it mated to a St. Croix Legend Tournament Bass Casting Rod and I think the combination is perfect though I'd like to try it out with a slightly lighter and slower action rod. I'll bet it can shoot a 1/2 ounce lure a half mile!

I didn't like my dealings with support. As I mentioned, you can engage or disengage magnets in the break system but I couldn't figure out how. The minimal instruction pamphlet didn't give any clues and neither did their support website. In fact, looking through some forums I'm guessing most people find access to the magnets obvious. But I didn't know how to do it and support responded with "Unfortunately, to experiment with the centrifugal breaks, you must take
the reel apart to access them." Wow. Helpful guys. Maybe I lost something in the translation. I don't know. Fortunately for me I feel the reel is so well built I'll never have to contact support so I'll just ignore them.

You can fish well with any nice baitcaster. This isn't going to put bigger or more fish on your hook. But you'll find each cast is a pleasure.

title: Not for me.

title: Early Review - 7.1:1 or 6.4:1?
text:
The specs here say this is the 7.1:1 ratio version of the Patriarch. What I actually received was the PATRIARCH64LP - the 6.4:1 ratio version of the reel. I believe this is important to some people and at minimum it is incorrectly described here. I will email Amazon directly.

Now - I have to say, 6.4/7.1 - doesn't make a difference to me. I'm not good or knowledgeable enough to let it bother me. On another site it says at 7.1 you are bringing in 28" per turn. With the 6.4 it is 26" per turn. I guess I will just have to crank a little faster if I'm in a lure race.

I wanted to deduct a star for the wrong spec but I can't. The reel is too too too nice. I decided to upgrade both my ultralight spinner (old Browning) and baitcaster (Abu 5500C) and settled on the Patriarch spinner and baitcaster. New rods too. I've been an on/off angler for about 20 years mostly from the shore in rivers and lakes. Now I live on the river.

This is an early review - one day (few hours) of use. I spooled up some 15 lb fluorocarbon line, put on a heavy Poe's diver and headed out to the dock. To start I had the dial up to 10 and the brake so I had to jiggle the rod to make the lure drop. Eventually as I got a little more confident with it I backed both down. One mild rats nest during the adjustment.

The feel on the rod is very nice. Compared with the 5500C this is a light and very small reel that fits beautifully in the palm of my hand. I've got it on a 7' MH rod and threw out a couple of sidearm casts. Distance wasn't great but the casts were smooth and backlash free. After each cast I dropped the brakes down a little. Eventually I went to some two-handed casts - one of which I got the mild backlash but was real happy with the distance at this point. I tried a few overhands but I need more practice as the distance was very short - like I was throwing the lure into the water.

One thing I noticed - I'm not sure if this is good or bad. My old 5500C3's eye - the part where it spreads the line evenly on the reel - would move back and forth when casting too. The Patriarch does not. I'm trying to think it through and can't really tell if there's an advantage of one over the other.

Reeling in the lure was smooth. You could feel this is a precision made reel. There was no gear rumble - smooth as glass. I was able to finely control the crankbait's depth and speed of retrieve.

By the crank is the star drag. On the 5500C I would have a little bit of a hard time adjusting the drag. The star was smaller and my fingers couldn't get much of a grip on it. The drag control on the Patriarch is big - almost kung fu weapon big. Easy to adjust but not in the way.

That's all I can say for now. I need more hours with the new reel and rod and different lures to see how it will work for me. The 5500C is a tank-like reel, big, strong and powerful. The Patriarch may have these features also but in the smaller package with the aggressive low profile shape it seems built more for finesse.

More to come... ask questions.

title: Very light and well built, but not for cold weather use.
text:
I loved how light they are. These are really well made poles, but I returned them unused. With no gloves on, I couldn't set the length, lock in place and lean on them to simulate a fall without them slipping. And no way could I lock them with gloves on. This is not a knock on the manufacturer. Twist lock mechanisms are bound to fail over time. These would probably be excellent in the summer when you are not wearing gloves. The foam handles are firm get giving. Not sure how absorbent the handles are.

The final thing I learned, which I'll try to confirm with other carbon poles, is that there is significant vibration when you smack a pole down (I was simulating on carpet). Man, these poles resonate! You feel it in your hands. This might not be a bad thing. For carbon fiber bicycles, the give in the material creates a dampening effect. This could be a great alternative to an active shock absorbing mechanism. We'll see...

UPDATE 02/12/2014
I bought Leki carbon poles and went did 4k+ vertical, 2k+ in snow. Yes, you want carbon. The lighter the better! I'm new to snowshoeing, so I fell a few times. They took the bend. The give in the poles is the right amount of dampening for me. Perfect.

title: Excellent chair at a good price, needs a couple tweeks to be perfect
text:
Very well designed chair. Very excellent value for people with back problems. At this price point you have to take a flyer with this chair if you have back issues!

My specific back issues allow me to sit in the chair for only a few hours. I let my chiropractor borrow the chair for a few days. Folks in the office either liked it or didn't.

I'm 6 feet. I definitely needed the accessory leg lift kit.

Two small issues:
1) The nuts that keep the metal retainer bar in place dig into fairly soft plastic and the torquing of the chair in use works the nuts loose. I'm always finding a nut on the floor and I have to re-tighten. Need to add a lock washer and firm up the plastic the nut interfaces to.

2) Two wheels come with locking mechanisms. No matter where you put these wheels you end up locking the wheels somehow. A couple Amazon reviewers recommend using the two back wheels, but I still lock one or the other. If you use the back wheels, then if you don't remember to check for locked when you sit down, then when you get up you will knock the chair over backwards since the chair is so light.

I found a workaround to #2. I Took pliers and twisted off the tab that controls the locking mechanism, then used a knife to shave off the locking lever plastic, to make sure shoes, etc. don't snag and lock the wheels. The locking mechanism still works fine, but now I have to use my fingernail to flip the lever. Problem solved!

I would definitely recommend you try this chair!

title: Will definitely buy again
text:
I bought this intending to keep it as part of my emergency supplies but ended up using it when I was laid up at home sick and didn't have the energy to go grocery shopping.

title: Tai chi ruler

I'm new to tai chi and this is my first ruler. Without experience of other rules to compare this to, I have to say that I'm satisfied with the product. I only have two complaints about the ruler, both fairly minor. One end of the ruler isn't quite finished. It's not so rough as to be unusable, but it's noticeable enough that I plan to sand it down and oil it. The other issue is that I didn't get a carrying bag like the one shown in the product description. To be fair, it's not something I need; I only mention it for shoppers who might want such a bag.

Overall, I'm pleased with my purchase, especially since I got a small discount on it. Experienced tai chi practitioners might disagree, but this is pretty much what I was hoping for and I look forward to learning how to use it properly.

title: Basically does what I need it to do
text:
I admit up front that I'm not using this to it's full capacity because my interests are more narrow: I don't want to check email or make calls from my activity tracker, I just want it to track my activities. However, more basic trackers proved to be cheap in quality as well as price, so the FitBit charge was a compromise choice for me.

For the things I care most about, it works well in general. It's good for tracking the activities I care about, and it only took it a few weeks to learn to recognize spontaneous activities that I sometimes do without starting the workout timer. It reliably buzzes to remind me to get moving every hour, another key feature that I needed, although I wish it were possible to set a goal of something like 10 hours out of 12 rather than a set number of straight hours. Still, that's a pretty minor complaint.

Sleep tracking seems to work okay, but I don't use it as much as I intended because I find sleeping with the band annoying. It's not uncomfortable; it's just not part of my sleep routine and I gave up on sleep tracking. I suspect that just knowing that I'm wearing it to track my sleep makes me slightly anxious, which in turn makes me less likely to fall asleep. However, for the nights I have worn it, the numbers seem to accord with my subjective experience of the night. One thing about this is that you have to be asleep for three hours before the tracking starts. I'm sure FitBit have good reasons for this, but it would be more useful to me if it started at the two hour mark.

The health metrics are interesting but aren't something I need.

I found the mobile app a little tricky at first but got used to it after several weeks. The website is nice for looking at everything on one big screen, but I don't have much use for it beyond that.

The GPS seems to work very well and consistently.

Battery life isn't great -- I charge mine at least every other day.

The band that came in the box was comfortable and worked well but broke after six months. Luckily, I was able to get a replacement from a third-party seller -- it's bulkier than the original but also more durable.

title: Fun but overpriced
text:
I've been using this for about two weeks now. It does what I bought it to do and I have a lot of fun using it, but there are certain flaws that lead me to say it's overpriced.

First the good: it's easy to put together and works as advertised. It took me a few tries to find the right fit (a little tighter than I first thought) and several practice attempts before I could get the weight spinning long enough for a good workout (but I was never that great at regular hula hoops as a kid). Playing with the length of the cord also resulted in a much better workout, and the catch is very strong; it holds whatever length I set no matter how hard or long I use it.

Snapping the links into position was moderately challenging, but my grip strength is relatively poor so no surprise there. Opening and closing the hoop for actual use is easy, and that's what's important. There's a novelty factor to this, of course, but I do find it fun to use, which motivates me to use it regularly.

Now the not so good: a few of the pieces arrived broken. Although I don't need those links now, it's disappointing that I won't have them in the future if need be.

A bigger issue is that this thing is loud -- not "wake the neighbors" loud but loud enough to disturb others in the house. I wasn't expecting it to be utterly silent, but neither was I expecting this rattling. This limits my use of it somewhat.

I got this as a cardio option other than walking or biking. I have posterior tibial tendonitis -- a fancy way of saying tendonitis of the ankle/foot; walking or running for long distances can irritate it, and biking isn't always an option for me. The weighted hula hoop is a very good alternative to these activities because I can get a good cardio workout without aggravating my PTT. Admittedly, I can't go as long with this as I can walking or biking, but I can make it a lot more intense. Besides, this is still kind of new to me, and I'm confident that I can build my stamina over time. Judging from the feel of the materials, though, I'm not sure how durable this device will be.

Prices here vary all the time, of course. I got this for about $35 altogether. Given the breakage, I'd say that was slightly overpriced; I certainly wouldn't advise anyone to pay more than that for this. It's a nice tool for your home gym, but I'd wait to buy it on sale or at least until February when most of us have left our new year's resolutions in the dust.

title: Great addition to my home gym
text:
I bought these in December 2019 and was very grateful to have them. Now it's December 2021, and I'm still working out at home with these as a key component of my strength training.

PowerBlocks can't compete with a full set of dumbbells like you get at commercial gyms, but they cover all of the major points that I need them to. Having my hands in a sort of box felt weird at first, but eventually I got used to it and can do most exercises as easily as I can with regular dumbbells. There are certain exceptions, like goblet squats. It's not that these moves are impossible, just extremely awkward. But this represents a very limited number of exercises.

There is a bit of rattle when the PowerBlocks are in motion, though they are secure. I don't think the rattle would be loud enough to disturb someone sleeping in another room with the door shut, though of course this is a subjective thing. When I compare it to the noise I'd make working with regular dumbbells, I'd say there's somewhat more because of the rattle (at least on fast move) but not at a high level.

Adjusting the weights is very simple and fast, but it is possible to misalign the adjuster so that it overlaps two weights rather than firmly latching onto one. This is easy to spot if you're paying attention, but note that it is possible to lift the weight when the adjuster is improperly set. I've done this a few times when in a hurry. At that point it's just a matter of setting the weight down and resetting the adjuster, but that's not something you'd want to be doing habitually for safety reasons.

After two years of use, the colored plastic bands on the tiers of weights are starting to get brittle and crack, but I'm not bothered by this. Actually, I'm surprised that these are holding up as well as they are given the humidity of my environment. More importantly, the metal is still in good shape and looks like it will continue to hold up for a long time to come.

With the weight levels properly set, the PowerBlocks are very stable and safe to use. I still wish this pair came out to 50 lbs rather than 48, but I think this is just how it is given the nature of the design. I'm lucky that I bought these before COVID hit, and I've certainly got my money's worth out of them.

title: Just couldn't make this work
text: Sending this back was a great disappointment because this tracker had the features I wanted and I quite liked the display. Sure, it would only do metric units and battery life was on the short end, but I didn't mind that. title: Still like new after one year's use
