title: Decent addition to my home gym
text:
I already had a Bowflex adjustable kettlebell that I liked a lot (though it's not perfect), but I wanted another adjustable kettlebell with lower weights for certain types of work. After four months of regular use, it's still in good shape and I'm glad I bought it.

Changing the plates is not as fast as on the Bowflex model, but it's easy, although the sliding tab sticks now and then. Still, it's fast enough for me to continue through a circuit without losing momentum, and that's what's important to me.

All the plates weight 2.5 lbs, and you can remove them however you like. That is, you don't have to take them from the top or the bottom. You will have to slot them back into the same place they came from, however, because they all curve in a certain way to give the kettlebell it's shape. The reviewer who mentioned sharp edges makes a good point, one worth considering for different exercises. For example, for swings it makes no difference to me where I pull the plates from, but if I'm doing shoulder presses, I pull them from the bottom or else I'll get my forearm unpleasantly poked and scraped as I use it. For a bottoms up carry, I find keeping the plates loaded at the top makes the weight more stable as I walk.

The plates make a slight rattle when swung -- that doesn't bother me, but it's something to keep in mind if working out within earshot of someone who might be disturbed by the noise. The plates do feel secure within the bell, but I still make it a habit to swing it so that the plates would fly away from me rather than at me if they came loose, and I swing them toward a wall or some other area where the plate wouldn't damage anyone. All that said, I'm sure I'm being overly cautious.

One thing I really like about this is the overall shape and footprint as compared to the Bowflex adjustable kettlebell. This one is a standard kettlebell size -- that makes it easier for me to handle, especially when it's in close to my body. The Bowflex is much larger, and that makes certain moves really awkward. It's not fair to compare these, though, given that they have very different weight ranges, but it's something I noticed. In those few places where the weights overlap, I almost always reach for this kettlebell over the Bowflex.

When buying exercise equipment, I'd much rather go to a shop where I can try it out in person and comparison shop. The pandemic made that impossible, so I crossed my fingers and hoped for the best. And it worked out. Even with its flaws, I've definitely gotten my money's worth for this.

title: Not perfect, but pretty close
text:
On the whole, I'm happy with my purchase and find it very useful when I'm riding. I've got a folding bike, which I love but limits my choice of mirrors. I tried different ones that attach to glasses or helmets, but I could never find one that quite fit; besides, I always worried they would drop off the moment I hit a bump. I figured the Myklops was my best option.

As others have noted, objects in this review are a heck of a lot closer than they appear. However, I've gotten used to this and find the mirror very helpful for spotting cars, trucks, and other larger vehicles in traffic. For spotting other bikes, skateboarders, and standing scooter riders (scooterists?), it's not as helpful. Being smaller, they're usually on me well before I pick them up in the mirror. Luckily, that's usually not a problem. With motorcycles and mopeds/scooters, it's a mixed bag. The bigger they are, they easier they are to pick out in the mirror. Usually it's the noise of their engines that I notice first, then I know to look for them in the mirror. So this mirror is helpful, but not as much as I'd like.

Sturdiness is hard to speak to without lots of time going by, but I've been using this regularly for over six weeks, tossing it into bags when I'm not riding with it, and it's holding up. I find the cover a little fiddly to close, but it does latch into place with a little patience. The biggest challenge was remembering to push the arms back into the base before taking by backpack off once I'd gotten to where I was going, but that's pilot error on my part. I don't yank at the arms or twist them hard, but neither am I super delicate with them. They feel the same as they did out of the package, so I'm hopeful that they'll last a while.

As for stability, I find the mirror to be very stable once I've extended the arms and positioned it how I like. The band sometimes shifts around my wrist as I ride, but I don't think this is a fault of the product. I usually wear long-sleeved shirts, the material of which is often a bit loose, so I need to be more careful about smoothing that down and not letting it bunch before fastening the strap. When I'm wearing shorter sleeves with tighter fitting sun gloves, the band stays in place. Also, I'm very pleased that the velcro on the band is on the gentle side. By that I mean that it doesn't have large teeth of the sort that often damage my clothes. Despite being careful, I sometimes catch my clothing on it, but so far (touch wood) it hasn't caused any pilling or tearing of the fabric ... and these are fairly delicate materials I'm talking about, so that's a major bonus.

I think it's impossible to make a perfect mirror that fits all my riding needs. But this comes pretty darn close. Funnily enough, as I sat down to write this review, I noticed that there's currently a nice little discount for it, no doubt for Black Friday/Cyber Monday/or other seasonal sales holiday here. I paid full price for mine, but I'm okay with that. At full price, I feel like I got my money's worth, and I would definitely buy this again.

title: Would buy again
text:
I've never been a regular wearer of helmets so I can't compare this to other brands, but this one suits me. The medium/large fits me well, and it's comfortable to wear throughout longer rides. It's also cooler than I expected, which is a real benefit as I live in a hot and often humid climate. And though it shouldn't matter, I like the simple design of this helmet as opposed to those that have a more aerodynamic look, so to speak. And I really appreciate the low-key logo; it's tasteful, not garish like you see on so many products.

But the most important thing for me is the fold. The main thing keeping me from wearing a helmet before was having to lump around a bowl. I know that's a bad reason, but it's the truth. This folds down enough to easily fit into all of my bike bags and even the small backpack that I often carry as a purse. Admittedly, it's a squeeze for the latter, and I don't carry much in that purse anyway, but the fact that it fits means that I'll use it, and using it is definitely safer than going without.

I was lucky to get a nice discount on this (for Prime Day, I think, though perhaps it was some other deal), but I think it's worth it at its regular price. Of course I hope never to give this the ultimate test, but it feels like a sound helmet and works for the way I bike. I'd definitely buy this again.

title: Just what I was looking for
text:
My use for this may be a bit unusual. I have an adjustable Indian club and needed something to put inside as a weight. I wanted something that would allow me to break the weight down into at least 0.25 pound increments but not so fine that I'd be sweeping up little bits of it every time I cleaned my floors (because, sooner or later, no matter how careful I am, I'm going to drop and scatter some of it). The material also needed to stand up to being thrown around inside the body of the club as I swung .

This stuff is perfect. It's large enough to easily find when I drop it but small enough to weigh out exactly in whatever increment I work. I weighed it out into 0.5 pound increments and put those into sandwich bags to make changing weights more efficient. Then I started a 21-day training program that required 100 swings per day. The bags needed replacing periodically -- which is understandable as that's definitely not what they were designed for -- but the pellets still look new. I should also note that I did not get 8 pounds as advertised; I got just over 8 pounds and 10 ounces.

I had no idea that plastic corn pellets were a thing until I started searching for filler for my club, but I'm very glad I found this. What I have now will keep me going for a while, but when I'm ready to up the weight, I'll definitely buy another box of this.

title: Nice little bag for my folding bike
text:
I've got a folding electric bike that I love, but I'm limited in the kinds of bags I can attach because a) the battery pack is mounted on the front and b) I have to think about how the bag might limit my ability to fold the bike (or how my need to fold the bike limits the kind bag I can mount). I wanted to buy a handlebar bag made by the company that makes my bike, but like so many items during the pandemic it was impossible to get. With some reluctance, I settled on this. Now I'm really happy that the company bag -- which was twice the price of this one -- was out of stock.

The velcro straps are strong and keep the bag in place even when I let the handlebars drop to fold away. Unlike some reviewers on here, the zippers have held up well for me so far, though the ones for the main compartment are still a bit stiff. I can use my phone easily through the transparent touch screen holder on the top, but getting it in and out of that pouch at first was extremely difficult. This has improved greatly over time, though. While my phone does fit even inside it's bulky case, it goes in much easier without the case on -- no surprise there, but it made me a little nervous at first. However, if I have my phone there on a ride, I leave it there and don't remove it until I get home and can return it to the case.

Since getting it, I've been caught in a couple of light rains and one heavier shower while riding with this bag. In all cases, everything inside the bag and it's various pouches remained bone dry. It does come with a rain cover, but that popped over my battery.

The only thing I don't like about the bag is that the stitching on the velcro patches on long exterior pouch (the one with the reflective stripe) aren't very well done. I don't use that pouch much, and I'm careful to slowly peel it open when I do, but I expect those to come off sooner rather than later. It was a bit disappointing to see the low quality work there when the rest of it is so well made, but there's more than enough space for me in the rest of the bag.

If I ever need to replace this bag, I'd definitely consider buying another one of these. The only thing I'd like to see changed (besides improving the stitching on that one pouch, that is) is to perhaps make the interior of the main compartment a contrast color rather than black like the exterior. Maybe that would increase the price a bit -- I'm sure it's cheaper to make everything the same color -- but I sometimes use the bag in low light conditions, and it can be a bit hard to find things. But even with the black interior, it's a good bag as it is and offers good quality at far better prices than many major brands.

title: Does the job
text: I wear these to keep my pants clear of the chain when I bike. I can't speak to the reflective quality as I only ride during the daytime, but it seems to do the job. The plastic clasp is holding up well to my opening and closing it multiple times a day, and the band comfortable to wear even on long rides. However, the band tends to creep down my calf no matter how I position it even though the adjuster itself seems to hold wherever I set it. Sometimes this means I have to stop to adjust the band to make sure to keep my pants leg clear of my chain. That's a little annoying, but I'm still glad I got it and feel like I got my money's worth. In fact, I'll probably buy it again to make sure I have one in every bag, just in case I forget to put it on before I go out.

title: One size fits all, some better than others
text:
Unfortunately, these just didn't work for me so I had to send them back. On the plus side, they're surprisingly well made for the cost. I used these regularly for a few weeks, rinsing them off by hand after every workout and throwing them in the washing machine a couple of times, yet they never showed any wear and tear. The padding on the palms was sufficient to prevent callouses from forming, which is the main purpose of hand protection for me for the gym.

Unfortunately, these were just too big. I'm a woman, 5'2", with hands proportional to my height. Other reviews mentioned having extra material on the palms, but I decided to risk trying these anyway since many buyers reported that this wasn't a big deal. That part wasn't a major problem for me either, but the finger loops were way too big. Also, I found that my palms tended to get sweaty while wearing these, though that decreased a bit over time; eventually, I think I would've gotten used to them and not sweated with them on, or at least not so much. Still, the oversized grips plus the tendency for my palms to sweat meant that I couldn't get a good grip, especially when lifting heavy or doing swings. That's why I ultimately returned them.

Although these didn't work for me, I think they could be a good option for those with slightly larger hands. If you're of at least average height, you'd probably be okay with these. And even if you're not, the generous return period means that you have enough time to test these for yourself at no risk. I understand that offering different sizes would likely mean a price increase, but I hope the company is able to do this one day. If they maintained the build quality, a small price increase would still make these grips good value for money, and I'd jump at the chance to buy a slightly smaller version of this product.

title: Excellent wrist support, inadequate palm protection
text:
The gloves fit fine and the build quality was good. It took a little playing around with the wraps to get the right amount of tension, but once I figured that out I found the wrist support to be excellent. Unfortunately, the palm pads didn't provide enough protection for me. I've no idea why as the padding felt more than sufficient for the job, but I continued getting callouses on my palms even using the gloves. The callousing was far, far less than I would have gotten with no protection, but the whole point of using gloves for me is to preserve my skin. My grip isn't unusually strong, and I've not had that happen with other good quality gloves. Most of my work with these gloves included kettlebells, dumbbells, and medicine balls, so I don't think it was the gear either.

Although I ended up returning these gloves, I think they could be right for other people. And I can't fault customer service since they accepted my return with no question. The time between receipt of the product and the return deadline is more than ample to try these out for yourself. If you're on the fence, I'd say it's worth giving these a go. It seems like most buyers really like the product, so odds are you may too and that I was just an outlier.

title: Somehow too big and too small
text:
I gave up gloves about 10 years ago in favor of pads/grips. It felt odd at first, but after a few weeks, I realized that I could never go back to using gloves. Gloves were bulky, bunched in the wrong places, and made my hands too sweaty and hot. Pads/grips gave me protection without adding bulk, were easy to take on and off when necessary, and held up longer. The only thing I didn't like was that they had a single strap that went across the back of the hand. Even if I laced my fingers through the strap, I could never get a firm enough hold to keep them on for things like medicine ball work. Everything else -- dumbbells, barbells, rowing, push ups -- was fine. So when I lost those grips, I ordered GymPaws because I thought that the individual finger loops would make for a solid grip.

Unfortunately, the GymPaws weren't a good fit for me. On three of the four finger loops, I could see daylight between my fingers and the material -- not a lot but enough that I felt the pads sliding when trying to do some fast work with the medicine ball. So GymPaws were too big for my fingers, yet they were also too small for my palms. I'm a woman, about 5'2", and my hands are proportional to my size, though obviously smaller than many other people's hands. The brand I used before GymPaws provided more coverage on the palm, but the GymPaws left a bit too much skin exposed at the base of my thumb. It didn't prevent me from getting a solid grip on the dumbbells, barbell, or rower, but it was often irritating.

Making a product like this has got to be difficult because you can only make so many sizes and still keep the price affordable. Having one size only is the easiest way, but then it's, 'One size fits all, some better than others.' For something like this, I think the only way to know is to order them and try them out for yourself.

Although I didn't like the product, I've got nothing but praise for their customer service. The return window is only 14 days, but you can return them even if they've been used. That's exactly what I did and I got my refund as soon as they received the package. Given that, I'd say that it's worth giving GymPaws a try. They didn't work for me, but they seem to work for a lot of people. Although I only had them a short time, they felt sturdy and well-made enough to last a while. But try them on every sort of gear you regularly use before the return window shuts, especially if you're transitioning from regular gloves.

title: Bright enough for day or night
text:
It's a wonder I didn't get myself killed riding around with that AA powered headlight for so many years.

This isn't even the brightest model they make and it's almost as bright as a car's headlight. It illuminates the whole trail or street. The side lights illuminate your controls a bit and provide better visibility from the side. The light is a crisp, neutral white. Not yellow or cold blue.

It's actually too bright on full for the bike trail. Even the lowest setting is fine. I rode unlit bike trails at night for years with a light that wasn't half as bright on full as the L&M 800 is on its lowest setting.

Riding in fog? Yeah, this headlight is bright enough to make you visible.

Treat your headlight like your phone and charge it daily. The only thing missing from this headlight is a really accurate battery level indicator.

You may not want this headlight if you're doing six hour rides in the dead of night. Or if you're riding so far out in the boonies you're miles away from an electrical outlet. Most city and town riders will love this headlight, as will bike commuters.

title: Good budget option for night rides. Great flash mode.
text:
If you need a taillight bright enough in solid mode for foggy/rainy daytime riding, this is probably not the taillight for you.

I used the old AAA powered Superflash for many years and it was good enough for my type of riding. Mostly unlit trails. Some city riding. I always used the flash mode which is very attention grabbing. Rain, fog, snow, whatever. Solid mode is still good on a clear night, but not for low visibility daytime conditions.

The old Superflash had a tendency to pop off when riding over bumps. Also had a flimsy switch.

This model has built-in batteries which means it's one solid unit that wont fall apart. The switch is improved as well. I don't think it's really any brighter than the old one.

Cosmetically it is improved from the old model due to the black plastic housing. White plastic looks grungy after a while.

I still consider the Superflash to be a good value for the money.

title: Not a good value with today's options.
text:
I have owned the Beamer 5 from Planet Bike for 8 years. The same one. I can give it points for durability but not much else. Years ago I would have given it a higher rating but there are many better headlights today for the same or a little more money.

The first problem is that you just cannot make a bright LED light powered by only two AA batteries. Every small and cheap LED flashlight I've ever owned used 3 AAA batteries. Even when this light was a newer model there were flashlights of just about the same size with much brighter LED emitters and better optics in the same price range. Only thing lacking there was an integrated handlebar mount.

Don't be fooled by the number of LEDs. The number of LEDs has nothing to do with how bright a headlight or flashlight is. The LEDs in this headlight can be bought in bags of 100 for less than the cost of shipping. A single, more powerful LED is almost always better because you can build a better reflector around it with a more coherent beam of light.

In today's market, there are many headlights that offer better value for the money. There are a great many options with built-in lithium ion batteries offering longer run times and more power that aren't much more expensive. In this day and age I would only be looking at a headlight run on disposable batteries as an emergency backup for long rides when you're miles between outlets to plug a USB charger into.

Now, I've run this headlight through everything from torrential rain to blizzards and so far as I can recall it hasn't failed me. It just never put out very much light. The weather sealing is a simple O-ring which can wear out, but the light is designed in a way that even if a bit of water got in it wouldn't really get near the electrical contacts.

It is just barely bright enough to illuminate a clean, paved, and straight trail on a clear night. It doesn't have a wide enough beam to light around corners.

It's not bright enough in the fog to be noticed by drivers. In a winter environment with ice patches and chunks of slushy debris everywhere, it's dangerously dim. Rather than a nice smooth beam of light you can see dim lights in the beam from the lens. Don't forget about other riders wearing all black at night with no lights. Or people walking their dogs on 20 foot leases wearing all black on unlit trails.

Realistically the Beamer 5 is about as bright as a $5 LED flashlight from the bargain bin. Far and away more durable, but still dim.

I've just compared the Beamer 5 to the Light and Motion Urban 800 headlight and the difference was comical! Now, this is a $90 headlight, compared to a $30 one, but anything less than 100 bucks that makes me safer on the road at night is a good deal. Do NOT go cheap on your lights. Getting a bargain on a light is not worth your life, or even a minor injury.

Pros:
Decent handlebar mount
Well sealed
Durable
Quick and easy to remove from mount

Cons
Dangerously dim in many conditions
Narrow beam
Poor optics leave visible dim lines through beam
No battery level indicator

title: It eventually failed, but I'll probably buy it again.
text:

Rule number two of lightweight bicycle components is everything must be installed with a torque wrench. If you read stories of Thomson components failing soon after purchase, the bolts have been torqued too much.

Seatpost looks sleek, though the setback version is an acquired taste. The adjustability is excellent and the side markers allow you to set your seat angle with a great deal of precision. I'll probably buy another one.

Cheap, light, durable. Pick two. That's the old joke. Thomson hits a certain sweet spot for price, light weight, and durability. But please see rules #1 and #2.

title: Incredible wedge - Can't recommend it enough!
text:
Being a lifetime hacker (22 hcp), I was reluctant to spend a lot of money on a wedge, but I was in need of one desperately. My short game is usually my downfall so I researched and found the Callaway Mack Daddy 2. I chose to go with the 60 degree "C" grind due to the fact that I love to hit flop shots as well as standard chips, pitches, approaches, etc. Check out the videos on callaway's website for more info on which grind is best for you.

The wedge comes in a matte chrome or slate finish. I chose to go with the slate finish as I liked the darker look and thought I would like the oxidation look as well. Looking back I think I would likely have chosen the chrome finish as it requires less maintenance. The slate finish will rust and require you to scrub off the rust as time goes by. Callaway recommends you keep a small patch of Scotch-Brite Purple in your bag for scrubbing it off. A lubricant cleaner can also be used to help keep the rust off the finish.

The handling of this wedge is amazing. As I said, my short game has sucked, partly because I haven't put enough time in and partly because my wedge always was a hand-me-down. After getting this wedge and practicing with it quite a bit I'm in love. I usually use hard covered balls because I hate losing a nice soft covered ball. Even with using a hard covered ball I'm able to get some pretty good backspin on the ball when pitching or approaching the green. Flop shots are incredibly easy with this wedge thanks to the "C" grind and I've improved nearly every aspect of my short game in part to this club.

The groves are the highest degree allowed by the USGA and the laser etched pattern really helps put extra spin on the ball.

Overall I love this club immensely. It gives you great control of the ball with whatever shot you are trying to hit. I'm planning on picking up a 52 or 54 degree wedge as well, in the future. Excellent club, can't recommend it enough!

title: Super comfy, installs in 30 seconds
text:
I'm REALLY pleased with this gel seat cover! I saw an ad for it in some local online newspaper, followed the link to Amazon, and checked it out! Reviews seemed fine, so I sprang for it. It's as good as it looks! Really thick gel that's the perfect cushion for my ROCK HARD bike seat. It appears very well made and comes with a "rain hat" to cover it.

I've comandeered my mountain bike to use as an exerbike during the pandemic year. I put that bike on a Wahoo KICKR, hooked it up to FulGaz virtual rides, pulled on my padded Pearl Izumi bike shorts and..... got EXCRUTIATING sciatica down my right leg for several weeks! I think it's cuz my ROCK HARD bike seat was killing that nerve as I ground away the miles. There's no other exercise I've done that would cause the sciatica. Once I got that painful issue under control with physical therapy, I got right back on the exerbike - but riding on this Zacro gel seat!

All I did is set the gel seat on top of my old bike seat and tie the straps it comes with in a square knot under the front end of my old bike seat; the back of the gel seat secures with a very effective drawstring to hold it snugly to the old bike seat. Took no more than 30 seconds to put it on! The seat does NOT wiggle, slide or shift out of position in a good 10-mi (50 min) ride. I have not had a single sciatica incident since using this gel seat, so I'm HOPING that took care of the problem.

Highly recommend this very practical, well-made gel seat cover for anyone who lacks padding where it counts and wants a comfortable ride.

title: NOT for swimming with snorkel apparently
text:

I had no lotion on my face or slippery stuff to loosen the cap. It felt VERY comfy on my child-sized head.

But. Minutes into my 40-min lap swim in the pool, I could feel water sloshing around my ears! I had earplugs in JUST IN CASE - but in no way do the flush design of the earplugs get in the way. My TYR earplugs fit in my ear canal with NO stick poking out.

Bugged, I kept swimming anyway. After my swim, I removed my cap and sure enough, a cup o'water poured out of the cap! The ear cups on this cap seem to HOLD water inside, and the seal on the cap appears not to be strong enough to keep water out. Again, it *could* be due to the snorkel mask and strap I had on, but really? I did better with a traditional swim cap with NO molded ears on it.

SO GLAD I kept my TYR earplugs IN, cuz that kept the pool water out of my ear canals. It would've been really gross to have that cup of pool water flushing IN and OUT of my ear canals for 40 min.

title: Great weight, ease and comfort for snorkelling
text:
I got my first Henderson Zip Shorty a couple years ago for snorkelling on the Big Island. It was SUPERB! There is simply no easier style for getting into and out of a wetsuit on hot, steamy days or peeling them off when they're all wet. It's super easy to step into one of the legs and then zip the shorty up as high as you like. There is JUST the right amount of give in the armpits so you can swim but not fill the suit with water. It's a brilliant design, actually. The 3mm thickness was absolutely perfect for swimming in HI's water - where temps averaged 71-74F for us.

After each use, I'd faithfully soak, then rinse the suit out with special neoprene detergent, then roll it in a beach towel and hang it up to dry in the shower stall. It would be clean, fresh, dry and ready to use within a couple hours - even in a humid place.

I wore a long-sleeved rashguard under mine for extra sun protection, but otherwise, was totally warm enough with great flexibility for swimming in this garment. At the end of our 3-mo stay in HI, I donated my Henderson - and the dive shop nearly cried for joy!

Flash forward 2 years, and I bought the identical suit for snorkelling on Kauai! If I was psychic, I never would've donated the last one, and now I'm going to be an optimist and keep this one!

CAVEAT!!! Be sure to soak, WASH, rinse your suit out before you try it on - seriously! I just wore mine for 10-15 min day one and woke up later that night with a shorty-shaped RASH on my skin. I only read about neoprene reactions after that - and immediately washed my new shorty. Err on the cautious side, cuz that was the one and only time I got a rash, and you can avoid that if you just wash it first.

Of course, if you don't want to remove the tags, you could also try your wetsuit on with a "skin" underneath - but be sure to wash that garment then to avoid any neoprene reaction.

title: Not enough SHADE or HEAD ROOM; corners need heavy weight to hold in place
text:
Ack, my husband and I just took our new Neso Tent down to the beach today ... and lasted about 45 minutes under scanty shade with not enough head room. We SO wanted to love this shelter, as it has a brilliant concept: idiot-proof setup and very transportable kit, with the fabric and two collapsible poles all in one tidy storage bag.

In looking at the videos and even pictures of this particular model of Neso Tent, it appears that WIND is a HUGE factor in one's satisfaction with the overall experience. Alas, we sat on a hot, sunny, windless beach by the lake, so we found the fatal flaw real fast: without wind to literally LIFT the fabric up in the air, it sits flat and low at back. We could barely fit our slim selves in two beach chairs under that fabric. With the poles lifting up the front, the back of the fabric slopes down so low that our heads literally poked into the fabric overhead like two beach balls. Duh.

Not only that, but even on a windless beach, you're gonna need some serious LEAD weight to hold the 4 corner ropes in place. We hunted around our beach and found 3- to 5-lb river rocks. Once you raise the poles under the fabric, it literally lifts the corner ropes up in the air unless they are weighted down GOOD. To show a few handfuls of sand tossed into each pouch doing the job is simply misleading, unless that sand is made from lead shot.

On top of which, in order to face the view - i.e., the lake - we had the sun slanting in from the side. As soon as we set the tent up, that meant that one of us sat with legs in the burning SUN the whole time. Yes, even with our chairs scooched back so far that our dorky heads poked into the fabric, the total shaded area of this fabric is simply too small, measuring about 6' square. We probably could've re-positioned the tent with our backs facing the sun, but then we would've been staring at two bikini-clad gals lying on their beach towel 5 feet away - kind of in-your-face? Nope. It was no go.

Frustrated, we packed the tent up and will be sending it back. I think the perfect beach shelter should actually be more like a camping tent, with full coverage overhead and multiple, collapsible poles strung through the structure. Ideally, this tent would have net sides to let the breeze come through (and probably filtered sun). Most of the tents I see here are simply too HOT and airless, cuz they're made more for all-weather camping. Or they're shelters like 8' tall and 12' wide, which - if the two of us parked that on our little lakeside beach - would encourage others to beat us with their rubbah slippahs.

Best way to enjoy the beach is to slather up in sunscreen, leave all the food, drink, books and stuff at home. Go with a towel and get in the water. Period.

title: Love this HRM's functionality, but it SERIOUSLY needs easier buttons to press - SERIOUSLY!
text:
Round TWO! I'd bought this identical HRM kit back in February 2014. From day one, I'd get WILDLY erratic readings on the heart rate - but that's ok, cuz I am actually from Planet Mars. No machine in any gym, nor any kind of heart rate monitor on Planet Earth works consistently on me. I either get zero reading (when my Martian paws are on the piece of exercise equipment) or I get rates that jump from 189 to 60 to 132, and so on. Don't tell the NSA, because I'm here on a secret mission: to see if my second purchase of this Polar FT60 HRM works. I should've registered my initial purchase back in Feb, but being a foolish optimist, I used the HRM daily - till it plain died on me long about August. I stopped getting any kind of reading between the transmitter and the device - even after new batteries were inserted. So I assumed it was a goner.

What I LOVE about this HRM:
- It gives me the data I need to stick with my fitness program: how many minutes spent in zone 1, 2, & 3 (based on initial VO2 reading and the 6-min fitness test I took first time I took it to the gym); my total calories burned and what percentage of them were fat; my average and max heart rate (which, on the first device I purchased gave the "accurately" bizarre ranges of 189 to 62, but I know why that is). That is ALL I need to know. I'm not a marathon runner or even daily runner. My goal is to burn 400+ calories in a variety of ways at the gym (or outdoors) on most days of the week. I don't need to know my footfall, cadence, how much foot is on the ground every nano-second, my GPS coordinate, or about 100 other functions that other HRMs provide (and which are no doubt of interest to the athlete wearing them).
- It's easy to find your VO2 (well, maybe it's based on a lame algorithm, but I have SOME number to work with)
- It's compatible with ALL the machines in my gym, so I don't have to keep looking down at my wrist every few seconds (like I did with the Garmin) to see what my heart rate is - a BIG plus!
- It's pretty intuitive to operate, once you spend 5 min learning the main buttons.
- It's a good-looking watch
- It doesn't drain the battery like some of the Garmin devices (unless you shut off GPS and turn the device off)

What I HATE about the device (Product Development: READ ME FIRST)
- the buttons are CRIPPLINGLY PAINFUL to press. It's ridiculous, but no kidding, I had to press the dang buttons against a flat, hard piece of granite counter to actually get them to depress.
- OUCH! OUCH! OUCH! OUCH! OUCH! I have short nails, but they'd just slip off the button if I used them, so I use the fleshy tip of my now CRIPPLED, broken finger to press the idiotically STIFF buttons on this watch. I mean come ON: spend a nickel more and get some decent springs under these buttons, so I don't get arthritis from pressing them every day.
- These painful buttons drove me to THROW the whole kit away when it stopped working (my duh) and go buy a Garmin HRM right here at Amazon.com. Unfortunately, that device seems to require a PhD in Rocket Science to call up the right screens to find the few bits of data I was interested in. PLUS that device also gave very erratic readings, given that it was not made for a Martian, but rather an Earthling.
- I think that for the money paid, the Polar FT60 should *in theory* last longer than a scant 6 mos? The warranty is for 2 years, but I've read elsewhere (mostly from a few years back) that other folks complained about their device conking out.

I'm going to register this HRM and take good care of it, cuz despite the NUMBINGLY PAINFUL buttons, it is the only device that gives me the exact data I want to see after each workout.

Please Polar: Make these buttons easier to press, huh?

title: ROCK SOLID!
text:
The UPS deliveryman carried this box to the front door with ease, but I quickly learned that a 108 lb., smooth, cardboard box is NOT that easy to maneuver. So just be aware this is a heavy shipment!

I was worried this was going to be a cheap and flimsy bike, but that's not the case in any way! This thing is welded, heavy gauge steel with a thick paint job (probably not powder coated). The handles are equally solid with a thick rubber grip, probably hot dipped. Basically, no amount of sweaty hands are going to cause the grip to deteriorate. The mechanics are practically silent.

Assembly is a cinch. There are 4 bolts used to attach the feet, three adjustable handles to attach the seat and handle, and two pedals to screw on. All of the required tools are in the box.

I've only ridden on it once, but the seat is soft (not that it matters if you're standing). The electronic display is of utmost cheapness, though. I was afraid that I was going to break it when installing the (included) AA batteries. It provides very basic information such as time, distance, "speed", and "calories" but there is no input for height and weight.

I'm waiting on a cadence sensor that will attach to one of the crank arms, and plan to use that with an app to get better feedback on pace. I also downloaded the Peloton app (30 day free trial) and was able to follow along just fine with the beginners ride. The resistance knob doesn't have a numeric scale (just +/-) so you'll have to judge for yourself based on how it feels.

Final thought is regarding the maneuverability. The front wheels are a bit small and made of a hard plastic so it will be hard to roll across carpet. You can tell from the photo we have a hard floor, and if it gets caught on debris, it may easily get stuck or scratch the floor.

Overall, I'm impressed with the build quality, assembly and performance. Only negatives are the ultra cheap display, lack of any integrated wireless technology (BYO), and the small wheels to move it around.

title: I am IMPRESSED!
text:
I ordered another titanium bottle last week and was extremely underwhelmed. I was afraid I'd have to spend $150 to get the Vargo version of this, but nope!

The quality on this bottle is impeccable. This isn't thin titanium, this feels closer to my Ti bike frame than the other bottle I'll be returning which felt closer to aluminum foil.

Pros:
It's made of titanium
It weighs 8.6oz/243g (for comparison, a Hydroflask 40oz is 19oz/538g)
Compatible with Hydroflask or Nalgene lids.
Great matching and finish

The machining and finish is really impeccable - easily as good as anything I've seen.
The lid and mouth in particular are incredibly precise - the little lip that retains the o-ring is EXACTLY flush with the o-ring. The lip of the mouth is rounded on the outside and chamfered on the inside. Of course the lid alone is 2oz/57g, so if you REALLY want to go lightweight, get yourself a plastic lid.

Cons:
It's heavier than it probably needs to be. This thing can take a beating, but... does it need to? I don't think it needs to be this thick-walled. Heck, just make it double-walled at this point, with a thinner inner wall.
The lid is a bit noisy, likely because the threads have the same texture as the rest. I wonder if you polish the threads, it'd be quieter.

Let's be real... this is overkill. Realistically, if EDC is your goal, you don't need this, just get a Hydroflask. If you're trying to go UL for hiking/backpacking, you need a reservoir/water bag/Hydrapak, etc.

But if you like nice things, things that feel good in the hand, have the right balance of light weight and solidity, and have a great finish... you can't go wrong.

title: I used the 1-liter for a 1-bag trip and loved it.
text: For what it is, this is a really nifty vessel for drinking water from. I used it recently for a trip where I wanted to take only one backpack with all of my clothes and gear. While I *probably* could have crammed a water bottle in my bag, this definitely was a defining factor between making my bag too tightly jam-packed and just right. It becomes practically nothing and so lightweight when it's empty. Surprisingly, it stands well on its own when filled and due to the shape and rigidity of the sides, you can pick it up relatively comfortably and tilt it like a normal waterbottle. Of course, you can also only partially fill it, which makes it rather "flat" and slides into a small space on my backpack, which is great. It can make it a little more awkward to drink from. Ultimately, I wouldn't say this is "the best one handed water bottle" and it certainly isn't insulative and it surely can't be the most durable or the easiest to clean. But if you're just looking for a water bottle that can slip away into nothingness but be at the ready, I was more than happy to use this for a week+. Especially for the price. title: Best tent experience ever! (6 person version)
text:
You can stand up in it. All of it. The ceiling is super high. Laugh at all the other dome tents that require crawling into, that you might be able to awkwardly stand just in the middle!

The door is wonderful. Going in and out of the tent has never been easier. It actually acts stiff like a hinged door would, making quick pops in and out so much easier than with a floppy zipper door. This of course does have a zipper the whole way around (which works smoother than my other cheaper tents) with flaps to block rain. Not only is the door action flawless, I was impressed with how it kept bugs out without using the zipper. While we definitely zipped up when not using it for extended periods, we could easily rely on the velcro and stiffness popped up under the rain flaps to make a fairly decent seal. It wouldn't keep tiny crawly bugs out, but it definitely does a good job keeping flying bugs out.

The windows in this thing are awesome. There's like seven of them and they simply zip up and down as panels. They're great to gaze out of on a lazy afternoon. They work well to keep rain out, too.

The rainfly (roof) also works well. Although it seems like it doesn't cover much but the top, it doesn't really need to do much more. In fact, we didn't even use the rope tie-downs for it - the velcro seemed to keep it plenty taut. We had moderate short bouts of rain overnight and it was 100% dry inside.

The closets do add a nice bit of space, though they look a bit weird on the 6-person version. They're nice to shove things out of the way. There's so much space in this tent compared to other tents I've been in. My last "4-person" tent isn't really that comfortable for two people. This is luxurious for two people. We called it our little airbnb in the woods.

Also, I LOVE THE COLORS. The thing just looks awesome.

Setup is moderately more complicated than a simple 2-rod dome tent but it's actually quite clever and intuitive. I set it up by myself (awkwardly in my basement, it was wet out) as practice. Basically, a spidery bit arcs out 6 (I know, not 8, not a real spider) flexible rods, which meet in a macaroni-type elbow at each corner and mid-front and back. Stiff poles prop up each side/corner and meet at the elbow. That's really the fundamentals. The rest is just clips and rainfly and extra rods for the door and closets. It's REALLY fast with two people, especially if you know what to do.

The paper instructions are kinda hard to parse, so I definitely recommend a practice setup so you're not caught in a rainstorm doing it for the first time. Youtube videos were helpful for me here.

One of my flexible rods actually shattered as soon as I tried to use it. Luckily it was just for one of the closets - not a big deal at all, it just looked weird on the outside. I'll have to figure out how to get a replacement. I hope that isn't happening for one of the structural rods on anybody's.

I didn't originally realize there was a 6-person version of this tent and almost bought the 8-person. There's only two of us and I'm really glad I went with the 6. Not only is it much cheaper, it's still got loads of space even with a queen airbed in there. I'm sure if we needed to accommodate another person or two it would have been little issue and still have been comfy. (Yes, I'm sure you could cram 6 people in if you really wanted.)

I'm really enamored with this tent. It was my girlfriend's first time camping and we had an amazing 3 days and nights with this tent!

title: Severe rash from band
text:
I had high hopes for this device. I think it's aimed at people who don't want a gadget to play with, but a useful and attractive minimalist activity tracker. It qualifies as attractive and, if all you want to do is count steps, it is useful. Ultimately, I had to quit wearing it because it caused a severe rash on my wrist under one side of the band. I have reached out to Withings and I will update this review when my issue is resolved (or not). At this point I just want to return it for the following reasons:

1. The rash was severe. I've now gone 2 weeks without wearing the watch and it has barely diminished. I'm not allergic to silicone, so I wonder what chemicals are in or on the band.
2. The lack of contrast between the hands and the face result in a watch I can only read in good light. In a dimly lit room it is completely unreadable.
3. A big reason the watch appealed to me is that I can wear it while swimming. It is supposed to log swim time, but it was unreliable to the point of being useless for this purpose.
4. I was intrigued by the sleep tracking, but it has quirks that make me doubt it's usefulness. For example, if I sit on the couch reading or watching TV for an hour before bed, sometimes it logs this as sleep, including deep sleep.

The watch counts from 50% to 20% less steps than my Samsung app. I can't say which is more accurate. I like the idea of an elegant and simple tracker/watch, and this was almost it. Ultimately nothing else matters because I can't wear it. The negatives add up to the point that I'm not interested in resolving the rash problem with a different band.

Update: I reached out to Withings. They responded quickly and seemed genuinely concerned. They dealt with my problem promptly and fairly. I'm upping my review from 2 stars to 3 stars because of the customer service.

I bought this hiking stool, to see if it would work well for this purpose.

I can happily report that for me, it works PERFECTLY for this task! I do not need back support while meditating, and for my height (5'6") I am able to sit on this stool with my legs at a comfortable roughly horizontal position to the ground. For a taller person, you may have to cross your legs, and they will not be horizontal to the ground, but that may be OK for you.

The stool is lightweight (I have no problem carrying it around for several hours, and there's a handy strap so it can just be slung over my shoulder) and presents no issues as a hiking companion. I did a nice sit with it yesterday for an hour in the woods at a park here in Baltimore. Lovely!

While there are a couple of inflatable zafu-style meditation pillows available on Amazon, I actually think for my purposes, this stool is superior. It will continue to come with me on hikes I intend to meditate during. I got mine on Prime Day, and I think it came to roughly five dollars with a ten dollar discount. text:

I am male: 5'7" - 155-160 lbs - 30-32" waist. I thought I would end up in a Medium because normally I wear Medium in most everything and buy pants with a 31" or 32" waist; but once I tried on the Medium, I was concerned it would allow a little too much phone-bounce (I have an iPhone 6S). So I purchased the small, and it fits me great. If you are not sure of which size to get, I would go smaller. But it also depends where you plan to wear it. If you are going to wear it at or below your hips (vs. your waist), you may want to buy true-to-size or even size up a size. The company has a great return policy, according to the FlipBelt website, should you end up with the wrong size. And if you get it on Amazon or REI, I doubt you would have trouble exchanging sizes as long as you didn't wait too long.

I took a photo of the sizing chart since everyone seems to be posting pictures of sizing charts. I guess there was some sort of sizing misprint a while back?? Anyways, the sizing chart I used worked great.

Overall, this is a great product that is made in the USA, according to the tag. I am very happy and will update this review should any issues arise (which I am not expecting).

title: They thought of everything
text:
This is the lightest tent I've ever had. My back is broken. I can't carry hardly anything. But at a pound and a half, I can finally carry my own tent. And it's so easy to put up. Most trekking pole tents require you to estimate the stake placement and possibly have you move the stakes multiple times (I'm in the desert with hard rocky ground, no way.) They also require multiple guylines just to keep it upright. Not this tent. 4 to 6 stakes, two poles... good night. The washers to protect the ultralight weight fabric from the trekking poles was a long time coming in the camping world. A vestibule large enough to cook in. Built in guy outs. Huge vents.... that you can open and close... from the INSIDE! You can clip and unclip the inner tent from the outer... from inside the tent! And lastly, when its raining you have THE ABILITY TO PUT UP YOUR OUTER TENT AND INNER TENT FROM THE OUTSIDE. Keeping your sleep area dry.
It's ultralight and it sets up ultra fast. And it's the most affordable tent in its class, but, in my opinion, they created a class all their own. I've never seen a single tent do so much, weigh so little, and be so affordable. I think its going to be my forever tent.

text:
These are impressive laces. They are stiff, strong and can be pulled tight. I have been using two new pairs in mid and full size hiking boots that were a little large and I wanted them too fit snugly. They are working fine except for the length (longer than should be for the boots) and the bows can slip. I have been experimenting with tightening and using double knots. Each pair came with a different cord lock The metal one designed by Rhino so far seem too complicated to use and is time consuming setting it up. The plastic ones already broke. So, I like the laces and they are working the way I expected. I do need to master a better way to tie them.

1/5/15-After using these laces (two pairs on high and low hiking shoes), or trying to use these laces for 6 weeksI have given up and replaced them with waxed hiking laces. As noted, the two different style cord locks that were sent with each pair of laces didn't work, I then bought two other styles of cord locks, which were useless. As a result I had to continue to double knotting them, which prevented slippage and untying but due to the stiffness (like wires) I had to repeat the tying process several times, which was time consuming, and because of the stiffness of the laces, couldn't tie them tight-in fact that were always loose.

Basically, these laces will work for someone that is concerned about exposure to fire-I was not. I bought them because I try and support Kickstarter products and assumed that they would work. They did not for me. Over time the laces develop kinks, like wires and this memory remains. The result s very frustrating if you knot them, as I did.

I assume that they would work as intended with an appropriate cord lock, which I gather the inventor of the laces is trying to develop.

title: Finally a legible display! Plus a 2-Year Update
text:
A winner at last. I like it and recommend it. My F11 was a confusing, hard-to-read, and somewhat inflexible Polar monitor. This FT60 makes up for those past frustrations. The display uses bold characters and is easier to read. No longer do I have to deal with those awful timed training sessions such as Normal 1, Short 1, etc., ad nauseum. Now I can exercise as long or little as I like in a week and if I'm being a little too carefree the watch will suggest what I should be doing differently to stay on track to my goals. This monitor is, as you have seen, rather expensive but if you are really serious about wanting to pursue a healthy or more healthy lifestyle I think this is a worthwhile purchase. My only minor complaints are that I dislike Polar's wrist bands as a matter of personal preference. I like a watch to be able to lie flat and face up but you can't do that with the fairly stiff, curved Polar band. A washable woven nylon band would be nice perhaps with a Velcro closure. I wish the monitor's beeps were louder (even when set on Very Loud) as I really can't hear it well but my ears are old so that's just me. I like the accessories available that may be useful to me should I purchase them in the future. I am happy with this purchase and recommend it.

2-YEAR UPDATE:

Well, I've had this trainer for a bit over 2 years. It is still working fine. I've replaced the battery twice myself and did not suffer any problems from that experience. The watch back is a bit hard to unscrew. I have done it with a large flat-bladed screwdriver (really large). The best tool to use is a spanner wrench which is two pointed rods mounted to a crossbar. This makes the back very easy to remove. I got mine here at Amazon. It is sold by Micro-Tools and costs less than twenty dollars. It occurs to me that if you have needle-nosed pliers, you could hold the jaws open just wide enough to fit the tips into the holes around the cover. Twisting the pliers should spin the cover open.

I also recommend putting a little silicone grease on the o-ring before you screw it back together to keep water out and to make it easier to remove next time. Don't bother trying to remove the o-ring too as it is fragile. Leave it in place on the battery cover and just smear a bit of grease on the cover's threads and the surface of the o-ring. Don't use petroleum jelly.

I know from reading the reviews that some folks have had disastrous problems after replacing the battery. I've found that my watch remembers all my workouts and training data after replacing the battery. I did have to enter the date and time again. If you have problems after changing the battery you can try a 5-button reset. Just hold all the buttons down for maybe 15-seconds (I'm a little fuzzy on how long exactly; the procedure is in the manual, though) and the watch should come back to life and will only lose the date and time. I have heard good things about Polar support if you get into real trouble. I've heard it is a waste of time trying to e-mail them. The way to go is just to call them.

I've replaced the battery in the transmitter once and I'm not sure it really needed it but it seemed like a prudent thing to do after a year. No problems with that at all.

I still like this monitor very much. I feel that Polar supports it well with their website and forum. Also their training videos are informative and helpful. The training programs are sensible and I have lost weight and built up my stamina using this product. It still looks like new. Unfortunately, the crystal is a cheap piece of soft plastic and easy to scratch. I only wear my watch during workouts so I have only a few scratches. If you are going to wear this a lot you might want to take precautions against scratches. (Plastic polish does a good job of mitigating the scratches.)

title: Awesome ride-- our first electric bike and we are loving it
text:
At first, the power and quickness of the electrical assist surprised me, but I got comfortable in no time. I hate to admit it, but I find myself using the electric mode (which requires no pedaling) more and more everyday. It is much like a scooter and very fun. Overall the bike handles like a cruiser and pedals with ease given 7 gear options. The shifter works well and does not get hung up too often. 

The bike is heavier with the battery but it is not that noticeable. The battery can also be removed when you know you won't be using it, or when you're charging it. It is GREAT that this has disc brakes to slow down the power of an electric bike. I kept track and for over one week, 1 hr/day, ~15 miles using assist and electric only mode, the battery indicator shows half life. It folds down to a more compact size, which is so useful if you want to transport it in your car, or fold it up for storage.  We got this initially for grandma to be able to keep up with the kids.  It turned out to be too high for her legs at the lowest setting (she's 5'1"").  My wife (5'4"") has no issues and loves using this bike with the kids. Overall, we never expected to be so won over by electric bikes; this is a great ride, and at a great price for what you're getting. There are other 'bells and whistles' included like a very loud alarm and front/back lights/accessories that add to overall biking safety and comfort.

Unboxing the bicycle was easy and the package included all the tools needed for assembly. It took about 30 minutes to put together (handle bars, seat, front wheel, fenders, pedals, air pumped into tires). There was no instruction manual in the box and the QR code led to nowhere, but I was able to find how-to videos on other similar models.  I also later found that they emailed me some tips, which were helpful.  Speaking of the seller, we contacted them because of an issue with the battery and they resolved it quickly; we were happy to see that they offered good customer service. Would be a perfect commuter's bike.

title: Multi-functional hand warmer, flashlight, massager, and power bank in one
text:
I have switched our family to electric hand warmers and am not turning back. My kids were putting the disposable hand warmers ('hotties', the kind you shake up to activate) on their faces and it made me realize how toxic those must be, and how much trash we are making by using them. This particular item is one of the fancier ones we've purchased. I got the pink color; it is shimmery pink, and the part that goes around the outside of the hand warmer is a shiny, metalic looking pink (although it is plastic). It serves as a hand warmer, a flashlight, a power pack (comes with cord), and a vibrating massager.

- Press the button once for power (four blue indicator lights show battery life)
- Press and hold for heat (press again to change between 3 heat levels)
- Press twice for flash light
- Press three times for vibration

Once you're using the heat setting, you'll see it starts you off at the highest setting (60- this one is too hot for me). I usually use the middle (50) or low (40) heat settings. I like that it has a wrist strap for added security. I'll also add that the size of this item is bigger than others we have so it doesn't fit as well in my hands but is a good size for my husband. The size probably also contributes to it's power and longevity of the battery pack. As for weight, the difference is negligible. My whole family loves these electronic, rechargable hand warmers and we don't leave the house without them anymore now that it is cold (the cold has not slowed down my kids from playing outside for hours at a time)!

title: Awesome light show via our kids' bikes while they exercise-- well made and entertaining!
text:
(This is the 3rd set of various bike lights we've tried, so we feel like we can really talk to this item)
I have two kids who love to ride their bikes; I put one on each of their front wheels and they LOVE them. Each theme/mode is on for a few seconds then it switches seamlessly to the next. I like that I'll never have to change the batteries.  When the batteries run out, recharge them using one of the many USB cords you probably already have, or the pair that come in the box. Also, the lights are motion activated, so you can simply leave the switch 'on', and the lights come on when the bike starts moving (and turn off when stopped).

Very easy to install and I really like that they don't need to be screwed onto the air valve-- this is great because I don't need to worry at all about it causing leaking air from the tire.  The on/off button is easy to access and press, unlike other bike lights we've had-- where you have to press the plastic covered ball HARD and also change out the batteries (and those other ones are always sliding down too).  The changing colors/patterns are awesome; we are the envy of the neighborhood right now.

title: Wow, my favorite!  Beauty of a stainless tumbler - so nice to use.
text: I just have to say, I love this stainless tumbler.  It is 30 oz and has a pleasantly tapered shape, with smooth, comfortable indentations at the bottom third of the cup.  It keeps things very cold and hot, like other stainless vacuum tumblers, but the smooth dented grip really sets this apart.  30 oz. is too big for hot beverages (for me), but I love having cold water or even iced tea/coffee out of this one, with plenty of ice.  It is easy to stay hydrated even in steamy Northeast summers, because this preserves its cool even in the car.  I have a number of other stainless vacuum bottles/flasks/tumblers, by various other manufacturers - and this one is the nicest in my hand, by far.  While I have large hands for a woman, this should be comfortable for most every adult.  I tried another 30 oz tumbler by another manufacturer, and it is simply too big to be held comfortably (and is being sent back).  If you are in the market for a stainless vacuum tumbler that will be enjoyable to use as well as thermally effective, would suggest this one over the (many) competitors out there.  There is also a nicely fitted rubber or silicone pad inset in the base, so this sits softly on surfaces.  Due to the thermal properties, there is zero condensation - today is a 100% humidity day, and the exterior is dry as a bone even though it's filled with ice.  A keeper!  Hand wash only (like all similar ones).  Hopefully they will make it in other colors, would definitely buy another one.  And it would make a great gift for a number of people I know.

title: Requires a air compressor with a HUGE amount of PSI.
text: I'm a diesel mechanic I work on things everyday at work. Hydraulics are something I deal with on a regular basis. I figured swapping these out would be a easy though a moderately technical adventure. So I ordered them and set them aside with my leaky brakes waited till I had a friend over whom had the same brake set. Perhaps I could teach my friend thru my rebuild in the case he needed to rebuild his in the future. So we sat down one night and went for it... I got the small air compressor from the garage and brought it into the basement shop. I figured the reviews here stated some guy mentioned the possibility of doing it  with a bike pump how bad can it be. The AVID manual makes it sound so easy. Face the caliper piston down to a rag in one hand use compressed air to unseat the piston. Well we shot 70 PSI... nope waited for it to charge some more. 90psi nope... At this point we were really struggling to hold the blow gun against the caliper and not have any leaks. So we decide the little air compressor was no longer going to pull it off. I run the air hose from my 125 psi unit in the garage. I think this time the piston will move for sure. I pin it up against the basement wall put my whole weight into the rubber tip of the blow gun. Pull the trigger, no leaks at all no movement of the piston at all. Friend decided he would try with pliers while I was off taking a leak, despite me knowing full well that it would crack with all the warnings on this site. He wound up chipping the piston. The kit looks quality as its OEM but man its really bad to install. I'm still left brainstorming ideas of how to remove the piston. I ended up getting thru the riding season this winter its going down. Almost need hydraulic pressure air compresses.

title: Insanely slippery
text:
The first time I received this product, it was packaged badly so had some unnatural indents that weren't going away. After a few days, I complained to Amazon and they promptly sent me a new one. The new one was in perfect condition, and I was very excited to try it out. I diligently did the salt scrub that they suggest in the instructions, then gave it a try once the mat had dried.

IT WAS SO SLIPPERY. Like insanely slippery. I do not have sweaty hands or feet, and have never had a problem on cheap yoga mats. I am very disappointed that when I finally decided to invest in an expensive yoga mat, I'm met with all of this unnecessary slipping and sliding. It is slippery to the point where it is actually dangerous to use.

I went online and found that this is a very common problem, especially with the prolite mats. I'm now starting on the arduous journey of trying to 'break in' this mat - a process that people say can take months to a year of intense use. Some people online said that they had more success using some soap as well. I have just recently done a very hard scrub using laundry detergent and salt to try to get rid of what they call a "protective film from the factory" that is causing the slipperiness. This process involves finding an outdoor area, spreading your mat flat, sprinkling salt, then scrubbing the mat using the rough side of a sponge for at least 10 minutes with the laundry detergent or dishwashing soap. I will update this post with how many times I have to do this process to make the mat sticky (hopefully not too many times! I might end up giving up and buying a different brand if it takes too much effort)

I really want this yoga mat to work, so I'm going to sacrifice some time and energy into 'breaking it in' just because so many people have told me how their manduka yoga mat has been life changing for their practice. I am still disappointed that it takes this much time and energy though. For how expensive their mat is, the company should be doing the break-in process for us.

Unless you are willing to put in the time and energy to 'break it in' - don't purchase this product. I have heard the Pro (heavier) yoga mat is not as bad as the prolite with it's break-in process, but I haven't bought the pro so I wouldn't know.

Out of the box, this mat is unusable with how slippery it is.

I was concerned about it not being able to hold enough weight and did not trust the fact that it requires no screws but I haven't had any issues with it whatsoever. As long as it's installed properly, you won't have issues either!

To install the bar, just twist it and keep twisting until it locks into place. Tighten as much as you! Now try to make sure you do your pull-ups in the opposite direction of the twist. Otherwise each time you use the bar, you're pulling it and loosening it. Keep this in mind when installing it so you're able to do your pull-ups in the direction you want to be facing.

title: Perfect for cycling; reasonable for running

While cycling, I've almost never had any slippage or inaccurate readings, so I can't complain there.  While running though, the band's enclosure system is more difficult to synch tight and keep properly when you're running and sweating heavily.  It's a detriment of soft straps, but my old Garmin had pads that 'stuck' more to you.  All in all though, I'm super pleased; my work-around is just to make it really tight and then it'll loosen a bit as I run.  Data quality is very high (have compared to other HRM simultaneously)

title: Most Comfortable Helmet Ever
text:
I just received this from my wife as a Christmas gift. I have gone on 3 rides ranging from 20-60 miles and this helmet is great. A few months ago I went into my favorite local bike shop asking about helmets because I seem to have an unusually large head......yea, a mellon head. The unique helmet features a "adjustment dial" that will fine tune the fit to your head with laser percision. This helmet is much lighter than my old Bell I used to wear. You might not notice this on a 10-20 mile ride but if you ride any longer distances you will feel it. During the summer months, I live in Michigan, I try to do one century a month and ...BOY, I can hardly wait to do my first one this year. Another very important feature about this helmet is ....IT LOOKS COOL!! Even my niehbor who likes to make fun of cyclists because of there "pointy hats" said this one looks cool.

Don't look at another helmet. This is the best I've EVER worn. If you cycle a lot, don't hesitate. It's a bit more money but for the serious cyclist it's worth every penny. I try to ride at least 100 mile a week during the good months. If you ride simply with a family or short distances you might want to concider a cheaper model.....unless you have a big fat mellon head like me.

title: Great lantern for a great price
text:
I got this product in the mail and was very impressed. It is a great lantern for the price. And it uses 3 AA batteries instead of D cell batteries.

Build - It is built very well. It is a sturdy construction that can withstand normal use and some heavier use. it is not indestructible but based on the price I would not expect that.

Convenience - This lantern is a good size. And when you store it away you just push the lid down to turn it off and it compacts to a smaller size to take up less space.

Low power - It uses 3 AA batteries and will stay lit for 12 hours. Once the batteries get to a certain point the lights dim to conserve what little power is left in the batteries. I do wish that the LED lights were is sections so once a section is pushed in so far that section turns off so it saves batteries and is less bright than you need it. but that would make the price go up.

Handles - I like that the handles will fold down when not in use and you can use the handles to hang the lantern however you need to hang it. The handles are metal and are somewhat sturdy. I think the handle could be better. Make it a hard plastic and build it into the lid.

All in all this is a great little lantern and I love that is runs off AA batteries. I will get a lot of use out of it.

title: I like this so much I bought two
text: I know I should drink more water. I want to keep a bottle handy at my desk so that I don't have any excuses, but I hate that less-than-fresh taste of water that's been sitting around, even for a day. This Larq bottle solves the problem by using UVC light to kill any germs left from sipping your water. Don't be fooled; there are a lot of imitators, but THIS one has actually been tested and works to keep your water fresh. I have one for my desk, and 1 in my bedroom.

title: It really keeps the water fresh
text:
It's important to first say that I returned this large bottle and bought the smaller bottle BUT the functionality is the same. I want to keep water handy but I hate the taste and smell when water in plastic bottles sits around. I was already aware of the value of the UV-C light zapping bacteria, so I was curious as to whether this bottle was worth the price. The short answer is Yes. I like that it's stainless steel rather than plastic; it will keep water cool for several hours (I usually put the bottle in the fridge overnight). And having left the bottle out and unrefrigerated several days after drinking from it, I again found the water to be as fresh as if I had just filled it. So it does work!

Be aware, there are a LOT of copy-cat bottles on the Internet that do NOT do what the Larq bottle does (nor have they been tested to prove they kill the bacteria). Spend your money on THIS one if you can find one -- they've been sold out lately. Good luck!

title: MAJOR disappointment over previous editions
text:
I was expecting to be disappointed by this map because for decades, New Hampshire and Vermont were two separate atlases. The 2015 edition is the first time the two states have been combined into one.

Here is what has happened:

THE GOOD
- colors are awesome and are a huge improvement over previous editions. I'm very thankful for this.
- the northern NH roads and roads in wild/remote areas have generally been significantly improved
- names of many streets have been added (although many were also removed - see below)

THE BAD AND AWFUL
- over 75% of the waterfalls listed in the previous editions have been removed (this makes no sense to me)
- more than 50% of the zoomed-in city/town maps of the previous editions have been removed, including the busy tourist town of Manchester, Vermont (this was a huge disappointment)
- more than 50% of the small streams/brooks have had their names removed (this makes no sense to me)
- many major tourist attractions still are not listed (how on earth is Diana's Baths and Santa's Village STILL missing from these maps?)
- many small streets in rural areas have had their names removed (another huge disappointment)

Garmin bought the DeLorme company a few years ago and I'm hoping a major overhaul of these maps takes place. There is a lot of room for improvement. Overall, this map gets a C/C+ whereas previous editions were B-.

title: I WANT MY MONEY BACK. BROKE EASILY AND DEFECTIVE. HAD TWO!
text:
My first Charge 2 was wonderful until it stopped reading my HR correctly after 5 months. My Charge 2 would tell me that my HR was 130+ when I was sitting or not even wearing it. On top of that, the wristband broke around the same time. I contacted support and they tried to fix the problem by having me restart my Fitbit however it did not work. Customer support was nice enough to offer me a replacement after going back and forth a few times.

Unfortunately the replacement Fitbit sent me was defective. I put the Fitbit on and tighten the wristband and position the Fitbit to the correct spot on my wrist but the Fitbit would not pickup my HR. After a few hours it started to read my HR however the reading was completely off. I took the Fitbit off and it continued to give me an outrageously high HR. It said my HR was 150 when I was just sitting or not wearing it. That's riduculous! I tried resetting the Fitbit many times but it did not solve the problem. I ended up wearing the Fitbit for a few months to see if it was just a one time fluke (I was also too lazy and feeling too frustrated to contact customer support AGAIN). Unfortunately the Charge 2 continued to read my heart rate incorrectly. To add onto the problem, this new Fitbit would think I'm walking when I'm just driving. I understand that most Fitbit will do this sometimes but mines was doing it all the time! No way I walked closed to 10000 steps each day. I've been lazy as F and I've been doing a lot of sitting these past few months LOL.

I finally found some free time today and hollered at customer service. They asked me to reset my Fitbit, so I did, but as I was doing so, my Fitbit battery suddenly drained and my Fitbit died. WHAT? After waiting for my Fitbit to come back to life the rep asked me to fire up the app and sync my Fitbit to the app. We tried 5 times and even reset the app but it didn't work. UGH this is now the FOUTH issue I'm having with this Charge 2. What a nightmare.

The rep quickly offered me a 50% discount for a new device or get my Fitbit Charge 2 replaced. NO WAY was I willing to get a THIRD Charge 2 and risk having to go through the headache of contacting customer service again if my THIRD Fitbit turns out to be defective too. I pestered the rep to see if she could give me a better discount, refund me, or give me credit to upgrade to a better model. Sadly, the rep and the supervisor did not have the power to offer me a better deal.

*When I asked for a refund or credit for a better model, the rep responded with this:

"I really understand your frustration Kimberly, however please be assured that our product team is constantly working to ensure that our products go through rigorous testing so that they can last and endure as expected."

LIES! Obviously Fitbit doesn't tell well enough if I've received two defective Charge 2.

*I asked if my warranty will be extended if I obtain a THIRD Charge 2:

Rep - If the device is out of warranty we will be unable to replace it and we may offer a discount to purchase a new device.
Rep - I understand your concern Kimberly, but if you decide to use the 50% discount to make a upgrade the new device will have a new warranty.
Rep - When you receive a replacement device, the replacement device has 30 days of warranty or the remaining of the original warranty.
Rep - So if the device fails which is not something that we expect to happen you have 30 days from the moment that the device is received in order to contact us again and get a replacement if necessary.

Sigh, this offer is not good enough. I wonder if I can sue for giving me a headache if my THIRD Fitbit also turns out to be defective...

*I then inquired about what happens if I have to claim a FOURTH Fitbit?

Me: would I qualify for a different model at that point
Me: or just another 50 % off discount
Rep: That would be a very unusual situation Kimberly and to answer your question, the amount of replacement devices that you receive does not makes you applicable for a free upgrade since that is a program that we don't have at the moment.
Me: Is it unusual that I received two fit bits that do not work
Me: Or is this fairly common
Rep: The reason is that the two devices that you have received failed in different areas Kimberly. Even this is not an expected situation.

Uh huh....

*Lastly, I asked if I will be sent a refurbished Charge 2 if I choose the replacement option:

Rep: Depending on available inventory, we sometimes issue factory-certified refurbished products as warranty replacements. These are typically products that were returned to Fitbit unused for reasons like wrong size and wrong color.
Me: Well that's not good
Rep: In most cases however, warranty replacements are brand new products that we package without accessories for easier shipping.
Me: how Do I guarantee that I get a NEW one
Rep: Since that depends on the warehouse Kimberly we have no control about if a new or factory-certified refurbished device will be sent.

I really wished Fitbit had a better buyer protection plan for unfortunate people like me. If you're reading this Fitbit, I would really like my money back or an upgrade to the Blaze or Ionic.
