title: Great folding panniers!
text:
Some background - I purchased an electric Pedego Interceptor bicycle for my better half. Pedego's frame also serves as a bike rack, and does an awesome job of protecting the battery. The challenge is that tubing is so thick, that 99% of all panniers will not work because the pannier hooks won't fit over the frame tubing. So, I bought a Topeak Uni Super Tourist Fat Disc Frame Mounted Bicycle Rack to mount above the existing Pedego rack. There was some custom work involved, but it turned out great! This pannier fits perfectly on to the Topeak rear rack.

I needed a folding pannier that a standard backpack would fit into, to make it easier just to plop a backpack into the bike (instead of having to load the panniers everytime, then take all the stuff out afterwards). I did a lot of research, and there are very few folding-grocery panniers that have the width of the Bushwacker (Dimensions: 14" Length x 9" width x 10.25" height). Of those that are also this jumbo size, I read that most do not hold their shape very well when loaded up.

This Bushwacker is rock solid, having steel-reinforced tubing to hold it in place. It has a nice bungee-hook set-up to keep it secure, and is adjustable to increase tension.

Tips:
1) If you use a backpack in this pannier, use a good carabiner (we used the sturdy, easy-to-open-and close, Black Diamond Oval Caribiner) to help prevent the backpack from flying out when hitting bumps. Simply plop the backpack into the pannier, attach the carabiner to the top loop of the backpack, and then hook it on the cloth handle of the pannier. Another option would be to use a bungee cord through the backpack, and attach the bungee to the frame.

2) To help prevent theft of this nice pannier when the bicycle is parked, I attached a small cable to the handle (OnGuard Akita Seat Leash Cable - 53 cm x 5 mm), and locked the seat leash to another cable (used to lock the bike seat to the frame). Though it's a very thin seat leash cable, which could probably be snipped easily, it does help prevent someone without tools just walking off with it. Next, I used some heavy duty zip ties to attach the plastic clips (bottom / backside of pannier) to the Topeak rack. So, I don't take the pannier on & off the bike - I just leave it in place.

FYI - I only used one of these panniers (keeping the other as a backup). On the other side of the bike, I built a custom, locking, waterproof hardshell pannier out of a Pelican 1430 case. It's awesome, and it's great to store the heavy chain & u-lock, tools, extra tube, pump, lights, and extra batteries. I used the terrific latching mechanism from Arkel (10 inch length), and also used a seat leash and zip ties to secure it in place (I leave this pannier on the bike also). Happy riding!

title: Presta valve stem failed
text:
I ordered two Sunlite (Kenda) Thorn resistant tubes (700c x 18/23) with removable presta core in July of 2015. I wanted a thick (puncture resistant) tube that allowed me to remove the core (with a chain tool) to allow me to inject tire sealant into the tube.

In the Southwest, we have nasty thorns called 'goatheads' that cause many flats. As part of my defense system, I use: 1) a thick, thorn resistant tube, 2) tire sealant (Flat Attack); 3) a high-quality, super puncture-resistant tire (Schwalbe - Marathon Plus Tour, Marathon Supreme, or Durano Plus - depending on the bike).

I waited a while to see how these Sunlite tubes would hold up. Unfortunately, after about a year and a half, the front tube failed. The presta valve stem separated from the tube, rendering the tube unrepairable and useless. The rear tube got a flat, but due to the tire sealant, I was able to simply pump up the tire, spin the wheel, and it sealed itself.

I had high hopes for these tubes, but I will look for other alternatives.

TIP: One reason that many of these tubes may be failing at the stem is due to the threaded, round 'nut' on the valve stem. The nut is really helpful when inflating the tube for the FIRST time, (i.e., when there is no air in it). However, once inflated to full pressure, I would recommend REMOVING this nut and setting it aside. The problem is that when riding with this nut tightened down on the valve stem, it creates added pressure on the stem at the base of the tube, increasing the likelihood of separation & failure.

title: The Modern Approach To Sighting In Your Firearm
text:
Yes, this SUNYA Laser Bore Sight is specifically designed for rifles in 7.62X39 caliber. With ammo currently costing what it does (avg 50 cents per round of 7.62X39) the purchase of this handy boresighter can save you a lot of money -- especially if you need it for more than one rifle. Or perhaps lend it to a friend and build up a few brownie points.

Simply twist off the end cap, insert 3 batteries, and twist the cap back on. The laser should light up. Make sure that your rifle is unloaded and the charging handle is in the back position. Insert the boresighter and line up the laser to your of point of aim. Do not pull the trigger or release the charging handle. Either can cause damage to your boresighter.

Then mount your scope (red dot, holographic sight) and adjust the point of aim to the laser. Now you have a good frame of reference for when you go to fine-tune your sights at the range. Easy to use, saves on ammo costs, and allows you as much time as you need at home to line up your sights without having "range pressure".

You can purchase boresighters for virtually any caliber of rifle/pistol. Just remember that you're going to zero your firearm at a certain distance and with specific ammo. Changing the distance or trying different brands of ammo will result in differing results. However it is easy to repeat the steps to help zero any change in ammunition.

You get quite the package for the price: the primary set of glasses and lenses, two extra lenses (yellow and grey), a tiny screwdriver for removing and installing a different set of lenses, both a hard case and soft cases for protective storage, a set of retainers to keep them safely on your head, and a brief instruction manual. They also provide a small plastic eyeglass frame that can have your distance prescription mounted in and then attached to the inside of these sport frames. Novel idea if they are held securely!

Lightweight, good snug but comfortable fit, wide eye shielding with UV400 protection, two extra lenses and a bunch of accessories, these ITSCOOL Sports Sunglasses are quite a package. title: I Would Call This A Beginner's Red Dot
text:
Do you want to see what all the fuss is about concerning adding a red dot to your firearm? Decent quality in red dots doesn't get much cheaper than this. For only $37.79 you get a well built red dot sight, both a one inch riser mount and a 45 degree offset mount, a polishing cloth, a battery, scope covers, an allen wrench, and a rudimentary instruction manual.

This is everything you really need to mount your first red dot and learn how it works, where it should be placed on your firearm of choice, and what positives and negatives use of a red dot offers. I've got to say that for the price this ohhunt unit offers a well constructed scope that is easy to mount and operate. I wouldn't expect it to handle the recoil of anything powerful, but it should do fine with small caliber firearms. In fact I'd recommend trying it out on a .22 plinker first.

When you turn it on one of the first things you will notice is the shape of the dot itself. If your vision is "normal" then you should actually see a round dot floating on the front lens. If you have astigmatism, cataracts or other eyesight problem, you wil get a different shape. For me it's more like a star shaped pattern. While a 2 moa dot that is mildly distorted somewhat is probably still useful to you, it will be a clear indication that you either have a faulty unit -- or that your eyesight is compromised.

Have others in your family (or circle of friends) try it out to find out what they see when looking through the scope. If most of them see a perfectly round dot, then the unit is not at fault. If you determine that your eyesight is the problem, then you will want to try out a holographic sight in a gun store to see if that offers a better sight picture for you. Holographic sights are quite a bit more expensive but the type of sight you mount and use has to provide you with the confidence you need to hit your intended target.

title: How Good Is This Stool For A Large Person Working Outside?
text:
A bit of a conumdrum here with two ways to look at it. I am 6'3" and currently weigh 225 Lbs. Not a lightweight but as my Pulmonologist informs me "you're no longer clinically obese, you're just obese". Thanks Doc! A left-handed compliment if I ever heard one.

And there lies the rub. The first time I shook this out I had mild difficulty in getting the tabs and latches to hook up-- like I did just now. That seems to inspire a little less confidence in how safely it will support me without crashing down. Once it is expanded and set up it appears to be pretty sturdy. The color also makes it easy to see in the yard.

But having just had double knee replacement I was a bit concerned that it would hold me without making me faceplant in the yard. When I asked my wife to watch me sit on it in the kitchen she said "don't do that!". The sight of me pulling it out and clicking it together didn't inspire confidence in her either.

It did hold me while sitting still although I was a bit reluctant to shift my weight around on it. That would be my major sticking point. On a yard that is not completely level I know that I would have to be careful. The other part of that is that leaning forward or to one side suddenly puts additional stress on whichever part of the base is sitting on the ground. I am not convinced that leaning over wouldn't cause the stool to buckle and me to fall over.

So there it is. It seems to be a smart design and should solve the problem of having a stool available when needed. However plastic is not indestructible and will often bend as it is stressed over and over again. Good idea, decent execution, but it doesn't inspire any confidence for someone my size.
