title: This Is Not A Good $300 Hawk -- But It Is A Great $50 Hawk
text:
I own several Condor sharp-edged tools and have never been disappointed in any of them. My collection of Hatchet/Tomahawk/Breaching Tools includes cheap models from United Cutlery to expensive tools from RMJ Tactical and the Busse family. You can break the cheaper ones with little effort so it's important to distinguish between "pretty or tacticool" and durable/useful. If you want an all-purpose tactical rescue tool this $50.00 Condor TRT is probably the cheapest one that I would trust to perform consistently in a tough environment.

It came out of the box razor sharp -- as in sharp enough to slice a piece of paper. There is a nice sheath that fits over the head but you'll need to stretch it and work it to snap the first time. The sheath also has a belt loop on it for side carry. Now why would I give it four stars instead of five? First off the paracord wrapped handle is slippery. You can remedy that with some sandpaper and create a grip that you are comfortable with.

But the biggest problem is in the weight distribution. This is a full tang hawk with a hollow steel handle and the head is offset to one side. Strange construction that but probably an attempt at keeping this TRT hawk from being too heavy. The strength and durability of this tool is not a concern but the strange (lack of) balance is. Shifting more weight to the head would balance it more properly and make the damage inflicted by the downward strike all the more devastating.

All-in-all though this $50.00 Condor TRT is probably worth twice as much as it costs. Just be aware that it has some drawbacks that might affect your performance with it. If things get too bad you can simply turn it upside down and grip it just below the blade to deliver a heavy handled blow.

title: Glossy Black Or Flat Black -- That Is The Question
text:
Things sometimes get banged around a bit and the resulting small chips can be distracting. When I mounted a buffer tube and Sig Sauer SB-15 on my CZ Scorpion I got a little careless and put a little chip on the rear of the Scorpion. No problem I thought, I'll just order the glossy black Birchwood Casey Touch-Up pen and hopefully a little dab will do it.

Unfortunately the glossy black didn't match the flat black on the Scorpion although it was easy to apply and certainly was an improvement over leaving the chip untreated. Now I just have to order the Birchwood Casey pen in flat black and do it right this time!

title: Hang It By The Door And Grab It On The Way Out
text:
5.11 is a well-known and highly regarded supplier of tactical equipment. This is a well-constructed bag made of a double-stitched tough nylon material that uses heavy duty zippers and large Velcro fasteners to keep everything locked down. It will hold six 30 rd mags of .223 ammo (or several other ammo combinations) securely and within easy reach. I put a piece of old towel between each pair of mags to help minimize any noises while moving around.

Behind the mag pockets is a deep compartment that can hold an effective combination of equipment. If you're like me, you'll want to also isolate any equipment in that main compartment to avoid shifting and noise generation. Each side of the bag has an additional zippered compartment that can hold pistol mags, a flashlight or other tools. The padded and adjustable shoulder strap can be configured to hang around your neck and allow the bag to be centered on your lower belly and there is a Velcro belt loop on the inside of the bag so that you can anchor it to a 2" belt. I prefer to have the bag centered so that I can get to what I need quickly with either hand.

This 5.11 Tactical Bail Out Bag is a well-made and practically designed grab bag that can be filled with critical supplies should you need to get out of your home in a hurry. The main problem I see is that the very bottom of the main compartment seems to be constructed of a thinner material. Unfortunately, because this large main compartment will hold a lot of stuff, the combined weight and/or sharp edges of whatever is being carried is likely to wear through that area first. This area needs to be reinforced by sewing in extra fabric or by the insertion of a fitted piece of foam. Either quick fix should add extra durability to this weak point. I'm very surprised that 5.11 didn't pay more attention to this part of the bag. Perhaps in the near future their bags will come out with some type of reinforced bottom.

title: You Might Be Able To Find One Good Way To Use This Holster -- Just Don't Think That It Will Solve All Of Your Carry Problems
text:
I'm always concerned (and skeptical) when someone develops a product that can perform three different ways. Very seldom is anyone successful with this format unless it's of the Swiss Army Knife variety. Trying to make something function three different ways always involves some compromises involving the different uses. As an example, BMW wants to be that perfect combination of a sports car and a luxury car, but in my opinion misses both targets (pun intended).

Like many other hobbyists/professionals, I own several holsters but only use a few. We live in hot and humid Southwest Florida and my normal daily wear consists of shorts and a short-sleeved shirt. Heat and sweat are enemies of guns and holsters and my normal shirt/short outfit doesn't provide a lot of concealment. Therefore I choose holsters that are light, breathe well in the heat, and aren't about to reveal themselves unexpectedly and become visible. Printing is also a potential problem so extra caution has to be used in that area too.

The holsters I use most often include a Sticky Holster for my Kahr CM9, another Sticky Holster for my NAA .22 Magnum with laser, and a StealthGear IWB for my Springfield XD Mod. 2. I also use an ActiveProGear Hybrid Defender Concealment Holster for several small pistols and revolvers. That is a "belly band" type holster that can be adjusted to fit invisibly while still being comfortable. Originally I carried my NAA .22 mag loose in my pocket, but doing so with the laser mounted resulted in the laser being pushed out of alignment. Not a good thing.

Blackhawk is a maker of many quality products, none of which has ever disappointed me. This Blackhawk Leather Tuckable Pancake Holster naturally drew my attention for its proffered flexibility as far as carry. While I don't own a Smith & Wesson M&P Shield, this holster fits both my Kahr CM9 and my Glock 42. Given that these two pistols are almost exactly the same size and have the same magazine capacity, I prefer carrying the Kahr in 9mm (instead of the Glock in .380). While I can see how several owners might be able to adjust this holster to fit many of their own personal needs, I am not completely comfortable with some of its construction.

First off, and very importantly, this holster utilizes large polymer (plastic) clips as fasteners. While they appear robust and have inherent fexion, the continuous heat in our location and the constant shifting/movement will eventually put enough stress on them to cause failure. In my experience, this often occurs at the worst possible time -- which can be embarassing and/or sacrifice concealability. The second concern I have is the lack of breathability in the leather. While the leather is soft and has a nice scent, it does not have the padded and breathable finish that my StealthGear holster has. The other disadvantage of the Blackhawk holster is the smooth leather on the inside of the holster. Heat and sweat will no doubt cause it to become slick and stinky over time. While this might not be a factor in your location, it is a major concern here.

title: The Gun You Have When You Need It Is Better Than Having No Gun At All
text:
I have carried a NAA five shot .22 magnum in my pocket ever since Florida allowed concealed weapons carry. Being small and constructed of stainless steel makes it a perfect hot weather weapon to have with you regardless of how light your clothing is. There are not many firearms that you can carry completely concealed in a swimming suit. Loading it with the new .22 magnum defense rounds gives you five shots that can do a surprising amount of damage to an attacker. I certainly wouldn't want to be hit by it -- and having it beats having nothing.

When it became available, I decided to put the new LaserLyte grip on this gun so that I could extend my effective defensive area. The short barrel makes it pretty ineffective to use rapidly on any target beyond about 7 yards. Adding the LaserLyte allows you to hit point of aim quite a bit further out. The problem I encountered is that while carrying it unholstered in my pocket the laser would bump out of alignment. Not a good thing if you have to depend on it eventually.

So I purchased this Desantis Pocket Holster to protect it. Unfortunately this Desantis holster will not fit around the laser grips. But I also noticed that when the NAA .22 magnum was placed in the holster, the holster was too tight to allow coverage of the trigger. That's not good either. After looking at the holster for a while, I realized that I would have to remove three partial rows of stitching to make it fit. However that would result in the gun sliding around in the holster. After the integrity of the stitching is compromised, it would just be a matter of time before it continued to unwind. Since the holster is designed to stay around the gun as you pull it out of your pocket, it is necessary to make another move to pull the holster from the gun. The Sticky Holster that I use with my Kahr CM9 stays in my pocket when I draw the gun. And the Sticky Holster is about the same size as this Desantis although the Sticky has a much larger space for holding the gun.

Looks like I'll be contacting Sticky Holster instead. I am really happy with their products and I feel very comfortable that they will make a holster to properly fit this combination.

NOTE: 5/11/16 I ordered the proper Sticky Holster after emailing the company and telling them about my problem. They told me to order the holster designed to fit the NAA Pug. It fits perfectly, the trigger is properly covered, and the gun pulls out of the holster leaving the holster in your pocket. Good Job Sticky!

title: THIS IS A REVIEW OF THE 250 LUMEN FLASHLIGHT TAKING 3 AAA BATTERIES.
text:
Lots of confusion on the reviews concerning this product mostly because two very different models were submitted to reviewers. This review is for the smaller 250 lumen model that takes three AAA batteries. It is short (about 3.75"), sturdy, and comes with three AAA batteries and a lanyard. The case is attractive with an industrial look but probably too smooth as far as texture for some people to work with. And yes, the package was relatively difficult to open, probably to discourage five-fingered shoppers from stealing them off the shelves. Unfortunately there are no instructions included for those who may not intuitively figure out how to install the batteries and use the three lighting functions (high, low, strobe).

Being short, slippery, and not confidence inspiring as far as using it -- and only having an estimated 2.5 hour battery life -- what is this really good for? The functionality is in its small size and very bright light. This would be an excellent tool for those working in small and dark spaces, casting enough clear and bright light for close detail work. Working under a sink with a Maglite LED 3D Cell Flashlight just doesn't cut it. This Energizer is small enough to prop up against anything in your work area to help focus the beam while freeing both hands for whatever task you're undertaking. The light beam cast by it broadens quickly and the choice of a "high" and "low" setting increase its usefulness. Believe it or not, it can actually be too bright for close work using the "high" beam.

This 250 Lumen Energizer is fine for short operating periods either inside or outside the house. However its very limited battery life restricts it to use as a back-up flashlight. For overall effectiveness as an emergency light source (blackouts, storms, indoor/outdoor security) nothing really beats a Maglite LED Flashlight using 3 D batteries. For $22.72 (compared to $14.99 for this Energizer) you have a 168 lumen light which casts a beam as far as 412 meters and has an eight hour battery life. We have several in our home that are red in color which makes them easier to find in a stressful situation. Not only that, but the Maglites are hefty enough to use as a striking weapon if need be. It's certainly better to have in your hand than nothing at all.

title: Practice In Your Backyard Without Your Neighbors Knowing It

title: Testing This Product Means A Lot More Than Spraying It Into The Air
text:
Let's say that you are confronted by an attacker who demands something of value from you. You whip out your "police strength" red pepper get and hit him full in the face even though he is still eight feet away. After a second or two, he begins to laugh and keeps coming at you. What went wrong? The spray deployed exactly as you tested it, yet this guy seemed immune. It was made by a reputable company. And all the reviews you read were extremely positive. But what no one bothered to do was to test the formula on themselves.

Test this on myself? What kind of stupidity is this? Think of it this way. Would you buy a gun and depend on it to defend yourself and/or your family without testing it previously? Of course not. The problem here is that it's easy to test guns, knives, clubs and other weapons by hitting something with it and assessing the damage. No one gets hurt and yet you can become very comfortable by mastering the proper delivery and seeing the expected results. But pepper spray is another matter entirely. No one in their right mind wants to spray themselves in the face. Certainly not the first 21 reviewers of this product. They all seemed to be perfectly happy that the spray deployed as advertised. No offense to any of them but some of you might end up trusting your lives to this product.

But it's really pretty easy to test on yourself. I was a product development manager for a small defense corporation about 40 years ago. I had to vouch for any product that we developed and sold. Putting a defective product in the hands of someone who truly needed it (even back then) would result in a substantial lawsuit. One of the items we developed and eventually sold was one of the first self defense sprays available to the average consumer. We would pay volunteers to take a full shot in the face as we developed and improved the formula. When we began production there was always the problem of if the canisters were filled with the proper formula. Since I was unwilling to shoot myself in the face while randomly sampling dozens of these units, I would test out the sprayer on the back of my hand.

If you want to truly rely on this product, here is what you need to do. Find a sheltered (from the wind) outdoor area away from people and animals. Your back should be toward any (even) minor breeze. Hold your left hand out from your body, unfasten the safety trigger, and shoot a small stream onto the back of your hand. Hold your breath while doing so and then step away from any residual mist. Your hand should have a large orange spot on it and you should immediately feel a strong tingling or burning sensation on the back of your hand. There were no instructions that I could find that told you to shake the canister first -- so I didn't.

Unfortunately nothing happened! No stinging or burning. Even though I was just recovering from a bad cold, I put my nose within an inch of the formula and took a quick sniff. Nothing! I tried the whole exercise again after this time shaking the canister first. The results? A more consistent mixture on the back of my hand, but again no deterrent that I could detect. With my damaged and tender nose and still sore throat, i would have been expecting discomfort of an epic nature. So my guess is that this particular canister was faulty. On the other hand, no other reviewer has tested this on themselves to corroborate my findings. Perhaps the company will contact me to try and figure out why it doesn't work. This isn't my first rodeo, but it is my only shot at life. If this product failed me at the only time I really needed it, I wouldn't be around to ask for a refund.

NOTE: There was a direct sale company (We Care America) back in the late 1970's that also sold a personal defense spray. 60 Minutes (or some other news program) proved on a televised segment that the spray didn't work as advertised, taking what was once a viable company into bankruptcy. Thousands of those canisters were sold to people who believed that they were going to be adequately protected by WCA's product. That's when I knew that I had to test these things for myself.

title: Great Design Elicits A Lot Of Questions.
text:
This patch is great! It is very high quality, well made with a great design, is a nice size, and glows subtly in the dark. This is not the typicaI cloth stitched patch. The front appears to be composed of molded rubber stitched to a velcro backing. The design itself is nicely executed with great detail and is raised to give it a 3D look. This patch does not look like the green color in the picture on the product page when it is not glowing. Instead it normally looks like the emblem is gold instead of green.

I love that there is no wording on it! That makes it both mysterious and official looking at the same time. No monkeying around here!

title: Show Others That You Care For Your Country
text:
Our current government is disappointing me, but I still love our country! I bought this patch to mount on the front of my Tru-Spec Contractor's Boonie Hat. This is a right-facing patch intended for the right shoulder of a uniform/shirt. However it has also been interpreted as "first into battle" and is appropriately attached to my hat.

title: Different Tools Excel At Different Jobs.
text:
I spend a lot of time cutting back invasive vegetation in the wetlands surrounding our Southwest Florida home. The Brazilian Pepper tree is a non native plant brought into Florida in the mid-1800's for use as an ornamental plant. Their bright red berries and brilliant green foliage are used frequently as Christmas decorations. However this tree is a member of the same family as poison ivy and can cause reactions to those with sensitive skin as well as respiratory problems for some people when the tree is blooming. These trees can grow up to 10 feet per year and their root systems and canopies expand so quickly that they rob the surrounding vegetation of both water and sunlight. They currently dominate about 700,000 acres of land in Florida.

They also sprout limbs vertically and horizontally and create a very thick network of branches. I have often used a reciprocating saw (with green wood blade) and my Esee Lite Machete to attack the outside perimeter of these trees. But since the areas closest to the trunks are very tight, I couldn't get a full swing on my machete and had to look for a "chopper", something that this Silky Yoki excels at. I have several Silky saws (including folding saws and a pole saw) that are built better and last longer than just about any other saw that I've tried. So I thought that an investment in this chopper was a pretty safe bet.

Machetes are designed for slashing with a full swing. Choppers are, well, made for short and abrupt (primarily) down strokes. Think about a butcher cutting up a side of beef. The weight is concentrated on a shorter blade and of course the blade itself has to be razor sharp. You should be able to achieve the same results with a chopper in a tight space with about the same effort that you'd use with a longer machete in a more open space. And I'm happy to report that the Silky Yoki Chopper performs as well as I expected it to.

The grip is very comfortable, the blade holds an edge all day, and the brush hook on the end helps draw vegetation towards you for disposal. It comes with a hole in the blade for hanging and also a carrying case that matches. The blade is easily touched up with a butcher's steel as long as you follow the natural line and don't get too aggressive. Even if you do abuse the blade, replacements are available. This is a good tool to take with you when hiking, hunting, camping, or clearing brush. It would also make a pretty good defensive tool if you find yourself in a bad situation.

title: It's Kind Of Like Having A Squirrel On Your Leg -- It Just Doesn't Stop Moving
text:
I wanted to try a drop leg holster for some time and came across this model in desert camo through another vendor. For the price, and because I had heard good things about Fox, I decided to take advantage of the reduced price and see how good (or bad) this holster really is.

The first day, after strapping it on and making all the adjustments I could, I carried around a mini ball peen hammer just to try to get used to it. Why did I choose a hammer? While I am CCW licensed, Florida does not currently allow "open carry". So I had to put something of measurable weight in the holster without alarming the neighbors or anyone driving by on our street. I could imagine someone seeing me with a drop leg holster and calling our local law enforcement, not knowing that their was no gun in the holster -- but assuming there was.Yes, the weight of the hammer head made the holster cant backwards, so I switched to a rubber mallet. This provided a much better balance.

Then I switched to a Glock 23 and a Springfield XD-45 MOD 2 and alternately carried both around inside our home, After trying my darndest to get it to fit properly, I came to the following conclusions:

1. This is a cool looking and well constructed rig. The desert camo design is well done, the material is light and flexible, and the various
clips, belts and fasteners work like they should.
2 The holster accommodated both the Springfield and Glock perfectly and the strap easily fastened over the gun butt.
3. It is very light and designed to fit comfortably against your thigh.
4. And of course it easily carries a lighter weight weapon like a Kahr PM9 and a Glock 42. In fact the smaller and lighter pistols eliminate
the bounding around explained below. But who wants to carry a "pocket pistol" in a drop leg holster?

But, and this is a "big but" for me, the single strap that fastens the holster around your thigh just couldn't keep the holster secure and steady. It bounced while walking and really moved around when running (even at my slow pace). I tightened the thigh strap so that over 14" of strap was outside the buckle, but it just never felt secure. No one wants that feeling -- you want your gun to be right where it's supposed to be -- all of the time.

This holster really needs two improvements: 1. It needs a second strap to go around the thigh, one high and one low. 2. It also needs more vertical adjustment so that it can be carried a bit higher on your belt. Both of these changes would result in a better fit and should eliminate excess movement.

title: It Not Only Looks Official -- It IS Official.
text:
My two daughters went to UF and each enjoyed themselves tremendously. Obviously my oldest daughter enjoyed herself more since it took her five years to complete her education instead of four. Both have a Pandora bracelet and this charm should be a perfect addition for each of them.

I was a little leery of ordering this charm because of its reasonable price but the fact that it was officially licensed helped a lot. We have a lot of UF gear and this charm looked like it was using the proper design with the correct colors. The charm is about the size I expected but presents larger because it has two pieces. It is well constructed, has great colors, and will be greatly appreciated by both of my daughters.

If you're looking for a Florida Gator charm as a reasonable present for a recent grad, of for any UF grads in your family, you can't go wrong with this one.

title: Solid, Secure, And Yet Flexible.  Great Deal For Very Little Money.
text:
This is a simple but effective modular rack that securely holds three large pistols without scratching them. The soft foam allows you enough "wiggle room" to fit some of your larger pistols in the rack without damaging either the guns or the rack. Mine currently holds a stainless Desert Eagle (44 mag), a Glock 40 (10 mm), and a Smith & Wesson Backpacker IV (44 mag). I really like the fact that it securely holds these guns for display.

I use the Hyskore 3 Gun Modular Pistol Rack on my storage shelves to help keep things organized and easily visible. Now that I know how sturdy and effective they are, I'm ordering a second set. If I would have known in advance how well built they are , I probably would have ordered the 7 gun model. This is a surprisingly good product for the money.

title: Good Looking Gloves With A Good Level Of Comfort And Protection
text:
Once in a while a product comes along that looks like it might pose a solution to a different problem than what it is actually intended for. These Ringside Gel Wraps are obviously designed to protect your hands while either working out or sparring in the ring. But I ordered them for a different unrelated purpose -- protecting my knuckles while cutting/trimming trees in our wetlands. We live in Southwest Florida where the brush grows all year around and not only grows quickly but also tries to choke out its neighbors by fighting for the available sunlight and water. That makes for tight quarters and a lot of "barked" knuckles while maneuvering tools and changing positions.

There are pros and cons to how this product is constructed:

PROS
1. They fit your hands ergonomically without limiting your flexibility. I am actually typing this review with the gloves on.
2. The gel padding on the knuckles is positioned for proper protection and provides a feeling of confidence and security.
3. There is a stretchy strap just below the knuckles that helps keep the glove in position.
4. The glove fastens around your wrist with an adjustable velcro strap.
5. There is a second strap that fastens over the first one which holds the velcro strap in place and actually provides good wrist support.
6. The gloves are breathable and machine washable.
7. Last but not least, they come in several colors: blue, grey, pink, and red.

CONS
1. Even though I am a bigger guy, I have always worn a large size in every type of glove. Be warned that these gloves run small.
2. While the overall construction is quite good, the sewing around the cut-off fingers is not uniform. The point where the gloves are
cut off (on the inside of the hand) are folded under and stitched together -- at least that was the intention. However the stitching is
"balled up" in different parts and loose strings are evident in some of the fingers. That appears to be a quality control problem.
3. I am assuming that since the gloves are too small for me that the smaller size carries over to make the fingers too tight for comfort.
Perhaps that will loosen up with wear and washing.

So overall I think that this is a great product for what it is intended, but at 65 years old I'm not the guy to punch someone with them on or
to test them out in any manner that would hurt these old bones. At my age I'm trying to protect myself, not break my hands. The manufacturer might want to take a closer look at how the fingers are sewn together, but overall this is a good looking product that should serve its purpose quite well.

title: Everything Has To Work Together Perfectly For Effective Concealed Carry
text:
I needed a BDU belt that would effectively fit my cargo shorts and hold up my IWB holster while carrying a Springfield .45 Mod 2. After researching various belts it became obvious that I needed a 1.5" wide belt to fit my belt loops, it had to be flexible enough to be comfortable around my surgically repaired abdomen, and it had to be strong enough to hold my Mod 2 in the right position for an effective draw. Since Florida is a concealed carry state, although they are currently considering open carry, my rig has to avoid printing so that it doesn't point out that I have a CCW in my possession. No sense in attracting unwanted attention from the public and law enforcement.

Over the years I have slowly moved up from carrying a NAA .22 magnum to a Kahr 9mm. The NAA .22 magnum is easily carried in any pocket with no printing issues. Stepping up to the Kahr 9mm was as easy as using a Sticky Holster inside my right front pocket. But carrying a far heavier and bulkier .45 took a little planning and trial and error. The clothing and belt have to be right, the carry position simple to access, and the weapon has to be concealed from public view.

I have the correct combination now thanks to this Spec-Ops BDU belt. It fits my regular belt loops, fastens securely around my waist, holds the weapon and holster in the proper position, is very comfortable, and instills the confidence needed when carrying a heavier weapon. I highly recommend this belt as a cost effective solution to carrying bulkier weapons.

As another interesting observation, each belt comes with a one page instruction sheet with illustrations. I have received many different products where an instruction manual/sheet would be very useful, and of course didn't get one. Spec-Ops wants to make sure that you get to use all the benefits of these belts. Smart!

Note: I like this belt so much that I now have it in three colors. Made in America no less!

title: Great Idea That Could Be Executed Better
text:
I have been carrying a NAA .22 mag probably for 25 years now. In hot and muggy Southwest Florida, having a stainless steel mini revolver tucked in your pocket allows you to carry concealed without anyone knowing. It's light, holds five bullets, is easily controllable, won't rust when damp, and can be brought to play in seconds. NAA as a company stands by their weapons and have reconditioned mine twice for free. The biggest drawbacks to this gun (although no gun is perfect) are twofold. While a .22 magnum bullet is considerably more powerful that a .22 long rifle, the extremely short barrel of the NAA doesn't allow the bullet to reach the higher velocities that it is intended to provide. In addition, the sights on the gun don't allow for more than a "point and shoot" at short distances with any accuracy. Of course you could quibble about the size of the gun, the slippery grips, the lack of bullet capacity, and any other shortcoming that might affect your choice of weapon. My philosophy has always been that any gun when you need it is better than no gun at all.

The recent introduction of short barreled ammunition has helped punch up the power of the .22 magnum through the NAA guns. While everyone knows that being shot with a regular .22 LR can be deadly, having a short barrel .22 magnum round fired at you will arrive with a lot bigger punch. And then of course the sights on the NAA guns are relatively useless because of the very short barrel. Laserlyte came up with this nifty idea of putting a laser sight in a grip that replaces the standard grips on the NAA .22 magnum. When properly mounted and used, this extends the useful range on this tiny weapon enough to keep any assailants at a greater distance. The sight of a red dot on someone's chest can be a tremendous deterrent, even without knowing what gun it's mounted on and without a shot being fired. That should give an assailant pause and also allow you to tactfully retreat to a safer area.

The Laserlyte NAA .22 Mag Grip Laser comes well protected in a hard plastic package with three batteries already inserted in the grips, three extra batteries for your first replacement, an instruction manual showing how to remove the old grips and install the new ones, and three hex wrenches--a larger one to fasten the grips together and two smaller ones to adjust windage and elevation. Installing the new grips took a little extra effort on my part. The hard plastic that the grips are made of were slightly too large to fit smoothly against the frame and gently cranking down the fastener left some gaps in the fit. I ended up taking them apart and putting them together about four times before they finally slipped into the proper alignment with no gaps remaining. There are a couple of things that LaserLyte could do to upgrade the grips. It would of course help if they were machined to a slightly looser tolerance. Putting some kind of texture on the grips would be helpful by making them less slippery. Alternatively, using a softer molded plastic would give a better fit and grip at the same time.

I haven't had time to go to the range to adjust the windage and elevation yet. When I do, I'll be sure to follow another reviewer's suggestion to "gently" use the hex tool on the tiny screws provided in the grip. We're talking really tiny here and it appears that it wouldn't take much pressure to strip the screws and render them useless. If that works out for me and brings the sights on target, I will be a pretty satisfied buyer. But the hard plastic construction of this product is a recipe for disaster. There is nothing robust about this design and it probably wouldn't take much to crack the grips or break off the small laser housing. This is a good start by LaserLyte but they have to come up with several improvements to make their product more durable. An oversize grip wouldn't be asking too much, would it?

NOTE: If you pocket carry this little gun with the mounted laser, you can no longer carry it without a holster. Carrying it without the holster allows the gun to jostle and throws off the laser sights. Not good! Please be advised that mounting this laser on your NAA .22 mag will not allow it to fit in many holsters intended for this firearm.

title: This Is Not Your Father's Backpack!
text:
WOW! That's the first word that came to my mind when I opened the box this pack was delivered in. The last time I wore any backpack was when I was a Boy Scout--and that was about 55 years ago. I remember thinking what a great backpack that was. Its ability to swallow massive quantities of camping gear and personal items was impressive although there never seemed to be space for enough food to keep a growing 12 year old happy. The later addition of the first rudimentary frame was considered a luxury although comfort took a back seat to utility.

This ALPS OutdoorZ Extreme Traverse X Hunting Pack (whew) is the "Swiss Army Knife" of backpacks, providing enough features to be adaptable for several potential uses. It's a lot like one of those "pop out" RVs that provide additional space by expanding, but only when you need it. Otherwise it's a neat and efficient package. The frame is a molded of structural foam that fits the curve of your back, the wide straps are padded to ease the burden on your shoulders, and expanding the "wings" increases the comfort by keeping the pack stable around your middle. The construction is robust and uses high grade materials for the fabric, zippers, and buckles. A versatile design allows you to tailor its use to your particular needs. The camouflage pattern allows you to fade into the forest/wetlands should you need to make yourself unnoticeable.

Right now I am using this to carry guns, ammunition, water, insect repellent, sunscreen, targets, and various tools to the shooting range. Because I have a bad back, carrying a heavy duffle bag on one side of my body is a recipe for muscle spasms. Instead I can shoulder this pack, carry all of the stuff I need, and not risk hurting myself. Once I have really gotten comfortable with how to stuff as much as possible into this pack, I will start configuring it into my "bug out bag". If/when the SHTF you need to be able to shoulder a pack at a moment's notice with all the practical stuff you need to survive on your own until things cool off. Of course you also need to know that whatever you choose to take with you can be evenly distributed in your pack and that the weight doesn't become a limiting factor.

This pack is strong and versatile enough to be put to many different uses, and you can be comfortable knowing that it's built to last. This isn't just a hunting pack, it's an extremely versatile carry system.

title: Perfect For Sighting In Rifles And Handguns
text:
When you get older, some of your senses start to fail. Fortunately my weakest sense is my hearing, not my sight. Although I will admit that I can't see quite as well as I used to. But similar to using hearing aids to improve your hearing, you tend to search out other solutions to make it easier to complement any shortcomings aging has thrown your way.

Sighting in a new firearm can be frustrating, time consuming, and relatively expensive--especially if you can't see your target well. These 12" Splatterburst Targets make it easy to see your points of impact and then adjust to find your zero. I use scopes a lot for precision shooting and the combination of the these targets and good scopes eliminates the need to buy and carry a spotting scope or to walk back and forth to your target to determine proper hits.

I also bought some black target hole stickers to cover up existing holes and extend the useful life of each target. While not a perfect solution, it does cut your target use about in half.

title: Not Just Throwing Knives
text:
I'm a knife/hatchet/weapon collector with probably over 400 blades in my collection. My first strong impression is always from seeing the blade, some just jump out at me from a visually striking perspective. In my experience, if they look good in a picture, they'll feel good in my hand. Very few times have I been disappointed in a blade purchase--if so, I just give it away--but I've learned to trust my instincts. I'm not talking about the weird fantasy stuff you see out there, I collect practicable and usable blades both old and new, some inexpensive but a good value, and some unbelievably expensive and worth it only for the investment value.

First off, I own three SOG products: a large Creed knife, an SOG Access Card, and a Tactical Tomahawk. All represent good value for the money and are well-constructed for their purpose. So it was a no-brainer for me to order the SOG Throwing Knives. But wait, these are more than throwing knives. Let me point out a few positives:

1. They are well designed, made of relatively thick steel, have a long cutting edge, and are well balanced.
2. The long cutting edge makes them much more than only a thrower, the grip is comfortable and the choils help prevent your hand from slipping forward to the blade.
3. They can be comfortably and effectively handled with stabbing, slashing, and back handed grips.
4. They will obviously handle any cutting chores assigned to them--once you sharpen the blades properly.
5. If not used to make tent pegs, they are long enough to be used as tent pegs in a pinch.
6. The paracord on the handles could be unwrapped and used for a multiple of purposes in the field.

And of course there are some negatives, but they aren't deal breakers considering the price:

1. Mine did not come sharp. That is easily rectified with a proper sharpening and can quickly be brought to the desired edge.
2. The sheath, while of a practical design, is not strongly made and I would expect it to not hold up long under constant use.
3. Although well balanced, I prefer throwing knives that are double edged at the tip and that are also longer and with more weight. At my size these feel insubstantial.

But I have to say, for this pricing point, this is a nice package to consider including in your bug out bag. You can wear them on your belt, they don't weigh much, and you get three strong blades for the price of one. Just make sure that you also have an excellent folding knife, a sharp and durable fixed blade knife, and a strong tactical tomahawk in your kit. It's always better to have too much of something than nothing at all. And by the way, almost anyone with moderate coordination can learn to throw a knife effectively. Just check out the You-Tube videos and try it out. Lots of fun!

title: OOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOPPPPPPPPPPSSS!
text:
Discounted or free product
is it good or bad?
I'll make the provider/author
either happy or sad..........
and sometimes even mad.

First off, I received this unit free from the distributor in exchange for an honest and unbiased review. Unfortunately this review is more along the line of "what were they thinking" when it comes to this product. I get the concept, but both the pricing and execution are way off. First off, I thought that this would simply be a way to securely mount my iPhone 6 (with it's case on) to my road bike. That makes a certain amount of sense. You could keep it in sight instead of stashing it away in a bag or sweaty pocket, allowing you to either listen to music or make/receive calls without missing anything. In actuality, it doesn't work this way.

The first thing you have to do is remove all the components from the packaging--something it took me five minutes to do without harming either myself or the product. I don't know if all of these are delivered with such "unfriendly" packaging, but if so a good place to start would be to make it easier to unpack. Once you get it opened and inventory the parts, you find that there are no written instructions. There are pictures and arrows pointing to various places, but instead of using them I simply looked at the components supplied and figured out how to put them together. After getting the product unpacked and understanding the mechanics, you have to remove the perfectly good protection case you've already purchased and replace it with the rather stiff rubber sleeve provided with the mount. I call it stiff because unlike the stylish LUVVITT protective case I currently use, the molded black rubber contact points of this TIGRA case are not designed properly to allow you to use the protected buttons easily. Added to this problem is having to put on a flimsy plastic front cover that also has stiff plastic moldings over the operating buttons. Now the operation of your Iphone 6 is twice as difficult compared to my original (and preferred) case. It compares roughly to my wife's Otterbox Defender--only worse. The combination of cases makes it harder to turn your iPhone on and off and also to input instructions.

Things get a little better when mounting the case holder to your handle bars. You can mount it in either portrait or landscape form and the double lock on the mount holds your phone very securely. Good design and well implemented. However, the combination of how far you have to reach to use the mounted phone combined with the difficulty of inputting instructions (because of the stiff buttons) causes the rider to take his eyes off the road, makes him unsafely shift his/her balance, and prevents him/her from operating the phone in a safe manner. In my humble opinion, listening to music while riding is an unsafe practice. Things are dangerous enough out there and having your hearing impaired by listening to music only increases the potential danger to you, other riders, walkers, and those operating motor vehicles.

As a final comment, this is a $19.95 item masquerading as a $49.95 product. It is made in China, which probably results in the poor construction I commented on, and the profit margin has to be huge. Suggestion to TIGRA: Bring out a simple mount that attaches securely to a bicycle and allows you to simply snap your Iphone 6 with existing case into the mount and remove it the same way. Less parts needed, simpler and more efficient operation, much more user friendly. Problem solved.

title: Good Transition Tool From An NAA Minigun To A Kahr CM9
text:
Living in hot and humid Southwest Florida means that you get pretty darn hot and sweaty twelve months of the year. Since concealed carry became legal in Florida, I've been depending on a North American Arms .22 magnum stainless steel mini revolver for personal defense. Wearing shorts and any kind of shirt allows you to simply pocket the gun without any "printing" issues. No one knows that you have it, which is the way it should be. Until now I've been reasonably happy carrying this five shot .22 magnum loaded with high velocity CCI segmented ammo. It is impervious to sweat, is very light weight, and if anything ever goes wrong with it NAA will fix it for you--for free.

Now however our world seems a little more complicated. While most defense situations take place within three yards, my little .22 magnum is going to leave me out-gunned in capacity, stopping power, and potential range. With those thoughts in mind, I purchased a Springfield Armory XD Mod-2 Subcompact in .45 acp. It has everything that I was looking for but is considerably heavier. Rather than jump from one extreme to the other, I decided to buy a Sticky Holster for my Kahr CM9 (9mm) and work with that first to adjust to IWB carry with a heavier and bulkier pistol. I'm a big guy, so wearing a light fishing shirt untucked with cargo shorts is a common sight here. While I am able to carry my Kahr in my right front pocket without printing issues, it is a little more difficult to draw it smoothly and consistently. And since pocket carry won't work for my new SA .45, I have been experimenting with placement inside my waistband.

I've been using the Sticky Holster now for over a week and no one has noticed that I'm carrying it--not even my wife. It works exactly as it's supposed to and I have not yet had the holster come out when I've pulled the Kahr. So I've found this holster to work as advertised and I've learned to become comfortable with the extra weight and size. Using this holster has also allowed me to learn where to place my new Stealthgear Onyx IWB when I decide to step up to the SA .45 Subcompact. My thoughts were that I would ditch the Sticky Holster when the Stealthgear comes in, but it is such a good fit for me that I'll probably also use it in the future. It's nice when something works as advertised.

title: My Eyes Are 65 Years Old--And So Are My Reflexes
text:
It's really nice to see what you're looking at without having someone else point out the results or to have to use a spotting scope. While I use the smaller Splatterburst Targets to sight in new .22 rifles and pistols, I prefer the larger ones for heavier calibers. Yeah, they work well for long-range target shooting, but for me they are priceless for 7-15 yard practice with my concealed carry weapons. I use a similar drill when sighting in my new .22's, taking the initial shots at the large center mass target and then fine tuning my shots using different ammo manufacturers/configurations to find out which ammo performs best in which gun.

I used to think that a North American Arms .22 magnum revolver would be all that I'd need to defend myself, but slowly I've come around to having enough stopping power to either intimidate someone or put them down with one shot. At a minimum I'll carry a 9mm but I prefer a subcompact .45acp. The trick is to properly conceal a larger weapon so that it doesn't "print" so that someone notices it AND have the ability to easily pull it from concealment and put into service. Whatever weapon you choose, you need to practice being smooth and consistent to develop the efficiency and confidence to bring it into play effectively.

These Splatterburst targets allow you to immediately see what your results are each time you engage it. While shooting paper is not the same as defending yourself in a highly stressful situation, knowing your weapon and what you are capable of doing with it comes with a lot of practice.

NOTE: My apologies to those who might not think that concealed weapon carry is important. On the other hand, "when seconds count, the police are only minutes away".

title: I Saw These For $15.00 Per Package At Two Gun Shows
text:
I use these splatter targets whenever I have to sight in a new .22 rifle. Each rifle I buy has a threaded barrel so that I can attach an AAC suppressor and do the shooting in my backyard. Using a 4X scope or higher allows you to easily keep track of your hits without having to rely on another person or a spotting scope. Since no one has a clue as to what I'm doing, I can take the time to do a good job with each rig.

First off I use a boresighter on the larger center target to zero each gun in properly. When I'm satisfied with my efforts, I'll then use three bullets from a different manufacturer--or a different configuration from the same manufacturer--on each of the four smaller targets to determine which ammo each gun likes best. I usually have about eight different types of ammo on hand so it takes two of these splatter targets to get the job done.

When I put each gun back in the rack, I tape the bottom of each stock with the name of the ammo that seems to work best in that gun/scope combination. After a few days I'll take the newly sighted in guns back outside to try the different types of ammo once more--just to be sure. Since I'm able to do this in my own backyard it saves me a lot of time driving to/from the range and waiting out the other shooters to change targets. I've also used this method to break in some suppressed .22 pistols.

Great targets, easy to use and easy to see.

title: Summers In Southwest Florida Are Always Hot
text:
This is a versatile and effective tool to use in the harsh conditions of Southwest Florida. While a lot of people use these for fishing, I have found it great to wear when mowing/trimming my yard. If you have allergies like I do, breathing in dust created by your lawn tools can create a real problem. So I wear this over my mouth and nose to cut down on my exposure to allergens.

The other big problem is both the heat and humidity. Using this as a mask will cover your neck and face giving extra protection from the sun. It is hardly noticeable because of its light weight, and it wicks moisture off effectively. I have also used it as a sweatband to keep my eyes from getting irritated. Good price and quality. You can't go wrong.

title: Every Knife Collector Should Own One--Especially At The Price I Paid
text:
I have been collecting knives for a long time and never got around to adding this particular Ka-Bar model. Part of the reason for that is that I did purchase one of their "Zombie Killer" knives and was sorely disappointed in the design, balance and durability. But it was obvious that the review I wrote ruffled the feathers of some die-hard Ka-Bar fans who evidently didn't understand what attributes a dependable knife should have.

This knife is a way different animal than the "Zombie Killer" and is an example of a great knife. The design, balance, and mostly durable construction make for a good tool to carry whatever the need. It is comfortable to hold, has a razor sharp blade, and just feels right in the hand. Anyone facing this knife knows that the threat is not to be taken lightly--especially in the hands of an expert.

The one concern I have is where the full tang of the blade becomes thinner where it enters the handle. I tend to be rough on my tools and depend on them to perform as needed. This particular construction creates a weak area if the knife is used for leverage. I don't want to be let down by a broken knife, but most owners will not put it through the paces that I would. Comes with sheath.

title: All Big Knives Are Not Alike--And Neither Are The Users
text:
This knife was designed for Outdoor Edge by Jerry Hossom, a highly respected big knife expert who makes some awesome custom knives for big bucks. (Search the internet for "American Kopis" and you will see what I mean) His biggest emphasis is on self-defense and martial arts.

This particular knife is really cool looking and immediately inspires confidence when holding it in your hand. To check out how it functions I compared it to one of my Esee Lite machetes, a big knife that I have used for hundreds of hours after trying out several other large knives/machetes/hatchets/saws trimming trees and cutting brush. The Esee can be found for between $60.00-$70.00 and the Brush Demon is available from $50.00- $70.00, close enough for comparison purposes. The Esee is made in South America and has a lifetime guarantee. The Brush Demon also has a lifetime guarantee and is made in China.

The Esee has micarta handles, a blade length of 17.25", an overall length of 23.5", a blade thickness of .065", and weighs about 17 oz. The Brush Demon has a rubberized handle, a blade length of 13.5", an overall length of 20.08", a blade thickness of .160", and weighs about 18 oz. Both blades use a medium grade carbon steel that is black powder coated. These carbon blades are tougher, durable, easy to sharpen, but also susceptible to corrosion.

Blades are a bit like cars: some people like one design, some like another, some owners drive their cars gently, and some drive them to the edge of abuse. So when I give you a perspective on a knife, it's simply my perspective based on how I use it. My height, my weight, the length of my arms, how strong I am (or not), and the type of swing I use all come into play. So here is what I found after using both knives to limb trees and to chop into trunks. Most people would probably use hatchets or saws for this type of work but I have found that a big knife is more effective and can be used for a longer time without arm fatigue.

For me, the Esee Lite is the hands down winner. It is about 3.0" longer, resulting in better weight transfer with a full swing. The blade itself is about 4.0" longer and is markedly thinner and sharper. Having a blade that is less than half as thick as the blade on the Brush Demon results in more energy being driven deeper into the wood. If you compare the cut made with the wide blade of a hatchet to that of a good machete, the thinner blade of the machete will always cut farther into the wood with less effort. The same holds true when comparing the thickness of these two big knife blades. I also noticed that the blade configuration of the Brush Demon resulted in a much smaller "sweet spot" when cutting wood. The best cuts were made when the wood was impacted at the belly of the blade. Off-center hits were noticeably ineffective. The Esse Lite was better balanced and similar to hitting a golf ball with an over-sized driver--even a relatively poor impact had good results.

So with apologies to Jerry Hossom--and still lusting after an American Kopis--the Brush Demon doesn't stand up to the Esee Lite machete for the type of work I use it for. On the other hand, the pointed Brush Demon would probably do much better against soft targets--especially for stabbing. If I could only carry one survival knife with me, it would still be the Esee.

title: Always Buy The Best Tool You Can Afford--Especially For Manual Labor
text:
This is by far the best machete I have owned and used during my 33 years living in Southwest Florida. I am a big knife collector and ran across this machete by chance when researching other big knives. Previously I had used several Cold Steel machetes which were quite satisfactory--until I discovered and started using the Esee Lite Machete.

Yes, the price point is higher, but what you get is a long, well-balanced, razor sharp, light weight, and flexible blade that cuts through 3" to 5" limbs like the proverbial "knife through butter". Besides that, all Esee products are guaranteed for life. While I haven't abused one to the breaking point yet--although I've tried--all you have to do is send it back to the company for repair or replacement (at the option of the company).

I take two of them into the wetlands with me when cutting Brazilian Pepper trees. Sharpening them is simple with the proper stone and they hold their edge far longer than lesser machetes made of softer steel. You can use them for hours with minimal fatigue because of the good grip, fine balance and light weight. The only better knife that I can compare it to is my Busse Nuclear Fusion Battle Mistress which costs upwards of $500.00. However, the NFBM is considerably heavier and has a thicker blade. This causes shallower cuts and quicker arm fatigue.

So ante up a few extra bucks and enjoy the superior cutting power of the Esee Machete. You will never buy another cheap machete because you will be spoiled by your new Esee.

NOTE 02/15/15: I finally found a drawback to the Esee Lite. The areas I work in are so thick that if you drop the machete or put it down and forget where you put it, it's almost impossible to find. So now I spray the handle with fluorescent orange paint which makes it much easier to see and recover.

title: I Taught My Daughter To Shoot .22 Semi Auto Pistols And Rifles In Our Backyard--And No One Knew It!
text:
I'd been wanting to teach my youngest daughter the basics of gun safety and help her get comfortable firing a weapon. However, I didn't want to take her to a gun range with its attendant loud noises and general confusion. I only wanted her to concentrate on the weapons and on what I had to tell her. We live in a neighborhood where the homes each sit on 2.5 acre lots--and most of them have surrounding fencing. While I could have set up a target range in our basement, I didn't want to deal with lead and gunpowder, and I also wanted to be able to push the boundaries to make her comfortable and capable with a rifle.

So I bought this trap and mounted it on two heavy duty pallets, put two more tall pallets behind it, and hung some heavy cardboard behind the target in the trap. Behind the pallets are some mounds of fill dirt and 100 feet of thick brush. In addition, there are no neighbors behind us for over two miles. The heavy cardboard was to stop any bullet splash back and also to help lower the sound of the bullet hitting the trap.

The final key to keeping all this a secret was to use two legal suppressors I have on the semi autos. You can use a variety of ammunition in both the rifle and pistol without having to deal with the "crack" of the bullets, giving you the opportunity to match each gun with the best ammo for it. And no one is the wiser. Mission accomplished!

title: Living In Southwest Florida Does Have A Few Drawbacks
text:
Being blond and light skinned is a bit of a hazard living in Southwest Florida. Add in allergies to grass and pollen and you've got a potential disaster waiting every time you mow the lawn. If I knew then what I know now, I would have done a much better job protecting myself from the sun over the past 60 years. Now the cumulative damage is putting my Dermatologist's kids through college--and maybe medical school.

Besides wearing hats, sunglasses, and using zinc oxide and 50+ UV sunscreen, I decided to invest the princely sum of $10.39 to try out this flap hat. Turns out to be just what the doctor(s) might have ordered. The hat and flaps protect my head and neck, the front mesh keeps pollen and dust from entering my mouth, and the hat can be adjusted/manipulated to fit your needs. Add in that it's made of a lightweight (and breathable) material and has 50+ UV protection, and you're talking more about a hat "system" instead of just a hat.

Use a good pair of sunglasses and some zinc oxide (if you wear the front flap lower), a lightweight long-sleeved shirt and pants, and you've got great protection against the elements. An added bonus is the protection the hat and flaps give you from mosquitos and biting flies. The less distractions the better when you're running power equipment. If you're looking for extra protection from the sun at a very reasonable price, this is your hat.

title: "There's A Sucker Born Every Minute".  Unfortunately It's Me!
text:
Ok, you can decide if I'm either stupid or desperate. One of the biggest problems encountered working in my yard during the summer in Southwest Florida are these insanely aggressive deer flies. They bite hard,even through your shirt, but they seem to particularly like your cheek, neck or lips. They don't stop pestering you until they are either able to feed or you manage to kill them. The best method I have found so far is to patiently wait for one to land on you and then beat the crap out of it. The problem is that I encounter several of them every day.

So I fell for this flypaper on a hat deal, hoping against hope that it would work where other methods have failed. I have used it for four hours every day for five days in a row. The results: NOT ONE DEER FLY CAUGHT! They continue to buzz around me and I continue to impatiently wait for them to settle so that I can kill them, but not even one deer fly even managed to trap itself on the flypaper by accident.

The product headline says "Repellent Strips" but also discloses that it contains no chemicals or odors. If the product has no chemical on it, how does it repel the deer flies? The only way I can see this working is by attaching the strips to a tennis racket and swinging it at the incoming deer flies. At least I'd get some more exercise and maybe kill a few before they can bite me.

title: It's All About Practicality, Speed, and Flexibility
text:

text:

title: Something Wicked This Way Comes
text:
I collect knives and hawks. There are two ways that I judge the effectiveness of any sharp tool. Number One is how it stacks up to a good machete. At this point if I could only take one blade into the wilderness, it would be a high quality machete. It has reach and a long cutting surface, is fundamental in design, and can create a large protected area around the user. In addition it cuts through things easily and doesn't typically get hung up in/on the target, unlike other implements. Number Two is judging how I would feel if I were threatened with the tool. It does look wicked, it has two effective blades, it comes sharp(!), can be swung in any direction, and is well built. It's inherent light weight will allow a lot of use before arm fatigue sets in, but it does have some negatives.

On the con side, it is short and its lightness doesn't make it feel substantial in my hand. The cutting surface is much smaller than that of a good machete and of course you can't really stab with it. It is a swinging tool that will allow an experienced fighter to step inside of the swing. Although I haven't tested it, it's hard for me to believe that it can stand up to the abuse that a large man can generate. The M48 probably wouldn't last long against a hard target (breaching doors or cutting wood or metal) but it should prove to be easy to carry and extremely effective against a soft target. I certainly wouldn't want to be hit with it. The best part of the M48 is the value. It is simply one of the most cost effective blades that I have ever bought. And darn, it just looks and feels cool!

title: You Can't Go Wrong.
text: This is a well designed knife that is solid, attractive and balanced. Being a knife collector, it isn't all that often that you hold a knife that inspires confidence no matter what the task.  The Creed would prove to be devastating as a cut and thruster, has a long enough blade for slashing purposes, and could even prove effective as a chopper.  If I were forced to take just one knife with me into the wilderness, this would be one of the top candidates.

title: A Knife to Be Proud Of
text:
I collect knives and hatchets--but I think that my wife considers it hoarding. Probably a fine line there. I had previously looked at a Benchmade Infidel, an OTF automatic, but found it to be of lesser quality than my Microtechs. It also had a lot of blade play (slop) which always makes me doubt the construction quality. I finally got seduced by a picture of a Benchmade Bedlam. It just plain looked wicked and I had to have it. Unfortunately it also lacked in quality.

Benchmade's fixed blade knives have always had a great reputation. I saw the Nimravus at a gun and knife show and was impressed by the weight and balance. It was solidly built in the mode of my Busse fixed blades. It is sinister looking, built like a tank with a very sharp tanto blade, and has the look of a weapon that would get my attention immediately if it were pulled on me. The overall size is almost perfect, it fits my hands well, the construction is robust, and it is extremely well-balanced.

Always remember to use extreme caution when handling knives. An old-timer once told me that they are just as dangerous as guns because they are always loaded. One slip can have disastrous results. So until you can go to Walmart and buy a new finger, or can print one with a 3D printer, be careful out there.

title: WHOA BABY!!!!!
text:
Just received this knife as a gift from Cold Steel Special Projects. I had ordered a discontinued Spectre ($400 knife for $100)directly from them but the final shipment didn't meet their standards. As an apology, they shipped me a Pocket Bushman. By the way, the Special Projects web site offers great deals on discontinued models (like the Rajah) for significant savings.
My first thought was "what's a Pocket Bushman?". That was quickly answered when I slid it out of the box. Very strong and utilitarian looking tool. But I still didn't really get it until it opened with a bang and locked up fast and tight. It's just over 10 inches long when opened with a 4 inch razor sharp (and I mean RAZOR SHARP)blade. I told my wife that it was sharp enough to shave with and then immediately cut myself by trying to close it without looking at the instructions. You'd think that I would be smarter than that at my age. One quick swipe and the tip of my index finger started leaking blood through a cut that you could barely see. Blood everywhere.

This is a big cumbersome tool that will handle any task you set it to. Cold Steel's motto seems to be "If it's worth doing, it's worth overdoing". If you have to pull it out in a defensive situation, your opponent is going to think twice about engaging you. The intimidation factor is impressive--and it inspires confidence in your hand. Take my word for it. It's not for amateurs and will do accidental damage quickly.
"If you find yourself in a fair fight, your tactics suck!"

text: I have been using one of the original Fitbits for about five years, having received one free from my health insurance company. I was a bit disappointed that the company no longer offered the original Fitbit One, so bought this to replace it. I actually love it, except for the clunkiness of the look. Because of the mechanics and sensors in it, it sits up rather higher on my wrist than a normal watch does, and I am not especially enamored of the look of the band itself. I have thought about getting one of the leather bands, as it might look a bit nicer, but all in all, the looks of the thing are the only draw back. While the Fitbit One tracked steps, stairs and sleep, I had to actually remember to push the button to track sleep, and it wasn’t especially accurate because it only sensed movement. With my new Fitbit Charge 2, it not only tracks sleep automatically, it also detects deep sleep, light sleep, and REM sleep based on pulse rate. title: Except for the seat....
text: I bought this bike to upgrade after purchasing the GX2.0 last year, which I had been completely delighted with.  I am so glad that I didn't order this bike first, because the seat is SOOOO uncomfortable, that I had to purchase a sheepskin seat cover just to ride it!  The description on this page as I am writing says, "...features an adjustable, oversized cushioned seat," which is completely untrue!!!  The seat is HARD!!!  The front edges of the narrow part of the seat are sharp, and when I first sat on it, I could feel them scraping my thighs so much I couldn't ride it.  I planned to give my GX 2.0 bike (with its VERY comfortable seat) to my daughter when I got the new one, and was glad I had not, so I could continue my daily riding.  Even with the sheepskin cover installed, this seat is way too hard, and I am going to have to purchase some cushioned biking shorts in order to be as comfortable as I was on the other bike.  I had been riding up to 71 minutes (for a 61 year old woman who hated to exercise, that was great), and today I was only able to ride 30 minutes.  I wish that NordicTrack offered other seats that one could purchase for this bike.  It was really a disappointment in that respect. I am hoping that the company will fix this terrible seat, and put the same one on that I had on my original bike!  All in all, it will most likely cost me another $100.00 for the sheepskin cushion and bike shorts I will have to get.

title: Insane wheel tire design
text:
You will be singing praises to the designer if this wheel if you ever have to repair a flat or ever just add air. I have 4 different pumps and none will fit the design of the wheel and tube stem.

To repair or replace the tube - good luck! You need to remove one bolt through the hub, holding the same allen bit on both sides at the same time (hope you have 2!). There are two little hub components that fall out when the wheel comes out. Don't lose them! Then there are four bolt on one side of the wheel and four nuts on the other side. Don't drop any! When you get the wheel apart there is ANOTHER loose hub part that falls out. How many pieces are we dealing with now? Not counting the two bit sets I have out. Yikes!

Hopefully you have a spare or patch kit. After you fix or replace the tube, you have to line the wheel halves up with each other, and the tube stem. Don't forget to put the inner hub lose piece in. And don't worry about lining it up because there is no way to. You'll end up just rattling the wheel around until the bolt finds it's way in. But first you have to hold all those nuts in while you screw the four bolts back in. THEN hold the wheel to the scooter AND the two outer hub components while you put the FINAL bolt back in - also holding both ends so the bolt will screw in. Remember, you have to shake the scooter and all those components until the bolt finds it's way to that inner hub piece. It's helpful if you have two other people to help.

So now that you have it all back together get your needle nose pliers to pull the stem out so you can attach a pump. Pump up to 60 PSI and cross your fingers. Oh, the patch didn't take? Don't worry, just repeat all those previous steps!

Try not to think how you just paid $130 bucks for a scooter, or how the designer is on the beach in the Caribbean.

One star left only because my kid likes it. LOL

title: This Workout Produces Results
text:
Measurements Pre-P90x: 6'4, 212 pounds 16% body fat.
Measurements Post- P90x: 6'4, 207 pounds, 11.5-12.5% body fat.

This workout works. I had heard about P90x through the infomercials and thought I would give it a try. I have always been in decent shape but I wanted to get "ripped". The first 2 weeks are grueling, you are sore everyday but it feels great. I could do every workout but sometimes I had to do push-ups with my knees or pull ups with a chair, go at your own pace, even if you do 1 rep you will still see results if you keep at it. Tony Horton is great, sure some of his lines are corny but he keeps you motivated. By week 4 my arms were the most defined I had ever seen them, by week 6 my abs were coming in pretty nice, and by week 12 WOW. As far as the diet, this was equally important, I did not follow the diet plan to a T but i did do a low carb diet for the first 4 weeks and it helped shred fat. Try this workout, i wish I had done it earlier and will do it again in the future.

2 other points:
(1) Try beachbody on demand, this allows you to pay $40 to stream the workouts for 3.5 months, which is cheaper than the CD's (i used the streaming service).
(2) Don't worry if you gain weight in this program, I went up to 216 after a month because I was burning fat and gaining muscle (i went from 16%-14% fat in month 1). Even so, I looked better at 216 than 212.

title: Good bottle, cap can be improved
text:
I just received this bottle today (I went with the "carbon" color). Overall, I like it, but I think the sip cap can be improved.

First color & design: The carbon is a shade darker than the image conveys. I'm pleased that's the case as I'm a guy. Also, the mouth of the bottle is quite wide and doesn't look like it will be difficult to clean. I haven't dropped it yet, but the glass is thick and I think the plastic cover will protect it (i'll write an update after I drop the bottle a time or two - it's only a matter of time). The carry handle seems to be medium duty - It'll do the job. Finally, the bottle is big so it'll hold a good amount of water. If you're looking for small and dainty - this isn't the bottle for you. I like the size and feel of it.

The cap is well made and has an o-ring to stop it from leaking. The flip top covering the sipper though seems like it *might* be the weak spot. I'm not sure if that's the case and time will tell if it will leak. I wish the bottle had an pressure relief valve to let air in as you drink. As it is, you can't suck the water out like you can a squeeze bottle and you have to let it pour into your mouth. Not a huge deal, but it feels like it could be done better.

Overall: it's a good bottle that feels like it'll survive some wear and tear. If you're looking for a glass bottle: this is one to get. Sure, the cap can be improved, but all-in-all it's a bottle worth considering.

title: Good bottle but cap is flawed
text:
I have owned no fewer than 4 of these and have gone to Camelbak several times for replacement lids. The weakpoint of this bottle is the cam and bit valve.

The Good: the cap itself does not leak and the bottle is BPA free. It also looks good and is easy to carry.

The Bad:The bite valve will leak over time and the flip mechanism will get weak to where it will not stay in place. Also, you can get some mold inside the flip mechanism.

Is it a bad bottle? I'd say no, but I'd expect to buy a new one every 6 months or so. If you're ok with that, it's a good bottle for you.

I should note: camelbak is pretty good about sending you replacement lids free of charge if you need them.

title: Simple bottles that do the job
text:
I used these bottles to carry homemade juices while on a 60 day juice fast and have owned them for 4 months at this point. At 18oz they were the perfect size - not too big, not too small. There were times I wished they were 20oz instead of 18, but not enough for me to warrant saying they're too small.

The mouth is wide enough to easily fit a bottle brush into them. Also, they are not to tall to where the bottle brush would not fit into them.

The caps do not leak. However, I wish the waterproof seal used was better designed. The cap and the seal (i.e. o-ring) are two separate pieces and the o-ring has a tendency to fall out at times. It's odd, it can be really hard to remove the o-rings yourself, but on occasion I find that they did drop out while washing. This, however, is a minor inconvenience.

Overall, highly recommend these.

text:
This is a great way to store 12 sets of polyhedral dice for D&D and similar games. I'm not sure if you strictly-speaking need waterproof storage for that, but while the O-ring may be overkill, the locking clasps and overall durability are a cut above what you usually find on parts organizers. This is never, ever going to come open unexpectedly and spill its precious contents all over the place!

With the dividers installed as shown in my photo, 8 areas hold a set of 7 polyhedral dice perfectly. Five of those will also hold a set of 12 six-sided dice. The four larger areas hold somewhat more; I have 10 d20's in one of them comfortably.

The downside of this approach is that you're certainly not going to sneak up on anyone while carrying one of these full of plastic/resin dice. And if you're into metal dice, or the sort of gemstone dice where each of them costs more than this whole container, then this probably isn't how you want to store them. (But you could probably pad them properly with a bit more work.)

Color of the O-ring seems to vary. I have two black and one blue, but the Plano part number stamped into it is the same for all three.

If you are the sort of person who needs to compactly and securely transport a lot of dice, this is the best way I've found to do it.

title: Good secondary lock for extra peace of mind - lock up your seat and front wheel!
text: Great lock for securing secondary components like seat and front wheel on your bike.  I live in Baltimore where bike theft is an issue, but not as bad as it is in bigger cities.  The general recommendations are U-Lock your frame and rear wheel first, then secure the front wheel and seat with something like a cable or chain lock.  I needed this longer length chain to secure my seat, and I use the shorter Abus steel chain lock to secure my front wheel to the frame.  This may be a little bit of overkill, but it is not unusual in Baltimore to see locked up bikes with the front wheel missing, and I overheard a woman in my LBS who was coming in to buy a new seat because hers had just been stolen.  These things can/do happen, and the harder you make it for thieves, the more likely the thieves are to pass you by for an easier target.  Seats and quick-release wheels are easy to steal when left unsecured, and they are expensive to replace.  A cable lock costs about as much, but is significantly easier to defeat than these chain locks.  I like these Abus locks (this one and the shorter one) because they are a small investment for a lot of peace of mind.
