title: Laser or GPS??? I finally decided on laser.
text:
I spent a lot of time researching lasers and GPS devices to replace my original Sky Caddy device. Several times I almost pulled the trigger on the Garmin Approach 6, but in the end I went with the Callaway Razr. In short, I am very happy I did. I love the device, it is easy to use, and gives me the information I need to hit my next shot quickly.

Comparing this to the Bushnell line, I selected this based on price and my trust in Nikon optics. I have limited experience with Bushnell, but in that experience I found it hard to sight the pin at distance. Most of my friends have Bushnell, and we all always get the same yardage. I think it is just personal preference and ergonomics when selecting between the two.

One of the key deciding factors for me was the driving range. When I am warming up, I like to practice my distance control. This is not really an option for GPS, because most ranges are not marked. Sure you can do it your self for your home course, but that takes time that I was not willing to invest, and when I travel it does not work. With the laser, any target on the range can be measured and used for practice.

On the course, I have been using this laser for a month now, and spotting flags has been quick and easy. This was one of my chief concerns, because I have had issues with older lasers being difficult to use. On the Razr, the cross-hairs are easy to align, the image in the view finder is nicely magnified, and the display is easy to read. I have been able to 'shoot' every flag I have aimed at, and get a quick reading. Also, the manufacturer reports a range of 600 yards, and I have spotted flags that are 400+ yards out.

The laser has also been quick to give readings off of false fronts, bunker lips, barber poles (150 yd markers), my bag and tee markers. I am sure I have measured a few other things by now too. These were other areas where I felt like GPS had an advantage, but now using the laser, I like being able to pick where the measurement is taken. This Razr scans for 8 seconds, so it is easy to run the target over the bunker lip to get get a couple yardages with one click of the button. I am very happy with my ability to get carry distances.

This model reads down to the tenth of a yard, which I do not find necessary. If you can save money on a model that only reads to a full yard, I would not pay for the extra, perceived accuracy.

Battery life is another advantage for the laser. I love that I don't have to worry about recharging my range finder on a regular basis (at least once per weekend) so I can use it. There were multiple times I raced out the door to the course and had to double back to get my GPS off the plug or had to play without it. I have used the Razr heavily for a little over a month and there is no dent in the battery yet. I expect to get at least the summer out of it before needing to replace the battery.

One area you will hear the GPS is better is when you cannot see the flag. In my experience this claim is wash. A lot of times, if you can't see it, you should not be shooting for it. :) The laser will give you a better chance of getting a distance to a punch out location, or a lay up spot. In cases where you need to walk to the top of a hill for a blind pin, shooting the distance to the pin and then to your bag (which you left next to your ball!), gives you the info you need. Some of the newer GPS units that allow you to pick a spot and get a distance are probably at a little bit of an advantage here.

Where may GPS still be better?
The laser has been less useful in determining distance to the front/back of a green if there are not markers, like bunkers, in the area. Particularly on courses with a fair amount of elevation change.

GPS is a little faster. By the time you walk up to your ball and start to assess the shot facing you, the GPS will have yardages to the middle of the green and several landmarks up and in front of you. You will see many arguments about their accuracy in your research, but I never had an issue with mine.

Stat Tracking is also a strength of many of the GPS systems. If that is important to you, you should still consider a GPS unit.

Summary
I am a former GPS person that went laser. I am happy that I did. The laser is easy to use and accurate. I have not missed my GPS unit yet, and I really thought I would. The Calloway/Nikon model is good looking and durable. Overall I am very happy with my purchase, and I am very comfortable recommending this product to others.

My particular sample/shipment didn't come with the Klickfix handlebar mount. Popular in Europe. So I was stuck with a handlebar bag I couldn't mount. Enter XXcycle of France. They carry Klickfix parts. So I order the mount, my credit card issuer charges me a buck for the monetary exchange, and now I have a 'lockable' handlebar bag, which I wouldn't have if there was supposed to be a mount included in the box with the bag.
As for the bag, the main compartment will hold a sixpack of talls and is insulated with removable insulation pads, about 9 1/2 by 5 inches. It also has two thinner pockets in front of that, for maps, cellphones, thin stuff like that, taking the dimensions out to 7 inches. 10 inches high. Comes with a rain cover zippered underneath.
In my opinion, not an example of good value as there are plenty of handlebar/camera bags out there with more space for less money. But then, how many lockable on the bike handlebar bags do you know of?
And/so give XXcycle a browse. They saved me a world of frustration.

title: What you'll be getting.
text:
Two very handsome collapsible grocery-bag panniers, highly water resistant if not classified as waterproof, & an "overnighter" sized suitcase.
I cannot verify the stated 57 liter capacity of this set-up. I can testify that my measurements came to 51.5 liters, thereabouts. A standard large grocery bag is 6.5 inches by 11.5 inches...then there's the length...these panniers are 11/11.5 inches high. Doing the math comes to 1719 cubic inches for the pair...more of less.
The suitcase measures 19 by 12.5 by 6. so that's 1425 cu. in. Add it to the panniers comes to 3144 cu. in. or 51.5 liters.
Aside from this little discrepancy about capacity this is a well made good looking carrier system. You can toss the suitcase in the closet and still have a competent set of pannier bags that will attach to any rack. And you can still plunk your rack-bag of choice on top. I think they were called trunk bags also. Kettler took the terminology out to the proper dimensions by designing the suitcase. Velcro plus buckles hold it on top.
The panniers come collapsed inside the suitcase. All you need do is slide the ends of the plastic stays away from the thread band...you don't need to cut the thread...you can leave it in place, and then tuck the plastic ends all around the inside the pannier. And wah lah a firm & rigid pannier body all around. I did say good looking? How waterproof I don't know. No instructions. We're on our own.
I wanted a set-up like this some time ago. My delema is getting six loaves of bread home. Light but lots of volume. This system seemed the way to go. But the original price stunk. Once again Amazon to the rescue. Thanks one more time Amazon. And thanks as well for the price for the "trunk" bag from Topeak as well!

title: Make sure you have an 8mm key
text: I was torn between these and the Shimano 105 pedals, but decided to go with the more budget friendly Look pedals in the end. I'm pleased with my purchase, but don't really have any similar pedals to compare them to as these are my first clip-in pedals of this type. Unlike other bike pedals I've purchased, these adhere to the spindles by tightening with a typical 8mm Allen wrench; perhaps beneficial to those who don't want to splurge on a bike pedal wrench or don't have one, but kind of obnoxious that it doesn't come with such a wrench: I had to dive through my basement box of old Allen keys and fortunately found one. After that, installation was easy. The clip system feels snug on the included cleats, and it's easy enough to clip in and out. I've noticed these have more float (left/right rotation allowance) than previous clipless systems I've tried, so keep that in mind while making your decision. The cleats are plastic, and have become a bit beaten up already after just a few weeks of riding: specifically, the more rubbery stick on pieces on my left shoe fell off almost immediately (I use that foot to "push off" from a dead start which I think wore down the glue pretty quick). If you're really *really* into weight savings these aren't the lightest, but likely you wouldn't be looking in this price point anyway. For the money I'd say these can't be beat.

title: Nice entry level pedals
text:
I'm not really much of a bike rider, but lately I've been going on some longer trips (about 20 miles once a week or so) and decided that it might be worth my while to invest in some clip in pedals. After reading about the two main types of clipless systems, I decided the SPD-style pedals would better fit my bill and budget, and desire to stay around $100 together with shoes. Installation was a breeze, once I purchased an additional wrench to get my unexpectedly heavy old regular rectangle pedals off, and these Venzo brand pedals slipped right into place.

I haven't had any issues with the tension of the clipping mechanism after three solid rides so far, though I did have a bolt fall out of my shoe causing the shoe to get stuck clipped into the pedal -- I releasing the tension all the way got the shoe out but the small metal piece which the tension screw screws into is rather difficult to get back into position if it happens to fall out.

The included cleats fit nicely on the shoes I bought and other than some embarrassing falls and general awkwardness getting in/out of the pedals, I haven't had any issues with these pedals. If you are a beginning cyclist like myself looking for an affordable entry to clipless pedal systems, these fit the bill well. I also have taken some shorter trips with regular non clip-in shoes with these and they are acceptably fine.

text:
I had trepidation about purchasing such a joist-mounted pull-up bar, but decided it was the only real option I had for my basement gym. Assembly was difficult, but not from any fault of the product. Big question to ask yourself first:

Are you joists spaced far enough apart so that you can actually fit a drill w/ bit in between them to make the holes?

Turns out mine weren't, or rather, that almost all of them weren't, except for one awkwardly overspaced gap right up against a dividing wall that almost had enough to room to squeeze the drill in there and make holes. Anyway, after a few hours of cursing and intermittently giving up I finally got the thing up and it feels great. The handles are a good distance and offer many positions for hands to do chin/pull -ups. My joists are standard 2 in thick and about 10 in deep, I have the screws mounted about 4 inches up and so far it seems very sturdy. Hopefully nothing breaks, but thus far my expectations are high.

title: Decent belt
text:
I purchased this belt on a whim--I'd never used a weight belt before. I was squatting around 300 lbs at the time. The belt helped a little with increasing weight, by giving a solid surface to push your gut into. I use it on my heavy sets now for squat and deadlift and it works fine.

The belt has a good thickness and width. I have a 33" waist and use the fourth from the last set of holes. My fiancee is able to use the same belt (she wears size 0 womens) albeit on the tightest set of holes. It'll take a week or so to loosen up and will continue to for awhile. After a month or so of regular use my belt is still a little starchy.

My complaint is the double latch. It's difficult to latch and unlatch. Don't be that guy walking around in a belt the whole time you're at the gym--the belt is really only that useful for heavy lifts. I resorted to just buckling the top one instead of wrestling with it after each set.

Compared to other belts, this one is substantially cheaper. It feels solid enough to last a few years at least. I'm satisfied for now.

text: This stuff works well. I've used this on many outings and walks through thick woods. If applied carefully, along with taking other precautions, it is very effective. For the average person this product should keep enough insects away to keep you comfortable, but If you're pregnant and seeking to avoid the Zika virus, you don't want to get even a single mosquito bite. One application of this quality product should not be your only defense. To be safe when pregnant, pair the use of this product with other measures to keep from getting bitten. text: Some people in the reviews were saying that the fan did not keep them cool...if you’ve got a bigger tent, honestly that should be obvious. This is a lightweight, battery operated light with a fan to help circulate the air more than anything. I hung this from the lantern hook in the center of my tent ceiling and it worked beautifully. The light is very bright and bends different directions as well. It also runs for a SOLID amount of time. I want to say we accidentally left the fan running for like, 10-14 hours? Never replaced the batteries for the entire weekend. Bring a fan that plugs in if you actually want one for cooling down, but this one definitely does the job it’s supposed to.

title: Take Your Time, It’ll Be Fine
text: [[VIDEOID:d5ccfbabc09f5934207a6fc4cf8dbfe4]] I bought this as a gift to my boyfriend for us to build together. He is a MASSIVE Buckeye fan, so I knew he would fall in love with this! We started to build it together, but I honestly feel like it’s easier to go by yourself...the pieces are very small and the directions are initially overwhelming. HOWEVER. If you take your time with the project, it will come together beautifully. Organize and count ALL of the pieces out at the beginning to make sure you’re covered for everything, then take things slow and steady. Double check that you’re placing things correctly, because it’s hard to get the pieces apart once they’re down. It’s a time consuming project, but it’s a lot of fun and you will feel so accomplished and excited at the end. His stadium proudly sits on his desk at work now and it’s the HIT of the office! :)

title: Great Company / Cumbersome Boat
text:
Purchased this boat directly from Sea Eagle. They offered a 180 day risk free trial. Returned it after 2 1/2 weeks and they accepted my return for a full refund, no questions asked. A very smooth transaction. Would definitely deal with them again.

The 370 hull is 32lbs, not 26 as in Amazon's description. They confused the 330 and the 370.

As a 5'2" woman, I found that I couldn't manage all the transport and packing of this 12 1/2 ft long boat comfortably on my own. Even with the help of a friend, we had a difficult time repacking everything. And we never did get it back in the carry bag. 32lbs of a solid object is easier to handle than 32lbs of 12 1/2 ft long deflated rubber.

And keep in mind that if you are buying this because you live in an apartment or condo and lack outside storage space, you'll need to rinse and hand dry the boat each time you use it before rolling and repacking it.

Having said that, the boat is sturdy and stable when inflated and I never felt ''tippy" in it.

Of course any inflatable takes more paddling effort than a hardshell and that needs to be considered too. But the paddles provided were fairly lightweight and easy to handle.

Tracking was just okay.

IMHO this makes a good vacation kayak. But wouldn't want to deal with extra maintenance and packing on a regular basis.

title: Uh... OK Fitbit (revised)
text:
Brand new out of the box, trying to set it up, and this thing is already presenting challenges. If you're thinking of getting one here's what you need to know: the charger is magnet so it attracts the charging prongs to the device easily HOWEVER, the magnet isn't strong enough to hold onto the device. If you set it down, it pops off the charging cord. You have to lay it down, propped on something, veeeerrrrrry carefully. I haven't even worn this thing and I can see that this is going to drive me nuts!!! I may deploy some high tech hacks - like a twist tie or some masking tape - to content with the charger design. :-p I'll come back and write more once I've set up and worn this thing.

You should know, I"m a devoted fitbit user and wear my devices out - they retire off to wherever beloved exhausted devices go after their life ends. I'm so sad my Alta HR died. I want it back! I still have my old Flex as a backup. I've never considered buying another brand of tracker and probably never will.

2/8/2020 - I'm back and I've upgraded stars from 3 to 5. The magnetic charger thing is still a bummer but absolutely everything else about this tracker is phenomenal. I can't believe this thing has so many features at its price point. Interaction with the screen is intuitive. The features available on-screen are a step up from the Alta HR. There's a Breath/relax/meditation function, a Timer, you can view and enable/disable the silent alarm settings right on the device, you can see how many steps you have left to meet the Reminder To Move target. I simply ADORE this thing!!! Fitbit, you really brought it with this tracker. I thank you.

7/7/2020 Back again with more information. Exactly 6 months after purchase, the device won't sync so I tried pairing it again to Bluetooth. The device won't pair so I tried resetting it per Fitbit product help web pages. The device won't reset. Now what? I loved the features on this device but it's hard to love something that won't work. Back to 3 stars.

title: Charge 3 is so disappointing
text:
I'm a Fitbit lover. I track everything with it; steps, heart rate, activity, sleep, food, BMI, body fat. All these metrics warm my geeky little heart and help me achieve my health goals. I own a Flex, an Alta HR, and the Aria 2 scale and have adored all of them. Because I love them so much, I gave my husband a Charge 3 for his birthday. I'm sorry to say, this Fitbit product is a total dud. The tracker will not sync with Fitbit's app. It worked for about 1 month then just stopped syncing with the app. We've tried every flavor of delete-reinstall-reset possible, all to no avail. There are hundreds, maybe thousands, of people who have this same issue, who have reported it to Fitbit, and the response is unfortunately not in keeping with the company's usual excellent customer service. All they will offer people is another Charge 3. You can't even swap the tracker for a less expense, older model that works with their app. Without the app, without the ability to track and review a history, the Charge 3 is little better than the freebie plastic pedometers your employer's health insurance plan hands out at their annual Open Enrollment fair. What's more than a little irksome is that Fitbit seems unwilling to admit there's a major software problem here. Seems obvious when one reads the Help forums. Why not 'fess up and tell us an estimate of when we can expect a software update? I don't get it. People will likely be patient and wait for the update if they know one is in the works. What is to be gained by pretending nothing is wrong? A lot of very unhappy customers, that's what.

Long story short: Don't buy this tracker. Get a different one. Maybe even one not made by Fitbit (sorry, Fitbit!)

title: Fine fine-weather car-camping tent.
text:
I've had this for about 3 years now, and I really do enjoy it. This is the go-to car-camping brought-way-too-much-stuff tent for fine weather. My husband likes it because he doesn't have to crawl to get around in it. I love that I can get it up in a few minutes without help. It's roomy and comfortable, but there are caveats.

-This is a single-layer tent without a rain fly. You can't leave the windows open in damp weather, and you WILL get tons of condensation in wet or cool conditions. It hasn't leaked badly in the rain for me, except when the rain has blown through the top vents. Keep your things away from the sides if you don't want them wet.

-I absolutely don't trust this thing in stormy or windy weather. It's just way too high profile for that sort of thing.

-It's bulky. I can easily fit it into the bag it came in (without needing to open the expander), but it's still large and heavy for a tent of these dimensions.

In short, this is a nice tent for a weekend with a fine weather forecast. It's not a tent for when you're going to be hours from civilization for longer than you can trust a weather forecast. Get yourself something low-slung with a fly that goes to the ground for that kind of camping.

title: My All-Time Favorite Water Bottle (and I consider myself a water bottle connoisseur)
text:
My entire life I've carried a water bottle around with me but never found a good water bottle that didn't leak or break quickly in all of my 34 years. Well, not until I found these bottles nearly 2 years ago at a Walmart. Contigo is my favorite brand now and all my bottles are this type (push to drink and pour into mouth). I used to prefer bottles that you can sip from, but changed my mind when I tried this model of water bottle. The fact that it stays sealed even without the lip on is great because my son is always knocking it over. You can even lock the button you press to drink if you don't want little hands making messes. I love the handle - super easy to carry and you can even hook it onto something like a belt loop because it has a little carabiner hook. I love the size of this bottle as well and now I'm so spoiled that I get frustrated with most other water bottles which generally hold half the amount of water this one does. I always put ice cold water in my bottles and the condensation is minimal, which I cannot say for any other bottle I've tried.

By the way, the last water bottle from Contigo I had (exact same model) broke after about 1.5 years of rigorous use. This was constant use, all day, several times a day, every day of that 1.5 years. The way it broke was that the flap-lid broke off but everything else worked fine. I've dropped this bottle a lot and it's been durable enough to never crack. Yes these cost more than your average water bottle, but honestly, they've saved me a ton of money in the long run because I've not had to replace ever few months like all other water bottles I've used.

title: I was going to get the Carhartt bag that looks just like this one BUT...
text:
According to NPR news I read, Carhartt was forcing it's employees to take an injection if they wanted to remain employed.
I, for one, have a mom who has allergic reactions to most medications and completely understand why some people would fear taking a jab. Because of this, I wanted to keep my support away from Carhartt. Plus, it didn't hurt saving myself $35+ at the time of writing this. I was actually about to buy everything Carhartt I could find that I needed since I've been buying a lot of supplies for work but, hey, I have found some great stuff from these "little guy sellers" and this bag is top notch.

This bag caught my attention because of it's obvious similarity to the Carhartt bag. I received the bag within one day of ordering and the bag looks very well made. No smell as some people complain of smell with products, mine was super clean and well cared for packaging. I wouldn't be surprised if the two brands' bags were made in the same factory - pretty sure both say country of origin is China.

Quality of this Lyweem bag and its zippers appear will be durable. It is comfortable to wear on my shoulders thanks to its padded wide shoulder straps; they don't get all twisted when I put it on like my old bag did - something so annoying I almost never put the old bag on but with this bag no problem.

However, the bag is not completely perfect, at least, perfectly suited for me. Things you may want to consider:
First off, the phone holder is too small for my cell phone. I suspect it would maybe hold phones with up to a 6" screen that are in a case and still be able to zip because mine is very close to fitting snug but nowhere near to zipping but with the case on it's just short of fitting all the way in. My phone is 6.6". (Moto G Power).
Second, I work a job where I have to work out in the rain sometimes and I needed the bag to hold a FROGG TOGGS Men's Classic All-Sport Waterproof Breathable Rain Suit that I also bought from Amazon (the one with the blue jacket is currently only $26). It will fit but it's very tight fit. I thought the bag would be a bit roomier than it actually is. But I also have on top of the suit: 2 pairs of gloves, toothpaste, toothbrush, toboggan, a cloth mask, eye wear, 2 drinks in the side, ibuprofen and sinus medicine, work hat, spare pen and paper with my lunch occupying the bottom.
Third, the bottom section is quite small. I got about 2 2"tall bowls in the bottom. One about 2x6x6 on top of one about 2x8x6. Nothing else but the silverware will fit in the bottom. Can't fit ice packs in with these two sandwich lock n' lock bowls. And with all this said, this is a pretty big bag, honestly. It just takes me more room than I expected.
Fourth, like others have said the bottom section is very awkward how it unfolds but so is the top section (compared to what I am used to). Definitely be aware of this. I am not a fan of how the bag unzips in half at the top. I've only used it once, though, so I might get better used to it. But it zips in half and is just hard to get stuff into it without having to hold it in while I zip it back up. And the bottom unzips and the whole top end just falls back or the bottom falls down. I am sure the Carhartt is just as awkward. So while I am sure they are both great bags, I am not truly a fan of the design as much as I thought I would be. Maybe it'll grow on me? Compared to my other regular backpack this one is tougher to pack.

Lastly, if I had it to do over again for my personal needs, which is a lot of space to carry a lot of stuff - an absurdly lot of stuff I will admit, I would skip this bag and get the Lyweem Duffel bag that also works as a backpack. I think it is $27 and looks like it has a ton more storage space. I would probably get a separate cooler to keep my water and ice packs in. I was thinking about doing this before I bought the bag but I was hoping I wouldn't have to carry 2 bags. I believe I will end up having to get another bag anyway.

At the time of writing this, if Lyweem will continue to make quality products as they have here, this company should go far and last a long time. I will search Lyweem for other needs and support the company as they have supported me with great value. GREAT QUALITY FOR A GREAT PRICE!! DESPITE MY NITPICKS, THIS PRODUCT IS A WINNER!!

title: Early Review: First Impressions
text:
The things I was curious about before buying these:
A) How they sound.
B) How they feel.
C) Compared to Howard Leights by Honeywell as well as the BT edition of the Walker Razor.

I have not tested the Noise Cancellation yet but provided it works as it should I wanted to get out my review in case anyone wondered what I did. My hand's on impressions have been fully positive.
If you get these and wonder how to open the package: I just bent the package in half. This caused the cardboard to split open and the plastic clamshell is not sealed - it is 2 parts and the headphones came out super simple.

How do they sound? (I own Sennheiser HD600 compared to those:)
A)Surprisingly good. Not audiophile but not bad.
B)Bass is light. Not much bass from these. Bass seems purposely reserved, truth be told probably neutral.
C)Slight emphasis on mid-range. But not annoying in any frequency.
D)Highs are present but not pristine.
E)Overall, they sound good for a $43 set of headphones that do so much more. I am pleased with it. I can listen without irritation.

How do they feel?
A) A little tight on my medium-sized head but the muffs are plushy and do a good job of distributing the clamp pressure.
B) I can't imagine wearing these for much more than an hour at a time but it might be ok for longer but probably no one will actually want to.
C) Headband doesn't rub my scalp.
D) No hair pulling or "pinchy parts".
E) The hinges that hold the muffs look thin but they work (so far). Durability could be a concern.
F) The hinges are adjustable. I collapsed then down about 2/5ths of the way so they could possibly fit larger heads but wider heads may have more clamp pressure?
G) Again, the clamp pressure is pretty tight. I am surprised how tight they are. But they stay on the head when moving my head which is good. It is a good thing they are tight but it could cause them to fatigue your head after a while. Be aware they are pretty tight on the head but I don't believe it will be a deal-breaker.

How is the enhanced hearing:
A) Fairly natural. I can rather accurately distinguish sounds.
B) I never knew what a bee flying sounded like other than Bumblebees right in my ear. I heard the bee and I will learn that sound but I wouldn't have known what it was had I not seen the bee and heard the sound.
C) You will discover new sounds you haven't heard before.
D) Unfortunately, the sound is mono-sounding like everyone has said. Determining the origin or placement of noises does not work out so well.
E) I questioned whether to get these or the Howard Leight by Honeywell. I decided to try these first after listening to YouTube videos. I have read reviews that say the "Howard's" better determine which direction noises come from but some videos said they do not do it better enough to choose them over these.
F) These are supposedly more comfortable than the Howard Leights.
G) They are cheaper and look better IMO than the Howard Leights.
H) I might buy the Howard Leights just to see if the sound placement is better because I think that would be a big deal but from what I have read and heard the hype may or may not be all it is cracked up to be. The reviewers mostly chose these over the Howard Leight.

Overall, I am impressed that these are only $43.
Be sure to get a 3.5mm to 3.5mm male to male wire to use them for music.
I wanted to get the Bluetooth version but after reading how much problems people were having with the BT dropping or not working, I decided to get the wired version.
The BT version has 4 mics which, on paper, seems would give better awareness of surroundings but from things I heard it didn't quite work as well in RL as it seems it would. I still would like to try those because it would be worth the money to me if they worked like they should but if they didn't I knew I would still be getting these.

title: Very handy and convenient lights that are extremely lightweight and easy to use.
text:
When I first opened these up and saw them, my mind started racing because I was imagining all of the different uses for these cute little lights!!

First of all, they're really easy to operate. They have a pretty flexible clip that you can use to attach them securely to just about anything - including the velcro straps, which are included. If you wanted to put them on your bike handles, for instance, then you'd use the straps since they can't clip on something that wide. However, they are perfect for clothing, dog leashes (or even the color), bags, pants, purses, etc.

These are super lightweight and you'll probably forget that you're even wearing one or have one attached to you. There's a single button that is used to turn them on and off. You can press it once for a steady light and again for a flashing light. With these being water-resistant, you can use them in any type of weather. I'm impressed.

Best of all, the BATTERIES ARE INCLUDED and you even get an extra battery for each light! How generous is that? title: A pretty solid watch with useful features, for the most part. Heart Rate Monitor, though? I think NOT!
text:
I've thoroughly tested this watch and used it for about a week before handing it over to my husband to wear daily. I'm on the fence between giving it 4 or 5 stars. I'd prefer to give it 4 ½ stars, but that isn't possible. Why? Well, I give it 4 ½ stars because the “heart rate monitor” in the name is a bit misleading; it’s not as advertised. Also, the instructions need work and there are a few things I still have questions about and don’t know what they’re for (ie. What is “Sig”).

For starters, this is a little more than just your average sports watch. It has some additional features that do come in handy - especially if you're very active and like to stay fit. Even though the watch seems to be a bit on the masculine side, I can definitely see females wearing it too. Along with a heart rate monitor (ahem, more like a pulse reader), it also has a pedometer fitness activity tracker (to count your steps, count calories, etc), chronograph stopwatch, countdown timer, backlight, and not one but two alarms!

I have to admit, going through all of the features and setting everything up is not just time-consuming but a bit confusing at times. I hope you have a good memory! :) Luckily, there is a pretty thorough guide included with the watch. Although there are a few spelling and grammatical errors due to them being broken English (probably translated from another language), you should have no trouble figuring out the important stuff.

The watch itself seems to be all plastic, but it’s very thick and feels very strong and durable. The face is large and easy to read. The four buttons are also large and easy to press, although, again, it can be a bit confusing remembering what each one does. So far, I’ve found everything to be pretty accurate besides the pedometer. It seems to count movements (when just standing or sitting still) as steps as well, but changing the sensitivity level helps with that.

Surprisingly, my favorite feature is the pulse reader (even though this is advertised as a heart rate monitor, which actually IS different) because it’s so quick and easy. I thought this watch would constantly track your heart rate, and I was sad at first to see that it doesn’t do that. However, after testing out the pulse reader I think I prefer it the way it is. It’s pretty much an on-demand thing. Whenever you want to know your pulse, you place your index finger at 12 o’clock and your thumb at 6 o’clock. I have not had an issue with it displaying my pulse.

title: Functions well but too bulky
text:
This is the 2nd pedometer I've owned. I bought this Omron to replace Walk 4 Life (W4L) unit I used for the prior 7 months. I was happy with the W4L pedometer except that the clip broke twice on it. And, because the clip is part of the basic W4L housing, you can't just purchase another clip - the unit is basically ruined (unless you want to risk carrying it loose in your pocket and opening it with your thumbnail). Therefore, since this Omron pedometer fits inside a separate hard plastic clip housing, I decided to try it.

It functions well, accurately tracks your steps, and has a nice memory feature to review the past week. However, it is close to 3 times the size of the W4L and, therefore, too bulky to wear under nice clothes. I was able to clip the W4L to my bra under a relatively tight fitting top, and it was undetectable; the Omron looks like a growth is projecting out of your chest. This seems to defeat the purpose of tracking all your steps if you can't (or choose not to) wear it, let's say, on a night you go dancing. In addition, although there's much less chance of the clip breaking, it's uncomfortable against bare skin and seems to me to be much bulkier than necessary.

In spite of these design flaws, it's a nice little unit for wearing around the house or in a casual/workout environment. In general, I've found pedometers to be a fantastic way to motivate individuals to just stay active, which is much more effective than exercise alone. If the only way pedometer manufacturers can prevent the clips from breaking is to make them as Omron has, it's far better than W4L's clip design.

If Omron could reduce the size of the unit, the bulkiness of the clip, and have the unit sit low in the clip housing (instead of half of it sticking up over the top), I'd give it 5 stars.

title: C+ front light; A- rear light
text:
Overall, I'm happy with my purchase as I feel I received good value for the money spent. Both lights operate as described and (mostly) provide me with the light I was seeking for my very early morning or very late night rides. I am a full-time bike commuter who lives and works in the suburbs and drivers here are notoriously distracted and inattentive.

Specifically, the front light has a great mount, better than I expected. Holds well to my odd-shapped handlebars. My rating of a C+ is based on two issues I have with the beam of the light. It seems to loose its stated 900 lumens brightness about 30-40 minutes into my ride. It's almost as though I can see it getting dim as I ride. Additionally, it shines a large circle of light rather than an oval-shaped beam that I grew used to on my Cygolite and Cycle Torch lights on my other bikes. I much prefer the oval beam for seeing a nice wide angle. As for the tail light, I'm very pleased. It offers great brightness by night and day, which here in the 'burbs is very important. My only knock on the tail light is that is must be charged after every use. The battery life is 60 minutes tops.

If you don't mind charging your lights after every use, even short rides, and a circular headlight beam meets your needs, I think you would be happy with this light set. I would absolutely purchase Nite Rider tail lights again, however because of the round beam and the dimming of the headlight after just a short while, I don't know that I would buy another head light from this company. Too bad because I think I like their mounting strap better than any other I've used.

I bike to work even day and lock up onto a wide-tube bike rack so I needed more space that a U-lock provides. The ripstop cover is quite heavy duty and robust. Overall, I'm extremely pleased and have recommended it to a friend who also bike commutes.

title: Best storage solution
text:
I've owned this brand and style of water container for almost 17 years, it's my go-to for camping and day trips where there might not be any water. I have almost always had at least 2 of them, one for drinking water, the other for potable water (cleaning dishes, cooking, dog water). Recently having to purchase two more, I guess the one that's put on the age and seen places finally developed a crack on the bottom. Not bad after 7-8 years being lugged around.

Pros: Lots of water on hand - Easy to use - Stack able - Durable - Trusted brand -

Cons: Heavy once full (7gallons x 7lbs per gallon of water + container = 50lbs) - spigot almost never lines up pointing down no matter how many ways you screw on the cap - price raised by $10 in past year

Points to look at when choosing: If you can't lift 7 gallons, get the 2.5 or 5 gallon model
(Here is an example per the National Park Service) 2 gallons a day per person when camping, you can figure the same if the water at your house is shut off during a emergency event. You might add an extra gallon for toilet flushes.

I'm glad this bag comes with straps on the sides, I would be afraid the sack might split from the pressure of this sleeping bag. I might update this after the trip is over and I stuff the bag back into this compression sack. Maybe even take a picture with it in the side pannier for size comparison. For size - imagine this; you cannot fit a regular size coffee can over the opening of this sack and have enough fabric to pull over.

Update: After my journey out, and my journey back. For a sleeping bag this size; you have to roll it a few different ways until it works. Fold it in half until its bag width, then roll it as tight as you can. Proof is in the pudding, the bag fits just perfect and still fits into my side bag on the motorcycle. Not really sure what to put into the little pocket on top, maybe an extra pillow cover? Or small flashlight. Hope this picture helps someone decide what they need. I would buy again for other things I need to compress down.

text:
I didn't get any pictures like I normally donate toward the cause, it was a dark night and a rush in the morning. I watched the assembly video about 2 months prior to using the tent, unless you have a terrible memory...it helped. I didn't even set up the tent at all once I received it in the mail, I just took it out of the box and strapped it to the bike for camping 2 months later.
It's a very small package, almost perfect for a medium-weight backpacking trip or a motorcycle trip. The first night we arrived at the site I unpacked everything; it was getting dark fast so I immediately started the tent, I pulled everything out and just started to dump the contents on the ground.

Within 8-10 minutes - the tent was set up and I was ready to crawl inside! Very little rainfly, it only covers the 6"x8" air vent at the peak of the tent. If there is a blowing wind with rainfall you will get wet. I suggest getting two "footprint" ground covers and use the first underneath and the second one as an additional rainfly. It is a perfect size for a single person, I'm 6ft and I had a few inches of space above and below me while sleeping. Enough room to get dressed standing while bending over, or to be on knees and likewise. I had my backpack, sleeping bag, boots, extra clothes and still had extra room on sides of me to roll around at night. Very simple and nice design, I would get another.

title: Get a 4 pack for each cooler!
text: I bought 2 coolers for camping. One 5 day cooler for food and one 4 day cooler for drinks, I used 5 pouches in each cooler. I put pre-chilled food and drinks in the coolers upon leaving for the site. The night before I put cheap ice packs in the coolers to chill them, as to prep so the packs wouldn't start melting the moment I put them in there. I removed the cheap packs the morning before leaving, and placed the packs on each side and bottom of the coolers. Filled the coolers and buttoned them down for the ride. It was an average of 75-90 degrees through out the days we were out camping, I kept a shade cover over the trailer that contained the coolers as it was bear country. So no direct sunlight was on the coolers at any time. We were camped for 3 nights and 4 days, upon leaving for home...both coolers were about 80% gone of food and drink and the packs were just barely cold and already sagging from loss of ice pack. The first morning I opened up the cooler to get a propel, it had a small frost layer inside the bottle. If I was rich enough to afford a Yeti, I bet these things would easily rock 5 days no problem. It's worth it!

title: Good intro to Zumba
text:
I am a 65 year old female and new to Zumba. This is an easy introduction with 3 different cd's. One shows the actual steps to salsa, merengue, etc. This shows you how to do them, some of their variations, and a quick run through to some music. This is a purely instructional cd. Ignore Joy, pay attention to Beto. I'm not sure why she's there.
The next cd is the Cardio. This will start you out with a warm up routine and then into some dance routines using the above steps you learned. Ignore Joy and watch Beto. I always do the cardio and then decide how much dance I want to do. I might do this 2 or 3 times a day.
And the 3rd cd is the toning cd that includes using the very lightweight toning sticks. They sound a bit like maracas. You don't have to use these, just do the workout routine without them.
Remember, this is for those of us who prefer a slower pace, but it still gets the heart rate up and counts as exercise. Don't complain if you were expecting wild and crazy; this is not that.

text: I purchased the Lanshan 1 Pro in green from the 3F UL website and it arrived within 2 weeks. Overall I am very please with the tent. The sleeping area is generous compared to my old tent. I purchased the footprint as well which I recommend. My problem is that the sil-nylon cannot be seam sealed at the factory and it is a must for a single wall tent. I completely ruined the cosmetic appeal of the tent using a highly recommended silicon seam sealer from a big name company. For the love of whatever ultimate supreme being that you believe in, use a thinned silicon to seal or it will turn out to be a mess. I felt completely defeated with the end result. Its a nice tent, the weight is perfect as advertised and the accessories are quality. I hesitated to buy a sil-nylon tent and I wish I had bought it sooner. Too bad my seam sealing trashed the clean aesthetics of the tent. I highly recommend this piece of kit. Price, weight and quality converge for once and the tent is roomy. The vestibule is useful and the mesh around the perimeter of the tent tub floor provide adequate 3 season ventilation. I have not had issues with condensation yet.

title: Great tent but seam seal is a must
text: This is a good tent. We like the vestibule and sit in it in our folding camping chars when the bugs are out. I can almost stand up straight in the middle (5'9"). We did seam seal everything from the windows down. The rain fly is seam taped from the factory but the tub seam and corner seams leaked a bit after 2 days of rain the first camping trip. I greatly appreciate the reflective guy lines as pictured for reference. The stitching looks good for the price point compared to much more expensive tents. I love the stake out loop at the middle of the vestibule screen door so i can open and close with 1 hand. People complain about things getting wet in the vestibule but maybe they forgot its basically a screened room. Its like an airlock to keep bugs out. We had zero issues with interior condensation after seam sealing. Its roomy for 2, almost a palace. 6 people would be uncomfortable, maybe 3 or 4 at most but for 2 on a queen mattress its basically a bedroom. We uses our camping storage totes as end tables. We like this tent and the vestibule is one of it's best features.

text: This review is for our second RCP Trekker 1 we purchased. The first 1 was a gift for my father inlaw so we could backpack a section of the AT together. I was so impressed with the tent that I purchased a second one for myself. It's not the the lightest backpacking tent nor the smallest. It is however a heaver nylon material with great seam stitching and seam taped to keep you dry. You still need to seam seal the exterior seams. The vestibule is HUGE and plenty to store our packs and shoes. The rear wall is full mesh double wall with bottom vents. It is a hybrid between a single wall tent and a double wall tent. Best bang for your buck if you are new to backpacking or if you want a solid trek pole tent and don't mind the weight.

I'm still slow going down steep descending loose footed trails but my balance and stability with a 60L pack is greatly improved. Next week my father inlaw and I are going on a 4 day section hike of the AT which would not be possible without my Trail Buddies!

My new trail name is "Tortuga" because I'm slow like a tortoise and wear my buff like a pirate. Happy trails!

title: Absolutely amazing for the money!
text:
For under 100 bucks shipped you get everything you need to get out on the water minus life vests. The skeg has been improved as it now has a new locking mechanism and silhouette. The 86" paddles are well made for the price, nicely curved, have an adjustable paddle angle and float (as we found out accidentally) so paddle leashes are recommend. The boat is stable when inflated properly using the pressure gauge "measuring strip" and did not rock too bad when standing up in the aft position with an adult seated up front. The boat has a drain plug in the stern which has to be closed as mine was shipped in the open position. The 30 gauge PVC (Vinyl) has a nylon like backing and appears to be rugged enough for large lakes and mild moving waters. Not sure I would personally use this on class III+ water but some reviewer's have reported their own success stories. It tracks well on flat water with the skeg and okay with a peaceful river current without. Seats are more comfortable than I originally imagined when purchasing. Watch out for over inflation as we pumped her up at 64° and by the afternoon the temp had increased to 74° which caused the inflation gauge to read 5-10% (0.5-1 cm) higher due to air expansion. Over all I am impressed for the cost of purchase. It comes with one 3"x3" self adhesive patch similar to "Tear-Aid type B" (looks like a square piece of yellow card stock) and two 2" clear patches that require you to use your own PVC cement. The pump tube can be stored inside the pump itself by unscrewing the end and coiling it around the pump shaft. It packs up into a Blackhawk tactical bag that I have as the Intex bag was uncomfortable to carry since it didn't have a shoulder strap. The boat is 22.2 lbs without the seats, 25.8 lbs with both seats not including other accessories. Takes about 10 minutes to setup with the included air pump or 5 minutes with the 12v Intex pump (which has deflate mode too!!!).

Things to remember include closing the drain plug and monitoring inflation to prevent over inflation related seam tears. If you know the temp will increase throughout the day by 5-10° i would recommend under inflating by 5-10% (0.5-1 cm) on the inflation gauge which is approximately 10 cm long when fully inflated.

title: Good fenders for Fat bike tire coverage, but the mounting system isn't 100% stable.
text:
The inner fork mounting system is ok, but the fender will move around some horizontally not covering all of tire if you are doing any kind of jumping or trail riding.
I modified the fenders, getting rid of the single expansion screw mount. Removed some metal from the mounts, bent them 90 degrees, and both peices of the front fender now bolt horizontally through the Fork hole (where U brakes used to bolt to on the forks). Testing it on my full rigid fat bike, hucking down some dropoffs and over major roots, the fenders now stay perfectly in place.

I left the rear fender unchanged. However, I put on some grip tape on my seat post where the rear fender mounts to by way of strap/cam. Before the grip tape, the rear fender would move slightly side to side. It is now nearly as stable as the front fenders while still allowing quick removal.

title: Poor quality control - FRAME/Fork
text:
got Megalith on 1/5/2015 directly from STATE bikes. used 20% coupon so got bike for $560.
Bike is not worth $700.
IS mounts F & R were hugely off from being perpendicular to Axle centerline.
I had to modify these myself to fix and get decent alignment with the Hayes Prime and 203mm discs I put on immediately.

Bike may work tubeless with the extra heavy CTS tires the bike comes with. However I could not get Vee Missions to work as they fit too loosely on the wheel to hold bead until you can inflate.

I heard from another owner that the stock headset is absolute crap. I noticed the headset myself was bit crappy and fit seemed weird, but have not ridden the bike yet, so i'll take the word of another owner and also upgrade the headset to a Cane Creek Forty
Again. Even though I immediately upgraded parts, the poor quality control of the frame (*disc mounts) has kept me from even being able to ride the bike yet, as I've had to massage it with my 4.5" dewalt grinder

I would be a bit more Annoyed if I had paid the full $700 price. And if I wasn't fabricator with all kinds of tools/welders, I would not have been able to fix some of the issues myself at no cost.
This other owner also told me their is non existant support from STATE. Also if you can't prove it was professionally assembled, he said they will not honor any warranty.
I knew this was a gamble as it's an "internet" only available bike. and also I would be assembling it myself.
I think if I had taken this to a professional bicycle mechanic, they would have laughed and most likely try to sell you another bike, or possibly charge a bit to fix the issues (typically $25 per end, $50 total)

If you plan to upgrade to 1x10 drivetrain, etc, don't waste your money on this bike. Pay more up front and get a better bike that has better components
The only other fairly inexpensive Chromo fatbike I was aware of was Bikesdirect Lurch. Not sure of their quality but wish I had purchased that instead. Surly of course makes chromo bikes but the cost of frame is about what I paid for full Megalith bike (you get what you pay for). Aluminum bikes you have much more options. BD boris, Charge Cooker, Framed, etc.

text:
Pro:
- warrantee
- durability
- thickness
- comfort
- length options
- no weird smell

Cons
- Price
- weight
- slickness

So, the mat MUST be salted and let sit once you first get it, otherwise it will be very slick. Do not skimp in the salt.

The price for the mat is high, but it has a lifetime warrantee and last FAR longer than most other mats.

It is not as soft as some other mats I have used, but it also isn't squishy like a lot of cheaper mats. I have great stability on the mat (once it has been salted). It is cushioned enough that I can do table and the like on my knees without too much discomfort (yay, old knees).

It is heavy. This is not a mat I would want to use for a long walk to the studio. It is great for home or if you always have close parking.

As a taller person, I really liked that this mat is very long. It adds to the weight, but it means I don't have to adjust where I am on the mat most of the time.

I used to carry the RTIC 20 hard cooler and it will definitely keep ice longer and would last longer as well. But damn that thing is heavy. The soft pack loaded is not much heavier than the hardsided 20 empty.

title: Reasonably sturdy, very comfortable, perfect for ice skating
text:
I use these gloves for ice skating daily. They keep my hands warm, but not too warm, and they are very comfortable. I like the rubber grips on the palms so that when I put my hands on the boards, they don't slide all over the place. The thumb and forefinger tips work well enough for my phone. Not to type, but to push play on music or skip a song..that's about the extent that you'll want to use the tips for. Any more serious typing and you'll need to take a glove off. I find that heating up the finger tip helps even more (which is cold because of the ice rink).

I got my first hole in the gloves after about 2 months of daily wear. I'm pretty tough on the gloves and they're put on and taken off multiple times a day, and frequently touch the ice or sharp skate blades...so one minor hole on a seam after that period of time seems reasonable to me. Sewed it closed and ordering a second pair so that I have a backup for the future. I got the grey ones so they're easier to find in my bag than black would be.

I preferred the size for packing for a trip since they didn't take a ton of room in my suitcase, but when I was out in the ocean I got a little tired quicker than I expected because of the lack of power due to the length. They weren't as difficult to walk in since they weren't so long though.

title: The purple color pictured is inaccurate, but the bag is great.
text:
The color in the picture AND on the Grit website is INACCURATE!! It is NOT a royal purple like shown. It is a much, much darker color purple and not bright at all like the picture shows. I wish I had gotten a different color and will be writing to Grit regarding this mistake. Purple is a new offering so I'm the first one with this new color at the rinks, but I'm annoyed that it's not as bright as the pictures show.

Color aside, the bag is wonderful. The 36in is just the right size for XL gear. Any larger and I'm not sure if it will fit. I love the removable garment bag but I do wish it was a tad bigger. It BARELY fits my undershirt, pants, socks and jersey...and will not fit my hockey socks so I have to shove them in a pocket.

The middle shelf holds my elbow pads and shinguards. My shinguards are ALMOST too long for it...so if you're taller than 6ft, this may not work for you. My pants and chestpads fit in the bottom section. I shove my gloves inside my helmet since they won't fit anywhere else. The pockets are nice for accessories tape and other stuff.

It BARELY fits into the trunk of a mustang. I was actually concerned that it wouldn't fit when I first tried because the base is so large. Thankfully the bag twists so I'm able to just barely squeeze it in and out of there every day.

title: Occasionally FLINGS WATER ALL OVER YOUR FACE.

While exercising or at home...this isn't much of an issue but when you're at work and you get a strawful of water down your white blouse, it's a pretty significant design flaw.

I don't know what causes the issue...perhaps if the bottle gets turned upside down in transit to work or something. I don't have any leaking issues and for the most part, the straws seal fine. Occasionally one of my bottles will have a leaky straw issue where it's hard to suck the liquid out of the bottle because of air seapage but for the most part...it's reliable.

But having liquid flung in your face a small percentage and totally at random is unacceptable.

title: Comfort for a larger person!

I'm still working up to longer rides...but going from 20 minutes to 45 minutes overnight was incredible.

title: So far, so good
text: As a replacement for the worn out OEM coil fork on my 29’er, this has been great.  The improvement in ride quality is very evident.  An area I frequently ride has sections where tracked vehicles have left long stretches of washboard terrain, which previously were a jarring, miserable riding experience.  Now, they’re really barely noticeable.  I have only a couple gripes.  The fork comes with absolutely nothing in the way of instructions for installation, maintenance or setup, or even contact info.  However, installing it is extremely simple, except for the brake cable issue mentioned below.  And there’s quite a bit of torsional flex in the fork. I would hesitate to tackle any black diamonds with this fork, but for intermediate trail riding, it’s a nice, affordable upgrade.  As mentioned by several other reviewers, you may have issues with the brake caliper needing a lot of patient adjustment to prevent the rotor banging into the caliper body; this is a pretty basic manufacturing issue, and a millimeter or so extra distance between the brake posts and the axle drop out would be helpful.  Be aware that the fork is likely to be quite a bit longer than OEM forks on most low- to mid-range bikes (it was almost 3.5” longer than the original on mine) and this does manifest itself in a changed geometry and frame height, as well as necessitating a longer front brake cable.

title: Probably ideal for road/hybrid, not so much for MTB
text: These grips definitely relieve pressure by giving more surface area to the palm and repositioning the wrist.  Quality of construction appears quite good, and I’m positive they’d be great on a hybrid that you’re riding on paved/smooth surfaces.  However, there is a tradeoff if you’re using them on a mountain bike and riding any kind of rugged terrain: you will feel each and every bump transmitted straight up your arms due to the fact that your palm is now the primary point of contact.  Whether it’s something tolerable long-term, I can’t say; it’s my initial reaction after a fair ride on rocky trail.  The gain of comfort on relatively smooth stretches of trail may be worth suffering the bone-rattling over more unforgiving terrain.  It may be that I end up putting these on my hybrid for long-distance comfort and going back to round grips on my 29er.  Also, I suspect that if your hands are wide, you’ll eventually take issue with the grip ends.

title: Comfortable and grippy glove.
text:
I’ve played a few rounds with this glove and so far, I’m very pleased. There’s no discernible sacrifice of grip vs leather, and it’s comfortable. The real test will come in another couple months when I’ll see how it is in Florida summer heat, when you’re continuously sweating; that’s where a standard leather glove starts to fail. Can’t rate durability until it’s had adequate use to offer a rating, but one can easily see that these gloves are more easily washable than leather, and so won’t develop the nasty aroma that leather/synthetic leather gloves invariably get even when washed often.
Update 7/2022: After two years of use, these gloves are in essentially the same condition as new. These wash up very well, threw them in the dryer with my other clothes and no shrinking or wear. Definitely the longest-lasting golf gloves I’ve had.

text: This driver definitely will boom out the big drives you'd expect from a 460cc head.  For the price, that's a miracle.  But - don't fool yourself into thinking this is high-quality gear.  The paintwork is cheap, the head is a generic design that shows up in other mfrs' clubs (albeit at a higher price) and its overall feel doesn't lend one to believe it'll hold up more than a couple seasons.  Most crucially, though, I've taken mine out a fair amount in the last six weeks and it already shows clear signs of stress fracturing and surface cracking on the face, right around the sweet spot.  I hit a consistent 270-280 yard drive with the club - for now.  But I don't hold much hope it's a club that'll live long if used often.

title: Great club to have handy
text:
An awesome little tool for those shots off the fringe, where a wedge would be too dicey and putter can't get through the grass. But where this really shines is those approach & recovery shots where regular clubs are just useless - behind/under trees, off hard turf where a wedge would just bounce - anywhere you can't easily get under the ball or don't want a lot of loft. It's become a much-used club in my bag and I'd say it's cut several strokes off my game. Quality of the club exceeded my expectations. I used it yesterday to punch a shot off dirt, in a cluster of trees, 80 yds steeply uphill to put the ball on the green. There's no other club that could have made that shot work, period.

ADDED: after having several months of playing time with this club, I still can't say enough good things about it. Here in the northeast, this last season offered two basic turf conditions: dry as concrete or soggy, muddy slop. Neither condition makes it easy to use a wedge for those close shots under 75 yards. I've played through the winter where the soil's been frozen, as well, and the chipper makes those shots so much easier. It's well-built and it's really become a favorite club.

title: Clubhead falls off first time on course?
text:
OK - my own fault as by now, I know you get what you pay for. On this basis, buying a $20 hybrid is more experiment than sensible purchase. But based on prior reviews, I thought, why not?

Here's why not: I received the club on Wednesday, put it in my bag and went to the course on Thursday. Looks like a Taylormade Rescue, but with really poor detail. Well, looks don't get the ball down the course, and it was $20, so who cares, right?

First shot, nicely impressed...second shot, the same. Third shot, I feel something...odd. Ball pops straight up in the air at almost a 90 degree angle to my lie. Look at the club, and there's the answer. Clubhead is an inch down the shaft from the ferrule, and with the slightest tug, it pops right off. So much for the experiment.

Maybe I'm crazy, but there's just no excuse for a clubhead falling off within three shots; six swings total with practice. None. Zero. I'm surprised it actually made it through shipping without coming off. Maybe they used cornstarch to glue this on instead of epoxy? Who knows. The only saving grace is that I hadn't yet thrown away the box, so it was easy to return this dismal thing.

title: Bulkier than I imagined
text: I used the belt for the first time today, after the particular weight vest I bought turned out to be a total loss (and cost me $12 to return to Amazon, thank you very much).  This belt was an improvement, but that's not saying much. To begin with, the strap that attaches to one end of the weighted tube appears to have been sewn or attached vertically, rather than horizontally.  This means that when you attach the belt to its fastener on the other side (which is attached properly-i.e. horizontally), the strap is twisted. So there is minor discomfort even before you've done any exercise. The belt does cinch nicely, and shifts just slightly side-to-side during (my relatively mild) walking exercizes- however, I did not try any moves that involved jumping up and down, specifically because I was afraid that the weight would bounce up and down and be very uncomfortable .  The darn thing is just bulky- about as big around as a water bottle, and rests right along the hips. All the weight is in the back, which throws off your stride- also, you can't move your arms very freely,and you have to make a pretty conscious effort to keep your swinging elbows from whacking the thing each time you stride.  I may try it a time or two more on days when I am only doing moderate walking exercizes, but I'm probably going to return it and try to find a decent vest that will stay put during exercize and not choke me.  It is ironic that the initial 5 lb. vest I bought at TJ Maxx 2 years ago has been far and away the best device I've used for loading the body during exercize.

title: May work for some, but not for me
text: I currently use a 5 lb. weighted vest by Danskin that ai like very much. However, I wanted to increase the weight and challenge myself, and thought the 12 lb vest would be just the thing. For whatever reason, it fastens just about on top of my collar bones, whereas my other vest fastens under my bust- the high closure is uncomfortable and also shifts during exercise, until it ended up nearly around my throat.. And the whole vest shifts and slides around whileyou're exercising, which is incredibly distracting. I'm returning this best and am going to try a heavy weighted belt instead. Good luck to anyone trying to use this vest- it,s too bad, because the weight is ideal and the item appears to be well-made otherwise.

title: So far very pleased
text: So far so good.  I will say this is an initial review so I will mostly cover set-up and first impressions since I've only ridden the bike once so far.  Will do a follow up review later to better rate how it holds up.  Other reviewers have said two hours to assemble, and I found this to be extremely accurate for one person.  If the bike will go up or down stairs, recommend opening the box near the door and taking the individual pieces one at a time.  The design was smart for an assemble yourself device, as they put most of the mounting bolts in the places they go to make things easier.  All the tools you need are included in the box, but I highly recommend bringing your own socket wrench with a 13mm socket for the seat mounts at minimum.  This will make things a whole lot easier for you.  I used the included tools for everything else which worked fine.  I did use the seat extender because I'm 5'11", but it was a tough call for me since my wife is 5'8" and it is recommended for folks that are 5'9" and taller.  But with my socket wrench it will be easy to remove if she can't reach the pedals.  The seat is not particularly easy to adjust up and down, but I sprayed a little WD-40 on the metal and it made it slightly better.  It's sturdy once you have it at the level you want it.  The seat back folds forward, and has a lock bolt to prevent it from moving backwards, or to adjust to your level of comfort.  I took out the lock bold and used one of the extra adjustment knobs which fits in that hole too and seems more natural to use, and I put the nut from the lock bolt on it to secure it.  Not in the instructions, but it works better for me that way.  The massage bar is useful to me for added stability too.  You can hold onto that instead of the desk, or use it for added stability for your forearms when using your laptop or tablet.  I threaded the securing band through the top upper hole and only use that for a laptop since I have a pillow style holder that sits nicely on the desk for my tablet.  Typing is pretty seamless on the lower resistance levels, although I expect to be watching Netflix movies most of the time so I have a better handle on my riding time without paying any more attention to it than length of whatever show I choose to zone out to.  I did connect the meter and it seems to work fine, but so far I don't pay any attention to the calorie counter or other readings.  I had thought about ordering a rubber mat to go under it because of our squeaky hardwood floors, but the seats on the bottom sit quietly and the machine doesn't make much noise.  I would recommend having a towel handy though as this does offer a real cardio workout and you will perspire unlike the guy in the picture Amazon has here.  My last comment relates to the value.  I pondered over the $6499 Expresso bike available here on Amazon long and hard because it seems to be the latest in VR bicycle technology before choosing this machine.  The high tech gadget lover in me drooled over that at first glance.  In the end analysis I just couldn't justify paying that kind of money and then possibly finding out I couldn't dedicate the required willpower to get on it regularly.  For less than 5% of that cost I really think I will use this one, and won't have to worry about signing up for an expensive membership once the free trial expires on that other choice.  This machine makes a whole lot more sense to me in the long run.  I absolutely think it is worth the cost- so far.  Once I get into better shape with it, I'll add more to this review- and hope this is helpful to you for now.

text: Darn! Rain every day this week--and I was soaked to the skin the other day--and now I have my new umbrella and it's dry.  Humid, but dry.  It is black and classy looking with a soft-grip handle and is 36 1/4 to 36 1/2 inches long, closed. The difference is because the end of the handle is angled. The tip, bubble-wrapped, almost 2 inches long  with the slip case on and and 2.75 inches with it off, is covered with the same perforated plastic (I guess nowadays nothing is made of rubber!).  Then there is a .75 inch metal ring holding everything together. The umbrella is in a fairly heavy plastic slip case to protect the nylon case inside.  The nylon case is a slip case, not one of those that needs something to hold it onto the umbrella. Inside, And the bottom has a tab to make it easy to pull off. The velcro band around the umbrella is almost 1.25 inches wide. The jewel-like opening button is also protected by plastic.  The only flaw I've seen is that there is some glue that ran onto the bottom of the handle, from, I guess, when the handle was glued on to the whatever goes inside the handle. The fancy button provides a quick opening, but closing needs to be done manually.  The label indicates that it is coated with Teflon and there is a 2 year Peace of Mind Replacement Guarantee provided it is registered within 30 days.  I'll be back in a minute. Since it's not raining for a change :), I'm going to go outside and test this with my hose.  The water beaded up quickly and quickly ran off. It also provides nice shade against the 90 plus temps here.  I taped the hose's shower function on the umbrella, but may or may not attach it, since this was my first time to video anything on this phone. And it was impressive. I have no hesitation in giving this 5 stars. It was my absolute pleasure to get this at a discount in exchange for an honest, unbiased review. And I hope you appreciate the blood (mosquitoes) and sweat that went into this review. I hope it rains soon, now that I am prepared :) I've tried to add photo several times, with no luck, so hopefully these will work. If there are duplicates, please excuse me.

text:

update
ok so the negative vote i got made me think and i realize most of the review is about how regular beds suck and not how this bed is awesome, so time for an update. one of the great features i already mentioned, no stretching or leaks so the bed stays firm. another good feature is the connections inside the bed. the system they use allows for a fairly flat surface because the seal points are not form top to bottom but have a linkage that allows the bed to inflate to a fairly consistent depth across the surface. the image shows it well. other air beds have deep pockets where the weld connects the top to bottom piece. that is a major deal if you have ever slept on an airbed like this. flat surface is key. this bed seems to have the most advanced welding. the only real issue i have is that the bed is so light weight that it moves around easily on the frame. that can be annoying. Costco sells this same item and i sell to Costco so i know how intensely they review items for consideration to sell. this is the best airbed on the market today, period.

title: Happy to ride again!
text:
I was gifted this from a good friend of mine. Wow! It took 4 hours to install it on my Cannondale Mt Bike. I have tested it on very steep paved roads around my house and it works very well. The battery is very strong for about the 1st 2-3 miles on the hilly area. After that it will start to get a little weaker but still last me about 8 miles with hills. I weigh 216 pounds and I was running it on 2.1 knobby tires on a bike specifically designed for mountain biking - i.e. not road riding. I took it on single track to see how well it would do with some hills, does great! After having it for a couple of months, I got a flat - slow leak. I purchased a thorn resistant tire, Slime tube and Mr Tuffy liners. As other people have said, you do not want to get a flat. But I also carry all of the tools necessary to fix it out on the road just in case. I am no dummy, I have ridden thousands of road and single track miles through the years and flats are a way of life.

I can not over emphasize the ABSOLUTE JOY in riding this thing!! I had lost interest in biking because you always had to get all dolled up just to go for a ride. Not anymore. I wear jeans, Carhartt jacket if its cold and tennis shoes. Ha! I love it. Snap the battery in and I am good to go! What a great way to run to the grocery or hardware store or...

I purchased the second battery. Well worth the $100+. I can now go for a ride and when the first battery dies, click over to the second one and work my way home. I have been riding it on rough ATV trails here in Arizona and beating the heck out of the system. My rim has stayed true and the rack and batteries stay snug.

As a rap up... JOY in riding! Now I am always riding down hill. That use to be one of the things I loved about biking in Colorado where I lived. You ride up so you can ride down. Now the flat stretches are like down hills!! Woohoo! LOVE IT! I feel like a kid again... and it gets me out of the house.

Happy trails...

title: Easy to assemble and room enough for my two carts bags
text:
I put this together in about an hour while watching a movie in the man cave. So basically it could go together a little quicker if you keep yourself organized. I recommend that you do the following . Remove all the pieces from packaging (assuring that you have all you are supposed to have). Match up all the screws and nuts to make sure you have good thread matching. This keeps you from dropping them and/or losing track in the midst of the assembly. The instructions are not the best I have seen but they do give you enough information to get the job done. The pieces seem to me to only have one way to put them together and if you have a remote idea (remember the instructions) it should go together rather quickly. Avoid tightening the nuts and screws completely until you have the all the screws and bolts for the pieces you are working on in place. When you do snug them up and move to the next piece. A couple of them will make you wish for a third arm but if you have someone there to lend a hand on the trickier ones, it should be a breeze. I was working on a carpeted area so I did some flipping around to help give me the angles I wanted. The carpet allowed me not to worry about scratching the floor or the metal. After putting this together, I think I could put one together in about twenty minutes without distraction.
I like the look of the organizer and it had plenty of room for my old Mizuno cart bag and my new Sun Mountain cart bag. It seems like it will be plenty durable although I guess that remains to be seen over time. It was light to move around (unloaded). I am most pleased with the end product.

title: I’ve been using these for about a year now…
text:
With a chronic migraine that hasn’t gone away in years, I’ve slept with a block of ice as the upper half of my pillow for almost as long. It’s just one of the things that really help.

Now, having a container that’ll stay ice cold all night without peeing the bed, that can be a challenge. These are the most durable water bladders I’ve found, and after a year of being frozen and thawed every day, filled to about 85-90% with a little room left for expansion, they show absolutely no real signs of wear. They’ve gotten dirty, and I’ve had to scrub them now and then, but they are very reliable. My only issue has been the tiny nozzle on the little cap, which will occasionally pop open and cause problems. That’s easily fixed with a piece of duct tape. Considering what I put these things through, I really couldn’t imagine finding a better alternative.

It would be nice if they could make the fabric covering a smoother texture, but honestly, that’s a particularly nit-picky detail that most people using these for intended purposes, couldn’t care less about.

These things last so long, if you don’t lose them and you’re not using them in active military service, I seriously doubt you’ll need to replace them for a long time to come. I bet if I’d had one while I was in the army, I’d still be using it. They’re far tougher than the 2-quart canteens I was issued, that’s for sure.

Then, when it was almost empty, my husband grabbed it to move it, and the seam split completely. It was kind of impressive, how quickly and completely it ripped.
