title: Inaccurate Pulse Ox monitoring. Doesn't count steps on treadmill desk. Very small wristband.
text:
1) The pulse ox measurements are SIGNIFICANTLY lower on this than on my fingertip devices that I know are accurate. This could cause false alarms about health. For example it read 95 when I was awake and took manual readings at a time when my fingertip one read 98-99. No matter how many deep breaths I took I couldn't get it to read above 95. Perhaps due to my dark arm hair? On the overnight it consistently read around 90 but I know that my pulse ox isn't consistently that low overnight from my sleep study, especially when my CPAP is in use which it was. Given that there is a vast difference between 90 and 95 and 98 in terms of body experience and health it's useless to have a sensor this inaccurate.

2) It is really silly that the only way to do continuous pulse ox monitoring is overnight when sleeping. Why can't it continuously monitor throughout the day and warn me when I need to stop and take some deep breaths? This is actually what I really want it for because for some reason I've been getting out of breath occasionally during the day time (covid? anxiety? allergies? who knows!). When I do I measure my pulseox and it's always a bit low and deep breaths help bring it back up. I'd like something that would pre-emptively warn me that I've gone low or that could tell me how often over the course of the day I go low. This will only do that at night.

3) The wrist band on the standard model is really small. Like child sized. I know there is a larger model available and I suggest any adult use the larger model. My wrists are not at all large but I had to use the very first hole on this band and it still left marks on my arm and was uncomfortable. I thought this nice slim band would be more comfortable than the bulkier watches but it's just too small.

4) I'm not convinced the sleep quality monitoring is meaningful. Mine suggested I had only gotten 1.5 hour of deep sleep in an 8 hour sleep session. Since I woke up that morning feeling refreshed and my CPAP didn't note any significant events and I didn't wake up in the middle of the night it seems likely that my sleep was better than the watch suggested. I suspect it picks up movement from the other person in the bed.

5) I use a treadmill desk for my computer work. Of course a wrist worn tracker can not pick up steps taken when your wrists are stationary on a keyboard desk surface.

6) The proprietary charge connector just looks very flimsy and I wonder how long it would last.

7) I'd rather have more raw data than these silly "stress" or "body battery" measurements. How am I supposed to know what those even mean if they don't tell you how they are calculated? Give me the underlying data, not some weird abstract aggregation. I already don't trust the accuracy of the sensors, why should I trust these numbers?

8) I thought it would be useful that messages can come from phone to the watch but they display sideways which makes them very annoying to read.

I returned mine after a day of use. It just didn't solve any of the problems I want it to solve.

Neat features - The find your phone feature is nice, I liked that it lights up the phone's flash light as well as making a loud tone. Similarly being able to trigger the watch to vibrate from the phone app is nice for finding the watch. Being able to control music on my phone is nice for avoiding the need to unlock and navigate to the music app just to pause.

There's a lot of good ideas here, it's just very unsatisfying in the details.

title: Easy to assemble, rock solid to use, but dangerously stops running suddenly after 99 minutes of continual use
text:
Easy to assemble, rock solid, delivery experience was good (they delivery guys went above and beyond and brought it all the way to the room where I needed it).

I think the shocks other reviewers are talking about are just normal static shocks from dry air and belt friction. It's not a dangerous kind of thing and I would expect any treadmill to have this problem in winter.

I've been using it for running and walking. I built a desk shelf for it and use it as a treadmill desk while working and as a running trainer at other times. I'm 240 pounds and it doesn't have any problem at all with my weight. I like the programmable workout programs that let you set up arbitrary incline and speed changes over the course of a workout.

The handheld heart monitors seem to be pretty inaccurate for me (dangerously underestimating my heart rate even when I'm working out really hard). I got the chest band heart monitor and it works great and seems to be much more accurate. You need to order the chest band from lifespan, I don't know if it works with other ones.

EDIT - I am deducting 1 star from this treadmill because for some dumb reason after 99 minutes and 59 seconds of walking it shuts down. It beeps and shuts down instantly, no slow down, which is jarring and unsafe. So this makes it not ideal as a treadmill desk (your workout isn't likely to be longer than 99 minutes, but your work day certain is!). I can't find any way in the settings to disable this flaw. I know there's only digits for 99 minutes on the display but there's no reason not to just let the belt keep running even after the display maxes out - could leave it stuck at 99:59 or could wrap around to 0 or could switch to hours:minutes at that point but instead it does the unsafe thing of immediately stopping.

EDIT2 - I am deducting another star because their customer service's response to my complaint about the 99 minutes issue was that I should buy another different treadmill from them! It seems like this would be so easy to address via a firmware update.

text:
We live in the country on the great plains. Keeping in shape during
the spring and summer is easy, but when the cold winds and snow start
to blow across the prairie, it is impossible to walk the 2 to 3 miles

title: Delivered promptly.
text:
I read every review on this item before ordering. There were some very good points that I needn't repeat in this review. I encourage anyone purchasing this dart board to read all the reviews to glean assembly hints.

The dart board came in one box and the box was a little beat up. None of the components were damaged though. Despite the outside condition of the box it was packaged well inside.

I read all the instructions before assembling. I utilized a small handle screw driver for assembly so I would be less likely to over tighten them and damage the press board. I did deviate from the instructions slightly. After assembling the main cabinet (the lower or base cabinet) I put the back on it while it was laying flat on the floor (be sure to line up the bottom of the back with the bottom of the bottom shelf, not the sides). This allowed me ensure that the cabinet was square before installing the door or the top. I installed the top section after standing up the cabinet.

Following the steps above should eliminate any door sag, or at least it did in my case. The completed unit is quite sound stable enough. However I did anchor it to the wall with a couple of L brackets at the top of the completed unit. I did not find it necessary to add any other brackets as others have indicated. We play on the board virtually every day and have had zero problems.

Why not 5 stars? The board has a function that allows you to play against the computer. It does not work on our board. Every thing else works, and it looks great. Best dart board I have ever had. I will be adding some lights in the canopy.

text: We have now owned several of these water bottles, as they are a really great size, and we enjoy the flip top feature; however, before purchasing, please know that the plastic lid has a weak point that will break if dropped on basically any surface at all.  While we try very hard not to drop our water bottles, accidents occasionally happen, and the lids of two of our water bottles are now broken.  I was hopeful that I could find replacement lids either on Amazon or on the Stanley website, but, evidently, they do not make replacement lids for these bottles.  I contacted the Stanley company just to make sure that they do not make a replacement lid (I explained that the lids were broken due to drops, and I was hoping to purchase new lids).  I received an email back stating that all Stanley products are covered under a lifetime warrant, and they then asked me to submit pictures and fill out a detailed form, which I did, though, it took me a long time to compile all of the requested information, and I had to resend the email 4 times as their email kept telling me that it was "undeliverable".  A few days later, I received an email saying that my "ticket" had been resolved and closed, but I had never received a response from my original email.  So, I emailed back stating that my issue was not resolved, and I resent all of the information that they had originally requested.  Weeks later, I received an email apologizing for how busy they are and stating that the warranty doesn't cover accidental damage, and that I should look on their website or Amazon for a replacement lid.  So, basically I just wasted a bunch of time submitting useless information that they never needed and never received an answer to my original questions.  So, that's that.  If you buy this water bottle, just know that if it gets dropped at all, the cheap, plastic lid will break, and you will be left with a very nice, but useless water bottle.

text:
So far, this is a great bell! I just installed it today after I received it in the mail. It looks and fits great on my 2022 Trek Marlin 6. I was in my garage checking out the new bell and ringing it a few times while my wife was about 40 feet away outside in the driveway talking with her friend who was parked in the driveway with her car running and they both said that they could easily hear the bell. Her friend was in her car and my wife was standing outside the car, mind you, that car was not quite with the cooling fans running and the wind was also blowing to create extra noise. Yes, this bell is plenty loud to get someone's attention. This bell also allows you to rotate the dinger in any position you want, which gives you the ability to position exactly where it is best for you. You just rotate the assembly below the bell and put it how you want it. This is a very well thought out design that works great!

Another example later that evening, I was riding down a pathway that parallels the roadway and as I was approaching a parking lot driveway, there were two vehicles stopped waiting to exit to the roadway. I decided to continue down the pathway between the rear of one vehicle and the front of the other vehicle. But just to make sure that the second car saw me coming, I slowed and chimed the bell three times to get her attention as I was approaching about 25 feet away. She looked up and at me, smiled and waved as I slowly rode between the two vehicles. The bell worked as designed. The construction seems to be sturdy, but time will tell. I would recommend this to anyone looking for a small bell that does the job.

title: Perfect for my needs
text: My first use of this tent was for a long vacation in the Cordillera Blanca of Peru. I didn't use it in the snow and I wouldn't recommend it for a winter expedition, but it is perfect, in my opinion, for a bit below 32 F and above. The tent is advertised as a three season tent and adequately fits that classification. It is well made. The materials are substantial and well sewn. The tent poles are sturdy and the shock cording makes assembly a smooth experience. It's very easy to erect alone. To anchor the tent I staked down all the floor loops, and used 2 guy lines in some stiff breezes. The fly installs nicely and fits snugly, allowing ventilation yet keeping rain out and helping to keep the interior of the tent warmer at night. The doors struck me as strange at first in that they are ovoid. I'm so used to classic triangular doors, as are on my other tent, a 22 year old Kelty. But the doors are large so getting in and out of the tent was no problem. The zippers worked flawlessly. There weren't so many insects at 3,500 meters and above, but I am confident that the netting will block bug entry. There are cargo pockets at both ends of the tent interior and they hold a good quantity of items. It's a 2-person tent and I backpacked it alone, but the weight of the tent was not a major concern. From my initial experience I expect years of reliable service from my Chaos tent.

text:
I am adding this paragraph after three trips. The bindings have lots of rivets, and
I wondered about their durability. After the third trip, when I took off the shoes,
one of the rivets holding the heel strap broke. Fortunately I was back at the car;
if some of the rivets fail out on the trail, the shoe could become useless. Other
reviews that I have seen have not mentioned a problem with durability, but now I
wonder. The rest of the review hasn't changed.

This snowshoe has lots of good points. The only negative, and the reason that I did
not give it 5 stars, is a lack of flotation. I cannot compare it to other snowshoes
of the "modern" solid decking type, or the "traditional" wood frame lattice decking,
though it seems to have less flotation than my traditional shoes. I got the 27"
model, and with pack I weigh under 165 lbs; the shoes are rated to 200 lbs or more.
In a soft, old snow, I sank in 8-12" breaking trail; sometimes I sank in more.

The shoe has some very good points. The bindings are secure and comfortable, and
they won't ruin your leather boots or give you blisters by clamping down on the top
of your toes. The traction is good. The toes snap up automatically, and you can walk
with a pretty normal stride. Because of the short distance between your toes and
the toes of the shoes, the lack of a long tail, and the crampons, you can climb
over deadfall very easily. There's no need to back up to free your toes, burying
your tail in the process. I like the heel lift, though I only tried it briefly.
The lift bars are very stiff to put back down. The shoes are lightweight and don't
carry lots of snow on their tops, so you don't have to lift lots of weight with
each step. The natural stride and light weight tend to offset the less than ideal
flotation.

Pros:
Excellent binding system, excellent or very good traction, very good walking
stride, light weight

Cons:
Flotation may be somewhat lacking - I can't compare to other shoes, just to an
ideal, which is not possible to achieve

title: Inexpensive, light, warm, 2-person bag
text: A well-made, cozy bag for two! It's quite light, and not difficult at all to get into the compression bag, which has sturdy, well-sewn straps. Although I bought the bag for my husband and myself in case of emergencies, I've discovered it's very roomy and cozy for a nap, too (and the cats love to come nap on it with me—you can even use it as a comforter). The zippers seem to be well sewn and durable, and they work easily. It's convenient to be able to separate the two parts and make them into two single bags, if you want to. It IS helpful to have a light mat and ground cloth underneath, as with any sleeping bag, and I wouldn't say this is the bag you'd want for climbing Everest. Nevertheless, it's roomy and comfortable for two average-size people, and it even comes with two little pillows that are comfy without adding significant bulk. I'd say it's warm enough for three-season camping in most temperate zones, though you'd probably want to be wearing warm clothes or jammies, too, in a cool spring or late fall. All in all, for the price, I think this is a great hiker's bag!

Mattress was in a plastic bag, inside of the little carrying case/bag that it comes with; unpacked it and laid it out to inflate it. I then found that there was a wire tie on the cord, but it was twisted around the middle of the cord, like you would to not lose it, but it wasn't wrapped around the whole cord to keep it coiled up like you find on new electrical products. We went on and inflated the mattress, even though we were getting leery that it was used, and upon further inspection noticed some grayish markings on the bottom of the mattress & on the bag.
Between these observations and the horribly strong plastic smell we decided that this wasn't the mattress for us. I can't afford to, and don't think I should have to, pay the full $150 for a less than new $150 product. title: Does not fit Wald type baskets.
text:
I have a big beach cruiser bike that I use for most of my transportation needs. I live on my boat in southern California so biking works very well for me.

I had an issue with my bike headlight casting shadows of my bike basket when riding at night and, if I have stuff in the basket, the light can be blocked. I bought this device to move the light to the front edge of the basket so the light would not shine through the basket.

Unfortunately it does not fit well on my standard Wald bike basked. I am sure it fits fine on the type of basked shown in the photo on the Amazon page but that type of basket provides a much flatter surface for this device to grab onto. With the Wald type basket the top rim is a thick wire and the smaller wires that make up the basked itself are bent around the wire rim. This device ends up attaching so poorly that it can move around when riding the bike. Having the headlight spontaneously aiming in different directions is not helpful.

I have managed to make it work by adding some plastic material under the clamp of this device but its not a cosmetically attractive solution and is not as strong as I would like.

This device is very nicely made. They put a lot of attention into the plastic molding but it was obviously not designed for they types of baskets I have always had on my bikes. Ill probably shop around for a new basket but am not sure I can find the type shown in the pictures provided on the amazon page.

It was shipped from Japan so it took a few days to get to me. The seller provided shipping info and the delivery time was OK but not what I usually expect from Amazon Prime.

title: Big Improvement Over My Previous Light
text:
I previously purchased a BLITZU Gator 390 light for my bike and it was OK but not as bright as I wanted. When the mount for the BLITZU light broke, after a few months, I was unable to get any response from the manufacturer so I gave up and bought this light to replace it.

This light is head and shoulders above the BLITZU light. The new light is incredibly bright. I find myself using it on its lowest intensity setting and have more than enough light to deal with beach front bike paths here in southern California. I would hesitate to use the brighter settings because I think it might blind other cyclists who are coming toward me. I can see using the brighter settings in strobe mode during the day if I am riding in places with automobile traffic.

The power pack is very much like a standard USB power pack like the ones used to charge smart phones. So I can carry a spare battery on the outside chance that the standard battery dies. My previous light had a built in battery and if it died I would have been out of luck.

The mount seems more substantial than the one on the BLITZU light but it is plastic so I assume it will degrade from sun exposure sooner or later. Fortunately the light attaches to the mount with a standard camera tripod type thread so there are lots of alternative mounts available on Amazon and elsewhere.

The light seems to be very well made of machined aluminum.

The only issue I have with the design is that it is necessary to thread the light onto the screw that comes out of the mount so you have to spin the light 360 degrees several times to attach it. This can be a problem if you have other things mounted near the bike light mount on your handlebars as adjacent devices can prevent the light from rotating.
I had to mount it farther off center than I wanted so it was clear of my cell phone mount.. I would like it better if the stud that the light mounts on could be rotated up into the light using a thumb screw.

The tail light that came with it looks to be decently made and is bright enough. The tail light runs off two flat mercury cells. There are no instructions for the tail light so it took me a few minutes to figure out that there was a thin sheet of plastic between the two batteries in the light that had to be removed before the light would would work.

The instructions for the headlight were minimal. There was no information about how to charge the battery and how many hours of light would be provided, for the various power levels, before the battery would fail. All the instructions you would need would probably fit on one side of a 3x5 index card and that would be a nice addition to the product.

The light came with a headband mount so you can use this light as a head mounted light. Im not a big fan of those lights because I find myself frequently shining the light directly in the face of people I speak with and that, of course, ruins their night vision for a few minutes.

It would be nice if there was some way to control the size of the beam for the headlight. Most of the time I would like it to be a little wider than it is. But I can live with the current design if making the beam width adjustable would impact the waterproof design of this light.

text:
These lights dont attach very securely to some places where I would like to put them. The batteries dont last very long and its a pain to replace them. Each light needs two batteries so buy plenty of spares. Spares are cheap enough if you shop on Amazon. I would not buy expensive spare batteries because odds are the batteries are going to be used up when I forget to turn the lights off.

Im amending this review after I was contacted by the seller with an offer to replace the lights or give me a refund. That level of customer service deserves mention. I have also had more experience using these lights since I originally wrote the review.

I decided to keep the lights.

I had problems finding places to attach them to my beach cruiser mostly because I have a lot of baskets and a rear rack on the bike. I frequently have my gym bag, or other stuff, on the rear rack so attaching to the seat post is not an option for me if I want good visibility from behind.

The other night my partner and I rode our bikes to the movies. We knew it was going to be dark when we got out. He had never ridden his bike at night so he has no lights on it. I took a couple of these lights in my pocket and attached them to his hybrid bike before we started home in the dark. They attached fine to the seat post and handle bars on his bike and provided a lot of visibility for our ride home.

I decided to just keep these lights and carry them as spares when I ride at night. Its hard to predict when my rechargeable lights will die and having a couple of spares with me will let me show enough light in a pinch. I figured out I can attach one of the red ones through the slots in my helmet so I can get my rear light clear of the stuff Im carrying on the rear rack.

These lights are fine for occasional use or to serve as backups to larger lights. Most people will find them serviceable in a pinch and certainly way better than no light.

You should look at these lights as a way to increase your visibility at night. The white light is not powerful enough to illuminate your path but in the strobe mode does make you visible.

title: Adequate for my purposes but probably not the best choice
text:
Shopping for a phone holder for my new Beach Cruiser bike was more work than I anticipated. There are too many choices.

I decided that the ones with silicon rubber bands that have to be stretched over the corners of the phone was just to much hassle so I selected this model that grabs the corners with brackets that ratchet in and out.

This device is adequate for my needs but if I had the decision to make over again I'd get the max miles machined aluminum phone holder.

The issues I have with this model are:

1. It hard to get the phone out of the holder in a hurry when I get a call. Its hard to do even when I stop riding.

2. It is attached to the bike by a thumb screw and that makes it just as easy to get off the bike if someone wants to steal it. I prefer accessories that at least require some sort of tool to remove.

3. I feel like I need to close the arms down when Im not using this mount because having the upper arms sticking out of the holder by a couple of inches leaves them very vulnerable to damage, especially by things riding in my handlebar basket.

4. Only time will tell how the plastic will hold up in the southern California sun but I think the max miles aluminum mount would last a lot longer.

PS. Three years later it's still working fine and my bike was stored outside, in the southern California sun, for two of those years.

Update October 9: As I mentioned above my partner dropped one of the keys for his lock into the water beside our boat. When the folks at Via Velo read my review they immediately contacted me for my mailing address and the key code. They shipped spare keys, from China, for his lock. They work fine. I had the new keys in less than a week so now we don't have to worry about breaking out the hacksaw if my partner dropped his remaining key in the drink.

In the time since I wrote my original review I have used this lock dozens of times and when I lock my bike at the gym I look at the other bikes with the $100 locks on them and cant see the difference between those and my Via Velo lock. When you add to the quality of the product the obvious commitment to customer service this company has, I am enthusiastic about what other products these folks might offer.

title: Great Bike for My Needs.  Strong, Stable and Easy to Ride.  Not Super Fast
text:
This bike has turned out to be a very good purchase for me.

I live on my boat in Los Angles and am able to attend to 90% of my brick and mortar shopping without using my car since this bike is beefy and has no problem handling a couple of saddle bag type baskets as well as a basket on the handlebars. A 36 pack of canned beer rides securely on the rear rack held in place with bungee cords

I bought the three speed model and am glad I did. Even though the area around us is pretty flat there are a few sloped ramps, on our great local bike paths, that make me appreciate the ability to shift down. Down wind on a level surface, or down hill, the high gear is useful. Some days the breeze off the ocean is strong enough to cause me to shift down when headed up wind. The three speed has no derailleur so the bike has a chain guard.

This bike is very easy to ride and takes a lot of the back and hand stress out of riding my bike. Im 72 and outgrew dropped handlebars about half a century ago.

It took me a few days to get used to coaster brakes again, after decades of cool bikes with hand brakes. But now Im cool with the coaster brake and really like the lack of clutter on the handle bars.

I added a bell, lights and a holder for my smart phone. I also added a really nice rear view mirror which is a great safety feature. I got a nice beefy lock on Amazon and really like the fact that I can drop it in my basket instead of going to the trouble of installing it on the mount on the bike every time I take off.

Since I live in southern California fenders seemed pointless so I skipped that accessory.

The bike is easy to ride with its big tires but is not fast. If you want a fast bike a beach cruiser is probably not what you should buy.

Unless I have some compelling reason to get in my car I do all my local travel on my bike. Its easier, faster many times, and there are no parking hassles or cost. I rode it 25 miles round trip to a doctor appointment a week ago. It was along the beach where there is a nice bike path and lots of scenery. It was not an exhausting experience but then I was not in a big hurry.

As I ride to the gym every morning Im passed by cyclists on high tech bikes who are bent into incredibly uncomfortable looking positions over their dropped handle bars. As they zoom past I reflect on the fact that I definitely bought the right bike for me and also that some people should not be wearing lycra cycling outfits.

The only negative about this purchase was that the packaging on the bike was not adequate to protect it in shipment. The three speed shifter on the rear axel had broken through the cardboard box and got scratched up in shipment. The damage did not look like it was more than cosmetic and I did not want o hassle with repacking the bike to return it so I went ahead and accepted as it was.

title: Sunlite Superior to Wald
text:
I live on my boat in Los Angeles. I am within a 10 minute bike ride to several grocery stores and wanted to use my bike for as much shopping as possible. The trip by bike is shorter (timewise) that using my car, parking is much easier, and closer to the stores and faster. Sometimes searching for a parking place takes longer than driving to the store.

I mention my location because weather did not factor into my decision grid when selecting cargo carriers on my bike. If I still lived in Seattle I probably would have gone for a rainproof option.

So when I bought my bike I immediately bought a Wald folding basket to attach to my rear rack. The design has several shortcomings but I was able to get it installed using wire ties, rather than the metal clips Wald provided, and it has served my purposes. The mounting hardware Wald provided did not fit the rack on my bike and was not the same color as the basket and my bike. .

When I decided to add a second basket to the other side of the rear rack on my bike I decided to try the Sunlite model because it had a few features I now knew would be valuable (experience with the Wald basket taught me a lot and made me appreciate the reviewer's comments on both products).

Here are the main reasons that I find the Sunlite product to be superior to the wald basket. I have uploaded three photographs that address my reasons for preferring the Sunlite product. The Sunlite basket is on the left on my bike and the Wald one is on the right.

1. The sunlite model is larger when open which benefits cargo capacity.

2. Sunlite thought out the attachment options better and even provided some beefy wire ties as an attachment option. I did not use the provided hose clamps because I thought they would scratch my bike and the black wire ties matched my bike. Sunlite provided a couple of really beefy wire ties but I had to use some of my own to finish the job. More wire ties would be nice.

3. The latch that keeps the sunlite basket closed is much more effective that the one on the Wald. One of the photos I uploaded shows the bungee cord work around I use to keep my wald basket closed when its not in use. In the photo you can see the damage to the finish on the wald basket that was a result of the latch scratching the paint. In the long run the Sunlite latch might not be any better but its starting out as way more effective that the one on the Wald Basket. One of the problems with the Wald latch is that it seems to have been designed for an unpainted basket and the layers of paint on the latch and basked wire makes the latch very difficult to rotate.

4. The mesh bottom on the Sunlite basket keeps my mail from falling through the bottom of the basket. That is a problem with the wald basket when I stop by our mailbox on the same trip to the grocery store.

5, The finish on the Sunlite basket is better than the one on the wald basket.

Both of these baskets handle quite a bit of weight with no problem. I have put three 12 packs of soda in my Wald basket and it has held them secure.

Reviewers for both products have mentioned the fact that you need to bend the outer wall of the basket outward to get the support for the bottom in place. This is mentioned as a disadvantage but I look at that as a feature that assures me that the bottom wont fall out of my basket when Im using it.

The Wald basket is slightly cheaper than the Sunlite but, in my opinion, it is not enough cheaper to justify the Wald over the Sunlite. On the other hand the Wald basket is serviceable enough that I'm not going to replace it with a second Sunlite.

title: Very nice, with a few issues
text: Let me start by saying that I researched literally dozens of fanny packs before settling on this one. Badlands,Fieldline, LL Bean, ALPS, Allen, Timberhawk, Browning, Cabelas .  .  . you get the picture. I use a fanny pack primarily to run and gun longbeards and to get my archery gear into my hunting locations with a Summit Open Shot Climber on my back. This pack replaces an old fleece 380 cubic inch Fieldline that served me well for many years, but was always just a tad too small.  I can tell you that there are a limited number of packs available that are between what I consider to be too small at 450-500 cubic inches, and for me, too large at over 1000 cubic inches. I don't carry enough gear to require backpack type straps, nor do I want the complications associated with them. Furthermore, many  of the packs that DO tend to fall inside this capacity range  have what I call a "hopper" style zippered opening, which to me makes absolutely no sense. You unzip it and your gear rolls out. I want a top loading pack that retains my gear. If I've just climbed 20' , gotten settled in, unzip my pack and all my gear falls to the ground, well, lets just say I'm not a happy camper. This is a nicely designed pack that met the majority of my parameters developed over 40 years of hunting. This pack, in my opinion, is the perfect size. Enough room for all my gadgets and grub. The side straps "fold" easily and stay "folded" for  easy placement at the back of my platform. Lashing straps top and bottom, check. Plenty of zippered organizing compartments, check. Side strap pockets that actually have some capacity, check.  Oh. . Did I mention this is a great looking pack?  Which leads us to one of my few negatives. The attractive green panels that you see on the front and top of the pack as well as  the entire pack bottom are Dyneema, a super strong synthetic fiber material. Noisy??  Not terribly. Tenzing claims these panels are used for durability, and while I'm fairly certain this pack will indeed outlive my remaining years in the field, they are . . well . . synthetic.  While in my application it means little, if I were using this pack primarily  to stalk or still hunt, it might impact my choice. Get one in your hands and see for yourself. Sizing issue: The reviewer that  mentioned this not cinching up to his 34 waist is spot on. The side straps, at least on the pack i was shipped, are simply too long. I am a 35 waist and can JUST get this pack tight enough. Overall I am extremely happy with the design, build quality, and my Amazon purchase. Nicely done Tenzing.

text: This product is extremely functional.  It is made of very sturdy material and houses all of my accessories without a problem.  I normally carry my cell phone, music device and house key along with my fit bit when I go out running or walking outside.  However, I was never able to take my water along with me and remain hands free until I got this running belt.  It has a place on each side (right and left side) that the containers fit into for easy access.  There are two water bottles included just as the photo reflects.  The water bottles are not insulated, however when I am out running in the Florida heat and need water, the temperature of the water is a non factor.  The buckle is heavy duty and adjusts to fit my waist.  It doesn't slip or slide up and down while I am running because there are non slip dots on the back of the piece where the main compartment sits.  This makes it really nice when I jump up and down during a tabata workout. Anyone that knows a thing about tabata workouts understands they can be high impact.  So the nonslip beads placed strategically on the back of the running belt are more than helpful.  The main compartment where I place my phone and such is large enough to hold all of my items, yet it is low profile enough that it goes under my shirt without sticking out too much.  The only exception is when I place the water bottles inside each side.  Those do tend to protrude a bit, however when I utilize the water bottles, I keep the belt on the outside of my clothes anyway for easy and quick access.  There is also a small opening for the cord so my earbuds come out which results with the ability to keep my devices dry and protected in case of rain.  This running belt is impressive for my needs. I would recommend this running belt to anyone.

title: Smooth tension, fast results and easy to use
text: I really like this product.  I have begun a strength training program and am trying to build up certain parts of my body and gain strength. title: Good kayak hooks, but use your own screws!

I also did the trick where I took a 2x4 and bolted it to the wall width wise into a stud. This provided a larger screwing surface area so all 12 screws were into wood and not drywall anchors. MUST do this!

Another trick is to take a bar of soap and roll a screw along it. Will help it slip into place. I was able to use their screws in the end, only broke one of the 12. Hand tightening. However, REALLY recommend going to home depot and getting some quality ones.

Overall, plan it out and these hooks are VERY strong. Didn't bend or buckle with my 80lb Kokanee kayak.

title: Works well!
text:
[[ASIN:B000VEBGBC Moultrie® Directional Feeder Kit]]

update: 2013-01-05, the unit is working well almost a year later. It spins 4 times nightly (2 or 3 seconds each time). The battery lasted until 2 weeks ago. It was still at 50%, but couldn't handle the size of the feed I put into the feeder, so it was getting clogged.
My application doesn't require food to be flung far. I have a plastic shield in front of the unit to keep the feed under the feeder. Without the shield, it tosses the feed approx 10'.

At purchase time:
Setup was pretty easy. A 5-gallon container, drill a couple of holes, add a pulley and some thin cable and you're in business.

I've had this feeder for approx 5 months. I first tried small dog food, but it clogged. Now I use small cat food and if I tilt the feeder towards the release area, it doesn't clog at all. Make sure the food is dry and you keep the lid on.

The timer works extremely well. I change it fairly often because I want to feed just after dusk and then a few more times during the night. Some feedings are 3 seconds, some are 4 seconds. 2 seconds seems to not be long enough and clogs the feeder. Atleast with the food I'm using. I have a camera on the feeding area, so I can say for sure the timer works very well.

If you have failures, you need to look at the spinner area and verify you have a clog or that the food isn't feeding down to the spinner, don't blame the timer, it's the food. Either too big or clumping.

title: 5 stars but I'm not sold yet
text:
This is a fantastic pickleball paddle. I have been really happy with many components of it but I am not sure that it is actually worth the price that I paid as compared to another paddle with a honeycomb interior structure.

I bought this paddle after watching the owner of the company explain the details of how they make it and why it is superior to a traditional honeycomb paddle but I don't know if all of the technical details have translated into a superior paddle.

Things I've noticed: I really like the longer handle and the shape of this particular paddle but I have had some signs of wear on the end of the handle where the butt of the handle rubs against the lower part of my hand near my wrist. I also have noticed that there is one small little section of the paddle near the top edge that appears to be dented in or chipped inward. I take really good care of my paddle and I keep it in a foam sleeve when I'm not using it. I also have only used this paddle indoors and there is very little sign of wear and tear on any other portion of the face of the paddle. This one small area seems to have chipped a tiny bit but the chip doesn't seem to have popped outward but instead pushed inward. If this continues to be a sign of wear that I see on this paddle I may push for a warranty claim on it.

Overall I feel like the paddle is a great paddle but I'm not sure if it has the advantages that I believed it had when I first purchased a paddle. The one thing that will probably make me want to keep this paddle and keep using it is the strength that it has as compared to a honeycomb paddle. I believe this paddle is much better built as far as the strength where the handle attaches to the paddle face. I don't believe this paddle will break anytime in the next several years like a honeycomb paddle might.

title: Sun Escape > Litespeed Quick Shelter
text:
I've used several other sun shades at the beach and at soccer games. This is in a category all of its own. This is an easy-setup tent that opens entirely or closes for privacy and camping. The door turns into a massive sun shade that can be adjusted in height. Attachable mesh panels offer shade from the side while maintaining visibility.

Pros:
Size - Larger than the Litespeed Quick Shelter. Much more shade. The Litespeed needs to be oriented in the correct direction for it to provide shade. Also, packs down into a good size for a large tent. You can actually fit the tent back into the bag it comes in.
Setup - Wildhorn includes good video explanations for setup and takedown but it was hardly needed. Setup was a breeze and there were no bow-and-arrow style pull cords.
Shade - The amount of shade this provides is far superior to other canopies like the Litespeed Quick Shelter. The Quick Shelter includes a large tarp to sit on but it isn't covered by the shelter. this provides more shade but only has a floor inside the tent.
Multipurpose - Can be used as a standalone tent. I couldn't get my kids out of it. They wanted to camp in it as soon as I set it up.
Privacy - This closes up entirely when you want it closed. You can put a napping child in the tent and close the door while playing at the beach. You can close it up and change clothes. You can close it up and keep valuables inside where prying eyes can see them. You can also open the giant door and windows to keep cool in the shade.
Adjustable Shade - Unlike other shelters you can adjust how high/low the sunshade rests. The poles are adjustable and you can simply roll up the door if you don't want to bother with poles.

Cons:
Great in sand but need more equipment for the backyard- If you plan on using this on solid ground you are going to want better stakes (the stakes aren't necessary unless it's windy). Also, If you want to use the poles to extend the sun shade you need to do it in the sand with the included pole holders (if you use a little rope and a stake you could do this on the ground but rope isn't included).
Take-down - There is a small trick to packing up the tent. Not difficult, but I recommend watching the video to avoid frustration.

Overall, a great shelter. Excited to take it to the beach in the summer.

title: Amazing experience - visibility, breathing, GoPro compatible
text:
[[VIDEOID:3a1d0e8884973fd7767817b61417e9f7]] I've been snorkeling a few places around the world and I've learned just enough to know that good gear and good locations make all the difference.

I've had the chance to try out the Seaview 180 snorkeling mask from Wildhorn Outfitters. The Seaview 180 is different type of snorkel mask. The mask fits around your entire face - covering your eyes, nose and mouth.

I've experienced snorkeling in the Gulf of Mexico, off a deserted island in south america, in Belize, Thailand, and Nicaragua and Costa Rica. I felt like I wanted my own gear that fits and works right every time - so I finally ordered Wildhorn Outfitters Seaview 180 after having kept an eye on it for a while.

Over the last few months I've tried out a few products from Wildhorn outfitters and I've walked away impressed every time. This time was no different.

After trying this mask I had one big regret - not ordering this mask a few months ago. I really wish I could have used it last month in Central America but I know I will definitely be bringing it on my trip to Belize next year. Here's why:

Pros:

Visibility - It's hard to describe how amazing the visibility is in this mask. It is a completely different experience than any other snorkel equipment that I have ever used.

Breathing - With this mask the breathing experience is totally different. I'm not worried about breathing at all - which is kind of weird. When snorkeling I usually have to think about how I breathe - through my mouth and not my nose - keeping a tight seal around the mouthpiece - making sure not to breathe in too late after going under the water... you get the idea. With this mask I felt so much more comfortable and normal. Because the mask covers your entire face you can breathe out of mouth or nose. Also, if you try to breathe in when submerged no water actually enters your mask. You feel the pull of trying to breathe in without air but that's it. Also, if you get water in your mask the water will drain out the bottom of the mask when you lift your head out of the water.

Fog - When I tried the mask on at my house it fogged up a little but when I actually got in the water I had no issues with fog. I was planning on purchasing some anti-fog spray but now I think I'll delay that purchase and see if I actually need it in the future.

Go Pro Mount - I've used wrist mounts and other types of chest, head, and handheld mounts with a GoPro before and none of them really capture the footage how I want when snorkeling. I often spend too much time adjusting the head mount to make sure it's filming what I want it to film. With this setup I can set it up just how I want it and not worry about it being in the way or not being aimed the right way. Adjustment is also quick and easy.

Ease of use - This is the easiest snorkel mask I've ever used. It is a little shocking how quickly I got used to it. My young daughters would absolutely love masks of their own.

Cons:

Facial hair - You do need to be aware of how much facial hair you have when using this mask. Sometimes when I travel abroad I don't bother to bring a razor but with this mask I would probably bring one. Since the mask covers your entire nose and mouth it works better when I have recently shaved.

Overall:
If you snorkel regularly or are thinking of picking up equipment for your first snorkel adventure I can't recommend this mask more highly. I can't wait to use my mask again.

title: Great Hammock. Even better Straps.
text:
[[VIDEOID:fb66ac480a81689ef9e9e056398f88ce]] ***UPDATE***
I just took the Outpost II and an Outpost I out on a sub-0 degree campout last week with some family. We used hammocks from multiple brands and many different types of suspension systems. The straps on this hammock were so much easier to set up in the cold with gloves on than any of the other types of suspension systems (including ENO brand straps and whoopie slings). Also, sleeping in the Outpost II was nice because it was so large. I wanted to keep several pieces of gear in my hammock with me so they wouldn't freeze overnight and it was so easy in a large comfortable hammock. Definitely a great, comfortable hammock.
_______________________________
I go camping in one of my hammocks about 25-30 nights a year. This year I've been in my hammock to temperatures as low as -8 F. There isn't much that can deter me from going camping in my hammock. I've only been in the Outpost II a few times so far but I think I have now found the hammock that I will be using 90% of the time (just not when backpacking).

The Outpost II is big. Really big. At 11 feet long it is so much more comfortable than other hammocks that I have. Before the Outpost II I used a Grand Trunk Ultralight and an ENO Doublenest. The ultralight was too skinny and short for me while I slept uncomfortably in it for a week in Canada this summer. The ENO Doublenest was my go-to hammock for a while but I constantly felt my knees hyperextend while sleeping in the hammock and I had to keep stuffing clothing under my knees to get a great night sleep.

Earlier this year I got tired of using 9 feet long hammocks and made myself an 11' long hammock that I use now. Unfortunately, it is a little too skinny. I've found that prefer using a double hammock when I'm sleeping overnight - I love having extra space and not feeling cramped.
Wanting an 11' double hammock is what made me most excited about trying the Outpost II.

PROS:
Long enough to get really comfortable
Wide enough to get a good diagonal lay
Plenty of space for 2 people unlike many double hammocks
Triple Stitched
Litespeed straps are AMAZING
Straps attach quickly - Can hang the hammock up in about 30 seconds
Straps are strong and wide - some hammocks use rope which isn't good for trees.
Straps are included and already attached to the hammock.
Easily adjustable buckle system
11 feet long straps - longer than most straps anywhere
Hammock and straps fit in attached stuff-sack
Weighs slightly less than smaller hammocks with shorter straps

CONS:
Bulky when packed up
Will probably use Outpost I when on long backpacking trips to save space in my pack instead of the Outpost II.

Overall a great hammock. The straps are fantastic and so easy to use. It's bulky but that's because the straps and hammock get packed into the same bag and both the hammock and the straps are longer than almost any other hammock/straps on the market today. Definitely a great hammock for beginners and experienced hammock users.

The only issue I have with it, as other reviewers have commented, is the end pieces will pop off if you use them to move the cot. Get used to just not ever touching them, or else they’ll pop off and you have to struggle through getting them back on. This is where the design of an Army cot has an advantage: they don’t pop out because of how it’s designed. But, I’m sure the Teton cot won’t fall apart in the middle of the night, so it’s a minor point.

title: Like so many of today’s products
text:
Update 8/21/17 - Just returned from a 5 day camping trip where I used this stove every meal and I have to drop my rating from 3 stars down to 1. Here are the reasons why I don't like this stove:
1. Extremely poor flame control. It's impossible to get and keep a low flame. If you manage to get it low enough, the slightest breeze will blow it out. Had numerous boil-overs and burnt food from the high heat.
2. No handle, or easy places to grab. This issue went from a nuisance to a real PITA the more I had to move it around.
3. No protection for the knobs/piezo lighter. They will eventually get damaged without protection.
4. Nowhere to easily hold the stove while depressing the piezo lighter with one hand. Again, a seeminly minor nuisance that turned into a real PITA - especially when the stove it hot from the left burner and trying to light the right burner.
5. No type of anti-skid on the bottom of the stove. If you're using any kind of slick surface, like a camp kitchen, it will slide all over the place especially when trying to light the burners.

I’ll jump to the bottom line first – if you’re looking for a high quality, durable camp stove that will last for decades – they don’t seem to exist anymore. Like so many of today’s products, they are manufactured to last a season or two and then replaced with the next great thing. To be fair, I’m comparing it to what it’s replacing: my 50+ year old Coleman dual fuel. But, the more I look at these new stoves, the more I think I’ll just stick with my old one. It still works great, I just wanted a new and shiny two-burner and the convenience of propane.

Here’s the highlights:

Pros
Stylish
Lightweight (can also be a con)
Size
Cleanup

Cons
Fit and finish
Shoddy workmanship
Cheap rivets
Poor temperature control on low
Plastic lid latches
Regulator
Poor two-burner flame on a small bottle
No handle

I did a lot of research and really wanted to love this stove (still do). My current camp kitchen consists of a Coleman 413E gas stove and a Coleman 5418 single burner propane stove. Little did I know that I’ve been cooking on vintage stoves for many years! I recently added a Camp Chef EX60 two burner Explorer with a large steel griddle. Yes, this was a MAJOR upgrade. It’s a beast and requires a big propane bottle. Don’t know what I was thinking, but I love it.

After the disappointment of this Camp Chef Everest, I did a lot more research and went out and actually touchy/feely’d all the other comparable stoves I could find at REI, Walmart, Target, etc. I’ll just say that I think all of these stoves, regardless of brand name, come from the same completely unsupervised and un-credentialed factory in China. There may be minor differences, but there are too many similarities to be coincidence.

So here’s the details on the Pros: It looks pretty. Sitting in your campsite it will be the envy of the campground. And when you splatter grease all over it when cooking, at least it wipes down fairly easily. It can fit a 12” and 10.5” skillet at the same time centered over the burners with the windscreens up. That’s nice. And it’s light - because it’s made out of thin stamped metal and lightweight pop-rivets.

Now for the Cons. I figured almost nothing else mattered if it performed. But it doesn’t, and so everything else does matter. Ask yourself why you think you need a “high output/high BTU” stove. Presumably to boil water faster. It’s certainly not for cooking because you’ll never use high output for regular cooking. And high output does not equate to better performance. I’ll bet there are 11,000 BTU burners that will boil water just as fast as these. Frankly, these burners just don’t perform very well at low, medium, or high settings. At the very lowest setting there is a huge yellow flame that just won’t go away. Same on high. Only somewhere in the middle do you find a sweet spot for the flame, but it’s too hot for normal cooking. With two burners going, the small propane bottle just can’t keep up and both flames become unmanageable. I didn’t try using the bigger bottle lacking a hose. Which brings me to the regulator. It’s garbage, I don’t trust it, and I’m sure it will fail in short order. Both of the points where the tube joins the connectors shows very poor quality control. Not to mention it’s crooked when hooked up to the stove – meaning the connector part of the stove is not centered in the hole.

All of the bad reviews you read about poor fit and finish are true. There are sharp edges where the drip pan meets the body. The wind screens don’t line up without actually bending the pieces to achieve a “custom fit”, but that’s easy because the metal is flimsy and they used cheap pop-rivets which insures everything is loosely attached. The hinges that attach the top to the bottom are a joke – stamped aluminum and poorly attached with pop-rivets. There is no way the plastic lid latches are going to last – I’m surprised they survived shipping. I can’t stress enough how un-durable this stove is. But, it’s exactly the same as all the others.

To test out the cooking ability, I’ve cooked 3 things: pan roasted potatoes, pan roasted cross-cut ribs – both in cast iron skillets, and scrambled eggs in a non-stick pan. All 3 of these require good temperature control at low to medium-low setting. Note: I can do all of these perfectly on my Coleman 513E. On the lowest setting, my potatoes were over-crisped before cooking completely through. The cross-cut ribs probably would have been ok, but I missed the sweet spot for a second and they over-cooked. The scrambled eggs actually turned out ok, but I was very careful and moved the pan on and off the flame as needed while cooking. All in all, I think you can turn out good food on this stove, but for me it’s going to take way too much attention and fussing. I think I want something with lower BTU burners that perform and adjust better.

title: Better than the white 3414 for keeping items separated
text:
I don't know why everybody is having problems with these 3214 boxes. I've been using them for years - at least 10 years - the brownish kind that's labeled "Micro Mag". I've never had a single problem with them and I prefer them over the 3414 soft plastic white ones, although these are slightly heavier than the 3414's. When I want to just carry one little kit in my vest or pocket, these are perfect. I've accidentally dropped them on hard surfaces without any breakage or cracks. Of course, I'm sure there's a limit to how much abuse they will take, but if you're careful with your fishing gear there should be no problem.

Since I gave two of them away to my son and wife, I needed a replacement. I tried to consolidate all of my trout gear into one, but found I could be a little more organized with two. I use one for all my terminal tackle, hooks and weights (separated by size) and I'll use the other one for all my lures. The problem I have with the white 3414 box is that the lids don't seal tightly. Every one I've ever had or inspected on the shelf has the same issue. The lids are slightly bowed out. So, when you put a bunch of tiny #14 hooks, swivels, and the like, they always end up migrating to another section. Really irritating. That NEVER happens with the hard 3214.

When I saw these green ones (I've never seen them in the stores), I thought it was perfect. I like the color and it differentiates between my brown one. Comparing it to my old brown one, it is exactly the same - except mine is not labeled Micro Mag like in the picture. The top is just kind of plain with a small Plano logo. I actually prefer this because it makes seeing the contents easier.

As far as all the complaints with the latches not catching, I have NO idea what that's all about. I've handled dozens of these things and never seen that problem, nor have I ever gotten one that didn't work perfectly. You'd have to have pretty poor quality control to let so many go out into the market as seem to be reported, and I personally think Plano has pretty good QC.

title: Not for hooks or other small, thin items.

title: No dealbreakers, just a few nitpicks
text:
UPDATE Feb 2018: We've used this tent a lot in the last couple years. I started out really liking it except for a few little things. But now, the more I use it, the more I hate it. The primary cause of that is the door zippers. They are a major pain to zip and unzip, constantly getting stuck. It just ruins the whole peacefulness of camping when you're fighting a stupid zipper. Next is the bag. One of the seams has completely ripped making the bag almost useless, and the tent really needs a bag, even if it's flimsy crappy quality like what it comes with. Dropping from 4 to 3 stars.

Have used this tent 3 times now for camping. Overall, we really like the tent, but there are a few cons...

1. This is a big footprint - 10' x 14'. Where we camp - in the Sierra's mostly - it's not always easy to find that big of a spot that is level. And you DO want it level. For one, you need to sleep on level ground. Two, the legs won't adjust very well to unlevel ground which makes the tent lean and be unstable.

2. Thought we would like the idea of the "hinged" door, but honestly it's just a pain. It comes with 2 fiberglass poles that fit into hard plastic cups in the door. The poles have rubberized tips to keep them from poking through the cups, but they inevitable get stuck in the cups and pull off the poles. Then they poke holes into the cups making the whole system useless. The long pole that goes around the rim is a real pain to bend into position. Then, once the whole thing is installed, the door doesn't fit well when closed. Kinda hangs at a wierd angle leaving gaps in the doorway so that bugs and critters can get in. So basically we ditched the poles and just use the door like a regular tent and zip/unzip whenever we go in or out. Leading to the next issue...

3. The zippers are not high quality and frequently get jammed up. Not fun anytime, but especially not in the middle of the night.

4. The storage bag, which we think is pretty essential, is junk. Very thin and flimsy material with lousy stitching. Ours split a seam on the first repacking. The material is so thin that it's probably useless to try and restitch it. We'll probably re-purpose one of our old military duffel bags as a new bag. Not ideal.

5. Kinda nitpicky, but there aren't any loops or hooks for hanging lanterns or anything else. Seems like an oversight.

6. Sloping sides makes it awkward to move around a queen mattress it you have it in the middle. Fortunately, there's two doors, one on each end.

What we like about it:

1. Super easy to set up and tear down. My wife and I can have this up/down in about 5 minutes, and I can do it myself easily. Just take a little time and make sure the legs are positioned correctly. There is no need to force anything, so if you're trying to force something, you're doing it wrong. However, there is no indication on the tent when folded that indicates where the main door is. When you've set it up once - use a sharpie on the top pole hub to indicate the direction of the front door so you can point it in that direction when setting it up. Again, it helps to have level ground so the legs don't get kinked in any weird directions. Watch setup videos a few times so you have it imprinted what it should look like.

2. The space is great. Just right for the two of us! We have plenty of room for a queen air mattress and separate spaces for each of our stuff. So far, we haven't found a big enough flat spot to give us flexibility in where we put the mattress (except in the backyard), so we haven't settled on the ideal mattress placement.

3. Love the top screen for star gazing in bed and all the windows.

title: Great mattress, hope it lasts.
text: I'm always wary of buying air mattresses since I've never had one last more than a couple seasons before constantly deflating during the night. I hope this one is different, and so far after 4 nights it's performed beautifully. The mattress is very comfortable and I noticed that part of the reason for this is that the air chambers go from side to side instead of lengthwise like some other models. This seems to different zones for support and I'll look for this in any future air mattress purchases. I experienced very little initial stretching which the instructions say is common for the first few nights. I slept on it for 3 nights and only added a tiny bit of air the last night just to see how firm it would get. A nice touch is that the sides are slightly higher than the middle, which is very subtle but I'm sure keeps you from rolling off during the night. It comes with a good quality storage bag which sould help protect it when stored. The rechargable pump works well for inflating and deflating and comes with an AC adapter, car charger, and a couple different nozzles. Actually, the charger is the only reason I didn't give it 5 stars - for two reasons. First, it has NiCd batteries which are pretty old school in terms of rechargeables and won't last very long, at which point it becomes a brick. Ominously, perhaps they are only meant to last as long as the mattress? Second, the charger and accessories don't come with any kind of stuff sack or even a pocket in the mattress bag. I nice little cheapo storage sack for the charger and accessories is really needed. Other than that, so far so good. Very comfortable mattress.

title: Great bag but needs better straps/stuff sack
text: I love these bags! Got two of them to zip together for a queen sized air mattress. First off, they are big and roomy. They're big even when packed in their included "stuff sack" - slightly bigger than a water cooler bottle. They are also extremely comfortable and I have no doubt they will be warm down to 25 degrees. But nicely, they don't get too warm either. The zipper can be opened from either end, and has a velcro flap at the top to keep it from coming unzipped during the night. Zippers work great and two zip together perfectly. The only reason they didn't get 5 stars is due to the elastic bands to hold it rolled up and the stuff sack. The elastic bands are sewn to the bag and I've had them before on other bags. After a couple of years, they lose their elasticity and are useless. Attached compression straps would be much better. The stuff sack is a little bit too lightweight to last very long and the seams are not reinforced, so it won't be long before it becomes torn up. I'm going to double stitch the seams to hopefully help is last a little longer. Overall, a great comfortable roomy sleeping bag that should hold up well despite a somewhat cheap stuff sack.

title: Works well (for some kayaks)
text:
The overall quality of this rack system is good. All the parts feel solid and it clamped to my factory Subaru cross bars nice and securely. The cloth covers for the rear saddles make sliding your kayak up easy and the straps, guylines and hooks are good quality. I used this product when I picked up my new fishing kayak and drove 90 miles with it home.

Now to the "for some kayaks" part. The saddles pivot and fold in or out to adjust to various kayak hull diameters. For a traditional kayak or canoe hull this would work really well and automatically center the boat in the saddles. However I have a Wilderness Systems Radar 135 fishing kayak. The hull is a fairly complex shape with the sides being almost square and continuing underneath into a pontoon section on both sides and a fairly flat bottom in the middle. The prow is pointed like a normal, but flattens out after about 2 feet. All these weird shapes combine to make it difficult to center the boat on the saddles and trying to adjust the boat once on the saddles is difficult. Will be looking for an alternative rack.

It's a good product, unfortunately it just won't work very well for the type of kayak I have. Anybody in the market for a used once kayak rack? :P

title: Great Deal!
text:
I used to be a very active and fit person. I spent 12 years in the Army and as recently as 10 years ago was still running 3 miles a day. However the past 10 years have not been kind; I've gotten older (51), I work at a desk all day and have gotten fat (50lbs+ overweight) and have started having problems with my feet and knees. I knew I needed to get back in shape, but running was out due to my feet and knees. Seeing the Peloton advertisements on TV got me interested in spinning as it seemed like an intense workout that wouldn't kill my feet and knees. Looking into Peloton and seeing the insane price for the bike and classes, and the fact that to use their classes you need an iPhone, iPad, or Apple TV I started looking around for something more affordable that would work with something besides Apple.

That research led me to the Sunny SF-B1110. Based on other reviews the bike had everything that I was looking for; heavy flywheel, sturdy construction, handlebars adjustable front and back and up and down, not noisy and the price was right ($279.99).

I ordered the bike and it arrived in three days. The box it arrived in had slight damage to the outside which is not unexpected with the weight of the item, but the bike itself was packed and cushioned quite well and had no damage. The bike comes 90% assembled, so the only things you need to put together are the front and rear stabilizer bars (the bars that sit on the floor, four bolts total), mount the handlebars and post, mount the seat and post, attach the pedals and you're done.

PROS:
- Price
- Solid Construction
- Fit and Finish
- Quiet Chain Drive
- Smooth Resistance Adjustment
- Front and Back Handlebar Adjustment
- Flywheel Weight

CONS:
- Seat
- Only Three Up/Down Handlebar adjustment holes

Once assembled the bike itself really good looking. The paint is thick and clean, chrome is well done, flywheel is well balanced and spins with no wobble. Chain is quiet and smooth and the resistance adjustment knob works smoothly (doubles as the emergency brake).

The seat that the bike comes with is one of the cons. It's hard, cheaply made and painful to use, especially if you are overweight. Some people will claim you just need to get used to the narrow seats that seem to be the norm now, but the kind of pain this seat caused you can't get used to. I purchased this seat for the bike, [[ASIN:B000H87PUI Sunlite Cloud-9 Bicycle Suspension Cruiser Saddle, Cruiser Gel, Tri-color Black]] and it made all the difference in the world. I highly recommend it and it attaches to the seat post with no modification.

The other con is the vertical adjustment of the handlebars. The handlebar post has only three adjustment holes (the seat post has five). I'm a little over 6 feet tall and have the seat adjusted to its highest point point which puts the seat higher than the handle bars at their highest adjustment point. This very uncomfortable, especially if you have a big belly like I do. I solved this issue by drilling two additional adjustment holes in the handlebar post. There was plenty of room for the additional holes, so why the manufacturer didn't do this is not clear. The handle bars now sit slightly higher than the seat and is much more comfortable.

I also purchased several other items to go with the bike. For anybody that's out of shape you really need to use a heart monitor to make sure you aren't harming yourself by overdoing your workout. I ordered the [[ASIN:B00INQVYZ8 Wahoo TICKR Heart Rate Monitor for iPhone & Android]] and it works very well with my android phone. I also ordered the [[ASIN:B00L9XNFPY Wahoo RPM Cadence Sensor for iPhone, Android and Bike Computers]] to help me sync my workout with the class I'm taking. I also added these clipless pedals [[ASIN:B0014UG3WE Shimano PD-A530 Sport Dual-sided Pedal]].

As far as the classes, I found SweatStudio online classes. Unlike Peloton, they work with Android, PC, Roku, Chromecast, etc. and they have more than spin (yoga, TRX, etc.). I cast my classes onto my 51 inch TV which is much better than some 9 inch tablet.

So for about $500 and some customizing I've got a full workout setup. So far I've lost a few pounds, but more importantly my heart and lungs are getting noticeably stronger. I can't recommend this bike more highly.

My main reason for wanting it was to ease into more motion after ankle injuries have healed but get aggitated if over-doing it. I can go for a little on the treadmill and then be right by my chair to sit and rest if it starts hurting or I feeled wind to where my asthma might flare up.

Working slowly off and on each day, I've gotten to where I can up it to a slow job speed for short amounts of time, slow back to walk, repeat until I can tell my ankles need a rest.

The key that you have to have on the dashboard for it to run did come apart during one of the uses. I was at a jog speed and my dog decided to stick his head in front of my leg and I partially tripped, the key went flying off. I'm not sure if it might have hit the handle when it happened, but I found the magnet on the floor - it had come out of the plastic part. It works just fine keeping the magnet on the dashboard, but you don't have that security that if you fell it would detach and shut off.

I'm extremely pleased with it and now my husband has started using it to stay in shape while he has a short layoff from work for winter slow down. The only reason I gave 4/5 stars for easy to fold is because you have to unscrew/remove the 4 bolts (with handles). I think pull pins (retractable-style) could be better, but I don't know if that would be feasible design-wise.

title: Recently updated skewer design ruins the security story for this bike rack.
text:
I bought one of these racks in June 2017 from REI, and have used it many times over the year. The rack is a good solution for my Mazda 5 roof bars, though it's somewhat challenging to get my fairly heavy Electra Townie on and off the car (I'm not a strong person).

I bought a second rack recently (December 2017). The new rack has a different "skewer" design than the old one. The old skewer had a "cap" on one end, and the locking/folding head screws on and off. The new skewer has the locking/folding head fixed to the bolt, and the cap on the opposite side screws on and off. My problem with the new design is that it's simply not as secure as the old one. With a lock core fitted and locked, the old locking head simply cannot be removed when a bike is clamped in (well, it could be by somebody with a hacksaw or something, but it's at least conceptually a sound system). Because the new skewer has a screw-off cap opposite the locking end, the lock is irrelevant: the screw can simply be removed and the bike is free.

The attached photo shows the old skewer ("A" and "B" for the locking head and the fixed end cap), and the new skewer ("C" for the locking head and "D" is the screw-off endcap).

Update: I heard back from Yakima support. Apparently there's a mechanism in the new endcap on the skewer that does pretty much what the spring-loaded sleeve on the old locking mechanism did. When the cap is tight against the fork, it actually cannot be removed at all easily. So two stars back :)

title: Functional Fenders
text:
I do not like to write reviews until I have an opportunity to use the products as they are intended to be used for a while. So, after several times that these fenders have been called upon to keep the road grime, mud and water off my bike I can say they have worked very well. They have great coverage as they extend down to the front and rear axels. I've ridden in some sloppy conditions and have come home relatively clean. The fenders are sturdy and can take a little bit of abuse without getting tweaked or moved out of proper alignment. And, in my opinion, they look good.
I am reasonably mechanical but I will say that installing fenders is truly an exercise in humility and patience. These SKS fenders did everything in their power to make the job easy. The instructions were OK. The amount of high quality fasteners that they provide you with is amazing. I was installing them on a new bike so I had the luxury of all the time I wanted to do it as perfectly as I could. And regardless of all the fasteners they gave me I still had to go to the hardware store to get some things to complete the install to my liking. Looking forward to years of use.

title: Can a Human love a bicycle tire?
text: In my case, that answer is yes.  The Schwalbe Marathon Supreme (700x38) is the prefect tire for my bike and the style of riding I do. I've used other tires, most recently a Continental gator skin (700x35)  that I put over 3000 miles on with no problems, flats or complaints. They were, and are, great tires for me. When I was getting ready to replace the Conti's I decided to throw on the old Schwalbe Marathon Supremes that came stock on the bike (700x40) that probably had well over 3000 miles on them and could not believe how much smoother these old, worn out Schwalbe's felt when compared to the old, worn out Contis's. Again- no knock on the Conti's. Just seat of the pants observation. The 700x40 were a little bigger than I wanted so I went down to a 700x38 as I never liked the way the 700x40 fit under my fenders. The 700x38 are perfection on my bike for my style of riding. It is like riding on a sure footed cloud. They roll so beautifully. I appreciate the added visibility of the reflective side wall. That is such a great safety feature for anyone who rides on roads in low light conditions. I find it hard to believe that I will ever use a tire other than the Schwalbe Marathon Supreme (700x38) on this bike.  I hope these prove to be as flat-proof as the two sets of tires that preceded them.  Beauty is in the eye of the beholder so I can say, without question, these tires are bicycling perfection.

text:
I've been working on pinewood derby cars for a while. I first started with my children, then the past 10 years holding derby car clinics.

Tungsten putty is important to get your car to maximum weight. I keep the unassembled car weighted at 4.9 ounces. I drill a shallow 1/4 hole under the car and pack in the tungsten putty to make up the last bit of weight. That way on race day you can make small weight adjustments without trashing your car. The fastest car is the heaviest.

I've been getting tungsten putty from the large online derby suppliers. I figured I'd save money in shipping, use Amazon prime, and try a new product. This putty is less dense than the putty I've worked with in the past. It seems to have more sticky binder and less tungsten powder than what I've used in the past. I ordered 3 units. They easily fit inside one container. I even mixed some tungsten powder to the 3 blobs of putty.

I prefer the stuff I got before but this will work
