Now when I go for a ride, I put this in my pocket, hit go on the companion app on my watch, and lo and behold, my heart rate shows up on my bike computer, just like I want it to.
So, why five stars instead of four? Well, the initial frustrations are real, but seem to be a thing of the past. Put that together with a very real and genuine interaction with the developer in which they did everything they could do to ensure I had an opportunity to experience the product working as intended, and any start which may have been removed for the initial frustrations was easily gained back.

title: Excellent, for what they are
text:
It's hard to beat the convenience of going to a rack and picking up a couple of steel dumbbells of fixed weight, and relatively compact size, but who wants to spend $1,500-$3000, not to mention the environmental waste of producing 800+ pounds of steel for a single person's home gym?

I purchased this set of multi-weight dumbbells for my home gym that I use 4 times a week. I've only had them for a couple of weeks so I can't speak to their longevity, but I DO believe these are an excellent alternative to a full set of gym weights, if you accept the small compromises that come with this type of device. Many of the criticisms I see in other reviews seem to focus on these compromises so I enumerate them here, as well as some advantages, for the potential buyer.

This set offers balanced dumbbell weights from 5 to 25 pounds in 2.5lb increments, and from 25-55 in 5 pound increments. One of the advantages of these weights is the ability to adjust each end of the dumbbell independently. From 5 to 25 pounds, each SIDE increases by 1.25 pounds. It is thereore possible to set a weight of 6.25 or 8.75 pounds per dumbbell, understanding that there is a 1.25 pound difference from one end to the other-not a big deal-especially at lower weights. From 25 to 55 pounds you can similarly increase weights by just 2.5 pounds to give even more weight options. I find this a big plus.

The entire set weighs just 110 pounds and takes up very little space. You COULD spend the $150 on the dedicated rack, or, if you have basic woodworking tools, for about $50 you can buy a 4' x 8' x 3/4 sheet of plywood and a box of 2" construction screws and build simple boxes to hold the weights. (see picture)

Compromises:
1. The length of each dumbbell is longer than a standard dumbbell. For many excersises that doesn't matter, but for some you have to make some adjustments to how you perform the motions-it's the trade off for the convenience of being able to dial in the weight you want on a single bar.

2. You have to learn to remove and replace the weights straight and vertically out of the cradles. Once you get the hang of it, it's not a big deal.

3. If you are using identical weights on each side of the dumbbells, you can replace them into the cradles without regard to which side is which. However, if you do want to set the two sides at different weights, you will have to replace them the right way into the cradles. It's not rocket science, but it's something you have to be aware of and get used to.

4. The design allows for a small amount of play between the weight plates and the barbell they are attached to. So they can rattle a little. It's not like they are going to fall apart, but it isn't a solid unit like a dedicated dumbbell....you get use to it.

Those are my thoughts on this multiweight set. For a few extra seconds of set up for each weight, and proper handling during removal and replacement to the trays, you get a full range set of dumbbells at a fraction of the cost, and weight, and space requirement of a full rack set.

title: Almost useless until updated
text:
The fitbit as it comes out of the box (in late 2020) has lots of bugs. The settings function will lock it up if you try to use it. The weather app errors. It will not sync reliably. You would be thinking about returning it right now. But if you do some internet searches, you will find that these are known bugs that it leaves the factory with. If you install the mobile app, sync it and wait about 2 - 3 days the nyou will get the update that makes things work as they should. Do NOT uninstall the weather function of the fitbit just because it won't sync. If you do, it will no longer be available to re-install when device is updated. Just leave it there and wait for the update. Then weather and settings will work and syncing will become reliable.

It's absurd that fitbit would release such a defective product, but they do and they don't make any effort to tell you about the needed update.

After updating, it is quite a handy little tracker. The only fitbit tracker with a built in gps so you don't need to take your phone along. However be warned that your battery if fully charges will only last 4 - 5 hours when using the gps. It also takes a lot of time away from the standby time remaining.

Another feature they don't try to explain properly is the Spotify integration. Your fitbit can act as a very basic remote control for Spotify, but only if you subscribe to Spotify Premium. This means that to use the Spotify remote control feature you need 1) a paid Spotify subscription and 2) you need to have your phone with you. No music can be downloaded to the fitbit. It is just a simple play/stop/skip remote function for your phone and Spotify paid.

So those are all the things that fitbit doesn't want to tell you even after you buy it. After you get it updated, it is essentially a Charge 3 with built in battery sucking gps and paid Spotify remote control.

If you are new to fitbit and don't mind all the hassles getting it working right, it is a great little tracker. If you are thinking about upgrading from a fitbit Charge 3, the built in gps and Spotify remotes are the main differences.

Update: After all this it would never sync reliably. I would always have to reboot the device twice in a row to get sync started again. This hat do be done about every 36 hours.

Returned. Not worth it.

Second, what others say is true. The included adhesive disk is garbage. The good news is this is easy to fix. First, through the included disk away. Second order proper gel reusable washable adhesive disks like these (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B079YV1ZWL/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o04_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1). There are others on Amazon too, but not many. I just bought these. Clean the suction cup and mounting surface with alcohol. Center the disk on the suction cup and with the suction lever up, press the mount firmly onto the mounting surface, while holding pressure lower the lever. Now it works the way it should!

text:

A number of reviews have stated that it is too big for their ankles. I suspect this is because they tried it on empty. It will certainly be too large for anybody when empty. One mistake in it's design is they stupidly put the hook material facing your leg instead of the loop material. This means that if it doesn't wrap around your leg with total hook/loop overlap the hook material will snag on your socks or irritate your leg. Totally wrong design.

It is large enough for wear over thin topped tactical type boots if you don't stuff too much in it. I carry an Israeli Bandage, a Tourniquet, a Chest Vent, a few gloves in a plastic bag, a large sponge, a small QuickClot sponge and a few other small items. It fits just fine on a socked ankle as long as you don't wear tight legged pants.

title: Solid as a brick once you get it properly assembled
text:
The only reason this stove did not get a five star rating is because it arrived in a sealed box almost fully disassembled. None of the screws or twist on fittings were still attached. The tank pivot screws were both loose inside as were the tank and heat shield floating around in the box. The tank cap was also loose as was the pump collar. In addition a lot of these have faulty NRVs (None Reverse Valves) whihc keep pressure from the tank backing into the pump and either leaking fuel or pushing the pump plunger back out after you have pumped it up. I would have thought a conscientious seller would hear all the little parts rattling around inside and done something.

This is both an engineering flaw and assembly failure to not have these things tight enough to make it to the customer. It took some time to assemble it properly as the parts diagram doesn't have enough detail to tell what order things went under the tank pivots. You have to search the internet and find what was next to the tank, bracket and shield arms. Then you MUST USE THREAD LOCK to keep this from happening again as the screws are too short and don't bottom out before being tight. When the tank is slid in and out of the stove it turns the screws and eventually they will come loose again. They should have used shoulder screws or longer screws like on previous models, then they could be fully tightened and left that way. Once it was properly assembled and the threads on the tank pivots locked and the NRV removed, repaired and replaced and properly tightened, all was good with the world.

Now to the stove. This is NOT a backpacking stove. It is a brick! You would think with the name "Hiker" it would be pretty light like the Svea 123 which is a little miracle, but not. However it is indestructible when properly assembled. The burner is very hot and also pretty noisy. The pot supports are widely spaced but most pots will fit without a problem. The stove has no feet, just the flat bottom of the case. You may need to use little rocks/sticks to keep it from wobbling.

Now to it's use. First it can use several fuels but not with equal ease. Choices are Naphtha (Coleman White Gas Fuel), Kerosene 1K, Diesel or if you have some laying around Jet Fuel, which is somewhat like Kerosene.

There is a bit more of a trick to lighting it without losing your eyebrows or hair for that matter. Until you get blue flame you have to meter the throttle often. First pump it up until you start to feel increased resistance, about 20 - 50 strokes. The plunger does not stay in after the last stroke like Coleman appliances. It works it's way back out about half way. That is normal. Now hold a flame to the bottom of the burner FIRST if you can and open the throttle until it lights then turn it back down and wait. Either the flame will start to die after a bit or you will start hearing the hissing of the stove starting to generate. Either way start opening the valve slowly again and let it create a flame about 6 inches high but not higher or the fuel can start running all over the bottom of the case and you will have a bonfire. As the flame starts hissing and turning blue you can start opening the valve more and more until you have a constant blue roaring flame. You are good to go now. You will need to add a few pumps as the flame goes down now and then.

When you are done close the valve and let the whole thing cool a few minutes, them push the pump in and slide the tank in. Drop the valve knob inside and snap the lid closed. If is going to sit more than a few months drain it.

Fuels: Although it will burn all listed, some work better than others. Also outside temperature has an effect on each fuel's performance. White gas is fastest to light and Diesel for fastest boil. Kerosene is a good middle point. Diesel.takes a LOOOOOOONG time to light. I didn't have any Jet A. Remember when changing fuels to drain the old fuel well and give it a quick rinse and drain with a couple ounces of the new fuel before filling.

Here are some fuel comparisons I made on a 90 degree day:

Fuel - Light time to max - Boil time for 2C tap water from tap temp
White Gas - 1 1/2 minutes - 3:15 minutes/seconds
Kerosene/Klean Heat* - 3 minutes and can bee sooty - 2:30 minutes/seconds
Diesel - 5 minutes ** - 2 minutes

* Klean Heat is a "Klean Strip" brand odorless Kerosene substitute. I like it for indoor wick lanterns as it gives off much less odor and is very clean burning. However in pressure stoves I don't see a difference in either odor or performance.

** I could not get the Diesel to burn a full blue flame. There were always yellow tips and it was not fully efficient as evidenced by the soot on the bottom of the pot. This is the only fuel which did this. I checked with the manufacturer and they said this is normal as Diesel is the dirtiest fuel. They recommended white gas as having the least problems and maintenance in the long run.

Enjoy your rugged little gas stove. It should last you a lifetime and still have life in it with proper maintenance.

title: No guarantees
text:
There are several Coleman Lanterns where their model number STARTS with 220 but can be totally different in size. This case fits the 220K, and newer 220F 220H and 220J perfectly and will NOT fit the 220E. The 220C and 220D are iffy. Even then there are differences between early and later versions of each model which may effect the fit.

So there are no guarantees. Make sure you buy it from a seller that takes full returns and don't damage the packaging until you have verified the fit.

Also this case is a newer one of the exact same case I purchased years ago. It is quite a bit thinner to make it cheaper, but that doesn't effect it's protection, only how easy it is to latch and unlatch the cover.

title: Very Limited Fitment
text: I have 6 models of Coleman lanterns. 3 propane and 3 gas. This only fits one model, the 200A.. The primary reason these will not fit the others is 1, the center stud or tube is larger than the hole in the bracket and 2, the lighting hole is horizontal not angled so you cannot mount it directly into the lighting hole.

title: Horrible.  Save up for a better glove.
text: These are not really any benefit over your bare hands.  They are made of a material like nylon stockings.  They snag on EVERYTHING including any tiny blemish on your fingers or nails.  Don't waste the even tiny amount of money these cost.  Instead save up and buy a good glove for more like $20.  If you are even a little serious about the sport ,you will be glad you did.

title: Very good replacements but with faster than factory self-discharge rate
text: Fit is as good as factory and total power seems comparable.  However side by side if you take these off a charger and the factory batteries and let then set without being connected to anything these self-discharge (lose voltage) at triple the rate of factory batteries.  But as long as you do not plan to keep these charged for standby use months later, these work fine.  Nimh batteries have a high rate of self-discharge anyway compared to LiPo, but that is a characteristic of that chemistry.  These are just a bit worse in only this area compared to fresh factory batteries all of which were power cycled (fully drained and then charged) twice before testing.

title: Warm but too bulky for phone use
text: These gloves are warm and comfortable.  However with the extra thickness of the insulation the finger tips are way to large and bulky to be able to tap the small areas necessary to operate a phone.  A finger tip will cover more than one shortcut making none of them or the wrong one activate almost every time.  A tablet maybe, but not a phone.  You are way better off using thin form fitting split leather gloves (like police search gloves) which will work a phone screen just as well.  They won't be quite as warm though if that is your primary concern.

These are NOT waterproof. They do not have a water tight closure. It is simply a double foldover with velcro retainer. If you drop in water and especially if it sinks, water WILL get in shortly. Also material is extremely thin and you will have to be careful not to snag bag on anything.

After it is only $3 each, so be aware of the buyer rule.

title: Flimsy and SHARP
text:
Think cutting up soda cans with scissors. Each panel is a little thicker than that but just as sharp. The edges are cut with a shear and have sharp burs and lips that will cut your finger to the bone if you slide it along the edge. So be careful. The included nylon pouch (not a case as described) is needed so these don't slice their way out of your pack. Also they are VERY soft so you have to either pack this in a protective box or between two flat objects or it will be mutilated when you unpack it.

Other than that, it does the job.

title: Well made with only one area for improvement

It forms a much wider base than the fuel cans and fits the small and normal base cans.  One area of slight weakness is that the little spring loaded slide lock is plastic.  If it were made of formed metal it would last through heat, sun and wear, but I don't know about this little plastic piece.  It works fine for now and is well molded out of what seems like a strong material, but it is still plastic.  If it doesn't have any UV protection, it may not last long outside.

title: Just what it says
text: This burner is exactly what it says.  A butane/propane mix canister stove LARGE.  This thing goes through fuel like a BBQ so stock up.  On the other side it generates more heat than any other pocket stove I have seen.  Just don't plan on using it with one of the little mini sized canisters.  It will be empty before your food is cooked, so moderate the fuel adjustment if you want your fuel to last.  And also as it says, no igniter.  That is really the only thing missing.

title: Had to Get One
text: This had so many good reviews and such a cheap price for something that usually costs $50 - $100, that I had to give it a try.  I have used a lot of backpack and portable stoves from the Svea123 on up.  This is the best bargain I have ever seen.  It works quite well and seems moderately sturdy.  I boiled 2C of water in an anodized aluminum 1Q cook pot in less than 2 minutes at sea level.  The new fuel tank was only maybe 10% lower from what I can tell by sloshing it and feeling the weight difference so it used maybe 0.5oz of butane/propane fuel to do so.  It's definitely hot enough!  The little plastic box is pretty crude and will surely crack after awhile, but it works.  The only area of concern I would have if you backpack with it is that the pot supports are not totally flat/even (pot wobbles a little) and they are not very strong.  They could bend easily, but could be bent back easily as they are just steel not titanium.  Also I have trouble placing the kind of trust you need in something so cheap when days back in the Wilderness Area, but I see no reason not to.  For that matter buy 2, a primary and a backup.  They only weigh 115g/4oz each in the box.  I have noticed that China is starting to come into it's own in manufacturing quality.  Most stuff from there is still low quality, but I am seeing more and more things of pretty high quality with a very low price.  They are about where Japan was decades ago where they had become very good at copying manufactured goods at a very low price.  A definite "do buy" recommendation!

title: Could be better.
text: Not the brightest and very bulky.  The light field is blue I the middle and dims to white going to the outside.  It is also very narrow.  In addition this light is deep enough to bump up against glasses and thick enough to be well down into your view especially if you tilt it.  Still looking for a good cap light.  The Cyclops Micro This is VERY good but not tiltable (though it point down slightly) and sits on top.  Top is very good unless it rains and the Cyclops is not waterproof.  For dry were it is the best I have found though.  Bright white diffused light, strong clip and very small/light..

title: Not very practical
text:
My use is for 1" diameter by 5" long tactical lights which do not protrude out the bottom. I also tried it with a 2 C cell light which protrudes out the bottom a lot.

I was looking for something either with a flap cover or a snug but easy to insert fit. This is neither. It has no cover flap, but has a VERY snug fit on this type of light. However it is made up of a series of internal flaps and elastic straps you have to guide the light through to get it into this case. You cannot easily do this one handed as you have to spread two internal flaps apart and hold them that way to insert the light. In addition if you have to sit/stand as in driving patrol or the like, the light works it's way out the top even if it doesn't protrude out the bottom. Since there is nothing to lock it in, the movement of sitting and moving around when seated pushes against the bottom squeezing the light upward like squeezing a toothpaste tube. Eventually it pops out the top. In addition if your light has a tailcap switch it will get turned on without your knowing it in daytime (you would see the light at night), draining the batteries, as there is nothing protecting the tailcap switch from being pressed against the seat bottom.

From my experience with it, this is pretty useless if you are going to be wearing it on a belt in the vertical position, whether a short small diameter or longer larger diameter light. As a temporary worklight holder it isn't bad, but how often do you need a worklight on your belt?

title: No Instructions

The finished product I would give 4 stars, but due to the lack of any instructions I rated it 2.

title: Very Nice Tactical Light With a Couple Gotchas
text:
This is a very well made tac light, very bright and compact. It uses a lithium battery which means it can sit around for years and still be ready when you need it. I like it, but there are a couple things to be aware of, especially for a tactical light, which means something that has to be 100% reliable and ready when you need it.

1) Hitting the mode you want is very tricky. You have to hit the switch just the right number of times (of course) and most tricky at just the right interval. The timing is VERY fast and it is different if you are going to use a particular mode temporarily (light press and hold button) or switching to that mode (press firmly and release staying on that mode). It takes practice, lots of it to hit the mode you want reliably.

2) When the battery runs out, there is absolutely NO WARNING. Either you will click it on and nothing happens or (most of the time) you will click it on and in a few seconds it goes dead. NOT a good situation for a tactical light. The only way this light can be absolutely ready for a critical situation is to put a new fresh $4 battery in it. Battery life isn't great, but that's the price for such a bright light running on a single CR123 battery. Just hope it is ready when you need it. A low battery indicator would be nice.

Still I gave it a soft 4 stars, maybe 3.5 would be more precise. It is a good light if you use it often enough to be good at hitting the right mode and if you have a fresh battery in it.

title: Large Size Suits My Needs
text:
I like this bag very much! I was not sure which size to order, given that I would like to take a compact camera with me on my excursions, so I settled on a large. The large contains 1.5 L I believe, and I was able to stuff quite a bit things in it without even expanding the middle compartment. I was not able to stuff my phone in there, but if I expand the pack. I am sure I can get the phone to go in as well.

One of the pictures shows how it fits on a ladies extra small frame. My only complaint is that the outer zipper when it is all zipped up dangles against the fender. I am not sure yet how annoying this may be, but I guess I can wrap some tape around it if it clicks a lot.

A flat kit fits in the bottom portion of the bag before it flares out, leaving the larger portion of the bag available for various items. I was able to fit a spare innertube, tire wrenches, a CO2 cartridge plus dispenser plus foam, with room to spare in the bottom of the pack. Then, I stuffed in a helmet liner, my camera, a pair of gloves, a compact lock, and my entire set of keys. Without the clothing I could probably get my phone in, and if not I could expand the bag.

There were a number of criteria I used when picking out this bag: size, a "click" type of attachment mechanism under the seat, angle of the back for mounting a rear light. If necessary, size, and how it fits on the bike. I was pleased to see that it is angled in a way so that it will not bother my legs while I am pedaling and also fits under the seat without a lot of bulk sticking out. I like the click attachment under the seat so that I can take my goodies with me if I have to leave my bike. It really cost a lot to assemble all these items and I would hate to lose them, especially the pack!

I found the locking mechanism easy to install under the seat, the slots for the seat rails are approximately 4 1/2 cm apart. It did not look like it would fit when I eyeballed it, but then it fit perfectly. I found that you can also get a replacement mechanism in case the plastic breaks.

I will update this review if this bag fails me, but so far I like it.

title: Good for Keeping Honest People Honest
text: I wanted a small, lightweight lock that I could carry with me on my bicycle. I didn't need a substantial lock for leaving my bicycle over the course of the day in an urban area, just something simple to keep honest people honest in my small town. I was surprised that this lock fit the bill just right in size and weight. I am including pictures of how easily it fits on my bicycle. It has an impressive barrel locking mechanism with four numerals which I believe amounts to 10,000 possible combinations. It also has a vinyl coated coiling wire. While the barrel is a little bit on the heavy side and the wire is a little bit on the light side, I feel it is perfectly adequate for my current needs. It will stretch to about 4 feet, maybe an inch or two more. It is easily long enough to lock my frame and rear wheel around a sign post. I am a satisfied customer.

title: Everything about West Virginia
text:
This atlas is a "must-have" for anyone wishing to explore the state of West Virginia. It is a hefty atlas, with almost as many pages as a national road atlas. This is because the state is broken down into 63 pages that depict in great detail what there is to be found there.

The first page shows the entire state, along with the major roads and cities. This map is broken into rectangles, each of which represent one page in the atlas. You can use this map to get oriented and to find the page you wish to examine in greater detail. There is also a legend, which depicts the symbols and details of the map, along with some information about the design of the atlas.

Next is a comprehensive listing of place names and map features. There are charts that list points of interest along with their map coordinates so that you can find them. These include national lands, state lands, scenic drives, unique natural features, bicycle routes, historic sites, covered bridges, etc.

When you enter the map portion of the atlas, the first thing you notice is the topographic features. Mountains and valleys, rivers and lakes all stand out so as to be easily identified. If you look closely, you can actually see the topographic lines faintly drawn on the map. All roads, down to the dirt access roads are depicted, and every town is shown. And there are symbols marking the points of interest.

West Virginia is a wild and mountainous state with much to offer the traveler and adventurer, and this map makes the ideal companion for anyone who wishes to explore the state in greater detail.

title: Seat Tips
text:
I started my hunt for an exercise bike by driving around town and trying exercise bikes in stores. What I learned from this exercise is that not all exercise bikes are equal, and that a lot of them have an uncomfortable geometry with regard to where the seat and handlebars are located. For this reason, I would not recommend buying a bike that you have not tried in a store, because what you get may not fit you correctly. I chose the Schwinn 140 because when I tried it in a store I was happy with its comfort and performance.

Overall, I am extremely pleased with this purchase. This said, I have some other remarks. With regard to the assembly, I took my time, followed the directions, and it ended up taking most of an afternoon to assemble. The screws and knobs were vacuum sealed to a piece of cardboard, so I do not see how any of the parts could be missing or damaged. One tip I have for would-be assemblers is to record the serial number before assembly. On this model, the serial number turned out to be on the bottom of one of the supports, and the bike would have to be turned over to get to it once assembled. Once I had it together, I found that a couple of parts were loose and I had to go in and tighten them the next day. However, once I hopped on to give it a try, I found that it wasn't working. There was no resistance when I peddled.

I called customer support, and found that Schwinn was a division of Nautilus. Nevertheless, I was soon connected with the correct support person, and she was very efficient at diagnosing the problem over the phone. She told me I needed a new motor and that it would be shipped from Oregon and arrive in a week. Also, she called a repair man who contacted me the next day about the repair. For this reason, I am glad that I selected a Schwinn as opposed to another brand because I doubt that I could've gotten better or even equal customer support anywhere else.

A week later, the repair man arrived to install the part. He was EXTREMELY competent, and he tore the machine completely apart and rebuilt it. He diagnosed the problem as being in the cable as opposed to the motor, and he was able to replace the cable from parts in his truck. At this point, I feel completely confident that the machine is in 100% working condition and will not fail, due to the competency of the rebuilder.

Once I was able to start using the exercise bike, I started encountering problems with the seat. The seat is quite large, and on first sitting it is quite comfortable as well. However, as the days went by, I found that my buttocks were rubbing together and creating a sore in the vicinity of my coccyx. I gave it a lot of thought and concluded that the seat was too big for me. I went to the store and purchased a ladies size bicycle seat to replace it with, and so far I am more comfortable. I would advise anyone buying this machine to not replace the seat right off. It is not a bad seat, and you should use it for a while to see how compatible it is with your own seat. If you find it uncomfortable, you may, like me, choose to replace it with an ordinary bicycle seat rather than an exercise bicycle seat. My personal feeling about gel padding is that it is unnecessary, though it is built to some extent into regular bicycle seats. However, after using your bike for a while, you may decide to go with the padding after all. The point I'm trying to make is that if you have trouble with the seat it may be because it was designed to look good on an exercise bike more than to function as a bicycle seat, and if you have trouble with it it might be because it is just too big and flat.

I like very much using this exercise bicycle. It is solid, smooth, and quiet, with gentle transitions between the resistance levels. I am able to track my heart rate by holding the handlebars in the metal zone. The computer took a bit of getting used to, and actually technical support at Schwinn helped me get it set up to begin with. They are very nice, and actually American, which was a pleasant change for technical support. There are a number of pre-programmed exercise programs, and you are also able to create your own if you feel like it. I have not gotten to the point where I feel like creating my own, so I use the pre-programmed exercises.

I would recommend this exercise bicycle to anyone contemplating this purchase. From reading other peoples reviews, it does seem that having an exercise bike shipped to you bears the risk of not arriving in working condition, but Schwinn is very good at making it right for you so that you don't have to figure out how to get it back in the box and ship it back. I did check exercise bicycles around town, and the local stores wanted to charge a high price for delivering the bike and an even higher price for setting it up for you, so buying it from Amazon is an attractive alternative.

title: Good price, for shorter people
text:
PROS:
- Easy to set up. I don't know why some previous reviewers say it takes 2 hours with 2 people. It took me one person (myself) about an hour with 2 wrenches. The manual has crappy pictures, but as long as you can read English and follow instructions then the written instructions are all you really need (while occasionally looking at the picture to get the general idea). The bench is very sturdy and sits level. It weighs about 25lbs, so it's not exactly light weight. All of the required hardware was present and some of the easier steps were already performed (e.g. the plastic end-caps).
- Versatile. There are leg pads for situps and the backrest angles from flat to about 30 degrees to nearly 90 degrees. It does not recline below horizontal.
- Price. Can't beat this quality for less than a Grant.

CONS:
-Smell. Ok. Yes, the rubber pads do smell like, well, rubber. It is fading, but if smells really affect you then look elsewhere.
-Length. This thing is short! I'm 5'8" and I just barely fit on this thing. Unless I wrap my legs over the top padded bar, my head is completely off the backrest. This can be uncomfortable during situps and chest presses. The width is adequate.
-Design flaw. The space between the sitting pad and the backrest is slightly larger than is comfortable and during situps you kind of sink into the space. I'm going to try using a towel to fill it and see if that helps.

Of note, there are two J-hooks on either side of the bench, which are meant to hold small dumbbells. If you use anything over 10 lbs, I doubt these will be used. They can hold a towel or water bottle however. They should have skipped the dumbbell holder and lengthened the backrest.

First, the arm band needed to hold the Fitbit as you sleep is uncomfortable if adjusted tightly enough to be sure it stays on. Second, the relative sleep quality it "calculates" differs significantly from my own perception of how well I slept. Even a very bad night (in my view) rated 97%! I no longer bother with it at night. title: Great load bearing straps, confortable padding, great water bladder.
text:
This is a comfortable back pack.
The selling point for me was that it was listed to be able to accept an additional water bladder. And for me, (I hike in the Phoenix, AZ area mountains during the midday summer heat) that is important. Two 3liter bladders are a standard for me. Normally, I have to move up to my 35 litter backpack during the summer because the straps on my other packs are too narrow to adequately support the weight of two 3liter bladders (6 kilos or about 13lbs) in addition to my emergency first aid supplies, food, phone, and anything else I have. In total, about 25lbs (a little more than 11 kilos).

So it was a pleasant surprise that the straps on this 20 liter pack were almost as wide as the straps on my 35 liter pack. Making this pack easily able to comfortably carry the weight.

Also the waist belt has molle webbing for attaching additional things. For me, that's a phone carrier on one side and a 4x6 pouch on the other for some trail snacks (if I need the nourishment on the trail). A big plus. I don't have to remove the backpack to have a snack or to put the empty wrapper back in the pouch.
The waist belt also helps keep everything stable when I am trail running (probably about half of my normal 10 mile hike is trail running)

The padding on this backpack is much better than any of my other backpacks regardless of size. (I have 3l,6l,12l,18l,20l,25l,30l, and 35l backpacks.) Yes, I have a lot because I've never been able to find a nearly perfect fit for my needs, until now.

The bladder - this is a high quality bladder. (I now have four of them.) It has a nice high water flow. I'm easily drinking more during my hike because of this high flow rate. With my other bladders, I averaged about 1 liter an hour consumption. With these bladders, I average 1.5 liters an hour consumption. I have my garmin watch set to give a reminder every 8 minutes to drink water. So with the old bladders and the new Source bladders, I was drinking at the same intervals, it's just easier to drink through the Source drinking tube than the other ones resulting in the higher consumption.

Strap management - this thing has elastic on each of the straps to hold the excess strapping. Wow, so nice. No Irish pennants (marine corps terminology referring to the the stray threads sticking out on clothing) flying all over the place

I do have one complaint though, it says that it'll accept a second bladder. But there's only the one strap in the water bladder compartment to hold a bladder. To accommodate a second bladder, you have to place it in the main storage compartment. But there is no strap to hold a bladder there. And you have farther to run the tube for this second bladder. I started keeping some storage at the bottom of the main compartment (sun block, towels, etc.) that manages to raise up the second bladder so that the drinking tube for that bladder isn't uncomfortably short to drink through. Otherwise the second bladder sits low enough that the tube is a little short (perhaps about 5 or 6 inches shorter than the tube for the water bladder in the water bladder compartment).

title: Decent quality for the price. Some parts of the set were above expectations.
text:
I normally don't review products this soon. I just recieved the items today.

Ankle straps. Wow! They're comfortable. I really want expecting much for this price range, and the ankle straps are definitely worth it. Time will tell how durable they are, but I think I'll get my money's worth out of them.

Wrist wraps. Again, I wasn't expecting much. Never used wrist straps before, but I did choose this bundle because, hey what the heck, they're included. I don't have experience using the wrist straps, so I have no idea how they compare to others. They do provide support to my wrists. The thumb loop should have been sewn in so that it wraps nicely around your thumb though. Instead there's the one side that had to fold over because it was sewn as a flat loop. I'll give them a try.

Resistance loops. They're thin. I guess I was expecting them to be a little thicker. They do give resistance and I'm sure I'll find ways to use them. The heavier ones do make me sore on the outsides of my thighs, so they are doing what they're intended for, adding resistance.

Resistance bands. They're thin. They do seem to have the appropriate ratings though compared to other more expensive resistance bands that I have. I was looking for bands with these kind of attachment points. They're more versatile than the ones that have to hook into their own proprietary handles and attachments.

I do wish that they sold sets of just the bands though. Because there's not enough of the higher weight bands in this set for all of my needs. I'll end up buying other set just for extra bands.

The towel. A decent towel for working out. Again, I've never used one in the gym. But I'll find a use for it.

Door anchor. This thing is not going to slip through the door unintentionally. Just remember to put it through the hinge side of the door. Doors don't have enough strength on the latch side or top.

Sliders. They're about the same size and basic construction as another set of sliders that I have. But the ones in this set seem to be tacky on the smooth side. So if you're using them on carpet, you'll need to wear shoes or socks with some grip. Otherwise, you're foot will slide off and the slider will stay put.

And just one general complaint. There are several pictures of overly photoshopped Asian models demonstrating the different items on the packaging and instructions. They're photoshopped to look caucasian. I don't care if your Asian, African, European, South American, American or what have you. I buy a product for being in an acceptable price to quality ratio that works for me. If I like it, I buy again. I don't care who is making it or selling it.

title: A well made, study bench for those on a budget
text:

Granted, this bench isn't as robust as the ones at the gym, but this one will never see the use that those ones do.

The welds on this bench are robotic welded. That's obvious from the clean consistent welds.

The leg support can be folded up under the bench seat when not being used because it's hinged on just one bolt. I like that since they usually just get in my way most of the time. But it's still easily brought down into a usable position when needed.

I did drill some extra holes for the seat adjustment pin to go into, adding a roughly 30° and 70° seatback position to the incline, flat, 20°, 45°, and 90° that the bench came with. This made it much more usable for me.

title: Great idea, bad design

Put them on your feet and try to get over so you can do some ab workouts is (let's just say) not easy. The large wheel and wide handle bars make for a difficult transition to roll over from sitting down to ab without position.

It's one of those pieces of equipment that looks like a great idea, but the reality of it just doesn't work out. I thought about buying a second one to use the second wheel for stability and cut down the bar to just what was necessary, but I've gotten other equipment that made that idea obsolete. I use it as an overhead anchor for other excersize equipment and for hanging upside down with some inversion boots (for relieving back pain and ab workouts).

title: Good quality overall
text:
Seems to be a good quality piece of workout equipment. Nice and versatile. The web strapping is a good thickness. Surprising how heavy it was in the box. I have a similar product from Golds Gym. This one from Anoopsyche is thicker and heavier.

Perhaps my favorite thing about this product is that the two handles are separate, which makes doing exercises (pushing, pulling, and foot in strap) much more comfortable than with one that is connected at the top.

A close second is the versatility in setting it up. It'll wrap around a bar or wedge in a closed door.

It also includes a strap that connects both sides to one mounting spot. Honestly, I'm not sure why. It's plenty long separated. Combined I think that it would be overly long unless your mounting to an extra high mounting spot. You could probably mount this thing ten foot off the ground with the additional strap without a problem. Personally, the handle sections alone are enough for me.

The buckles seem to be good quality buckles.

Deducting one star for quality control. The two handle straps are different lengths. Which is a mute point because the straps are adjustable. Just causes me to have to double check that I've adjusted both straps to equal lengths. You figure out pretty quick when both hands are in different positions because of different lengths. I ordered a second set at the same time for a friend. I opened that box to check the length of the straps. In that box both straps were the same length. I'll continue using the odd length ones and give the friend the even length ones for their convenience.

I am in the process of returning this scooter, as I purchased it for my daughter to ride across her college campus. Upon opening the package, it was clear that not only was the kickstand defective, it wasn't even made for this particular scooter so it couldn't be attached! Also, the paint on the bottom of the scooter was peeled off - as if someone had already ridden it and bottomed out. The foot grip pad began to peel off in chunks after the first TEST ride, which is another sign of poor quality and cheap material. However, most importantly, the folding and locking mechanism gets stuck, is really hard to undo, and doesn't even work sometimes - which is SO dangerous. If my daughter had have ridden this around school, it could have folded itself mid-ride and she could have gotten hurt.
All this said, I am incredibly disappointed that this scooter not only didn't work, but also has a high price point for such poor quality. Even if it could be fixed, I would return this on principle, because companies that produce such poor quality and potentially dangerous products should be held accountable.

title: An honest "unpaid" review
text:
My review is primarily geared towards people who are interested in learning the Nordic walking techniques and are looking for inexpensive, appropriate walking sticks. It is also a comparison of the sticks offered here and the so-called “crappy Chinese” anti-shock, telescoping sticks. I have purchased both and am including photos below.

I started Nordic walking about 3 or 4 years ago. At the time, I wasn’t sure that this was something I would continue to do and did not want to spend a small fortune on equipment that would, once again, end up unused in a closet. But I was having trouble walking even a short distance (100 ft. or so) without excruciating burning in my legs and back, so thought I needed to give this a shot. I sprang for the cheap sticks and boy, am I glad I did! Within a few weeks, I was walking a mile with very little discomfort. That distance might be laughable to some, but to me, it was a miracle!

But honestly, it had less to do with the type of sticks than it did with learning the proper technique. There are many videos available that demonstrate the technique and anyone interested should spend some time watching them. It is not difficult to learn. In fact once you get the rhythm it’s like riding a bike…you don’t forget how to do it.

As far as the poles go, I see little difference in them. Perhaps at a higher price difference there is, but it’s still more about learning the skills.

Cheap Chinese poles (the black ones in the photos): When I bought mine I made some modifications. The rubber tips that were included wore out quickly. I replaced those with the boot type of tip which has lasted all these years and many miles. The tips are deeply grooved like snow tires and they do pick up small pieces of sand. This will make them slip some on asphalt, but it’s fairly easy to flick a grain of sand out and continue your walk. I also replaced the sponge rubber grip just below the handle (because it tore easily) with some closed cell tubing that I found online. That wasn’t entirely necessary because you never or rarely grab the poles in that area. I should have just eliminated it altogether.

These poles are the twist lock telescoping type (not the clamp type), which is handy when you don’t know what length pole you need in the beginning. But once adjusted, it is a PITA to collapse or readjust them. They do have a scale on them that shows the length you’ve set them to, so if you get these, make a note or find some way of marking the length. I never collapse mine anymore, because I want to start walking immediately, not fiddle with adjustments. However, if you need to pack your walking sticks, and don’t mind messing with the twist locks, this is certainly a consideration when you buy. I have never had the twist locks fail or accidently collapse once snuggly hand tightened.

These poles also have the anti-shock springs. It makes them heavier and, yes, they make a rattling noise every time the pole hits the pavement. Their extra weight does makes their footfall more forceful. I see no advantage to the springs at this point, but I’ve heard that they are helpful when going down steep terrain. Can’t say, because most of my walking is on fairly level pavement. BUT, DO NOT let the noise stop you from buying if you don’t want to spend a lot of money in the beginning. Getting you walking again is far more important than any minor rattles.

The handle grips are very comfortable and include a strap for your hands to go up through. I found these straps were much more comfortable for me and more convenient to use. Just remember to insert your hand up from the bottom of the strap.

Overall, these poles have a bigger diameter than the “real” ones and are slightly heavier. However, I think the few added ounces actually give you a better upper body and arm workout than the lighter poles. So, to me, the extra weight could be advantageous. Cost for these poles was 14.95 for each pole (@29.90). The Leki replacement tips cost $17.31 with tax, and I highly recommend them. I’m not including the rubber grip which is not necessary, so my actual cost was $47.21 with tax.

Real Nordic walking sticks (blue in the photos): As noted above, these are somewhat lighter, thinner, nonadjustable, non-spring-loaded poles. It is important that you order the right length. They adjustable have glove like straps attached to the handle.

Personally, I’m not entirely pleased with these particular straps. As you will see in the photos, their design leaves something to be desired. I have circled the points where they irritate my hands. And here, I will have to make some kind of modification if I want to use these poles for an extended time. The gloves interfere with wearing my fitness watch and the binding on some corners should be more rounded instead of squared off. Strapping your hand in or out, by means of Velcro strips, is awkward; and should you need to let go of your poles if you fall, you’re out of luck. There is a means of length adjustment (by pulling upward on the handle top) which is lacking in the Chinese poles, but it doesn’t solve the rubbing issues, since the part which cradles your hand doesn’t change position. After I have used these poles more, I may try to fashion a strap comparable to the ones on the Chinese poles.

The handles themselves are thinner and (though you shouldn’t be clasping them tightly) may be more suited to smaller hands. I can’t say for sure, but they are still comfortable.

I have a gut feeling that the boot tips on these sticks will wear quickly, needing to be replaced often. However, they do not have the deep tread of the Leki replacement tips and do not pick up grains of rock or sand, so that is an advantage as far as sliding on pavement goes. I will most likely replace these stock tips with the Leki ones and just deal with the rocks.

The cost for these poles (before any changes I may make) is, at this writing, $77.45 including tax and/or shipping. I am, otherwise, perfectly satisfied with these “real” Nordic walking sticks. They are light, not noisy and do what they’re supposed to do.

Both poles need some slight modification, but their functions are identical. Once again, it’s about technique, not one type of pole compared to another. Please do not let any hype make your decision. It’s far more important that you get out there and start walking.
I'm awarding 5 stars to either kind of pole. Both work pretty much equally.

Even though some were damp, they lit beautifully and kept the fire going for a long time. at least 20 minutes without refueling. I cooked out for three days of power outage, got to use up all the perishables that were in the fridge before they rotted; and had a great time, without wasting money on eating out, or hotels, or tossing food I already had, and by staying at home during the blackout. So I feel like I really made a wise investment in this stove. It worked like it should, exceeding my expectations when I really needed it. You could say I'm a happy, albeit backyard, camper!

title: MEASURE your bike FIRST
text:
I will first say the build quality of the rack seems good, and if you can get it mounted correctly to your specific bike, it will likely be a good rack for you.

However the rack could have been designed to fit more bikes better with a little more forethought. The product description says this rack is 16 x 14.5 x 9 inches. Maybe it is, however the critical dimension is the length of the support post for tire clearance reasons. The distance from the center of the bolt hole on the bottom, to the bent bar on top - ie the clearance measurement - is 14 and 15/16 inches. A 29er tire radius is obviously 14.5 inches, so if you were to mount the bottom of this level with your axle bolt you would have only 7/16 inch clearance - less than half an inch. Most rack mounting holes are well above the axle point, but some are not much. I was using P-clips since my frame has not rack holes, and even though I was completely free to mount wherever I wanted, I had trouble finding a usable position with much clearance. Since most 29ers are used in the mud at least on occasion, a little more clearance would have been nice.

Secondly, the hardware included is stainless M5 x 0.8, and there are just enough assuming your frame has the proper mounting holes. If your using P-clips or any other method, a trip to the hardware store will be required, and you likely won't find stainless hardware in metric. It wouldn't have killed them to add an extra bag of hardware for other bike mounting methods.

Lastly, if you plan to use the Topeak accessories for mounting then the top of the rack will be great for you. If your not, the top of the rack is not flat like most racks (because of the MTX grooves for easy accessory mounting). If your not using topeak bags and such, you should still be able to make it work fine, its just not flat.

Unfortunately there aren't many racks out there yet for 29ers, so this still might be a good fit for many.

title: Good but not perfect for a mountain bike conversion - a little short to fit twist grip shifters
text:
These are a good product for the price. I purchased them to give myself a little more upright position on an old mountain bike. They do this pretty well.

The reason they do not get 5 stars is the top portion where you put your hand was about 3/4 of an inch too short to mount my original twist shifters and still have room for my grips, making the place where you put your hands a little shorter than intended. OK for me, and also wouldn't be an issue for maybe a different type shifter - like the trigger type, or no shifter at all like a single speed bike. However for someone with very large hands it might be a problem.

Beyond that they appear to be pretty decent quality for the price.

Don't underestimate the amount of change in position that you will get. I paired these with a adjustable quill stem, and I think one or the other would be sufficient, so if your changing out an old mountain bike I might start with one or the other, not both. Also, due to the longer reach you will very likely need to change your shifter and brake cables. My originals were cut too short for this handlebar. Its not a difficult job, but a fair bit of work. You probably will want to buy new grips also in case your originals like mine were hard to remove.

title: Great way to burn calories and stay active while sitting at your desk!
text:
I am a software engineer that sits at a desk for at least 8 hours a day. I wanted to way to keep my body from being idle for so many hours and also was looking for a way to help with my weight loss goals. The Deskcycle has been a fantastic solution. I pedal off and on throughout the day at a low setting (resistance of 3 right now) and try to aim for 50 miles at the end of the day (disclaimer: actual mileage seems a bit high to me but I don’t really care if it is accurate). Some days I up the resistance to push my legs a bit more and shoot for a lower distance. I am a 54 year old woman trying to lose 50+ pounds. In the past, even with healthy eating and routine workouts, my weight has been slow to come off (maybe a few pounds a month). Since I purchased the Deskcycle, I have lost 10 pounds in a month. I don’t know that I can credit the Deskcycle for this substantial increase, but it does feel like it is helping. I love it so much I am thinking of purchasing a second one to use for the days I work at home. I find myself feeling lazy if I haven’t pedaled throughout the day.

Pros:
Very easy setup
Easy to see and use electronic monitor with variety of settings to watch
Very low height requirements compared to other under desk bikes
10 resistance settings – can set to 3 or 4 and pedal good part of day or set higher for smaller bursts of pedaling
Can pedal forward or backward to hit different leg muscles
Very quiet (Coworker in next cubicle cannot hear it.)
Smooth motion, no clunkiness

Cons
Pricey compared to other under desk bikes
Takes a bit to get distance from chair adjusted

*The cons to me a well worth the benefits! The price is higher because it is much higher quality exerciser and will likely last longer as a result. The adjustment issue is one you would have on any desk bike.

title: Expensive, but worth it for frequent lap-swimmers
text:
Update 2 years: the replacement model still working without any issues. I have recommended this unit many times to other swimmers
************
Update 7 Months: I have swum probably 100 times with this snorkel, and it is the best on the market. After 5 months, I was getting a little mist in the air I was breathing. I found if I removed the rubber valve and cleaned it, this mist was mitigated for 40 laps maybe. Then I would take the valve cover off and clean it again (3 minute process maybe). I emailed Ameo and informed them of my issue. They said the first batch of these had a minor valve issue which was corrected in the next version. They offered to ship me a new snorkel of the new design for free. I have used the new snorkel 10 times maybe, and it is even better than the beta version. My air is completely dry. Great product, fantastic customer service.
************
The Ameo PowerBreather is the best swimming snorkel available. I have had the Finis Swimmer's Snorkel [[ASIN:B004O6ECL4 Swimmer's Snorkel Yellow]] for over a year, and it has improved my swimming endurance, but the Ameo PowerBreather is better.

I am a 39 year old man, I swim 1.5 miles, 3 times a week as 3 of my 5 cardio workouts for a week. A year ago, I decided I wanted to integrate swimming into my cardio routines. I swam on a team in 6th and 7th grade, but that has been more than 20 years ago. I started swimming and found I had 2 major issues.

1) I hated keeping count of my laps.
I purchased a lap counting watch to do it for me [[ASIN:B0031IHMFY Swimovate Pool Mate Watch Speed, Distance and Lap Computer for Swimmers (Black)]]

2) Turning to breath was making my neck sore, and reducing the amount of laps I would complete.

I first looked into a snorkel mask [[ASIN:B00ZSFDCYS Seaview 180° Snorkel Mask for Adults/Youth. Easy-Breathing Full-Face Design. Best Snorkeling Experience with Anti-fog and Anti-leak Technology. Huge Viewing Area! Tubeless Design Prevents Gag Reflex.]], but this said it was not for lap swimming, and would not work well for lap swimming.

I then found the Finis Swimming Snorkel (linked above), which has been great over the last year. With a lap-swimming snorkel (front mounted, not side mounted to keep in place while lap swimming) I have been able to consistently improve the quantity of laps I am swimming and the speed of those laps.

I have now moved to the Ameo PowerBreather. I am one of the first Americans to have this device. I have used it maybe 20 times in 2 months, swimming between 50 and 250 laps per swim.

A comparison of the Ameo PowerBreather to the Finis Snorkel:

Cost:
Finis =$30
Ameo=$150

Breath restriction:
Finis= very little. There is a cap to keep water out during turns [[ASIN:B0028AQLYE Snorkel Dry Top]], but I never purchased it.
Ameo= 30% breath restriction would be my estimation of how it feels, 50% restriction with one side using flip turn "blind cap". More about blind cap assy below. [Update: 3 months ownership: even with this perceived restriction, I can pull in more air. I breathe as hard and fast as I would running. My lungs are getting stronger, and as I use this device I find I have gotten into a similar breathing pattern as I would running; great for cardio.]

Comfort during swimming:
Finis= good, no swim cap necessary, goggles fit easily with this, have to adjust occasionally as tube moves.
Ameo= good, must wear swim cap as adjustment knob pull hair without a cap, goggles have to be adjusted differently as the PowerBreather is close to them by your temples. Does not need any adjustment over time, never moves.

Spit buildup:
Finis= every 40 laps maybe I would have to stop and clean out the Finis snorkel, spit would build up in the bottom and backwash a little when I was breathing.
Ameo= no spit buildup, no adjustment. I have swam 250 laps without adjusting the Ameo PowerBreather.

Flip Turns:
Finis= description says you can do flip-turns just blow out hard to clear water from the turn, but when I did them the Finis snorkel would change angle and I would have to adjust it, so no flip turns for me. The freestyle version that follows your head may be better at this.
Ameo=slow flip turns are great, no movement of the device, once you are back at the top of the water, breath normally, no hard exhale needed to clear. Fast flip turns seem to pull in a little water, you can stop this by putting the "blind cap" on your flip turn side (right for me). This blocks off one of your tubes completely, no water in on the flip turn, but now I would say the breathing restriction is 50% up from 30% with both tubes open.

Mouth fit:
Finis= I bit the mouthpiece enough times to bite off the small teeth separator parts, still works, but Finis requires jaw pressure to keep in place.
Ameo= completely held in place by the mechanism. Much more comfortable to not have to hold in place with your mouth.

I am liking the Ameo Power breather much better. If you are dedicated to swimming, I highly recommend it. If you are put off by the price though of $100, then maybe the $30 Finis will get you most of the benefit for a much lower price. Your fitness tools can drive your performance, if you want the best, pay the premium and buy the Powerbreather.

title: Wrestling match
text:
This isn't a folding cot that you can just take out of your trunk, open and sleep on. It has to be assembled each time you use it. The problem with assembly, and the reason that some of the reviewers say that it's easier to assemble after you've done it several times, is that the side rails are approximately the same size as the canvas sleeves you have to put them in. I assume that the canvas will stretch with several assemblies. So when you assemble it, you have to push on it until the canvas stretches to fit the rails. That is no easy task. Once you have inserted the side rails, you have to rotate them. I did that by putting a screwdriver in the holes that need to match up with the slits in the canvas and working it back-and-forth until the rails were rotated. Again, no easy task. Once you do that, you put one end of the spring steel legs in one of the holes of the rails, and compress the spring steel so that you can get the other end in the other set of holes on the other side of the cot. While I was doing this, I was imagining a trip to the emergency room if the spring steel leg slipped out of my hand.

If you can deal with all of this, then it seems comfortable.

I guess it will serve my needs.

title: Nice but not for cold nights
text:
First, I don't understand the complaints about the extra piece of the bag, the part that is used to roll the bag up and store it, interfering with comfort. That piece is thinner than a pillowcase and the bag is very thick; so even though that piece is under the bag near my head, I can't feel it when I sleep.

Secondly, and this is the real reason for saying that the bag is just ok, it's not very warm. The bag is roomy and the material is thick; so it doesn't really wrap you up very well. It takes a while for your body heat to fill up the large bag, and if you have to get up at night, if it's cold, you'll be up for a while shivering when you get back into the bag. I'm not sure how it would do in really cold weather - I tried it at 50 degrees and was kind of cold. I don't see how it can be rated to 30 degrees. I'd hate to just have this covering me at 30 degrees; it would be a long sleepless night.

So it's an ok bag for summer weather. Not so much for crisp fall nights. And of course, it's not down; so as I mentioned, it is very thick and large. Definitely not for backpacking.

title: Nice but won't last

I looked at other ways to attach the mount, and it doesn't look like there are any because of the way the round base of the computer fits into the mount. A twist tie would prevent the computer from fitting into the mount. I had a similar "O" ring that attached a bike pump to the water bottle holder on the bike and it lasted one season. I attached the pump another way after the band deteriorated, but with this, there's really no room to put a twist tie around the mount.

So it's pretty much a throwaway when the band deteriorates after one season I figure.

title: Great tent, though a little difficult to learn how to take it down.
text:
I picked up the 2 person version of this tent with the hopes that if would be a good tent for my 11 year old to use for camping. I was pleasantly surprised by how roomy the tent is for a 2 person tent. Two people can comfortably lay sided by side in this tent with out issue. As others have suggested be careful taking it down, watch some youtube videos to see just how to do it as the instructions on the package are not the best for demonstrating it and if you don't do it right you could easily snap one of the poles.

Pros:
-This tent does go up in 10 seconds like the packaging suggests, though it may take you an additional minute to stake it in.
-Very roomy for a 2 person tent.
-Once you learn how to take it down it only takes about 20 seconds to go from being fully assembled to being in its bag.
-I used this tent in moderate rain and had no issues water in the tent.
-While the tent does not come with a foot print for it the bag the tent comes in has plenty of room to also hold a foot print.

Cons:
-You must take it down just right so you don't twist the poles the wrong way and snap them, be sure to practice this several times before going camping with it.
-You need to have some height to be able to take the tent down. In order to take down the tend you end up standing it on its side then have to pull it down from the top, as I said at the beginning of this review I bought this for my 11 year old son and he was not tall enough to take it down.
-Learning to take down the tent is a bit complicated but once you learn it then it is no problem.
-The size of the tent in the package is a bit large, it folds down into a circle that is larger than I would prefer; however, since it is rather flat finding a place to store or pack it is not usually a problem. Though certainly not a backpacking tent.
-Due to the tension in the poles that keeps the tent up it causes the zipper a bit difficult to zip up and I am worried that the zipper is going to break over time. There are two pull tabs for each zipper and the tension is greatest on the upper sides of the the zipper close to where the zipper starts (or finishes), I found that if I have the two pull tabs come together at the bottom (middle) of the zipper then I can avoid a lot of the tension.

Over all I really liked this tent, though my original use for it is not going to work. There is no way my 11 year old can take this tent down by himself and I am looking for other tents for him now. However, I am now using this as my personal tent when we go on scout camp outs and I love it.

title: 2 bikes, 3000 miles, 85mph
text:
3000 mile round trip with 2 road bikes at 85mph and we couldn't be happier. It took me about 3 minutes to figure out the install and another 3 minutes to load up the bikes. The rack holds extremely steady with virtually no movement from the bikes and requires little, if any, tightening once underway. Just as other user mentioned, we did have some damage to the lower bumper, a slight indention and a little peeling of the clear coat, but I don't hold that against this product. Really its just the ABS plastic bumper that was the issue and its hardly a problem. As for the trunk lid, there was absolutely no damage or markings at all. The color of the product is slightly misrepresented in the pictures - its more of a flat, colorless black composite than a shiny black color. Again, this is no issue for me, just not exactly what I expected. I will say, I'd guess this product could easily be painted to match your vehicle if you really wanted a cool, custom look. One other unexpected issue was the loss of MPG. We were driving a Honda Civic that regularly gets 30+mpg and that fell to 25-27mpg. Once more, no issue with the product, just something to be aware of for those on a longer drive.

On the whole, this rack is super easy to use, looks a LOT nicer than other racks, heavy enough to feel solid, light enough to store with ease. Over he course of our 3000 mile journey, I took this on and off 6 times and I never begrudged doing it. I would highly recommend this bike rack to anyone that asked.

Tips: Make sure the points of contact are clean before putting the rack on. This will ensure no dirt gets trapped and acts like sand paper once moving. Use small bungies or velcro straps to secure your front wheel from spinning and one more to secure the pedals of the two bikes to each other so the cranks don't turn. The security cable is a very nice touch that I would have no problem trusting for cross town and short stops, but I still added a standard, coated bike cable to secure it to the rack to feel more comfortable stopping overnight as the provided cable could very easily be cut with a small bolt cutter. Load your heavier bike on first to reduce the leverage placed on the rack. Take a short test run before going a long distance.

title: An abombination!
text:
I should have listened to the other 2 reviewers. I am beyond disappointed in the condition of this item. First of all, the fact that all the pieces were separate would not have been an issue IF the items were packed properly. The piece of sod was thrown haphazardly into a very thin plastic bag that was completely wide open and not secured closed at all. There is almost as much dirt and grass in the bottom of the bag as there is on the piece of sod. I'm surprised that there isn't dirt and grass all over the box it was thrown into as well. Worst of all, the sod is absolutely NOTHING like the picture. it is a 3 inch round piece of mostly dirt, that is not a rich dark brown as pictured, but a dried-out, tan-colored crumbling mess. And, the grass is long, sparse and a mix of pale green, yellow and brown. Not sure what the freeze-drying process is supposed to do, but the grass and dirt are so dry that you can't even breathe near it without pieces of grass and dirt falling off. What a mess! AND it smells pretty nasty too.

The letter of authenticity is trash (or at least it is to Steiner). It was thrown into the box along with the packing materials, without an envelope or any other protection. From being jostled around inside the shipping box, it is now crumpled and torn in at least three places along the side. Granted, it is a thicker-weight paper, but an envelope would have been nice (especially for the price). The letter says that the sod was removed on March 14, 2009 and that it is "unconditionally guaranteed" - whatever that means. It's difficult to tell if the signature of "Brandon Steiner" is signed in ink or a copy. I don't want to damage the signature trying to figure it out.

The case is actually a baseball case and comes in a "single baseball glass case" box. When I first opened the shipping box, I thought I'd been sent the wrong item. The case IS made of glass, not acrylic, and supposedly has a cherry wood base. It also is not nearly as nice as the picture depicts. The wood is dry and dull and the joints are roughly glued together and uneven. Unlike one of the other reviewers (and the description), I did not receive a separate sticker to apply to the base. It actually has a metal plaque already attached. The problem is, the only words that are legible are "Yankee Stadium Artifact." There are three full lines of smaller writing below that but it is completely unreadable. I can't tell if the words got scratched off or if it was improperly printed on the plate to begin with. I cannot read what it says at all.

I'm not familiar with these types of cases, but there is nothing that holds the grass in place. The bottom is a slick mirror, and the slightest movement causes the sod to slide around inside the case, leaving dirt and debris all over the bottom. Unless its kept perfectly still, it will probably fall apart completely into a big mess in no time. My biggest regret is that I did not purchase this from Amazon. I paid only $59 from another source who is not nearly as easy to deal with. Although, I don't think it would have made a difference in the quality of the product or awful packaging, because this item ships directly from Steiner sports anyway.

I've posted over 80 product reviews on Amazon. This is the first time I've ever felt the need to post pictures or video. This item is so pathetic - you really have to see it to believe it, so I am going to post something tomorrow. I just wanted to post my review ASAP so that anyone considering buying this as a last-minute Christmas gift is forewarned. I initially felt too embarrassed to give this as a gift, but now I think the recipient might appreciate the "tragic humor" of this item. It would make a good conversation piece for sure! I will let him decide if he wants to return it for something else, or keep it as something to show to his friends and laugh about.

title: Very roomy and durable, some draw backs...
text:
I bought this for my husband who works outside and needed something to keep lunch plus multiple drinks cold all day.
PROS:
- Very large size - can hold 2 larger-sized gatorade drinks PLUS a 16.9 oz water bottle in the bottom compartment with an ice pack, and 2 sandwiches with 2 16.9 oz water bottles or more on top
- Very sturdy material - thick, tear resistant, very durable
- Comes with optional shoulder strap that fits perfectly in the front zippered compartment if you need to be hands free
- Looks more masculine than LL Bean-type of lunch bags so hubby actually uses it
- Front pocket is see through mesh and perfect to hold strap and a "tick key" tick remover for outdoor use
- At under 20 bucks, it's a real bargain! I bought an extra one and put it away for when this one bites the dust

CONS:
- Black color means it gets hot outdoors or in the car - especially if the sun hits it
- White interior shows every bit of dirt (although cleans up easily with a little baking soda-water paste on a sponge)
- Zippers are sturdy, but get "stuck" quite often
- Sides are soft so will the bag will sit lop-sided if unequal size items are placed in the bottom
- Triangular shaped top (with above mentioned soft sides) makes it so things on top are easily crushed
- Top handles are too small too fit a large sized wrist through so it must be carried by hand or shoulder strap

All in all a good lunch box for men (and women) who carry lots of food and drinks for lunch. I wish there were other color options- maybe an army green or tan- so it didn't get so hot in the sun. Would also be better if at least the bottom compartment had stiff sides. Also, a zippered pouch or compartment to hold a cold pack would be nice, so it didn't have to get mixed in with contents.

It's really hard to find a durable, masculine lunch box for guys who get dirty at work or work outdoors. I've looked for something decent for years and the selection is extremely limited. This fits the bill and is very reasonably priced. For under 20 bucks, you can't do any better than this!

title: The best type of drinking water filter
text:
The best type of drinking water purifier is a Steripen, in my opinion.

Filters: work well but you must keep them clean and sterile. This is hard to accomplish in a camp or when backpacking. I therefore rate that type last.

Chlorine tablets: These are slow. But the bottles are tiny a lipstick tube,so this is the most portable option. the tablets are protected and therefore always clean. No other system is as easy to keep the cleaning apparatus itself clean. Very effective. The big Con is that it puts a taste in the water. To me this is a small price to pay for all the other benefits. I rate this the best system for backpacking. And good enough for camping. But worst of all for emergency at home, especially long term emergency. Because slightly off tasting water is OK for 3 or 4 days, but who want to drink it for say three weeks? A missionary might have to drink poor tasting water for 3 or 4 years :(.

Steripen: The best all around system. I greatly prefer one that uses AA batteries instead of rechargeable. In emergencies or backpacking or camping long term: USB sources aren't necessarily going to be there. But penlight batteries last years until used and are very light and handy.

But it's not so foolproof as tablets because electronics can go wrong. But a teeny bottle holding 50 tablets has only one likely possibility of failing: the bottle is so tiny that you might lose it. Other than that: it is a foolproof system! But these tablets are dated: they do not last more than a couple years, they expire. So you have to buy more from time to time even if you aren't using them. But: they are very cheap!

title: Works Fine!
text:
The stand holds the bike upright and so it will not fall sideways.
Because it grips the front wheel so that it cannot turn right or left.

Nor slip backwards out.
And as you can see in the picture the bottom of the stand makes the bile roll back uphill,
and so gravity holds the bike from rolling backwards.

I do not agree with those who say this should work to hold a bike in the back of a pickup.
The bike could bounce out (overcome gravity) and roll backwards out.

In the garage, you will want a cover over the bike and stand to keep dust and dirt
out of the parts that have grease (the chain for instance).

Indoors you need a long pad (like an exercise pad to keep the dirty tires off the carpet.

Another (better for cleanliness) is a 'work stand' because these hold the bike in the air
and only the stand touches the floor (like a Park brand work stand). But these take about
15 seconds to load and unload the bike instead of 2 seconds like this Bikehand parking rack.
And work stands are much more expensive.
But a work stand hold bike so that you can do mechanical work on it, thus saving paying
hundreds to a bike shop for repacking bearings and such that you can do yourself with
a work stand and some specialized bike tools.

There are lots of other ways to go too, holders that mount to the wall or ceiling,
some have hoist ropes to raise and lower.

This stand is a very sensible and cheap solution, just keep in mind when the
bike is in a garage, then it needs a cover (cloth or plastic). Amazon sells
