title: Best headlamp on this price level? UPDATE: NO!
text:
My favorite low priced headlamp.
Not the quality of high tech wonder lamps. But there are no real faults. And the interface is very good.
All inputs on one button which is the best way to do it, fewer moving parts to go wrong.
3 inputs : momentary push, 3 second push, 6 second push.
If the lamp is on :
Momentary push cycles on/off.
Long push gradually dims the light in steps.
(when it reaches the dimmest it will flicker once to indicate lowest level,
then it gradually brightens the light, step at a time, flickers once on highest).
This works very well to set the brightness levels.

When light is OFF:
momentary push turns it on (two outer lights for flood, or center for spot. Repeat pushes will alternate: spot, off, flood, off, spot,...
3 second push : turns on the red lamp
6 second push: turns on the lock mode (locks lamp off until another 6 sec. push turns it back on. A blue light on the side will go on for a couple seconds to verify the lamp is locked).

I find the interface easy to use to get it to do as I like when I like.
5 different tilt settings from straight down to higher than straight forward. There are settings I find perfect for reading or watching your step on the trail. And they stay put.

Very bright on spot!
The flood is very spread out, lights up the whole room or tent.

5 stars.
------

Another lamp that costs about $10 more is the Princeton Tec EOS TACTICAL. The tactical model of the EOS line is military issue from several governments. Bulletproof and rugged, really waterproof. But the ergonomics are military rough: the button is very hard to push (so it won't wear out), the battery box takes a tool like a dime to open (so they could never fall out by mistake). A better choice if you going to climb mount Everest and your life depends on the lamp. Not as good as this BDSH for using in common outdoor camping, running, hunting, imo.

Those are the two under $50 that I like.

EDIT: I should have noted the reviews stating the tilt lock stops would fail. They failed in 6 months on one of mine of these. The other two I have are getting weaker and weaker (about a year old). Then the lamp just tilts all the way forward and points at your toes. No way to reset the tilt after the mechanism breaks. I changed my rating from 5 stars to 2 stars. I do NOT recommend these.

Powder storage: Fed. regulations state storage for over 20 pounds powder must be in wooden container that is not completely airtight sealed, boards must be 1" nominal thick. This box meets regulations, standard 1" nominal lumber boards is an actual 3/4" just like this box.
There are two lockable hasps, one on each side, which would take padlocks (not included). The hasps are fairly thin and so not burglar proof. Making it burglar proof might also make it sealed tight, which would not obey the standards to be open to the air. The boxes are required to be somewhat flimsy, I would say.
Can stack it 4 high with 1 pound powder containers, about 12 cans per layer = 48 pounds or so.

2 rope handles, one on each end.
For anyone desiring thicker sides, thin plywood sheets could be screwed down inside on each section of the box and lid, and secured with short 5/8" wood screws.
This same company makes smaller boxes, some of which are also available on Amazon.

I think this item is worth the money :)

title: too big...
text:
Using two or three 3 liter (3 quart) shower bags is a whole lot easier than one larger bag. Sun shower used to make a 3 liter bag. It had no hose, the spout was attached directly to the bottom of the bag and was easy to turn on or shut off the water.

It was so small and lightweight that anyone even a child could hold the bag over their head with one hand. Or move the bag down to direct the shower to say your feet. Meanwhile your other hand was free to hold the bar of soap or shampoo jar. Heating up 2 or 3 bags in the sun takes no longer than one large bag. And drying out 3 smaller bags takes less time than for one larger bag.

No tree branch or anything to hang it on was necessary although it did have a hanger hole. One side was clear plastic up to warm up from the sun. 2-1/2 gallons weighs twenty pounds. 3 quarts weighs six. Great for backpacking with only one small showerbag weighing 3 ounces, carry 6 pounds water from stream to campsite.

OK that is no longer made, but some brands of 3L hydration systems have a shower head attachment. Unfortunately the head is on a hose, not good. Easier if the shower head is directly attached onto the bag in order to make it a one hand appliance. By tying the hose end close to the hydration bladder does the same thing.

The problem is the price! The old 3L sun shower cost about $7 instead of $25 !

Optimus made smaller and lighter set of pans and windscreen to fit the 123 and 123R. This set is the Optimus 124. It is not as rugged as the Sigg tourist however.

Optimus also made a model number 88 set which was a combination of the 124 cookset and 123 stove (not 123R).

Both the 123 sized Sigg tourist and Optimus 124 appear for sale on Ebay regularly. The 88 set occasionally.

"Off Belay" magazine in 1975 published a 32 page report of high altitude stoves. Pages 16,17, refer to the 123.

Notice below the thumbnails for the Off Belay article is a reproduction of a letter by Harold Boyce describing a technique for safety with the Svea at extremely cold temperatures. title: A Quality Streamlined, Lightweight, & Comfortable Flat Water Life Vest (but not USCG approved)
text:
Night Cat [CE Approved] Life Jackets for Adults Kayaking Boating Vests Inflatable Lifesaving PFD, Survival Preservers, Lightweight Premium Quality, Automatic and Manual, 150KG/330LBS.
Sold by Nightcat-fishing $74.99

NOTE: We bought two of these life jackets in 2020, to use kayaking. Just bought another (March 2022) for a different family member. We have used them 2 years now, and are very satisfied with the product.

ORIGINAL 2020 REVIEW: I was looking for a more comfortable life jacket for flat water kayaking... our rigid foam Type II and Type III whitewater life vests were just too bulky, hot, and uncomfortable. These Night Cat inflatable vests were just the ticket: Slim, lightweight, and comfortable, all at a very reasonable price-point.

In particular, I liked: (1) the zipper pocket in the outer case that can hold a cell phone (it will accept a device up to 6.5 inches long); (2) the neoprene fabric collar that prevents the vest from chafing your neck; (3) the SOLAS-rated reflectors on the outside of the vest (there are reflectors on the air bladder also). BONUS: They come with a nice mesh and clear plastic storage bag.

This vest is perfect for recreational boating or other water activities conducted on relatively calm waters. The vests are very well made... almost identical to similar products costing 2 - 4 times as much. They arrive fully-charged and ready-to-use.

To be clear, the Night Cat vests do NOT carry a U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) approval label. These vests are CE approved, which means they meet standards recognized by most European countries (the vests also have an Australian certification).

Based upon the specifications of this vest (CE approved for off-shore use; will turn many (but not all) unconscious persons to a safe, face out-of-water position; 150 Newtons minimum buoyancy; hold full inflation for a minimum of 24 hours), these Night Cat vests are EQUIVALENT in performance to a USCG TYPE II inflatable personal flotation device (PFD) [i.e., a buoyant vest for general boating on calm near-shore and inland waters where fast rescue is likely].

However, if you absolutely must, by applicable federal, state, or local rules, have a USCG-approved PFD for your type of craft or activity, you may have to get something else... without a USCG approval label, the Night Cat vests probably would not satisfy these regulatory requirements.

For flat and calm water activities where a USCG-approved life vest is not mandated, these Night Cat life vests are perfect.

[NOTE 2]: From someone with technical rescue experience... if you are going to be far off-shore, in whitewater, or in swift water where there's the potential for "strainers", wear (as appropriate) a Type I, Type II, or Type III (or if applicable, a Type V) rigid foam life jacket

I also don’t like how the light is framed when I’m using it at night, it’s an off putting distraction that fails to provide a clean view of the areas where I’m shining the light —so it also means the view in the dark is very narrow.

I justified this purchase as necessary to look out for coyote eyes when I’ve got my pooch outside, which it seems like it can still do, just as long as they’re not lurking near the periphery of where I’m pointing this flashlight —since I’d never spot it in the dark band that surrounds the bright middle light —or in his “frame” just outlines the thick dark ring separating it’s outer thin ring from the bright inner light if that makes any sense. If it doesn’t now, it will when your light arrives if you got the same model as me.

I absolutely hate the gummy button as it makes it hard to hurry up and snap the light on —or to turn on the light with one hand. Not a total deal breaker, but added to my issues with the edge circles it is reason enough for me to stay on my continued search for a solid edc I can count on in any situation —instead of just scenarios where I will only need a partial view of what’s going on, as well as more time to fiddle with a power button, while I also have zero free hands.

title: Great sound, but the tube is very brittle in the cold
text:
I bought this elk bugle back in May in anticipation of my elk hunt this Fall. The call is pretty easy to use, and in terms of sound, it did a fine job. The only problem was that yesterday, it was about 30 degrees out in the morning, when I went to expand the tube, and it broke into two pieces. The tube got very brittle in the cold air. I would have thought Flextone would have field tested this design a bit more, but I'm going to contact them and see what they say. I'll post back what I find out.

Update - 12/12/2014:

I promised a follow up, and here it is. I kindly let Flextone know that the tube broke into two pieces, and I mentioned how other Amazon users had the same problem, and I also asked about replacement. I just got a response back from them, and here it is:

"We haven't had an issue with the tube. Unfortunately we don't have any tubing available, but we will have them available at the middle of next year. Please contact us then for pricing and availability."

I was pretty unhappy with this response, so I've lowered my rating from 3 stars to 1 star. It seems they think that if someone other than them has an issue, it's not really an issue. I've dealt with lots of companies that stand behind their products and are willing to accept a design flaw and bend over backwards to help the customer fix/replace it. Not Plano (Flextone). When I bought this product, it only had 2 good reviews, but you can see them getting lower over time now. Do yourself a favor and avoid this bugle. There are better ones out there.

title: Makes exercising your wrist and forearms fun
text:
Of all the things I saw at CES, this was the only item I decided to buy. I actually found their competitor, DynaFlex Powerball first but decided to go with the NSD Spinner brand instead because it sounded like they were more on top of customer service. I also liked that they had an affordable wind up version that didn't require using the cord. You wind it up by turning the ball in the direction of the arrow (see picture attached, the arrow is embossed into the green part.) I'd read these kinds of balls were popular with rock climbers as a forearm exercise and it was fun to use, so I decided to give it a shot

Pros:
- Don't have to worry about losing a cord. You can take this thing with you anywhere and give it a spin.
- Easy to use - I find myself picking this up while I'm watching TV or just walking around.
- Helps with wrist / forearm pain - I have pretty bad pain from using the computer too much, and I found using the ball helped me stretch my forearms and hands and helped reduce the pain a lot
- I can't validate, but when I have the ball spinning on high RPMS it takes a lot of effort to maintain my grip on the ball so I feel like I'm doing something to build up my strength.

Cons:
- If you have sweaty hands like I do, it's sometimes tough to wind up the ball
- Very confusing lineup of options. I recognize in the end reading and taking note of the titles is super important. Here's an overview of the lineup -

~$20 : NSD Power Essential Spinner
= regular ball, no counter to show rpms, no self starter, vibration free to 15,000 RPM

~$30 : NSD Power AutoStart Spinner Gyroscopic Wrist and Forearm Exerciser with Auto Start Feature
= regular ball, no counter to show rpms, w/ self start, vibration free to 15,000 RPM

~$40 : NSD Power Winners Roll and Spin Spinner Gyroscopic Wrist and Forearm Exerciser with Digital LCD Counter and Auto-Start Feature
= ball w/ rpm meter, w/self start, vibration free to 15,000 RPM **what I got**

~$50 : NSD Roll 'N Spin Rainbow Lit AutoStart Spinner Gyroscopic Wrist and Forearm Exerciser with AutoStart and Multi-Lit LED =
= ball no counter to show rpm, w/ self starter, has LED lights that light up to different colours depending on how fast you're spinning, vibration free to 15,000 RPM

~$75 : NSD Power Winner's Precision Sterling Spinner Gyroscopic Wrist (SILVER COLOUR)
= ball w/rpm meter, NO self starter. Vibration free to 15,000 RPM. Delivers more resistance than the plastic balls. Inertial resistance: 19kg at 10,000rpm (350Hz) 3.2kg at 10,000rpm (450Hz) "up to 41.3lbs"

~$75: NSD Power Ultimate Winner's Precision Sterling Spinner Gyroscopic Wrist (GOLD COLOUR)
= ball w/rpm meter, NO self starter. Designed to deliver higher RPMS. Claims vibration free operation at up to 27,000 RPM.

Overall, since these aren't expensive, it was worth it for me to try out.

Update: I still love this ball but I recommend not leaving it anywhere really hot. Since I take this ball with me everywhere, I'd left it in the car overnight in the hot summer weather and I think the glue that held the grip band to the ball melted. Now I can't keep the rubber grip on the ball when I spin as easily.

title: Great tracker, when not broken
text:
UPDATE 1/17/2015

I had this for a year, and loved using it -- until it stopped working. I had purchased 6 of these in total (5 as gifts), and at least 2/6 of these things no longer hold a charge. When I emailed support, because I contacted them just over the year mark (Jan 6th purchase date), the best they could offer me was a 25% discount. It's great when it works, but such a high failure rate within a year seems disappointing.

==========================
The Withings Pulse claims to track your activity, your sleep, and your heart rate.

If you're looking for something that is precise and accurate for exactly what you've done, this isn't it. I don't think the technology is quite there yet in any device.

But if you're looking for something that is effective as a motivator, and that gives you a consistent baseline to measure your progress, this is perfect for that.

I've been eyeing activity trackers for some time. Many of my friends choose the Fitbit while others chose the Nike Fuel band. I finally pulled the trigger on this device specifically for a few reasons:

1. Integration with a smart scale. I think if you're really motivated to change yourself - get more active, lose some weight, you want to get the smart scale with it to close the loop. It is that much more rewarding and encouraging to keep up with your daily goal if you see the results of your work (whether it's lower fat %, lower weight). The Fitbit also has a scale, but I liked that the Withings scale had been around for longer. Sure you could just get any scale and put in manual measures to your app, but I'm a lazy person and having all of that integrated and automatically synchronized is a big deal.

2. Works for both iPhone and Android. I can't find the studies right now, but it's far easier to get fit and stay healthy if everyone else is doing it too. So for group motivation and support, when I finally committed to the Withings platform, I went ALL in and got 6 trackers + the Withings scale as Christmas presents to myself and everyone around me. The fact that it works on both mobile platforms is a big plus. As was getting a group of us on this at the same time. Our friendly competition has definitely pushed me on the days I felt like slacking off.

3. Accurate enough. When I've gone on hikes and walks with friends who run, we've ended up with roughly the same number +/1 100 steps (albeit different calorie counts) at the end of the trail. So while it might not exactly match the listed distance on a trail you've gone in terms of miles, it is at least consistent enough with itself which is the most important thing. Also, while it might log a few steps as I'm moving the pulse from the strap to my pocket and vice versa, it consistently does that so I'm going to know on any given day if I've done net more or less.

4. Has motivated me. I wasn't sure how well this thing would work, but the simple act of having a concrete measure of my activity has motivated me to move and do more than any other system I'd set up for myself before. I periodically glance at my tracker during the day, and find myself adjusting (ok an extra-long route to the store, maybe stepping in place while I'm on the phone, pacing while I watch TV). Knowing exactly how much I've done means there's no excuse for me to "feel like I've done a lot". I know if I've been active. Or not.

5. Good customer service. I'd read online that people have had problems with their customer service. My personal experience was far from that. 5 days after I got the tracker, my clip holder broke. Personally I think it's poorly designed as the repeated act of taking the clip in and out of the holder every night to move put in your night armband for sleep tracking is going to add a lot of strain to the corner of the clip. Well I emailed customer service and they offered to replace my clip for free. I just sent them my proof of purchase and 9 days later a package arrived from France. I can't believe they sent the replacement from France but I'm happy to have the replacement.

6. Detailed app and web interface. I haven't seen the competitor apps, but for me, the web site and the app contain all the information I need. At a glance, I can see my overall trends (compared to the normal range), and I can see my weekly trends of when I'm sleeping, how well I'm sleeping, when I'm most active. I tried integrating MyFitnessPal. I couldn't stick with that kind of dedicating food logging, but if you're that kind of person, the integration gives you a complete in/out/impact picture.

7. Decent battery life. I'd say your tracker will last well over a week with regular use. And it charges back up quickly (maybe 15 minutes). The first days I got my tracker I was religiously syncing my tracker with my phone several times a day a few days later I'd only used about a bar of battery.

That said the device does have some limitations:

1. The plastic clip is really fragile. I've read reviews of people having problems with the clip falling out of the holder. To be safe, I keep the pulse in my pocket. At $99 (or $70 during the Christmas sale), I sure don't want to be dropping and losing this thing that often.

2. Some sort of data override would be nice. Given that the sleep tracker works by being strapped to your body, the assessment of light and deep sleep (or being awake) is measured by your amount of movement. I can be prone to insomnia, but sometimes that involves just lying awake and feeling frustrated. It usually doesn't involve thrashing around like a mad person because I'm so upset I'm awake. So the tracker has mistakenly taken my lack of motion to mean I'm in blissful deep sleep. I wish! It'd be nice in those cases to add manual entries (the way you can with weight) to add notes. But in generally there is a correlation where more deep sleep (or sleep overall) has resulted in feeling more rested the next day.

Bottom line: The results

How are the results? This was a gift to myself for Christmas. Since then, I've used the tracker every day and have committed to doing 10,000 steps every day. I didn't change my diet and still continued to eat a few pieces of chocolate and some kind of dessert once a day. This is not to say I prescribe this as the best way to get healthy. I just happen to have a healthy love of food and was also curious to see what straight up physical activity would do to my weight. I've never been overweight and lead a relatively active lifestyle, but 8 months of living off mayonnaise laden hotdogs while living in Chile did leave me a little plumper than I cared to stay

So 19 days into this I've walked an average of 73K steps every week and slept an average of close to 8 hours. I have gone from 111 lbs to a trendline average of 108 lb (naturally my weight will fluctuate at every measure but it steadily goes down.). I feel great and am feeling as motivated as I was on day one. Short of accidentally washing this thing or losing it, I'm going to keep using the Pulse and keep tracking! This device has been one of my favourite purchases in recent memory.

title: Rock solid stove! Used for roasting coffee, but the possibilites are endless
text:
Pictures don't really show the sturdy construction or impressive size of the Pro 30. I'm currently using it without the leg extensions, but they are just as solid as the rest of the unit. With a 14x16 inch cooking area, it can handle quite a load.

I do a LOT of outside cooking, including roasting my own coffee. I had been using a 12,000 BTU side burner on an old, rusted out gas grill to roast green coffee beans, but the side burner recently died and I had no interest in refurbishing the gas grill. I needed a new stove for roasting coffee beans. After considering all the options, I chose the Camp Chef Pro 30. I'm glad I did.

Roasting coffee beans on the side burner limited me to calm, no wind days for the quickest roast. Roasting a pound of coffee usually took 19-21 minutes; longer in any wind. The wind was howling with gusts to 25 MPH for my first coffee roast with the Pro 30, a true test of the stove. After adjusting the air intake behind the low-med-high knob, I had a flame that held up nicely to the wind. With the Pro 30, in the strong wind, I roasted a pound of green coffee in 12 minutes on the medium setting!

I've been roasting coffee for about two years, on average one roast every 7 days. The wind will no longer be a factor and the Pro 30 will save me a lot of time. I own the Camp Chef Rainier table top stove for camping, and can serve 2-4 people easily with it, but could not use it for roasting coffee with the 10" Dutch oven I use. With the Pro 30 and a big pot of chili, stew, or soup, I'll be able to serve a large family. For the $70 I paid for the Pro 30 here on Amazon, it is a GREAT value!

title: Read the manual and master the technique for great results
text:
We have three sets of kitchen knives; a low quality TV infomercial special, a medium quality Chicago Cutlery set, and what we consider high quality home knives by J.A. Henckels. Plus we have more working knives than I care to count. I have used a lot of sharpeners and edge straighteners over the decades but we only use those now for machetes that my wife won't let me use in the Chef's Choice 120. They'd fit too!

I bought the 120 for my wife two years after I bought her the J.A. Henckels knives. New, the knives were amazing; felt like they had a near surgical edge. I knew once they got dull or burred we didn't have anything that would restore them to like-new condition. Before we bought the 120 we took our dull Chicago Cutlery knives to a professional butcher for sharpening to see what we'd get back. We were not impressed with the results so I knew we needed to find a good knife sharpener.

After reading the reviews on sharpeners, I chose the Chef's Choice 120. We carefully read the directions and practiced our technique on the cheap knives. Wow, talk about impressed with the results. Then we put the dull Chicago Cutlery knives through all three stages on the 120. Several of the knives were so dull we had to three-stage them three times to recover the edge. When we were finished they sliced effortlessly through paper! They had NEVER been that sharp, even new. They are decades old knives and I will admit the 1st stage of the 120 did put some scratches on the blades about 1/4" up from the edge, but we didn't care. We just wanted a razor sharp edge on the old knives and the 120 delivered.

We tested stage two and three on some loose knives we had to see if those stages scratched the knife blade. They didn't. Most knives that are maintained properly only require stage two and three, or only stage 3. Once we were confident of no scratches we used only the Stage 3 polishing strop stage on the newer J.A. Henckels. Although the knives were two years old and still exceptionally sharp, they had not been sharpened since we bought them. Plus they had developed a few small burrs. The 120 Stage 3 strop stage removed the burrs, restored the near surgical, like-new edge, and no scratches either. My wife was thrilled with the results!

We use the Stage 3 strop stage on several serrated knives we own and they are noticeably improved and shaper. I've used the 120 on my working pocket knives too. I thought they were acceptably sharp using a diamond edge straightener but the 120 takes sharpening to a completely new level.

The 120 will get hot sharpening a bunch of knives one right after the other, but we typically limit our sharpening to ten knives or less. Stage 1 definitely does scratch the blade but that stage is only recommended for hopelessly dull knives.

Others may have issues with the 120. Not us. Once you understand the technique you need to use with the sharpener, it works great! We love it!

title: Easy to assemble, easy to use, solid and quiet.
text:
My wife had a gym membership that cost $60 a month. It was the best deal ever.........for the GYM! I've always been a workout at home guy. When our treadmill started failing after 15 years she cancelled her gym membership and we decided it was time to try something new. Due to hip issues (me) and knee issues (both of us) we needed something that would be comfortable, quiet, give the old heart a boost, and not aggravate our joint issues. The Exerpeutic 300SR exceeded our all our expectations.

My wife actually put the bike together when I was under the weather. The frame is strong and compact. The seat/backrest is comfortable. The mechanism is whisper quiet, quieter than any exercise bike we've ever used. Why lay on the couch watching TV when you can comfortably sit on the bike and do the same thing? The only weak part is the display. Hands off! It works absolutely fine but I can already see it breaking if someone tries to put their weight on it while getting on or off the bike. We've put a label on it that says "Not a handle - will break" to prevent occasional guests from making that mistake.

If the Exerpeutic 300SR lasts only three months, we're still ahead of what the gym membership cost. I suspect it will last much longer.

Update: 6 months and this baby gets a workout twice a day on most days, me in the morning and my wife in the evening. Still working perfectly!

title: Deoderant only.  No break down of solid waste.
text: We have a Vista Potty camp toilet with a 6.3 gallon holding tank.  If you are only looking for a deoderant for your holding tank, then this is the stuff to buy because it works great for that purpose and is eco-friendly.  Also great if you are only using your camp toilet for liquid waste.  If on the other hand you want a product that will deoderize, liquify solid waste, significantly break down single ply toilet tissue, and make dumping/cleanup a breeze, Reliance Bio-blu is NOT the product to buy.  Get Aqua-Kem instead which does it all except the eco-friendly part.  We used the Reliance Bio-blu once in our camp toilet for dual body waste purpose and will never use it again if we even suspect we might have solid waste in our holding tank (insert big shudder and gagging here for memories of dumping and cleanup).  We like to do our part for the environment and camp with a leave no trace philosophy, but our camp toilet will ALWAYS be charged with Aqua-Kem not Reliance.

title: Most comfortable sleeping bag we've ever owned
text:
After decades of backpacking with mummy sleeping bags, and never having enough warmth, we transitioned to 4WD tent camping. Although I never really minded the confines of a mummy bag my wife was never crazy about it so we looked for a bag with lots of space, width, and warmth. Weight and bag compression was no longer the primary criteria for purchasing a sleeping bag. That's good because this baby is relatively heavy and doesn't exactly pack small once taken out of the box, but that's fine for 4WD camping.

Experience has taught me that you want to purchase a sleeping bag that is rated at least 20 to 30 degrees colder than the coldest temperatures you expect to encounter. We occasionally camp in the mountains where night time temps drop into the high 20's and low 30's, but most of the time the night time temps are in the 40s to low 70s in a relatively dry Western-US environment, including the high desert. I was concerned we might overheat but my wife and I have remained comfortable across the entire temperature range wearing just a t-shirt and underwear or long underwear. She zips her bag up completely whenever the temps drop into the 40s or lower. I don't think I've zipped mine up completely yet.

We're no longer sleeping on a thin foam pad on the ground. We use these bags on cots with 3" thick foam pads. We both sleep like a rock. Our mummy bags have been handed down to our grown kids. As sleeping bags go, this one is a winner!

title: Nice water jug for the money for light use
text:
We debated whether to buy this water jug or another, more sturdy jug by another manufacturer for more than twice the money. We decided to buy the other jug when we found the Rubbermaid on sale at a local store for less than 1/3rd the cost of the more sturdy jug. For the difference in price we thought we'd give the Rubbermaid a try to see how it would perform.

The lower spigot on the Rubbermaid is solid. No leaks and easy to use. The upper vent spigot is a little bit of a weak point. It works absolutely fine, just remember to always close it so it doesn't get broken or let hot air cycle into the cold interior of the jug.

Although not an "extreme" cooler jug, once filled with ice and water we had cold water well into the second day in the desert. The cooler was kept in the shade the entire time.

If you need a rough and tumble water jug, look elsewhere. If you need something that will sit on a picnic table for a day or two, this will work fine.

title: Great stove, but it is the grill and burner only unless you buy the "Combo" stove
text:
When I purchased the unit I thought it came with the griddle too. It doesn't. I thought I'd be able to buy the griddle separately but it was readily apparent it was not available from Camp Chef or anywhere else. I thought about returning the unit because the aluminum grill material will not hold a pot or a griddle without being damaged. If you are looking to buy the stove make sure you get the Camp Chef Ranier Combo which includes the griddle. For some reason though the Combo stove is 40% more expensive than the base Ranier Grill Camp stove. It is for that reason I passed on returning what I had purchased and looked for a cheaper jury-rigged solution.

We solved the grill limitations by purchasing a $12 BBQ rectangle expansion grate from a local hardware warehouse. I removed the expansion arms and cut off two of the grates from one end with an angle grinder, but left the grate supports so the gratefree end had about a 2" extension on each side. The extensions fit nicely under the single burner grate and the adapted grill perfectly covered the grilling section of the stove. The adapted grate moves a little, but very little. We can use the grill section now for a griddle we already own or an additional pot. You cannot use the adapted grill for grilling though because the gas burner element in the grilling section is not protected from fat drippings. When we want to grill, we just remove the adapted grill and replace it with the original grill that came with the stove because it has the burner element protector built down the center of the grill.

Now, having said all that, we love the stove. We use it with the bulk hose adapter for a 20 lb propane bottle. The single burner quickly boils water and is relatively adjustable for pot/pan cooking. The stove burners light with one or two clicks of the lighter button. If all I wanted was the grill and stove I would have given it 5 stars, but the fact that the combo unit is so much more expensive and the griddle is not available as a separate purchase, resulting in a jury-rig solution, I gave it four stars

title: Wow, most impressive $40 cooler you can buy
text:
We keep one of these in the house at all times next to the kitchen to use as an extension to our refrigerator. We use it for both cold and hot food storage. For cold storage you can put a couple gallon jugs of frozen water in the cooler and it will keep the temperature between 37F and 39F for several days. We use the cooler to thaw meat, party prep, seasonal cooking prep, and anytime we run out of space in the refrigerator after a trip to the grocery store, big box store, etc. For hot storage we use it for resting hot smoked meats after they have been taken off the smoker. Cleanup and disinfection is a breeze.

We used three of these on a weeklong desert camping trip to an art and music festival, temps in the low to high 90s. These babies definitely keep ice for 5 days. We had one of them under our shade structure up off the playa surface with wooden blocks and the other two we kept up on wooden blocks in a covered cargo trailer. The one under our shade structure was opened and closed quite a bit because it contained our fresh food. The other two had alcoholic drinks and were opened less often because we were consuming mostly water. We bought ice on the 5th day but there was still quite a bit of ice present in the melt water. The ones in the trailer had lots of ice but they weren't opened as much. We drained the melt water to use for shower water and only charged them with ice one more time before we left the desert, and we did so just because it was relatively convenient and we wouldn't be unpacking them right away when we got home. Great coolers especially for the price.

title: Great for boiling water in camp and replenishing water in a smoker
text:
With only one coffee drinker in the family we didn't need a 3 quart coffee boiler for camp coffee. What we needed was an inexpensive, well built, 3-4 quart container for boiling water for cocoa, making coffee with a a one-cup Melita drip coffee cone, reconstituting instant oatmeal, and for easily adding hot water to our camp showers. The Graniteware coffee boiler was exactly what we needed. We fill it, use what we need for breakfast, then turn it off and set it aside. Later, especially if the day is cloudy or the solar shower water has cooled later in the evening, we'll add some more water, reheat, then add the hot water to our solar showers. We split it between two 2.5 gallon solar showers. The Graniteware Coffee Boiler was exactly what we needed and we've had absolutely no problems. Be sure to use a hot glove or pad when pouring if you just took it off the fire or the stove.

I also use it in my backyard for replenishing water in my smoker. I've learned the temperature of the smoker remains more constant when I add boiling water to the water reservoir. My gas grill has a separate pot burner and it is right next to my smoker. I just fill the coffee boiler with water, place it on the burner, and have hot water at the ready when I need to replenish the smoker.

title: Great product with lots of uses
text:
Like others have said this thing sets up in less than 5 minutes. I often do it alone but with my wife's help it goes up much easier and even quicker. We always travel with our own camp toilet and a 45" inflatable kiddie pool for catching shower water. Both easily fit in the enclosure. We use a small bench in the kiddie pool to sit and shower. The toilet fits in the corner and there's still room to stand and dress after showering.

You definitely need to stake the corners before using it though. It will stand alone but without being staked if you kick it when it is loaded with a camp shower it can twist and collapse, an oversight you'll only do once. "Hello neighbors!" (The voice of experience talking). In windy conditions I stake the guys so I haven't tried it without them as others have done.

Great product. Quite pricey compared to other options, and we did quite a bit of shopping, but this is by far the best product of all we saw.

title: Works like a charm and definitely does the job.
text:
We've evolved as backcountry campers from sponge baths to the solar shower. Taking a bath in the backcountry is a daily requirement for us. At the end of a long day nothing feels better than washing off the dust and the sweat. In the past we'd heat 2 quarts of water to boiling on the stove then dump it in 2.5 gallons of cold water in a collapsible bucket. Then we'd sponge ourselves clean. This camp shower feels downright decadent compared to our previous habit.

For spring/summer camping it heats up to a nice warm temp in about an hour in the sun when the outside temp is in the low 70's. I wash first and use less than a gallon to get wet, wash, and rinse. Then my wife uses the rest of the water for the same, including washing/rinsing her shoulder length hair. We have two of them and occasionally she uses some of the water from the second one to finish rinsing her hair, but not always.

The shower head is a two-handed operation to pull it open for full flow or push it closed to stop the flow. We haven't had any problem with it at all. Great product.

title: The best cot for the money - and comfortable!
text:
We have several 4WD truck camping trips coming up this Spring, Summer, and Fall. We wanted to move from inflatable mattresses to cots in our 10' x 8' Kelty Ridge 6 tent. We were looking for a durable, comfortable cot that set up easily, left plenty of room for storage below the bed, was at least 32" wide, and could easily support 250 lbs without feeling like it was always on the verge of collapse. We tried several cots that cost anywhere between $40 and $150. The more expensive cots were comfortable and fit our needs, but we were having a tough time justifying the price. We were starting to rethink the move to cots until we both laid on the Slumberjack Tough Cot, a cot rated to 350 lbs. We bought two immediately at a local sports warehouse because it fit all our parameters for a great price.

When we opened the boxes we realized there are no instructions with the cots. Still, it took us less than five minutes to figure out how the cot sets up, including proper installation of the end-cap support bars. Once we had the process figured out the second cot took less than a minute to set up. Breakdown and stowage back in the bag takes maybe three minutes.

The cot is solidly constructed with very little sway when set up. The bed material is tough. Yep, the cot is heavy, but hey, we're not backpacking. We picked up a 3"x32"x82" foam pad for $20 at a local hardware store, cover it with a sheet, throw down the sleeping bag, and crawl in for the night. Camping can often be an exercise in sleep deprivation due to the lack of comfort. NOT WITH THESE BABIES! My wife and I both LOVE sleeping on these cots with the foam pad mentioned. It feels downright decadent compared to the blowup mattresses we used to use. The Slumberjack Tough Cot was one of the best purchases ever for our camping fun.

We're looking forward to years of use from our Slumberjack Tough Cots.

title: Compare to the Fenix LD02 before you buy.
text:
BACKGROUND:
I am a big fan of Surefire products, and I have had a LOT of flashlights over the last 40 years.
I try to purchase products that are "made in America" whenever possible, even when they cost substantially more.
I have had a Fenix LD02 single AAA battery flashlight (under $35 at REI) for about one year now.
I ordered this Surefire, because it appeared to be about 3 times brighter, and about the same size, as my Fenix.

MY REVIEW:
1). Like many other reviewers, I have NO IDEA why they decided to make this out of brass. It feels three times as heavy as my aluminum Fenix LD02. That was just a very odd decision. Its like we went back in time to some point before the Bronze age...oh well...
2). In order to turn this on and off and to select the various brightness levels, you have to twist the cap on and off relatively slowly. It always resets to the lowest setting.
Here again, the $35 Fenix wins out--it has a button switch on the tailcap.
3). It is a little bigger than the Fenix, for unknown reasons.
4). Apparently, to achieve the 300 lumen setting, you need to use the included Eneloop Pro rechargeable battery (buy your own charger).
5). On the highest setting, the Surefire beam is noticeably brighter and wider than the Fenix LD02.

CONCLUSION:
If I had to do it again, I would have just stuck with my smaller, lighter, and easier to operate Fenix LD02 that (to me) appears to be about 50% as bright on the highest setting.

title: Workds great for me
text:
After reading some of the negative reviews about this product, I was hesitant to order it. After shopping the internet, however, I was not able to find anything that appeared to suit my needs any better. Eventually, I reluctantly ordered this Trangia Fuel Bottle as an accessory to my alcohol fuel stove. I received it promptly, and just finished testing it.

I filled it to the fill line with denatured alcohol and tested pouring it. Using the adjustable screw cap, I was able to adjust the flow from a drizzle to full open. For me, it offers a nice smooth stream/flow that allows me to fill my alcohol burner without spilling.

I placed it upside down in the sun, but did not experience any leakage. I think it is important to tighten the knob when not in use. This should prevent anything from pressing the pour valve open.

If this size bottle and spout work for you, I recommend this product.

title: Not the lightest, but a great bomb-proof multi fuel stove
text:
PROS:
I have tested this extensively with Kerosene, isobutane canisters, propane (using the LPG Adapter/camping Propane Small Tank Input Adapter from Peakway on Amazon), and Coleman fuel. It worked great with all fuels and it boiled water quickly. In my opinion, the isobutane canister and propane tank fuel provided the most even and quiet flame--it was perfect. The Coleman fuel was right there with the isobutane and propane. As expected, the Kerosene was the most difficult to light and it provided somewhat of an uneven flame, but it was still fine, and it did not produce too much soot.

CONS:
This is not an ultra light backpacker stove by any stretch.

CONCLUSION:
I did a lot of research on this, and I am very glad I purchased it. It is made well, and I doubt it will ever break. I don't think I will ever purchase another camp stove. If you are looking for something that will use the most fuels possible, with very little maintenance, this is it.

I'd prefer to give this cot 2 1/2 stars, but there are no 1/2 stars available in the rating process. so, I gave it 2.

title: Good quality rings, nice and high, very solid
text:
I used these to mount a 50mm whitetail scope on a .308 FAL. The clearance is not enough to also use the peep sight, but that's because the scope is 50mm -- a 40mm scope would have allowed me to still use the peeps.

We've put about 100 rounds downrange on two different outings after zeroing and the scope has held zero fine, so I know the rings aren't moving despite the .308 recoil.

Some people think these rings aren't solid enough but I feel they are great. Just make sure you tighten the hex screws and the mounting nuts tightly, AND make sure your rail mount is also tight. Check the fasteners periodically if you're using a high-recoil rifle.

Only complaint I have is that the hex screw sockets (the part the hex wrench fits into) aren't sturdy enough to really hold up to a lot of cranking. I noticed one of the screw sockets started rounding out and it became more and more difficult to screw or unscrew with the included wrench. If I ever have to take this scope off, I won't be surprised if have to replace one or more hex screws.

Still, a good quality product for the price and I give it 5 stars.

title: Excellent little kit, bore snakes are totally worth it
text:
If you've never used a bore snake, get one. They are totally worth it. No more rods to worry about! The snake is super easy to use and leaves the barrel in great condition after a couple of passes. You can then simply wash the snake and keep using it.

The rest of the kit is pretty nice as well. The little case pouch is handy and compact and has a pocket inside so you can carry a second (and maybe a third) snake in the pouch.

The can of solvent is a little small. It won't last very long if you have multiple guns and go shooting often. But the gun oil should last you a good while.

I liked the bore snake so much I bought one separately (without the kit) for 9mm and one for .22. The .22 bore snake is a bit of a disappointment because it actually doesn't fit down the barrel very easily -- the pull string is almost the same diameter as the barrel itself.

But the .45 bore snake is excellent and so easy.

title: Very Cool Product, Good price at $0.66 each
text:
At the time I bought this 30 pack the price was $20 delivered for a per-target price of $0.66 each. This is a great value, as the local Wal-Mart sells a pack that is about $1 each.

Each target is a peel-and-stick "label". It adheres excellent to cardboard and clean, flat surfaces. I adheres OK to rougher surfaces like old, splintering plywood. I affixed this directly to an old shot-up apple crate and ended up having to supplement a little duct tape to keep it on when the wind kicked up.

Every target has four "pasties" that you can peel off and affix to the target after you've shot it. Each pasty is large enough to cover 2 or 3 .45 caliber holes, depending on how close your grouping is. The pasties are useful enough to extend each target by at least one more shooting group.

Here is a great suggestion to really extend the life of each target -- if you have guns of multiple calibers, start with your lowest caliber and work your way up. You can easily tell the difference between your .22 caliber hitsvs. your 9mm vs. your .45 caliber.

Using this methodology, you could probably use a single target up to 6 times, unless you are a nail driver and shoot out your bullseye really quickly!

The only downsides I can say are:

1) These targets are much more expensive than paper targets, but they're so easy to see that they're totally worth it for practicing your shooting and making adjustments after each shot.

2) The pasties can sometimes fly off when they get hit. Make sure you give them a good press and seal.

title: great pedometer good software
text:
I have had my Fitbit for 3 months and It is the best pedometer I have owned and it does so much more. I was looking for an upgraded pedometer with the ability to track my activity over time and picked this over the body bug because it does not charge a monthly fee. The website is easy to use and allows for tracking of activities, sleep, food, weight, ect..

It easily clips to my clothing and is very secure. I have had no issues with it falling off. The step count is accurate and I have compared it to other pedometers included on my phone and a stand alone basic pedometer. I love that it can track changes in elevation to include data about climbing stair or hills. It is sometimes less accurate when it comes to stairs. I will take the same exact walk and it will vary between 10 and 12 flights. The sleep tracking is not very accurate because I will often lay awake at night not moving trying to fall asleep and this time is usually logged as sleep. I am fairly aware of my sleep patterns and it did not reveal any information that I didn't already know.

99% of the time it syncs every 15 minutes when I am home but I have had issues with syncing which required me to reset the unit to fix the problem. Also it can be a little touchy during setup but I was able to set it up in a matter of munutes and install all software and get a fitbit account.

The battery lasts for at least a week every time. This exceeds the manufacturers claim and I have been very happy. Also it charges quickly so you don't have to be without you fitbit for very long.

Overall I am very happy with my Fitbit and would recomend it to others.

title: I loved Pelican's protective cases.  So I decided to try their bottles.
text:
I guess I expected more from a company that makes such great cases.

Pros:
Finish is great. Grime and dark scuff marks came off very easily with a non-scratch sponge and normal dish soap.
Temperature retention is awesome. Holds ice for 10-12 hours in 95 degree Texas heat. Retains cold for a minimum of 24 hours. (per my non-scientific testing anyway).
Durability is great. The cap gasket is nice and thick and there's no o-ring to pinch and wear out. I have dropped it several times without denting the bottle or cracking the base or cap.
I didn't have an issue with tipping that other reviewers had. I have the 32oz.

Cons:
Cap is super easy to crossthread. It's very easy to screw on the cap crooked and not even notice it.
Mine has a vague, persistent metallic taste. I have cleaned it thoroughly 12+ times with a bottle brush, sponge and normal dish soap. I have filled the bottle with plain tap water, filtered tap water, multiple brands of bottled water. Never goes away. So, I'm positive it's the bottle. It's not a deal-breaker for me though, just super annoying. I hope I'm an outlier.

Another words, if you leave this cooler in your car while driving, and if it tips over or shakes in your car, this cooler will leak and spill. It is missing the countdown feature that I actually need for timing 1 minute sparring match, a 2 minute wrestling match, a 1 and a half minute boxing match for example.  Instead, it has a clock with the time of day and an alarm feature, like it's a portable alarm clock.  Why would I need a wakeup or reminder alarm clock in a stopwatch?  Also, I don't know how to power it of nor do I know how to change the battery which according to the manual, it says it's a CR2032 3V.  The manual is a little confusing too. title: Great 2-3 season family tent!
text:
As an adult who has just recently returned to the world of camping (I am a leader in my son's cub scout pack), I looked at LOTS of tent options before choosing the Coleman Montana 8 person tent. I checked out reviews on Amazon and CampMor, and talked to as many camping enthusiast friends as I could. My first year in scouting, I borrowed a Eureka 2-person tent from our local boy scout troop, which came up to (maybe) my waist, and just barely fit my full-sized air mattress. After struggling to change clothing while lying down (I could barely kneel, let alone stand), and suffering through a fairly sleepless/stuffy night in the Eureka tent, I decided that the following features were necessary for comfortable camping:

1. The ability to stand up fully. This meant that any tent I chose had to have a center height of at least 72", preferably more (my husband is 6 feet tall, and if I ever want him to join us camping, the tent needs to work for him too. The Montana 8 has a center height of 84" (7 feet).

2. Room for gear and at least two full/queen sized air mattresses. Although the Montana 8 states that there's room for 8 people, the diagram shows these 8 people sleeping in mummy bags very close together. From a comfort perspective, this tent will hold 4-5 people (and their gear) at a maximum, without feeling overly crowded. For the three of us, this fits the bill nicely.

3. Intuitive and easy to set up and take down. While I like camping, I am not an avid camper. Finding a tent that can be set up (and taken down) with only help from a 9 year old was key, and this fits the bill nicely.

4. Good cross-ventilation. After sleeping in a stuffy tent once, I didn't want to repeat the experience. Three windows (the two side windows and the door window) can be rolled down to allow for good air flow and ventilation. We rolled the windows down 1/3 of the way, which provided a very comfortable cross-breeze while sleeping.

5. Waterproof with a bathtub floor. Many of the reviewers stated that they had no problems with leaks along the seams without using any waterproofing sealant. After talking with others and reading some recommendations, I used the Kiwi Camp Dry Heavy Duty Water Repellent to spray the seams prior to our first use, as added protection. We had some light rain during the evening, and much heavier rain the next morning, and the inside of the tent stayed bone dry.

6. Quality. I wanted a tent that would stand up to occasional car camping trips, without having to be replaced on a regular basis. Coleman is a recognized brand, and after talking with folks who own Coleman tents and reading the reviews, I was convinced that this tent would be a good one for our family. So far, I'm pleased!

6. Price. Given that we don't do a lot of camping, I didn't want to spend hundreds on a tent. I purchased the Montana 8 in Blue (not the Elite) from Amazon in mid-May 2015, and paid $136.48; a surprisingly low price for this particular tent model/size.

Some nice features that this tent offers (that weren't on my list of must-haves):

1. A port for electrical/extension cords. While this tent does not have electricity, it does include a port near the door that allows campers to run an extension cord into the tent (for use with lanterns, fans, etc.)

2. A covered entry area. I looked at tents that had screened in areas, but opted for this one instead, choosing to have the extra room inside the tent rather than in a screened area. I had two camp chairs outside - in the evening, when it started to rain, I placed the camp chairs under the front rain fly "awning", on either side of the door. Despite the rain, the chairs stayed mostly dry, with only a few drops of water on them.

3. A "D door". This door has a pole that threads around the D curve, and another one at the hinge axis, which means that the door can function as a real door in terms of opening/closing, rather than a door that must be zipped open and closed. While there are Velcro closures around the D curve, we found that to keep insects from getting in we still had to zip it shut. However, we liked the easy entry!

All in all, my family and I are very pleased with our new tent, and look forward to many years of use!

title: Good all-around BPA-free water bottle with no leaks!
text:
First off, let me start by saying that I am a loyal Contigo customer. I absolutely LOVE my Contigo Autoseal West Loop Stainless Steel Travel Mug with Easy-Clean Lid, and sing its praises frequently. I purchased the Grace water bottle to throw in my day pack when working at my son's cub scout camp. Here are the reasons I chose it:

1. It's Contigo. I like their beverage containers, and they have wonderful customer service - they stand behind their products.
2. It was $10.40.
3. It's BPA-free plastic, and doesn't feel flimsy. I love my stainless steel mug, but since I'm going to be using this primarily in the woods, I didn't want to risk dropping my steel mug on the ground and breaking it.
2. It's easy to fill with both water and ice. We have water stations set up around camp, and I generally fill the bottle at home in the morning with ice, and refill throughout the day with water.
4. It's a streamlined design, and doesn't take up much room in my pack.
5. It doesn't leak when filled properly (note - you have to be attentive to where you fill the bottle - you don't want to fill it above the shoulder, or the bottle will likely leak).
6. It's easy to use & drink from.
7. It's generally easy to clean and has no funky odors.
8. It fits into my car's cup holders.

Here are things that would make it better:
1. Adding a carabineer to the loop, or having built-in carabineer as part of the loop for clipping onto a day pack or bag, similar to some of Contigo's other Autoseal bottles. I've done this for my bottle, but I had to purchase this separately.
2. Double-wall insulation. The thing I love about my stainless Contigo mug is that it keeps my coffee hot and my iced drinks cold (and my ice cubes from melting) for hours - with no transference of the heat/cold to the outer wall of the mug. The Grace bottle does not keep water cold, and it will "sweat" when it's filled with iced drinks.
3. Having an "easy clean" lid. My stainless travel mug (are you sensing a theme, here?) has a fantastic easy clean lid, with parts that swing out on hinges to get into all the crevices, ensuring a better cleaning.

But this bottle was $10.40, not $25. And for that price and my purposes, it works, and I'm happy with it!

Note - I purchased a Contigo Cortland water bottle with easy-clean lid for my son a few months ago, and it has begun to leak. I called Contigo, and they told me that this is a known issue with the Cortland design - not the design I am reviewing here. After I fill out their form and submit two pictures of the bottle (one of the lid, one of the entire bottle), they will replace it for me, even though I don't have the receipt anymore (it was not purchased through Amazon). Again - Contigo has great customer service!

text:
The Saris Super Bones 3 is a really fantastic high end bike rack. I've been using racks by Allen for several years, and while they have their issues, I thought they were a good value. This Saris model costs 8x what my Allen rack did. The difference in price and quality is quite staggering. I can't tell you if it's worth $400, but you do get what you pay for.

The most striking difference is the stability of the Saris rack. It doesn't have lots of loose straps to fly around, and the design makes it stay solid at highway speeds. It's very easy to adjust to each trunk. I can load it up with 3 bikes and it feels secure, even at 80mph. I could not say the same for my Allen rack. The Saris is also well padded to prevent scratches to the car. It also keeps the bike pedals far away enough so they don't damage the car. With the Allen rack, my pedals totally scratched up the Civic's bumper.

The disadvantages of the Saris rack are:
- The much higher cost
- Does not fold flat for storage
- Fits less cars, such as hatchbacks

This is clearly for the serious biker, so would use it very frequently to justify the price. You know who you are.

This is a very good quality air pressure gauge with some nice extras. It feels solid and heavier than you'd think. It's coated in a nice feeling material that gives a good grip but isn't sticky.

The air pressure gauge matched my other digital gauge, so it seems accurate. It has a backlight which is absolutely necesary. There is also a flashlight and a red light, both powerful enough for reading maps, etc. The seatbelt cutter and hammer seem like they'll do the job, but I hope I'll never have to use those.

This gauge uses AAA batteries (included), which is a huge plus over the units that use watch batteries. I can use my rechargeables!

title: Lots of potential, but falls a bit short
text:
The Pulsense seems like a pretty cool heart rate monitor in theory, but unfortunately falls a bit short in actual use. It’s easy to put on the wrist, and the M/L size fit me fine. It’s not too obtrusive, and while not sexy, it’s not horrendous looking either.

Setting up the device and syncing it with my iPhone was pretty easy. And it was comfortable enough to wear all day at first. But the lights and vibrations that notify you on your heart rate (what target zone you’re in) got annoying real fast – thankfully they can be deactivated. And I found myself reflexively looking at the unit whenever I wanted to know the time – but there’s no clock on it, doh! I really wish there was a digital readout that could toggle between clock and heart rate.

When it works, I like the Pulsense a lot. But I found a lot of lapses in data collection, specifically with the heart rate. At times, it shows that I was at a resting heart rate, when I know that I was actually very active. Not really sure why this happens, and I haven’t been able to pin point it to any specific activity, location, etc.

While there is a lot of potential with the Pulsense (especially not having to wear a chest strap), I’m not so sure that it’s ready for prime time. I’m excited to see how the next version will be improved.

title: Easy!
text:
A cap that monitors your heart rate and temperature? What a great idea! Much better than the chest straps I've used in the past that always manage to tug on my chest hairs.

The Spree SmartCap works very well in my experience. While the monitor can be worn without the cap, it's easier to just have it installed in the cap that you can just put on and go. It paired effortlessly with my Nexus 4 phone using Bluetooth (despite the package says it only works with iPhones, they do provide an Android app now). The heart rate and temperature data seem to be fairly accurate.

With the GPS on, it is also compatible with some of the fitness apps I have for tracking my runs and bike rides. You'll get distance, speed, etc. that you can correlate to the heartrate and temperature. Unfortunately, the device is less suitable for the bike riding since the cap and even the band alone tends to get in the way of a helmet, though I did manage to get the band alone to sort of work with some tweaking.

I highly recommend The Spree for a very easy to use body monitor.

title: Great watch, but some unexpected shortcomings
text:
The Timex Run Trainer 2.0 is great low profile watch with accurate heart rate monitoring and GPS tracking. It does have several unexpected shortcomings, especially when considering the price and its label as "Ironman".

Nice size. This is one of the smaller heart rate w/ GPS watched I've seen. It fits well, even on my smallish wrists.

Fast connection to GPS - usually took less than 15 seconds, which is pretty good I think.

The memory on this watch is too small, especially considering the price. It seems to hold only about 10 hours of data before it becomes full. Timex should really include a much larger memory chip - aren't they pretty cheap these days?

Biking: Even though there isn't a biking mode, you can switch from pace to speed, which basically makes it a cyclocomputer, in conjunction with the GPS data. You can use the data with online software, including recent support by Strava Cycling.

Swimming: This watch (eventhough it is an Ironman), doesn't technically support swimming. It is waterproof to 50m, which should be good enough for most swimmer. Unfortunately the GPS does not work underwater, even just a foot a water - so you completely lose GPS tracking while swimming. Major bummer. There is a work around I've read about: Place the watch under your swimming cap, so that it usually remains above the water. That seems to help with the GPS, but since the buttons on this watch are very sensitive, you do need to play around with the orientation of the watch so one does not get pressed unintentionally.

title: A decent workout watch with some ridiculous shortcomings
text:
A good heart rate monitor and watch for people into fitness but are not super serious athletes. You can also wear this watch as a nice, functional regular watch too.

The operation of this watch is similar to the basic Timex ironman watches with some additional features (it's necessary to read the manual to understand all the features).

Pros: Watch is very comfortable - it's big but it stays in place. The strap is very adjustable and should fit nearly every wrist. The heart rate strap is also comfortable. The large face is a bonus because it's that much easier to glance down and see the numbers when you're running.
Lots of features - Chrono counts time and records your total workout length or laps, and gives an average HR for each lap. The interval timer counts down and can do timed intervals (eg. run for 8 min, walk 30 seconds). The review feature will give you average HR, max/min HR for the workout, how many minutes you spent in your "target" HR and calories burnt, which is nice to see if you want to judge how intense your workout was. It also gives the average HR for each of your laps.

It has an alarm clock and a really good Indiglo setting for the dark.

Very easy to use the HR monitor, basically put it on and press the HR button on the watch and it automatically starts getting HR data.

Cons: The review feature doesn't give the time spent in each HR zone over the whole workout, only your target HR zone. This seems like a big oversight because it's as important to see how much time you spend in the high HR "red" zones as well as the lower zones. This means that if you're running up and down varied terrain, you have to look down at your wrist to see what your HR is and remember what zone that is for you and guess how much time you've spent in each zone.

If you're only using one of the interval timers, you have to set the second interval timer to 0, which is very annoying. It would be easy to have a feature asking if you want to use one or two timers.

It doesn't store more than 1 workout review in the watch, so you have to write the info down if you want a record of your workouts. This is ridiculous for a watch at this price point.

It's not ANT+ compatible, so there's no way to increase the functionality like tying it to a GPS device. I suppose they want you to buy the next level up if you want to record that type of fitness data.

title: Almost perfect
text:
Lezyne is a new player in the bike lights market, but they've got a pretty good reputation behind them with their other products. The Super Drive is a great commuting light with many advantages, and I highly recommend it. I spent too many hours reading up on commuting lights and finally picked the Super Drive over the Cygolite Expilion (350/400 models) and NiteRider MiNewt 600. I have no regrets about my decision.

The pros which led me to select this light over the others:

- User replaceable standard battery. The Super Drive uses a PROTECTED 18650 lithium ion battery of about 2400mAh. You can buy an extra one for backup from Lezyne and switch it in a matter of seconds. I'm assuming that any PROTECTED 18650 battery should work, but don't hold me accountable if it doesn't. The battery charges via a Mini USB connection on the light, but so do the competitor's lights - however, you can also charge the 18650 batteries separately with an appropriate charger if desired.

- Small and sleek design. It's 12.25cm long and 2.5cm in diameter. It's an all aluminum body, so definitely built to last, and works as a good heat sink to keep the internals cool. The body does get hot though, and you shouldn't use it as a handheld light or keep it on for too long while remaining still. It needs the air flow from biking to cool itself.

- The Super Drive light weighs 126 grams (without mounting hardware), which is much less than ~160g for the NiteRider and about the same as the CygoLite (~130g).

- Most lights grossly overstate the actual lumens. The Super Drive's CRE led tested as 421 lumens (vs. 450 claimed; tested in a MTBR 2012 lights shootout). The Niterider 600 tested at only 485 (vs. the 600 claimed) - yes, it's brighter, not many reviewers say that the high setting is usually too bright and unnecessary. On high, it's a lot of light for both models in most situations. I mainly use the Super Drive on medium setting (300 lumens claimed) when riding on dark, isolated roads. The low mode (150 lumens claimed) is best for riding in well-lit urban areas.

- The beam pattern is pleasing. There is a good spread of light and the central portion isn't harsh. You can compare how the light output actually looks on the road[dot]cc website.

- Easy tool-free mounting. The mounting bracket installs in seconds - it comes with 2 sizez for mounting on different diameter bars. It feels secure. The mount allows for the light to be adjusted left-right at will.

There aren't many cons against the Super Drive:

- There's no helmet mount included or available. They're supposedly working on it, but it seems like you can use some other mounting systems right now.

- Not much side illumination. So make sure you've got reflectors, side lights, whatever so that you will be seen from the side.

title: Awesome for rough city streets
text:
These lesser known tires are amazing. Like 1500 miles of riding in the streets of NYC without a single flat amazing. While being used as the rear tire, and ridden on wet roads. The tire does have lots of cuts from glass, and I've removed quite a few that have been embedded in the rubber. But none of them has made it past the inner layer to actually puncture the tube.

There are probably tougher tires out there, like the Marathons, but with the Serfas, I don't notice a tradeoff in weight, rolling resistance, etc. These are speedy tires with good flat protection and decent traction on wet roads - the best road bike tires I've used for fast city commuting. They're also easy enough to put on and remove, unlike some others, like the Gatorskins.

Like other Serfas I've had, these run a little narrower than stated. The 700 x 25 is more like a 700 x 23.

title: Perfect for Indian cooking. And for cooking one egg.
text:
I own lots of Lodge items, but won't bore you with the merits of using cast iron - especially since I don't think a pot of this size really demonstrates all the strengths of cast iron cookware.

I purchased this little guy for 1 main reason and I have not been disappointed. I cook a lot of Indian dishes - things like dal and meat/veg curries. A common technique in Indian cooking is to heat some fat in a little pot and quickly add spices, chilies, ginger, garlic, etc. for a minute or so. Then you dump the mix into another pot which has cooked the main ingredient - things like lentils, beans, etc. The technique is called "tarka" and is an easy way to add a lot of flavor to a dish. This little pot is the perfect size for this - not too big, not too small.

I have since discovered another use for the pot. It is perfect for cooking one egg! You need very little water to poach and the small size keeps the egg compact. It's great for frying too since the egg doesn't stick to the properly seasoned cast iron.

The only problem I have with the pot is that the bottom diameter is a bit too small. I have a hard time keeping it stable on my gas burners. I fix that problem by placing a small cast iron trivet between the pot and the burner.

title: Very bright light for being seen
text:
This is a great light for riding in cities. It's very bright for being seen by drivers and pedestrians and even for maneuvering though some rough patches of asphalt on dimly lit streets. While there are four modes, the only ones to use are all lit or all blinking (I don't see the point of having just the two outer or inner LEDs on). The battery life is also fairly long, but definitely not 100 hours as claimed, even on blinking mode.

I've used this light while riding through moderate rainfall and it has worked perfectly. The handlebar mount is very stable and it's easy to release the light when locking up (yet it has never fallen off due to bumps). The small size is another benefit when carrying it in your jacket pocket.

I've used the light as a headlamp while camping and don't like it much for that. The headband is very uncomfortable since there's no cushion on the mounting bracket. I'm left with a sore indentation on my forehead. The light also does not tilt like a good headlamp should.

title: Not very bright
text:

While it does reflect a little bit of light, the other parts of the bike actually shine brighter, especially the chrome. Compared to the reflective properties of the gray trim on my saddle bags, this tape doesn't even come close. I'm still not going to get the day-glow tape, but hopefully my bright blinkies have me covered.

At least they stick well and have not peeled off, even riding in cold and wet weather.

title: Junk!
text:
I did quite a bit of research before purchasing this bag for a 6 week trip through Asia. The first day I really used this bag was during a 12-hour layover in London, where I walked around the city much of the day.

I carried a Canon 40D with two relatively lightweight lenses, spare batteries, filters, and a small notebook. At the end of the day, while waiting at Heathrow for the next flight, I was shocked to notice that the bag was already beginning to fall apart! The outer fabric covering the shoulder straps had already begun to tear. So had the fabric above the zipper on the top pocket. The tear was large enough for someone to stick a hand into the pocket. I inspected the bag closely to see if something had caused these tears, but I concluded that the bag was just a piece of junk. It had begun to unravel itself under the weight of a bag that was not even half-filled!

Not having any emergency repair items on hand, the unraveling continued to get worse over the next day. Finally, I had the bag stitched up in Kerala, India, thinking that would be it. Nope! Bye the next day, the bag had unraveled in other spots as well. I had it stitched up again in Mysore, and then again in Bangalore. Thankfully, these minor fixes cost very little in India. By the time I was almost done with Bangkok, I had bought a small roll of duct tape to keep my items from falling out of the bag. I had also had countless thoughts about the negative review I would write on Amazon when I'd returned home.

I considered writing about the design and functionality of the bag, but there's really no point in doing so.

This bag is a worthless piece of junk. It's amazing that they get away with charging almost $80 for this. Naneu Pro should be ashamed for manufacturing such an inferior product, while marketing itself to be an innovative company that produces high quality goods. I'm truly shocked that Amazon and B&H Photo carry this bag. A $10 bag from the local discount store would have been more durable. What a total ripoff!

title: Nice if you don't have front fender mounts
text:
I've got a bicycle without any mounting holes for fenders. It also doesn't have enough clearance between the forks/brakes and tires to jerry-rig a fender. However, I hate not riding my bike because of light rain or a few puddles.

The Grunge Board was the best option that I could find at a reasonable price. It straps onto the downtube with a couple of rubber straps. I've got an 80s racing bike with tight geometry, and the dimensions of the board are small enough to clear the crankarms and the front wheel during turns. But just so (orientation makes a difference).

I've ridden through some big puddles and it seems to do a fairly good job of keeping my pant legs from getting soaked. I still put some scotch tape over the holes/slits around the bottom bracket to keep the gunk from getting in. The board is light enough that I leave it on all the time, even when it's not raining...just in case there is an unexpected puddle.

I have to take off a star because I think the mounting band should have been designed better. First, it hard to push the rubber bands through the narrow slots once they wrap around the downtube. The bands have slits in them that attach to nubs on the underside of the board. The nubs are not large enough to hold the bands in place perfectly securely. They seem to usually work, but the bands come off occasionally. If you have a small diameter downtube (as in most pre-90s, bikes), there are also a couple inches of extra rubber band that just flop around. It shouldn't be too hard for Planet Bike to redesign this retention mechanism, but it's also hard to complain for ~$10.

You can use a couple of cable ties instead of the rubber bands and they'd probably do a better job. You could also use a large soda bottle cut to size and get the same effect, though arguably a bit uglier.

title: Electronics ruined.
text:
Because of the near perfect customer reviews for this bag I gave it a shot. After getting our stuff stolen off the beach in Waikiki a few years ago I never leave anything on the beach anymore. I purchased this bag for an 8 day trip to Maui. For the most part I used it just as a backpack and left it on the beach while someone always stayed back to watch our gear. Kind of sucked that our full group of 5 could not enjoy the water together so on the final 2 days of our trip I took it into the ocean with us. The bag was never completely underwater. I would just let the bag float within an arm's reach near me.

After getting back to the beach and taking my gear out I saw water all over the inside of the bag. Yes, I was careful and folded the top at least 5 times before closing the clasp. I now have two ruined iPhone 6 pluses and a Panasonic point and shoot camera. I'm wondering if I just got a lemon.

This morning I tried the sink test. Dropped some hats into the bag, filled up the kitchen sink, tossed the bag around a bit, and gave the bag a good squeeze. I could see air bubbles immediately. If air bubbles are coming out that means water is getting in. This bag is certainly getting returned. Now I'm wondering who should be responsible for my damaged electronics.

It's also very important to place on as level a surface as possible. Due to our campsite configuration we couldn't get a perfect spot so I found myself fighting a little bit to not slip. You can easily get two normal length showers out of one bag. The bags are VERY heavy when completely filled. If you aren't that tall you may need some help hanging the bag.

Pros: Light, easy to set up, price
Cons: Once the shower bag is mounted, the end of the nozzle was already down to my chest. Get used to squatting, holding one hand on the nozzle and the other hand lathering or rinsing yourself. This can get very hard if you have long hair you are trying to shampoo.

Suggestions:
1. Make a more horizontal shower bag so that it doesn't hang so low.
2. A towel rack inside would be nice. In all honestly, there isn't enough water flow to get anything else wet. I used the mesh toiletry bags for my dry clothes.
