title: Compact, functional towel for mobile adventures
text:
This a handy towel for mobile adventures. It isn't as fluffy and snuggly as a thick cotton bath towel, but it's really absorbent, dries quicker, and rolls up into a much smaller bundle, making it a great alternative for taking along when space is limited.

The towel's compact portability is one of it's strongest features. It comes neatly folded and rolled up in a nylon and mesh drawstring bag. It's a bit of a thrash getting it back into the stuff sack folded up if you don't roll it nice and tight. I find it far easier to just stuff it in like you would a sleeping bag, starting with one corner of the towel and packing it in tight starting at the bottom. The packed bag measures about 8 inches long and 5 inches in diameter, so it takes up lots less room in your duffel bag or backpack than a regular towel. I've attached a photo of the packed towel in my hand to give you an idea of its size.

The towel is just over 5 feet long and not quite 3 feet wide. If you use it to lay on at the beach, your feet will end up in the sand, and not on the towel, unless you're under 5 feet tall.

The microfiber fabric is quite absorbent, easily drying me completely after a shower.

It also dries faster than my normal cotton bath towel. There's an elastic loop crudely sewn onto one corner of the towel to hang it by (see attached photo). I don't usually use the loop because you need a pretty high hook to keep the towel off the ground when you hang it by the loop. Instead, I just hang it by the middle across a peg or hook to dry.

The biggest drawback I've noticed is the feel of the towel aganst my skin. Instead of the soft, snuggly fluff of a regular bath or beach towel, this towel feels more like a sheet of suede or chamois leather. For that reason, it won't replace my bath towel at home, but I do think that it's a reasonable compromise for an efficient travel accessory. It seems particularly useful for carrying to the beach or pool, and for camping or adventure travel (staying in hostels, for example) where you'll need to provide your own towel.
If that's the kind of stuff you do, this towel should work well for you.

Let me know if you found anything in my review helpful.

title: Good paddles for mobile adventures
text:
Good paddle for my inflatable kayak. This thing is lightweight, sturdy, and equipped with drip guards to reduce (but not eliminate) water running down the shaft getting you wet.

I bought two of these, one shorter than the other, because I'm taller than my wife. Now I wish that I'd just bought 2 long ones. The sides of the inflatable seem to interfere with the shorter paddle some, so the reach of the longer paddle is helpful, and the greater leverage is always welcome.

Being able to break down the paddle into 2 pieces is important to me, as I do need to stow the kayak and paddles in small spaces. I also expect to ship them (or check them as luggage) to various adventure destinations.

Let me know if you find any of these observations helpful.

title: Fun and useful inflatable canoe
text:
Sevylor calls this a kayak, but kayaks traditionally have covered decks, fore and aft, with a cockpit that you sit in. That was before "sit-upon" kayaks became a thing. This Big Basin is an open boat that you sit or kneel in, which in my mind makes it a canoe, although without the upswept bow and stern of most canoes. Regardless of what you call it, I have found this to be a good size for paddling on reasonably calm water, with two people and a little bit of gear.

I purchased mine primarily for shuttling between my anchored motorboat and shore, for camping, picnicking, beachcombing, or whatever. It works well for that purpose. The inflated boat is light enough for one person to hoist onto the top of my bigger boat's cabin, and to get it down and launched without a winch, a helper, or other drama. I can easily paddle it myself, or we can fit 1 or 2 more people in, as necessary. There isn't a lot of extra room, though. two people and a couple of day packs (and maybe fishing poles) pretty much fills the boat. I don't think that I'd want to try a multi-day camping trip for 2 in it, unless it was clear from the start that this would have to be an ultra-light adventure.

The sides of this boat are fairly low to the water, so it isn't a particularly dry ride. My kayak paddles have drip guards, which helps some, but I usually plan to get wet when paddling this boat. Choppy seas can easily splash in. None of this should come as a surprise to experienced paddlers. I usually wear rain pants or waders when using the boat.

A big advantage is that this boat can be deflated and stowed, or shipped as luggage to a distant destination. I used a similar Sevylor a few years ago on a moose hunt, and found it really useful for paddling back and forth across a lake by camp, and for floating out a quartered moose in one trip (two people walking the boat through the shallows, with a line on each end). I haven't had a chance to use this boat that way yet, but I'm certain that it would work just as well.

I do recommend that you buy a good quality foot pump, and take it with you on whatever paddling adventure takes you away from civilization. The nylon cover fabric is tough, so punctures are likely to be rare, but you can always develop a leak from a loose valve.

Let me know if you find my review helpful.

title: Good bottle for hot or cold drinks
text:
[[VIDEOID:a948ab74a1bd5a1a9be7bc0535d12137]] This insulated stainless vacuum bottle does a good job keeping either hot or cold drinks at their desired temperature for several hours. The mouth is large enough to accept full-size ice cubes (see video), but also small enough to drink directly from it if you don't have a cup to pour your drink into. (You probably don't want to do that if you have really hot coffee in your bottle!)

I already own both Thermos and HydroFlask brand vacuum bottles, and the insulation ability of this Triple Tree version seems comparable (although I have not done a controlled test using identical temperature water in all three and monitoring temperatures over the course of a day or two). This is not a cheap imitation, though. I expect it would compare favorably in a real test. I can say that at the end of an 8-hour shift I still had a little bit of ice left in my water bottle, whenever I didn't drink all the water.

Part of what you pay for is packaging (see photo). Inside the Amazon shipping box was a corrugated cardboard box holding the bottle, which was in a foam sleeve to protect it from scratches. There was a little tag attached, and an advertising/instruction pamphlet. A fair (excessive?) amount of packaging. Maybe not a deal killer, but I put this in the minus column. There was also a spare silicone seal washer for the stopper top. That goes in the plus column, especially if I can find the washer when I need it in the (distant???) future.

The screw-top stopper has a small carabiner clipped onto the swiveling bail handle. The carabiner rattles against the metal bottle and makes some noise (maybe remove the carabiner for ninja work or bowhunting?). I think the carabiner may be useful for attaching the bottle to your pack, especially if you have one of those weak water bottle pockets on the side of your day pack. I find that water bottles don't stay in those pockets very well. This should help.

Overall, a decent insulated bottle that holds almost a quart. I'll keep using mine. Let me know if my review was helpful.

title: Easy to replace the old broken light
text: Perfect fit to replace the taillight on my boat trailer. Well worth searching out this model because switching it out was far easier than I had feared. Loosen a few screws, unplug the old wires, plug in the new ones, and screw it back together. Now to make sure that the boarding ladder doesn't hit the taillight again (unfortunate design conflict between my boat and trailer!)

title: Low profile to stay out of the way
text:
Great mount for Scotty rod holders. The flush mounts stay out of the way and work well. Be sure to mount them close enough to the edge of the gunwale to allow you to swivel your rod (have your rod holder and rod handy when deciding where to install the mount).

The backing plate that's sold separately is optional, but I do recommend it to give your rod mount a solid base. I wish it all came together. We shouldn't have to buy them separately.

Let me know if my comments are helpful.

title: Good quality budget braid
text:
Good line for trolling or jigging. This is an economy version of the spectra superlines that allow you to hold more line and go deeper with less drag and almost no stretch. This line holds knots as well as any of the superbraids, and better than some of the coated, slicker lines.

This probably isn't the best choice for a casting reel. I'd look for an 8-strand line because its a little smoother and should pay out better than this 4-strand braid. The newer coated lines probably cast better, too. For trolling or jigging, though, this stuff works great, especially if you're on a tight budget.

Be sure to check the prices on all the different colors once you've selected the weight of line you want. Sometimes there's a deal on one of the colors that makes it really affordable. You might want to check the prices of larger spools of your selected weight, too. Sometimes you'll find that they've discounted one of the colors in a bulk-size spool that makes it cheaper than the smaller spools of the same weight test. Good luck on the water!

Let me know if my comments are helpful.

title: Good line. Look for the bargains.
text: Strong line at a good price.  I bought the 250-pound braid to use for my downrigger and its worked well.  I have found that if you look long enough you'll usually find a vendor offering one of their colors at a price far below the others, for the same length and test weight. In this case, light blue, 250-pound/1,000 yards was the magic combination. I sometimes wonder if its a mistake, or maybe just an overstock they want to get rid of.  If you aren't picky about the color you can often find a bargain.  The same concept applies to parachute cord (p-cord), too. Amazon makes it pretty easy to check with lots of suppliers. Let me know if you find my comments helpful.

title: If you're looking for the best...
text:
What a great reel for big, powerful fish! If you target fish that measure in the hundreds of pounds, and you want the best tool for the job, this is your reel. In my case, it's the reel I use when we go deep for big halibut here in Alaska. This reel holds plenty of line to get to those shelves 400 feet down where the barndoors lie, with plenty of line left over to allow for long runs that those big fish make. If you hang up and break off, losing several hundred feet of line (it happens), you don't have to hang it up because the reel holds enough line to let you keep fishing.

I like the high-speed retrieve for pulling up from the deep when you need to check your bait or try something else. When you latch into a fish, though, a quick push of the button on the hub of the handle engages the more powerful lower gears, so you can really torque into the fish.

That new handle design is nice, too. It comfortably fits my hand, has a nice rubbery, no-slip texture, and helps spread the stress across the meaty part of my hand so long battles are just a little bit easier.

The open design of the "X" series frame (with no crossbars across the front of the spool) is helpful when there's a backlash to deal with (yeah, it still happens once in a while). These reels aren't cheap, but they're the best you can buy. Solid, reliable, and made in USA. No regrets here!

Let me know if you don't anything in my review helpful.

title: Great blade for big fish
text: This thing resembles a small machete, except that the blade is thin and flexible.  That long, wide blade is great for turning out beautiful fillets from big salmon and halibut. The blade is thin, coated with a slick black finish, and comes razor sharp so it slides thru a fish quickly and cleanly.  The big handle offers a good, non-slip grip with great leverage for twisting the blade to follow the fish's spine. I want to keep that sharp edge with frequent honing, but I'm a little bit afraid of messing up such a fine edge. This knife does cost more than many other fillet knives, but it is a quality tool in a size that's hard to find. No regrets.

title: Good for making up salmon and halubut rigs
text: I use mine for crimping aluminum sleeves and closing the eyes on hardened steel fish hooks (for salmon and halibut rigs). So far they do what they are supposed to do.

title: Light weight and effective.
text: Not as heavy duty as some of the more expensive foot pumps, but it works fine for my inflatable kayak.  Not sure how well it will handle saltwater. I'll update if I find that it rusts out quickly.

title: Vulnerable to cross currents
text: Nice that its iron (or steel) instead of toxic lead. The pancake shape doesnt have as much drag so it tracks under the boat a little better than a spherical cannonball, but I've found that it gets swept under the boat a lot more in cross currents.  I've lost several pancake weights to the prop when fishing where there are currents.

title: Decent lock thats easy to use.
text: Good enough to deter most thieves, unless they really want your bike. I don't have a high-end bike that would attract serious attention from thieves, but low-lifes around here will ride off on an unlocked bike if you let them. This cable lock works well to deter those cretins.

title: Great lure for halibut in 100 to 300 feet.
text: One of my favorite jigs for Alaska halibut. Just keep bouncing this on the bottom and when you feel a strike, set it hard. Usually you'll hook them on the underside of the mouth as they bite at the middle of the jig. This one requires more effort than a bait that you can just sit on the bottom, but in my experience it gets more action.

title: Easy install, works well
text: Worked well on my diamondback wildwood classic. I mounted it in the center of the frame, forward of the back tire.

title: Useful webbing from a good company
text:
Good quality strap that is lightweight, water and weather resistant, and reasonably strong. Nylon and polyester webbing are both stronger, but the 1-inch polypropylene webbing has a breaking strength of around 600 lbs, which is adequate for many light- to medium-duty uses, especially if you're using plastic buckles and hardware, which will fail at much lower loads than that.

Strapworks seems to be a good company, responsive to customer needs and offering a broad inventory of products at competitive prices. I don't work for them, but have used their products a few times.

title: Great line for boating
text: soft, floating line that works well for a bow line and dock lines. I've rigged my boat with color-coordinated lines all the way around. These are nice, substantial lines.

title: useful accessory for isobutane stoves
text: Really helps stabilize your stove. The pins are thin and I'm worried about durability, but so far it hasn't failed.

title: OK knife. Poor sheath.
text: Light and sharp. Seems like a good knife, but the rigid plastic sheath is almost completely open in the back, so the blade is exposed to things that could be sliced if the knife is stowed in a tackle box, pack, or pocket. Seems like a really poorly designed sheath.

title: solid and well made.
text: well made, but just a little bit too long to fit under the gunwale of my hewescraft. The bungie design makes it difficult to shorten the rack to fit, because I'll have to shorten the bungie cord, too. It looks doable, but I've been procrastinating.

title: simple and good
text: Nice, large bore holder that I use for my landing net. I wish that the mounting blocks on the back had a solid face, so I could use command strips (double-sided adhesive pads) to install this, instead of screws.

title: good accessory, but too small for my net
text: strong and convenient. I attached mine using removable, double-stick, outdoor-rated command strips, so I didn't have to drill holes in the boat. It wasn't quite big enough to accept the foam-covered handle of my landing net, which is what I bought it for, but it is still useful for the gaff, or the deck brush.

title: Convenient and effective
text:
This is the most convenient, effective downrigger release that I've found for salmon fishing. You do have to be careful, though, not to let it hit the downrigger pulley on the way up, or it could pop off and you'll lose it to the big green toolbox.

These are easy to clip onto the cable at any location - I like to run one about 5 or 10 feet above the cannonball, so that if the cannonball hit the bottom, the fishing line and terminal tackle is above that and is less likely to snag up.

title: Good, cheap line for big fish
text: Strong stuff. The finish is a little rough, so probably wouldn't want to use it for casting, but this is for my halibut rod, so it works fine. A good, cost-effective alternative to more expensive brands.

title: Well made, but I'm not using these
text: Nice, cast stainless. These are well made and an interesting design. I ended up storing my anchor in the bow roller, rather than installing these chocks, because it just worked out better for me that way due to the limited space in the bow well of my Hewescraft. I'm still not sure how well the cleat prongs would work to secure the shank of the anchor - ideally, the anchor chain itself would wrap around the horns of the cleat, but they're a little too small for that. Are we expected to use a separate piece of line? If so, there should be a way to secure the line to the cleat, so it isn't lost when the anchor isn't in the chocks.

title: Good quality and service
text: Excellent quality wire for a fair price, with good, quick service. As expected, with no surprises.

title: Just what it says - for Scotty downriggers.
text:
Works perfectly to secure my scotty downrigger or line puller. Lost one somehow (donated to the big green toolbox, I expect) and this replaced it as expected.

Now, if Scotty would just design their downriggers and line puller to position the handle of this bolt on the side of the downrigger opposite the power cord, instead of making us struggle with the tight space under the motor and power cord...

title: good quality, maybe just a bit smaller than I should have bought.
text: I installed this bow roller on my 21-foot Hewescraft, and use it to deploy, retrieve, and secure/store my 22-lb Danforth-style anchor. It works well, but I do wish it was just a little bit longer, to extend forward over the bow just a bit further. I like the spring-loaded retaining pin - its got a smaller pin on one end that keeps it secure in the frame so you don't lose it overboard when putting the anchor into the roller, or taking the anchor out of the roller. The stainless steel is still bright after the first season of saltwater use, so I'm happy with it so far.

title: Good for wet conditions.
text: Great price for a very useful pack. I work and play in the North Pacific rainforest, where you can count on getting wet outdoors. This pack is tough, and well designed for carrying a day's worth of gear, lunch, extra layers, books, or whatever. The suspension system is good, and the material is strong. I wish it came in more colors, but it's a useful pack that I can recommend.

title: Fun new way to camp.
text:
Lots to love about the DoubleNest. This is how all the cool kids camp now.

Hammocks are fun to play in and relax in. It takes more of a leap of faith to camp overnight in one, but they work great in many situations. If bugs are likely to be bad, consider buying a bug net. A tarp stretched over your hammock will protect you from the rain. I've used these accessories and recommend them.

title: well built tool
text: We bought this for removing hooks from sharks, but so far it's only been of hypothetical use, since we haven't managed to hook a shark yet. It's well made, but I don't know how easy it is to use yet. I'll update when we've had an opportunity to use it.

title: Check the prices for each color - you may find a bargain.
text: Good quality paracord at a reasonable price. There are lots of businesses trying to sell you paracord on Amazon. There's a wide range of prices and some of it is better quality than some of the imitation stuff. This is the good stuff.  If you aren't picky about the color, try checking the price on every color - I found blue at a greatly reduced price from this vendor. I'm pretty sure that it was a temporary price to reduce their stock of that color. I expect that other colors may be cheaper at other times. It was definitely worth the time I spent doing it, to see how much difference there was in prices for different colors from the same supplier. Let me know if you found this tip useful.

title: Useful stuff
text:
This shock cord works perfectly to suspend the bug net that's sewn into my camping hammock. I just run the elastic cord through the loops on the bug net, and around the trees at each end of the hammock. This stuff works well to suspend a tarp, too, because the shock cord gives when the wind hits the tarp, reducing stress on the tarp.

Let me know if you found this review helpful.

title: Good whistle with several uses
text:
Nice and loud, durable, and it won't rust. This is a decent-quality whistle that I use with my hunting partners so we can keep in contact without scaring away game. They have helped us find each other in the woods, and we sometimes use them just to help us keep track of where each other is, while still hunting. I've also used them to get a bear's attention several times, when I wanted them to see me along salmon streams in Alaska. That usually is enough to encourage the bears to move off and let me pass.

I also keep one on my boat, as a signaling device. Electric horns on boats are notorious for corroding and failing, and the Coast Guard considers these whistles as adequate, which has helped me pass boarding inspections a couple of times. For me, its just cheap insurance that I'll be able to get someone's attention if I need to, or to avoid a ticket in case the Coast Guard wants to do an inspection. I like plastic better than metal for a whistle because its usually more comfortable to use if its cold out.

Let me know if my review was helpful.

title: Simple, convenient, and effective
text:
This windscreen is tall enough to block the wind around a compact camping stove on top of a fuel canister, even the taller propane canisters, which is exactly what I was looking for. Many of the others are short, and don't have as many panels, so they don't work as well as this one. The price was good, the unit folds compactly and stores in a nice little drawstring bag, and is easy to use. Most importantly, it helps you conserve stove fuel by allowing more of the heat from your stove to transmit to the cooking pot, rather than being blown away by the wind. (Even a light breeze will significantly reduce stove performance.) A folded up piece of heavy duty foil is a little lighter to carry, and will work for the purpose (I've done that for years), but this is more stable and much easier to set up. I used it during my last camping trip in western Alaska, and anticipate using it on future adventures. It is fairly heavy, though, so I'll think hard about carrying it on an ultralight backpacking trip. Maybe I'll resort to the foil for those occasions.

Let me know if you find this review helpful.

title: Good idea, but not for me
text: We used this double sleeping bag liner in our sierra designs bags that we always zip together to make a double bag. The liner was plenty big enough, and perhaps too big for our double bag. I found it annoying to climb into as it was often bunched up, and it got twisted and tangled through the night. My wife liked the concept of crawling into the liner bag, but I often struggled to find the opening and get inside. After a few nights, we wadded it up and put it into one of our sleeping bag stuff sacks, to use as a pillow. Probably won't be using it in the future.

title: Well made, but baggy on slender to athletic builds
text:
These are well-constructed waders that have survived a 9-day moose hunt in western Alaska, and several short fishing trips so far. The fit is good, but a bit baggy (I'm a lean guy). The baggy cut helps them not restrict movement, I suppose, but they'd be quieter if they fit tighter.

Overall, these are good waders that come with a belt and gravel guards. They are a significant upgrade from hip boots because they allow you to go a bit deeper and more importantly, sit down without getting a wet butt (which is important where I live, work, and play because it rains a lot here in Southeast Alaska). They are more comfortable than chest waders if it isn't cold out, so I expect that I'll be using these a lot in the future.

Do me a favor and let me know if my review was helpful.

title: Good quality, holding power limited by the design
text:
These stakes are well-constructed and can be pounded into reasonably hard soil without damage. I haven't destroyed any yet, but I do try to be careful when I'm pounding them into rocky ground. (A small, 8-ounce hammer works well. Larger hammers increase the likelihood of bending or breaking your stakes). The round cross section doesn't have the holding power of some of the flatter stake designs, so they don't hold as well in wind, in my experience. They're longer than most other after-market tent stakes, though (9 inches vs the more common 7-inches), which helps compensate. I like to have a few of these in my stake bag for places that the y-shaped stakes can't penetrate.

Some users have complained that they can't get their tent guylines through the holes in the silver heads. That isn't how they are intended to be used. Wrap your guyline or your anchor loop around the shaft of the stake, just below the silver head, and angle your stake to point it toward a point several feet below the center of your tent. These are fine stakes. Would like to try some of this style in a longer, 12-inch version, for larger tents that catch more wind and require stronger anchors.

title: Nice upgrade, but treat them with due care
text: These 9-inch stakes are a welcome upgrade from the ubiquitous 7-inch versions, and offered at a reasonable price (at least when I bought them). These longer stakes work well in soft to moderately firm soil, but you still have to take care not to pound them too hard into rocks or solid tree roots or they'll bend. I like to use them with smaller tents on the windward side of the tent, to give a little better holding power than the shorter stakes offer, and on the sheltered side of larger tents, where you don't need such a strong hold (with longer stakes on the windward side). The supplied cord loops are a nice touch, making it easy to see and pull your stakes when it's time to go. Many suppliers don't include those cord loops, but I think it's a good investment to add them if they aren't included, so you're less likely to lose the stakes (because you can see the bright loops, and they make a good handle for pulling the stakes from the ground).

title: Attractive idea, but not for us.
text: We tried these on a recent 9-day trip, thinking that they'd save us washing the sleeping bags while increasing comfort in the bags. Only used them for two nights, though, as they tangled up and were more hassle than they were worth. We're wondering if genuine silk liners would be better, and if so, if they're worth the high cost. For now, we're going without liners. These are going to the second-hand gear shop, so maybe we'll recover some of our investment.

title: Better than some cheapo showers, could still be improved
text:
The Red Rock Outdoor Gear 5-gallon solar shower works well and avoids many of the pitfalls of other designs. I've used it camping and found that it heats up well when exposed to the sun properly (clear side to the sun, so the sunlight penetrates the water and absorbs into the black layer against the ground, NOT black side up like the instructions on the product tell you to lay it!). The hose doesn't kink as badly as many of the budget solar showers, and the spray nozzle has a push button that's easy to use with one hand.

There are no instructions on how to hang the shower, so you have to be somewhat creative. This seems like a design oversight, that could be easily remedied with the addition of a couple of dedicated hanger grommets, or a webbing sling designed to go under the handle, or something like that. I tied a loop in each end of the supplied nylon cord, wrapped the cord around a modest-sized tree stem with a clove hitch (as high up as I could reach) then put the supplied metal S-hook through a loop in one end of the cord, fed that through the handle opening of the shower bag, and hooked the S-hook into the loop on the other end of the cord. It was easy to hang and to get down after it was empty, but some in our party didn't see how to re-hang the filled bag without some instruction.

Another annoyance is draining the water and drying the bag at the end of the trip. It's difficult to prop this thing open to get good airflow. I'd guess that many solar showers get nasty inside because its not easy to dry them. We hang ours near the furnace at home, but a larger opening at the top would make it easier.

Finally, how are we supposed to store the rope and S-hook between trips, so that we don't lose it? The rope can be easily lashed to the shower's handle, but the S-hook is a loose piece that doesn't attach well to anything. At first I tucked it into the red "hinge" straps of the water filler cap, and closed the cap. It holds there ok, but doesn't allow the bag to air out. My more recent solution has been to squeeze one end of the S closed, so the hook looks more like a letter q (with a curly tail). I tied this onto the end of the rope, which has made it easier to use when hanging the bag, because it's secured to the rope and you don't have to worry about dropping it when you're wrestling a heavy bag of water.

It's nice to get a warm shower when camping, and this makes that easy if you have sunny weather. I'm not sure how necessary it is, though, as we've used water heated over the cook stove for washing up with a wash cloth and soap for most of our camp trips, and that doesn't require several hours of direct sunlight. For a more deluxe car-camping or base-camp experience, this is a reasonable addition. Where space and weight are at a premium, I usually leave it at home. For designers, manufacturers, or entrepreneurs looking for a way to build a better mouse trap, I'd seriously consider modifying this rather typical design to incorporate an easy, straightforward hanging system, and a way to drain and dry the bag between trips.

title: Useful compromise of weight, length, and strength.
text:
I was looking for a strong, lightweight alternative to the heavy-duty, 12-inch tent stakes that came with my big expedition tent. The bag of stakes weighed over 10 pounds, and I really wanted to lighten it up to keep the tent package under the airline's 50-pound maximum. There are a few plastic stake alternatives that I know from experience just don't last long before they break. And there are many 7-inch stakes of this design that are just too short. Finally, I found these 12-inch aluminum stakes. I used them on a recent moose hunt in western Alaska and found them to be adequate, for the conditions we encountered.

On the positive side, these were long enough to reach through the tundra lichens and reach the rocky soil below. I used a small (8-ounce) hammer to pound them in, and they held through moderate winds that we had one day. (The rest of our 9-day trip was gorgeous weather with only light breezes). They weigh about 1/4 of what the heavy-duty steel stakes weighed, which allowed me to add a ground sheet and floor liner to my tent bag, and keep the whole package at or below the original tent weight.

These don't have the surface area and therefore the holding power of the bigger, heavy duty stakes, and they will probably bend if you strike them too hard into rocks or tree roots. None bent on my recent trip, but I've used the smaller, 7-inch versions of these on other tents and have bent plenty of them, so I was being gentle. I expect that they'd do really well in good, firm soil, but they probably lack the surface area to hold well in sand or snow, and probably won't stand up to rocks and solid tree roots very well. I have, and recommend carrying, a variety of tent stake styles. I like to include a few bigger/beefier stakes to use for the high-stress areas of the fly and door, on the windward side of your tent. These 12-inch stakes would be good for those spots on smaller tents. I use the bigger aluminum military-style blade stakes, or the twisted MSR cyclone stakes (of stronger aluminum) for the critical areas on my bigger tents that require better anchors. I also like to have one or two of the original steel stakes for tougher, rocky spots where I need a good anchor.

Overall, these Camco 12-inch stakes are a good addition to my tent bag, but not a perfect solution by themselves. Maybe one day soon someone will make aluminum stakes this length with the width, surface area, and strength to truly replace those heavy but effective steel stakes.

title: The classic!
text:
I purchased this vest 6 years ago and it served me well in multiple ultras. It has just enough space for everything you need. I just checked the front zip pocket and it's just a tad too small for my Samsung Galaxy S7 Active, which is a thick phone. It definitely wouldn't fit an iPhone 6-7 Plus. The pack rides low enough on your back that there are no real issues with rubbing or chafing of the neck...from the pack. I did get a bit annoyed from time to time by the hose rubbing my neck, though. The side straps....what can I say? Over 6 years, I've never figured out how to adjust them well, lol. But it hasn't seemed to matter much. For a while, I used to over-cinch the chest strap but realized it can stay pretty loose and the pack is still not very bouncy. The front right pocket is where I've always tucked my phone. Although I admit sometimes I've used a SpiBelt with this pack to free up more pocket space for gels. You don't get a whole lot of space in the back pocket but it's perfect for those rarely used but "just in case" items I like to bring like an emergency poncho, extra sunscreen, lip balm, ginger chews, etc.

The bite valve on Nathan's bladder tube has always been problematic for me. I never really "bit" it hard yet within a year or so, it began to leak. After one race, my leg was covered in syrupy goo where gatorade and leaked and evaporated over the course of 50 miles. I swapped it out for the bite valve from a Camelbak and never had another problem. Like all bladders, be religious about cleaning this one post-use or it will gunk up very quickly. The closure system on the bladder takes some getting use to. You'll become a pro at it but for years I watched aid station volunteers stare in bewilderment, trying to figure out how to open it. More often than not, I ended up doing it myself.

I used to find after 100 milers that the top of my back would have a slightly chaffed feel to it, without anything being rubbed raw. I'm sure a light application of body glide or vasoline would have prevented that. But overall, this is a great, basic vest with plenty of fluid capacity. I recently replaced mine with Nathan's VaporAir, mainly for more pockets. But I could easily have bought this again and been happy.

title: WOW! 25 Painful Minutes!
text: I've been a pretty high mileage runner for the past 5 years (several marathons and ultras) and my body has gotten to the point where I can almost literally run sleeping.  As such, It has become harder and harder for me to keep from gaining weight even with a relatively stable diet. Several friends mentioned biking, swimming, P90x, or crossfit and the like as cross training to workout some underworked muscles and wake things up.  As a busy father of 3 school-aged kids and as someone who refuses to sacrifice my running for something else entirely, I was not keen on any of those options.  When I happened across a commercial for this, I decided I had finally found something that might be worth it.  I'm still in my first week and let me tell you, I am feeling pain in musclesthat haven't been sore in years.  The workouts are non-stop and intense.  There's a little timer in the corner showing you how much time is left in the particular move you are doing as well as the entire 25 minute workout.  I'm sweating more from 25 minutes of this than I do from a 5 mile run, for sure.  If you want to wake your fitness routine up without making any drastic life changes or flipping tires, this might be the workout for you, too.

title: Best small pack even with it's ONE flaw!
text:
I got back into distance running just after one of my kids was diagnosed with a chronic illness so once I started running beyond 2 miles, I felt I had to have my cell phone to stay in touch with my wife. I've gone through multiple packs and armbands for phones, gels, etc. My previous Fuel Belt and SPi Belts were ok but not spectacular.

When I gave up on iPhones a week ago, I opted for a much larger Samsung Galaxy S4 Active and topped it off with an Otterbox case. I immediately realized NONE of my belts/packs were going to hold the phone. Out of desperation, I ran over to Dick's Sporting Goods to see what was available. I couldn't believe my luck when they had the Nathan 5k and another belt, by Nike, that also fit my phone. The Nathan was the clear winner, though, because it had a wider, softer material for it's belt and it also was stretchier.

I have not regretted my decision! Despite having a giant hunk of a phone, I can't even feel this thing when I wear it. And it doesn't rub in the slightest. They only way I know it's there is I occasionally hear the zippers jingling a little. It easily holds my phone, house key, and gels.

I did say there was a flaw. It's minor but it's a real head scratcher. They belt includes enough material strap this belt to Andre the Giant's larger brother! And there's no loop to hold it. Unlike many other belts, the belt part itself doesn't loop back on itself, adjusted by buckles. Instead, it just cinches like an ordinary belt. I've got a 34 waist and there's probably at least a foot of excess belt strap. But I've tucked it in for the relatively short runs I've run so far and used a rubber band on a longer one. I'll cut it eventually but hadn't b/c I wanted to make sure I wasn't missing a piece. Other reviews echo my concern, so I guess not.

But overall (believe it or not), the best belt you can buy!

title: First time Kastking purchase - Defective drag knob - Sharky III 6000 Baitfeeder
text:
I don't write many reviews - typically when I do they are positive. I'm pretty disappointed. My wife bought me this this reel to go fishing with my kids for Father's Day. I had been reading about these Kastking bait feeders and it was much less expensive than a known Shimano. I watched some youtube videos about it that seemed pretty good and the amazon reviews seemed real good. We got to the pier and I had them spool it up with 20# mono. I like having my spools wound by the machine - it does a better job. The drag cap came off but it was difficult to remove. It seems like it took a good 2 minutes to unscrew... NOW it will not go back on - it freely spins and won't attach.
I posted a photo I can't tell if it's stripped or what is going on inside there. The threading appears to be fine.
The old timers that work at the pier fooled with it but said that's what I get for buying unknown name brands. I told them everyone started out unknown! I recently bought a penn battle II rod / reel combo and the rod was defective from the factory.
I wasted my $6 to get her spooled up with line but the worst part I didn't get to try out my new reel on father's day - I was really excited to use it! I'm glad I didn't get the other spool loaded up with braided line like I was thinking - I'd have been out another $30...
If the Kastking people make good on the replacement I'll test it out and will consider changing my rating. Right now I'm disappointed and wanted to gripe. Anticlimactic!
Is this rare or typical? We'll find out! Looking at other ratings seems like it might be rare (I hope). I'll update as things progress. - Wayne

title: Excellent covers - Recommended, but a design flaw.
text:
I would recommend these iron covers to anyone, but I have some reservations that get me to the 4 stars. Here's the breakdown:

Pros:
Slip on easily for most clubs.
Keep your clubs from clattering
Keep your clubs from causing dents and scratches to each other
Nice looking
The see-thru window for the club allows universal use - they aren't marked with numbers/letters, so you can use them interchangeably or replace them easily.

Cons:
A bit pricey for what it is, but certainly reasonable given the cost of most golf accessories.
Wedges are moderately difficult to put on, but they fit. They neoprene is forgiving.
The plastic windows don't always line up well with the club number (and I have Taylormade irons), especially wedges because of the lie of the club. YMMV. I worked the window into place, but that might get annoying over time if they don't gain some "memory" of the club.
The plastic windows are a touch flimsy. They are heat "welded" to the neoprene, but weak at the edges. I had one that tore immediately upon use but the seller replaced it. It seems to me it would be better to have the plastic on the inside of the sleeve. Not a deal breaker, but we'll see how long they last.

All told, I'm satisfied. They do what I want by keeping the clubs from rattling in the bag while carrying or in the cart or car and keep them from nicking or dinging each other. The cost is reasonable for name brand golf supplies, but should be $5 cheaper. And the Window should be a bit bigger and secured better. But it's a clever idea. Here's hoping they last a while. I like them and can live with the mostly minor issues, so 3.5 stars rounded up to 4.

title: Super compact with a multitude of uses - get one today!
text:
The Gerber folding shovel is really top notch. Its quality construction is much like any other Gerber/Fiskars equipment I've owned - it doesn't disappoint.

The shovel I have is actually a little more agressively pointed than in the pictures, so I'm not sure if Gerber has addressed this as an issue or if the pictures were off.

The top of the handle is high density polycarbonate plastic and has a horizontal design like a spade should have. You can still use the verticle part of the steel handle if you wish, but there isn't much of it. The plastic will absorb some shock compared to steel-only, and it won't freeze to your hands, etc. The polycarb handle folds down on itself, so that it actually has 3 segments (instead of several designs which have 2 segments). This means you can stow the shovel in the included cordura nylon belt pouch which is no bigger than the shovel head itself. The handle pivot point locks and since it's square, doesn't rotate or twist easily. The steel which connects the blade to the handle fits nicely inside the A angle cutout of the handle, so when collapsed it is really thin.

The blade is high quality steel with the hinged handle connected at the top. This does limit the depth of the shovel a little, but I don't believe it's much of a factor, except maybe in really solid soil where you lose a little verticle travel when the ground butts up against the hinge.

It's very compact, light, comes with a solid belt sheath (easily convertible to pack carry) and stows away easily since it's so thin. I can put it in the side pockets of my doors or in the very small space above my rear wheel well without any problems (Trailblazer 4x4).

I really can find no fault with this item, it delivers on all fronts: usability, quality, compact storage, and rugged design. I will almost certainly be keeping one in both cars and in my 72 Hour survival kit. They are even reasonably priced. 5 Stars.

title: BRAND NEW UNIT became warpy discolored on first use! SEE PICS
text: I'm very upset at the quality of this item I just purchased brand new.  I just used it yesterday for the first time along with my new Weber grill, filled it with plain charcoal only to where the top hole is on the top (we counted 50 briquettes), and THIS is what my brand new charcoal starter now looks like!  SEE THE PICTURES I JUST TOOK, 2 from the outside (left and right sides) and two from the inside (left and right). After the first 10 minutes, I saw that the charcoal on the top was still completely black with no signs of the flame touching them.  Just then, I saw a very strange chemical-type reaction occurring on the outside of the canister!  It was as if a magic invisible paintbrush with white paint on it was stroking heavy stripes of paint around the outside of it!  We were shocked to see this odd thing happening!  About 15 minutes later, We finally saw small flames inside that were approaching the top briquettes.  As soon as we saw the top ones beginning to get a little grey color, we emptied it out, and the whole process took 30 minutes -- not the 15-20 we were expecting.  After we poured in the briquettes, which were already fully completely white and falling apart at the bottom, we began to cook with what remained in the canister.  I don't think this thing was operating properly at all, and I knew something was wrong when I saw this horrible discoloration happening only 10 minutes into the process.  I feel like this was made with some cheap foreign material and am very upset that my new chimney starter was ruined and unable to perform on DAY ONE.  I don't even think this thing is safe, because if it's being compromised in this way and the metal is underperforming, who knows what's going to happen to the metal on SUBSEQUENT uses, the metal and the bolts that is supposedly holding the handle onto the canister??  Is this now going to melt and break off just as we're holding onto it and unloading it into the grill??

title: Great bow
text:
I've been hunting with Mathews compound bows for 20 years and reached a point in my age that I wanted to switch to a crossbow. I wanted to find the best bow for the money to start out. I like compounds but I wanted to stay as basic and simple as I could with the crossbow for service and maintaining accuracy so I wanted a recurve.
Long story short the Excaliburs are nice but to rich for my blood so I took a chance on the Wildfire II based on the reviews. I'm glad that I did.
Pros:
Excellent fit and finsh work on the entire bow. Definitely quality construction on par with any of the big name crossbow makers.
It seems as fast and they say it is. Once sighted in it is consistently accurate. I think this bow is on par with the Excalibur baseline bows Like the Axiom or Ibex if not better as this bow has a one peice Aluminum rail versus a plastic rail. Weight is not bad at all and it feels well balanced for free hand shooting. Soft touch Camo is awesome and a nice balance of pattern and color.
Thumb Safety just like a rifle. Not up on the side of the string latch like a lot of other crossbows and quiet as a mouse. Not a loud CLICK! when you take the safety off. The trigger does have some creep but is pretty smooth overall. The more I shoot the better it gets.
Shot noise is average and less than a pellet gun for comparison. It comes with factory installed limb dampeners that attach to the riser/limb. I also installed the SIMS LIMBSAVER kit and it definitely helped reduce the sound when fired.
Scope is actually very good quality and clarity. Super clean reticle and the adjustable illumination is great for early morning/late evening shots! I was thinking to buy a Nikon but this scope is really nice so I will keep using it.
Rope cocker, Arrows, quiver, and sling are very nice quality as well. Super sling swivels too!
Must haves:
Plano Soft bow case. Best priced case that actually fits the bow another really good option is the OMP Crossbow soft case. A little more in cost but has additional pockets for arrows etc.
Tenpoint ACUrope cocker (BEST). Compact and retractable. Works like a dream and has a belt pouch.
Carbon Express Bolts. Either the Piledrivers or if you want the best get the Maxima Hunters. Buy their lighted nocks for your hunting arrows.
Go ahead and buy the MTM bolt case for your extra bolts.
Scorpion Venom string wax. The bow comes with string wax but I feel the Scorpion is easier to use and stays super slick in all weather.
Rail lube. DO NOT USE STRING WAX! I did and it slowed down the bow and killed my accuracy. I had to clean the rail with rubbing alcohol and start over. Buy Excalibur rail lube and/or do some research on the bow forums on what the veteran shooters are using. Some recommend silicone spray and other types of lube. If you're going to hunt use something that doesn't have any odor. I ended up using Ultralube 4x. It's all natural and no odor.
NAP 100 grain Sptifire Edge mechanical broadheads. These are my personal favorite and for overall accuracy I prefer mechanicals over fixed blades for better flight at high speeds.
Target for field point is the Hurricane H25 hands down best practice target for the money. It stops the bolts no matter what and is heavy and stable. You don't need a stand for it.
Target for broadheads I recommend the Blobtarget or American white tale HybriMAT AP . They are both pricey (BT 18"x18"x10" $90 shppied) (HybriMAT AP 18"x18"x12" $129.95 shipped) but they will last you for years and years vs the cheaper ones that last a year and are still very expensive!
Update:
Bought a Prochrono on Amazon to check the speed of the bow and right now it is 315fps with the stock arrows and with the Maxima Hunters. Dyna Flight string should bring it up to as much as 330fps.
I ended up removing the limbsavers since they slowed it down (10fps!) and actually created vibration in the bow after the shot. To be honest the noise level is not much different without them.
Another update. Bow is shooting 330fps using Carbon Express 20" hunter maximas and 100gr tips. I switched to Black Eagle Spynal Tapp arrows and the speed is still on.
Final deer season tally is 3 does and i buck

title: Bought for repetitive stress injury relief
text:
A few thoughts...
*Some people don't understand how to use this. After you get it going, you have to keep rocking the ball back and forth, like turning the door knob, and the point is to keep the ball steady so it's barely wobbling around in your hand.
*For best results (i think), imagine the open face pointing outwards and keep that as perpendicular to your arm as possible. DON'T do the opposite and have it facing away from you. you will not generate any speed and it will stop.
*If you loop the string more than once, you risk getting the string stuck inside the ball and you either need to open it up (screws are under the grip apparently) or cut off an end of the string. The string only needs one reinforced end anyways.
*Difficult to start by the handstrike method. String method is pretty fail-proof.
*The rubber grip on my ball says "Anytime. Anywhere." That is a load of crap. This thing is noticeably audible, like an air fan set on the medium setting. If you're looking for something discrete, move along.
*There's nothing particularly fun about this... it's just another exercise. Perhaps interesting in the beginning but not for long.
*Overall I like the product. I can certainly feel my weak grip strengthen, though I have no idea if this will really help fix the tremor I got repetitive stress. Personally, I use this in one hand while reading a book held in the other hand.

title: The heart rate function really sucks, all other functions decent
text:
This fitbit counts steps well. The sleep tracking is far from perfect, but it does the job well enough to be useful. The stairs tracking function is a bit suspect, but ok for the most part. But if you want just those features, then there are other, much cheaper models that do the job. If you're thinking about getting the HR model, it's because you're interested in tracking heart rate, and this is where this fitbit fails miserably.

If you're just sitting around, it tracks your HR quite well, but of course you're not really that interested in your HR when you're just sitting around.
If you're long distance running at a steady pace, it's in the ballpark. If you're running intervals, the average of the entire workout is somewhat close to reality, but it averages your HR over a long timespan, so your peaks will be way too low (and too late), and your valleys will be too low (and too late). So for that, it's kinda useless.

Worst of all, if you're planning on tracking your heart rate while doing any non-running exercise like calisthenics, aerobics, weight training, or body-weight exercises, then forget about it. It's utterly useless in this department. Your HR readings will be either completely off, or it won't read your HR at all. It's kind of a known fact that when you do exercises where your forearm muscles move a lot, the Charge HR fails miserably, but even when doing planks, crunches, and other exercises where the arm is pretty much stationary, my HR readings are 30-50 points low, or just not displayed at all. These results are regardless of where I put the band. I've tried close and far from my wrist, on the inside or outside of the forearm, with different amounts of tightness, and even my leg. Readings are unusable regardless.

title: Great bike for the price!
text:
Ordered this from Amazon December 20, 2015 and it was delivered the following Sunday. I assembled the bike a few hours after it arrived without troubles.

For some reason there is a full page parts diagram of the entire bike that is shown prior to the assembly instructions. The diagram made things look way more complicated than they turned out to be. Turns out (most) of the hardware is already in place and just needs to be aligned and tightened (with the included tools).

I assembled this on my own and most people should be able to do just like I did. One note on assembly though: the main part of this is the bulk of the total weight of the entire bike. It's a bit on the heavy side so if lifting heavy objects is hard or risky for you you should seek out some help.

The pedals went on super quick and easy. They were clearly marked 'L' and 'R' and the instructions made sure there were clear on which way the bolts should be threaded.

I've since put 320 miles on the odometer on this, so, about 14.5 miles a day. I haven't noticed any mechanical problems or glaring defects. I enjoy the fact the the seat is adjustable to some degree and the adjustable tension works surprisingly well.

My reason for giving only four stars is because of the seat. It is very hard and after a while it causes pain. I'm going to get a nice cover for it and hopefully that will help some with that.

Other than that, this is a great bike for the price.

title: The Xtherm isn't that great for below zero use
text:
The Xtherm isn't that great for below zero use ..... here's way and a better way.

The Therm-a-Rest NeoAir Xtherm certainly is the warmest, lightest, most comfortable pad I own (of about a dozen in my family), and perhaps the toughest too, but I won't use it again for below zero F camping. Why? The R-value certainly is high enough... but its a different technology.... and thus cold.

The Xtherm is an air mattress, meaning air can easily flow from cold to warm areas as you roll, shift, or even breath. In very cold places, this is enough to chill you in a warm bag. With a foam pad, air doesn't move from warm to cold.

I've tested this a few times in the backyard when temps dropped to -10F. My bags were quite warm (usually didn't even need to close the inner bag) and below I had an EPS accordion (2" expanded polystyrene rigid foam board, R-10, 6' long, 2' wide). In between I've tested a variety of pads, mostly to make the rigid foam comfortable on these old bones. (If you search around, you'll see the R-10 foam is appropriate for -40F ish.) Air pads certainly make the board comfortable but they were cold, especially when laying my side -- which is when it should be the warmest b/c the fluffy bags wrap downward. It was old because the cold air had a way to get in, along the channels of the Xtherm. Using a decade-old self-inflating Therm-a-Rest or even a cheap foam pad isn't as comfy but certainly is warmer.

title: Fabulous design, changes the way you drink water !!
text:
I simply LOVE my insulated Eddy Cambelbak bottle!
I didn't have a clue what they were all about, nor how a bite valve worked, but I needed a water bottle and started reading up about them. I am converted!
This bottle is very well constructed, and although tall, it doesn't take up much space on a desk or side table, and it holds a good 0.6L volume of lovely iced water.....and it doesn't "sweat"! Fantastic!
It keeps my water nice and cool for ages, and it is so convenient that I find myself drinking a lot more water that before, which is a good thing.

For anyone else that doesn't know what bite valve is (can I be the only one??!) - the "spout" of this bottle is made of a firm silicon rubber and it has a closed hole that attaches down to the bottle's straw. When you bite the end of this spout or valve, it squeezes the hole open and you just suck up the water like drinking from a straw. The second you take pressure off and stop biting down, the hole closes shut again and - voila! - A leak proof bottle! It is a fantastic design - I love it! (see pic)

The valve part can be in an angled or upright position, so you don't have to tip the bottle sideways to get the water to flow, and it also pushes right back to a "closed" and flat position which is great if you have it in a backpack, beach bag etc. It is just a really innovative design and it really works so well!!
I highly recommend this bottle to anyone who wants a fantastic, no sweat, leak-proof, easy to use drinking bottle - 10/10 !

title: be careful when purchasing Rollerblade Twister skates  (sizing issues)
text:
The sizing recommendations say to purchase this skate 0.5 to 1 size larger than our shoe size, but when I did that the front of the skate was way too loose (big). The problem with the current generation of Rollerblade skates appears to be that they are making the plastic shells harder which makes them harder on our ankles and harder to adjust the front of the skates.

If you choose to still purchase a Rollerblade hard-shell skate (Twister...), be very careful about understanding the return policy. Amazon.com apparently does not accept back rollerblade skates that have at all been skated outside. If you purchase Rollerblades, do not skate with them outside your living room without first being 100% confident that you have purchased the right size because you likely will not be able to return them. There are third party stores that provide much better return policies for inline skates (new or used-once), and so google until you find a skate and a store that gives you peace of mind.

I have a 10.5 shoe size, and I tried the 2018 rollerblade hardshell skates in 10.5, 11, and 11.5, and they all had the same ankle position issue. The issue is that my ankle is always close to the shell edge where the laces are, and so this generation of rollerblade skates all cause ankle pain. The workaround is that I took my skates to an ice skating pro shop where they used a heat gun to adjust the skates (it took 3 trips and a pretty significant adjustment). When the 2019 skates arrive, I will again check the 11.5 skates to see if they have the same issue.

title: Slept well in winter camping!
text:
I was impressed at how warm I was with a 3-season tent, no sleeping pad, and "little hotties" in my socks on an Xmas camping trip with nightly lows in the mid-20's F. I usually wake up a million times during the night when camping. This time I only woke up once, and that was because of an earthquake!

This sleeping bag's material has a soft, dry feel to it; not at all sweaty and swampy. It works best, counter-intuitively, when you don't sleep with tons of layers on. I just wear my undies. If you're too cold, you're best off adding your coat and your other layers on top of your sleeping bag, not inside of it.

I'm not sure why I bought the 32 degree bag when much of my camping is done well below that... I also do some warmer trips so I'll probably keep this and also buy the heavier one, too.

For this bar tape, I tossed the ugly finishing tape and used thin strips of gold duct tape (true look-at-me gold color), and painted the end caps with a bottle of cheap gold nail polish from the drugstore + spray varnish.

If you want to know the true color of the bar tape, go check out the pictures on Bike Ribbon's website for the Carbonio bar tape.
